title: Tibetan, Chinese pro-democracy advocates adopt joint declaration at Dharamshala forum
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 3:A three-day forum bringing together Tibetan and Chinese scholars, policy experts, and human rights activists concluded in Dharamshala on Wednesday with a joint call for nonviolence, democratic reform, and sustained dialogue as pathways towards a peaceful resolution of the Tibet-China conflict. The “Democratic China and Future of Tibet Forum”, organised by the Tibetan Community Development Fund (TCDF) in collaboration with the Central Tibetan Administration’s official think tank, Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), brought together 29 participants from India, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, Japan, Taiwan, and Southern Mongolia. Convened to foster candid exchanges on democracy, human rights, and Tibet’s political future, the forum sought to bridge perspectives between Tibetans and Chinese pro-democracy activists and explore avenues for greater cooperation between the Tibetan and Chinese democratic movements. The forum opened on August 31 with a keynote address by CTA President Penpa Tsering, who spoke on Sino-Tibetan relations, the Middle Way Approach, the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, and the importance of cooperation between Tibetans and Chinese. The discussions culminated in five declarations covering nonviolence, a shared democratic future, Tibetan democracy and history, the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, and the legal and human-rights implications of China’sLaw on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress. The first declaration established nonviolence as a common guiding principle for addressing the Tibet-China conflict. Participants drew on the longstanding advocacy of the 14th Dalai Lama and Chinese democracy advocate Liu Xiaobo, emphasising peaceful resistance, dialogue, and pragmatic engagement as alternatives to confrontation. The second declaration called for a shared vision of a democratic future, urging closer interaction between Tibetans in exile and Chinese democracy organisations and individuals. Participants also highlighted the value of sharing the Tibetan exile community’s experience of democratic governance as part of broader efforts towards democratisation in China. Discussions under the third declaration focused on Tibet’s history, Tibetan-Chinese exchanges, Tibetan democracy, and the Middle Way Approach. Participants said greater understanding of Tibetan perspectives among Chinese audiences, alongside deeper Tibetan engagement with China’s democracy movement, could help build trust and create space for meaningful dialogue. The declaration also called for greater efforts to explain the Middle Way Approach to Chinese people. The policy, advocated by the Tibetan leadership in exile, seeks genuine autonomy for Tibetans within the framework of the Chinese Constitution rather than outright independence. The fourth declaration addressed the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, rejecting any role for the Chinese government in the process. Participants stated that the authority to determine the Dalai Lama’s succession rests with the Dalai Lama and the Dalai Lama’s private office, Gaden Phodrang Trust, in accordance with Tibetan Buddhist traditions. The fifth declaration raised concerns over China’s so-called “Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress,” calling for its immediate repeal. Participants argued that the legislation could have far-reaching consequences for the linguistic, cultural, religious, and national identities of Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, and other ethnic communities. The participants said the forum marked a step towards establishing a sustained platform for Tibetan-Chinese academic and policy engagement, with continued communication and cooperation envisioned as a means of building mutual understanding and strengthening nonviolent approaches to the long-running conflict. title: Book honouring Lobga Rangzen’s legacy launched in Dharamshala
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:Marking two months since the passing of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, a collection of 77 essays and prose pieces written by Tibetans in the aftermath of his self-immolation was launched on Wednesday at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The volume brings together writings that appeared across social media platforms following Lobga Rangzen’s death, documenting the reflections, emotions, and political sentiments expressed by Tibetans in his memory. Lobga Rangzen self-immolated on July 2, 2026, outside the UN headquarters in New York. In his message, the late martyr strongly condemned China’s repressive policies in occupied Tibet and its ongoing campaign to assimilate and ultimately erase the Tibetan people. He called on fellow Tibetans that restoration of Tibet’s independence is the only lasting solution to end the sufferings endured under China’s colonial occupation. Speaking about the motivation behind compiling the book, Loyak Tashi, who compiled the collection, said the idea emerged within a week of Lobga Rangzen’s passing. During that period, he noticed a growing number of essays and prose pieces being written and circulated online in remembrance of the activist. He said Tsering Logye, the editor of the book, approached him and suggested bringing the writings together in a single volume. The conversation prompted him to undertake the compilation, as he feared that many of the tributes and reflections would gradually disappear from public memory within a year or two. He said the book was therefore intended not only to preserve those writings but also to honour what he described as Lobga Rangzen’s “ultimate sacrifice.” Among the speakers at the launch was Dr Sonam Tobgyal, a researcher at Tibet Watch and an advocate for Tibetan independence, who said he had read most of the pieces in the collection after encountering them on social media. Reflecting on the writings, he said he sensed a renewed expression of support for the Tibetan independence cause among those who had written them. He contrasted this with the situation roughly 15 years ago, when, in his assessment, relatively few Tibetans were paying sustained attention to the independence movement. While acknowledging that activism around Tibetan independence had continued, he said the past decade had been particularly difficult for advocates of the cause. According to his observation, many activists within the Tibetan community have faced challenges while organising campaigns and advocating for independence at both individual and organisational levels. He further noted what he described as a growing distance among some Tibetans from the broader Tibetan cause, particularly at times when international governments offered limited support or when the situation inside Tibet deteriorated. However, he said Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation appeared to have rekindled a sense of urgency and responsibility among sections of the Tibetan community. He said the act had reminded people of the importance of keeping the Tibetan issue alive and continuing efforts on behalf of Tibet. He also pointed to what he described as a renewed engagement among younger Tibetans, saying that a strong sense of commitment to the independence cause had been largely absent among younger generations for some time. According to him, young Tibetans have often grown up hearing that achieving independence from China is extremely difficult, that China is too powerful, and that Tibetans could benefit by remaining within China. He said discussions about collectively working toward Tibetan independence had consequently received less emphasis in their upbringing and education. He argued that Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation had helped revive those sentiments across different sections of Tibetan society, with its impact being felt among both younger and older generations. Another speaker at the launch was Rangzen Dhondup, a close friend of the late activist and president of the Dharamshala regional chapter of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC). He said he had known Lobga Rangzen for nearly a decade through their shared involvement in the Tibetan cause. Recalling the day of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation, Rangzen Dhondup said the late martyr had called him at around 10 a.m. IST. At the time, he was attending the annual general meeting of the TYC in Poanta Sahib and was unable to take the call. He instead sent him a message explaining that he was in a meeting and would call him later. He said he could never have imagined that the missed call would come only hours before Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire. He learnt of the self-immolation from a friend early the following morning and said he initially struggled to believe what had happened. He recalled that Lobga Rangzen had served two consecutive terms with the Tibetan Youth Congress’ New York and New Jersey chapter beginning in 2017, before later becoming involved with the Tibetan National Congress (TNC). Rangzen Dhondup said the two remained in regular contact, frequently discussing campaigns, sharing updates on activities and exchanging ideas on advancing the Tibetan cause. According to him, Lobga Rangzen also consistently supported campaigns organised by the TYC Dharamshala regional chapter, including through financial contributions. He described him as a person deeply committed to preserving Tibetan identity and consistently advocating campaigns in support of Tibetan independence. title: CTA reaffirms democratic legacy on 66th Tibetan Democracy Day
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:The exile Tibetan government, officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), on Wednesday commemorated the 66th anniversary of Tibetan Democracy Day at the Tsuglagkhang Temple in Dharamshala, reaffirming the democratic institutions established under the visionary leadership of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. The commemoration brought together representatives of the three pillars of the Tibetan democratic system—the CTA President Penpa Tsering and members of his Cabinet, elected members of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, and judges of the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission—along with members of the Tibetan community and 30 Chinese pro-democracy activists. Among the Chinese activists was Dang Yang, a veteran of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests who was subsequently imprisoned twice by the Chinese Communist government. Addressing the gathering, the Tibetan political leader condemned China’s newly implemented Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which came into effect on July 1, warning that the legislation and accompanying policies warrant a firm and appropriate response. “These include severe restrictions on the Tibetan language; the falsification of history and identity; forced cultural assimilation at the grassroots level; the Sinicisation of Tibetan Buddhism; enforced ethnic integration; pervasive technological surveillance; political and social coercion; the political vetting of Tibetan cadres; the violation of regional autonomy rights; and the assertion of extraterritorial jurisdiction targeting organisations and individuals worldwide,” the Tibetan leader said. He said the Chinese Communist government’s policies since its colonial occupation of Tibet have consistently sought to undermine Tibetan identity, particularly through restrictions on language, religion, and culture. Urging Tibetans both inside Tibet and in exile to make the preservation of their heritage part of everyday life, he called for greater participation in institutional initiatives to safeguard the Tibetan language and cultural identity. “On our part, it is not enough merely to declare opposition and protest; we must expose and confront these malicious policies based on a well-informed understanding. We therefore urge all Tibetans to join the Central Tibetan Administration in these vital efforts,” he stated. Dang Yang, speaking at the commemoration, described the Tibetan democratic system as a model of democratic resilience and said its experience offered important lessons to China’s pro-democracy movement. “The Tibetan experience has demonstrated to the world that even without a territory under its actual control, without an army, a democratic system can still function successfully and generate powerful political influence,” Dang said. He contrasted the Tibetan exile administration’s democratic legitimacy with what he described as the Chinese Communist Party’s reliance on “violence, lies, and control.” “The Tibetan community in exile, by contrast, relies on the recognition of its people, democratic legitimacy, and the cohesion of its institutions,” he said. Dang sated that the Tibetan democratic system has helped unite Tibetans dispersed across the world and ensured the continuity of their political voice across generations. “It is precisely this democratic system that has brought together Tibetans scattered across the world, generation after generation. It has ensured that the Tibetan voice has not been silenced by the Chinese Communist Party, and that the Party has never been able to represent the Tibetans or determine their future,” he said. Dang also announced plans for the establishment of a China Congress, a proposed democratic representative institution outside the framework of the Chinese Communist Party. He said the initiative has not yet been formally established but has already attracted more than 1,000 founding electors. “We hope to begin a democratic practice belonging to the Chinese people outside the system of the Chinese Communist Party, and to accumulate experience about China’s future democratic transition and constitutional development,” he said. He said China’s democracy movement could draw particularly from the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile’s experience of electoral representation. “The Tibetan experience of election has enabled representatives with a mandate from the electorate to continue making their voices heard in the international community,” Dang said, adding that China’s democracy movement has yet to develop a representative institution with a comparable electoral foundation. Looking ahead to a possible democratic transition in China, Dang said a future Chinese political system must abandon coercive policies towards Tibetans and instead respect their cultural, religious and national identity. “A future democratic China must never again treat Tibetans through oppression or forced assimilation. Instead, it must respect the Tibetan people’s culture, religion, language, national identity, and fundamental rights,” he said. He called for future relations between the Chinese and Tibetan peoples to be founded on equality and peaceful dialogue rather than political domination. Dang further proposed establishing a sustained platform for dialogue between Tibetans and Han Chinese living overseas, covering political and cultural questions related to Tibet as well as the future spiritual and cultural relationship between the two peoples. He concluded by expressing hope that Tibetans and Chinese alike would eventually be free from authoritarian rule and able to determine their own futures. The Tibetan democratic system began taking shape soon after the Dalai Lama arrived in India in exile. The process formally began with the establishment of the Commission of Tibetan People’s Deputies in 1960, followed by the drafting of constitutional frameworks in 1961 and their promulgation in 1963. A major milestone came in 1991 with the adoption of the Charter of Tibetans-in-Exile, which established a democratic system founded on the separation of powers and independent institutions. In 2001, Tibetans began directly electing the head of the Kashag, or Cabinet. A decade later, in 2011, the Dalai Lama devolved his remaining political and administrative authority and transferred it fully to democratically elected Tibetan leaders. The postCTA reaffirms democratic legacy on 66th Tibetan Democracy Dayappeared first onPhayul.

title: Tibetan researchers, activists demand transparency from China over Kyirong flash floods
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 1:A joint press briefing in Dharamshala on Tuesday raised alarm over what activists and researchers described as an ‘information blackout’ surrounding the devastating flash floods in Kyirong in occupied Tibet, demanding that China release full and verifiable information on casualties, missing persons, displacement, destruction, and its emergency response. The briefing, titled “Asia’s Water Tower in Crisis: Tibet-Nepal Flash Floods Demand Transparency,” was organised by the International Tibet Network (ITN) and Students for a Free Tibet–India (SFT-India) at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The briefing brought together researchers, activists, and a Tibetan monk from Kyirong, including Dhondup Wangmo, Research Fellow at the Environment and Development Desk of the Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), the Central Tibetan Administration’s think tank; Dr Lobsang Yangtso, Senior Environmental Researcher at ITN; Jampa Palden, a monk from Kyirong; and Tashi Dhondup, Campaigns Coordinator at SFT-India. The speakers called on Beijing to provide complete, accurate, and timely information about the scale of the disaster, warning that withholding, manipulating, or selectively releasing information could endanger communities both within occupied Tibet and downstream in Nepal and India. Jampa Palden, who is from Kyirong, shared accounts received from family members in the region, claiming that the entire Lhende area had been severely inundated and that three villages along the Lhende River had been completely washed away. According to his account, each of the three villages was home to at least 30–40 households. He added semi-nomadic Tibetan communities predominantly inhabit the area and is also an important trade corridor linking Tibet with Nepal. Chinese state-controlled media have so far reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing. The discrepancy between limited official reporting and accounts emerging from outside Tibet was cited at the briefing as evidence of the urgent need for independent access and transparent reporting from the disaster zone. Dr Lobsang Yangtso said that while the precise causes and trajectory of the recent glacial outburst have not yet been scientifically established, the disaster should prompt scrutiny of the rapid expansion of infrastructure across the environmentally fragile Himalayan region. She argued that extensive construction of roads, bridges, and hydropower projects in high-risk areas could compound the effects of climate-driven hazards, including glacial lake outburst floods, ice and snow avalanches, and other forms of cryospheric instability. She also pointed to the accelerating effects of climate change on the Tibetan Plateau, describing Tibet as an exceptionally climate-sensitive region. According to figures cited at the briefing, the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan region contain around 63,000 glaciers, 25,000 glacial lakes, 766 identified glacial-lake flood hazards, and 716 ice- and snow-avalanche hazards. “These risks,” she warned, could pose serious threats to communities in the future, particularly as warming alters the stability of glaciers and high-altitude landscapes. She also drew attention to China’s ongoing construction of a proposed 60-gigawatt hydropower project in Medog County, Nyingtri Prefecture, Tibet, close to India’s Arunachal Pradesh border. She warned that large-scale infrastructure development in such an ecologically sensitive and climate-vulnerable landscape could have ramifications far beyond Tibet and across downstream areas, including India, Nepal, and Bangladesh. The speaker therefore called for an international moratorium on mega-development projects in Tibet, arguing that large projects should not proceed until Tibetans can freely provide or withhold their consent without fear of detention, intimidation, or other forms of repression. She further urged Himalayan countries to consider an immediate moratorium on large hydropower projects until comprehensive climate, environmental and disaster-risk assessments are completed. The briefing also scrutinised the role of multilateral development banks and international financial institutions in financing hydropower projects across the Himalayas. Lobsang Yagntso specifically raised concerns over international financing for the Trishuli River hydropower project in Nepal, arguing that financial institutions must be held accountable when projects proceed despite known glacier-related risks and insufficient environmental assessment. She pointed to the vulnerability of hydropower infrastructure to sudden glacier-related disasters and questioned whether lenders have adequately incorporated increasingly volatile climate and geological conditions into their risk assessments. She argued that financial institutions should not treat Himalayan hydropower projects solely as development or investment opportunities while overlooking their potential consequences for workers, local communities, and downstream populations. The briefing called for independent monitoring, real-time data sharing, and effective cross-border early-warning systems, including timely notification of dangerous glacier movements, glacial lake outbursts, sudden rises in river levels, and other foreseeable hazards. The speakers called on China to grant unhindered access to affected Tibetan areas to international humanitarian organisations, independent journalists, disaster-response agencies, and human rights monitors. They also urged Beijing to ensure that Tibetans who document the disaster or communicate information about the humanitarian situation are not subjected to surveillance, detention, intimidation, prosecution, or other reprisals. The briefing also appealed to international governments, media organisations, humanitarian agencies, and monitoring bodies to use Tibetan place names consistently in official statements, reporting, and documentation. The organisers argued that accurate Tibetan terminology is not merely a linguistic preference but a matter of factual accuracy, cultural respect, and recognition of Tibetan identity. They urged international actors to avoid uncritically adopting Chinese state terminology, including “Xizang,” particularly when reporting on humanitarian, environmental, and human rights issues. The postTibetan researchers, activists demand transparency from China over Kyirong flash floodsappeared first onPhayul.

title: China censors Kyirong flood footage, grossly under-reports death toll
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 31: Video footage capturing the terrifying moments when people fled a rapidly advancing wall of mud and debris at the Kyirong Port in occupied Tibet has reportedly been removed from Chinese social-media platforms, fuelling concerns over Beijing’s censorship of information surrounding the devastating Himalayan floods. The footage, which circulated online following the disaster, reportedly shows people scrambling to escape moments before torrents of mud and floodwater engulfed parts of the Kyirong Port. Copies of some of the videos have continued to circulate outside China after the original posts were reportedly deleted. Kyirong County, a strategically important trading gateway between occupied Tibet and Nepal, was among the worst-affected areas on the Tibetan side. The Kyirong Port, a major land crossing, suffered severe damage; roads, buildings, and infrastructure were inundated or swept away. As of Monday, Chinese authorities have reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in Kyirong County, according to reports citing official figures. By comparison, the death toll on the Nepalese side had risen to 903, with 4,247 people still missing. The stark disparity is particularly striking given that Kyirong was among the areas hardest hit by the catastrophic floods. The figures have intensified scrutiny of the disaster and raised questions about the true scale of casualties in occupied Tibet, where access for independent journalists and observers remains severely restricted. Reports by Indian and international media outlets have stated in their reports that several videos documenting the disaster disappeared from Chinese social-media platforms. Some reports also allege that accounts posting information about casualties and the devastation were removed or restricted. Chinese authorities, however, have rejected allegations that they are suppressing information about the disaster. Authorities have also taken administrative action against people accused of spreading what they described as rumours concerning casualty figures and the scale of the disaster. The reported removal of eyewitness footage is significant because access to Tibet for foreign journalists and independent observers remains highly restricted. In such circumstances, videos recorded by residents, workers, and travellers can provide rare visual evidence of events unfolding in the region. The disappearance of footage has therefore added another layer of controversy to an already catastrophic disaster, particularly as official casualty figures continue to evolve while hundreds remain unaccounted for. Meanwhile, Chinese state media coverage of the disaster has largely centred on rescue and relief operations, repeatedly showcasing images of emergency personnel searching through debris, evacuating residents, and delivering supplies. While such footage documents the ongoing response, the emphasis on rescue efforts, rather than the full extent of the destruction and human toll, has been criticised as presenting a sanitised picture of the catastrophe and potentially obscuring the severity of the disaster on the Tibetan side. The contrast between official coverage and eyewitness footage circulating outside China has further fuelled concerns about information control and the suppression of independent accounts. With hundreds of people still unaccounted for in Kyirong, observers say, the disappearance of videos and restrictions on information could make it increasingly difficult to establish the disaster’s full human cost. The postChina censors Kyirong flood footage, grossly under-reports death tollappeared first onPhayul.

title: China accelerates DeepZang AI upgrades under ‘ethnic integration’ agenda
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 9:China is accelerating upgrades to DeepZang, its Tibetan-language large language model (LLM), with plans to expand its use in public services, education, healthcare and local governance as developers seek to promote what Beijing calls “ethnic interaction and integration.” The proposed upgrades were discussed at a seminar on October 5 in Hohhot, the capital of China’s so-called Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, which brought together representatives from research institutions, universities, and enterprises to discuss advances in Tibetan-language AI and multilingual interpretation, according to Chinese state media. Tenzin Norbu, founder of Choknor, the company behind DeepZang, said the team would continue developing Tibetan-language AI technologies and expanding their practical applications, using “technological innovation to support exchanges and integration among China’s ethnic groups.” Launched in Lhasa in March 2026, DeepZang offers AI conversations, translation and speech-to-text functions in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese and English. Its developers say the model has been trained on nearly 70 million standardised parallel-text entries and more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan-language audio covering the three major dialect groups of U-Tsang, Kham and Amdo. The planned upgrades include improved adaptation to Tibetan dialects, real-time Tibetan–Mandarin translation and offline language functions. Developers are also preparing to expand the model’s application across public services, cultural heritage, education, medical services and tourism in regions occupied by China. According toChina Daily, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users and recorded more than 350 million visits since its launch. Its reported applications include helping medical personnel communicate with Tibetan-speaking patients, translating documents and assisting with Tibetan-language administrative work. The expansion of Tibetan-language AI comes amid concerns over how Chinese technology platforms represent Tibet’s history, political status and religious identity. In a report published on March 19, the Washington-based right group International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) examined DeepZang’s responses to questions concerning Tibet’s historical status, the Tibetan spiritual leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama, and Tibetan independence. The organisation said the model reproduced official Chinese government narratives on politically sensitive subjects and restricted responses to certain questions, including those concerning Tibetan political history and self-immolation protests. The findings raise questions about whether the development of Tibetan-language AI will primarily improve access to digital services in Tibetan or also reinforce the Chinese government’s preferred interpretation of Tibetan history and identity. China’s push to expand DeepZang also comes amid wider government efforts to promote a unified national identity among the country’s ethnic groups. The “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”, which took effect on July 1, 2026, has drawn criticism from rights advocates and exile leadership who warn that its provisions could intensify pressure on Tibetans and other minority communities to assimilate into the dominant national culture. Beijing, meanwhile, presents the law as a means of strengthening “national unity and promoting development” across ethnic groups. The DeepZang initiative therefore sits at the intersection of two competing concerns: the potential benefits of developing AI tools for a language with substantial dialectal variation, and questions over how such technology may be used within the state’s broader ethnic-integration agenda.

title: 8th Young Indian Scholar’s Conference on Tibetan Studies commences in Dharamshala
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 8:The 8th Young Indian Scholars’ Conference on Tibetan Studies commenced Thursday at the Administrative Training and Welfare Society (ATWS) in Dharamshala, bringing together 25 researchers from across India for a three-day conference. Organised by the Central Tibetan Administration’s (CTA) official think tank, Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), the conference is being held from October 8 to 10, 2026. Now in its eighth edition, the annual gathering gives emerging Indian scholars a platform to present original research and engage with fellow researchers working on Tibet, the Himalayas, and related fields. Welcoming participants, TPI director and CTA spokesperson Tenzin Lekshay emphasised the importance of strengthening Tibetan Studies among Indian scholars, stating that the field is significant not only for Tibetans but for India itself. “Many times they get confused. Therefore, it is very important for the young Indians to educate themselves about Tibet,” Lekshay said, stressing that the conference was not organised merely “for the sake of Tibetans” but to develop Indian scholarship on Tibet “for the sake of India” and “for India’s interest.” He noted that despite the longstanding historical relationship between India and Tibet, many Indians who sympathise with Tibet may lack a deeper understanding of Tibet’s geography, history and relationship with India. “It is very important for India to understand Tibet,” he said, urging young scholars to develop their expertise so they can eventually answer questions within India about the country’s historical and contemporary relationship with Tibet. The conference was formally inaugurated by Prof. Sat Prakash Bansal, Vice Chancellor of the Central University of Himachal Pradesh (CUHP), who highlighted the importance of strengthening academic research on Tibet, the Himalayas and India-Tibet relations. Prof. Bansal said the conference’s themes—including strategy and security, historical relations, Buddhism and technology, and cultural heritage—reflect issues that extend beyond academia and are closely linked to India’s history, national security and future. Describing Dharamshala and the Himalayas as a “living lab” for research, he emphasised the region’s historical role as a bridge for the exchange of knowledge, culture, philosophy and traditions between India and Tibet. He called for renewed academic engagement with this shared heritage while encouraging universities to connect traditional knowledge with emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, digital humanities, climate science and environmental studies. He also urged young scholars to move beyond viewing Tibet solely through geopolitics, Buddhism solely through religion, and the Himalayas solely through geography. Instead, he called for interdisciplinary research linking history with contemporary politics, culture with technology, Buddhism with peace studies, and traditional knowledge with sustainability. Calling on universities to play a greater role in contemporary Tibetan and Himalayan scholarship, Bansal said academic institutions should not merely preserve knowledge but “interrogate it, reinterpret it and make it relevant to contemporary society.” He pointed to the potential for interdisciplinary research connecting traditional knowledge with artificial intelligence, digital humanities, climate science, environmental studies and emerging technologies. “We cannot survive without adopting new technology,” he said, while stressing the need to remain connected with traditional knowledge alongside technological development. He highlighted the Buddhist intellectual tradition’s emphasis on inquiry, debate, logic and examination, and referred to the Dalai Lama’s advocacy of examining Buddhist teachings through reason and investigation rather than accepting them blindly. He also pointed to the potential convergence between Buddhist analytical traditions and scientific inquiry. He said the Central University of Himachal Pradesh plans to collaborate with the Tibet Policy Institute and other institutions in the region on joint research projects, archives, fellowships, language programmes and digital repositories. He also proposed greater collaboration between universities and institutions through joint research projects, archives, fellowships, language programmes and digital repositories, with the broader aim of making the Himalayas a centre for interdisciplinary research and peaceful knowledge cooperation. He said such initiatives would strengthen academic cooperation and help establish the Himalayas as a centre for interdisciplinary research and peaceful knowledge exchange.

title: Jetsun Pema honoured with Christmas Humphreys Award for lifelong service to Tibetan education
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 7:Jetsun Pema, popularly known as Ama (Mother) Jetsun Pema, the sister of His Holiness the Dalai Lama was honoured with the prestigious Christmas Humphreys Award on Wednesday at Upper Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV) in Dharamshala. The award, presented by the Buddhist Society, London, recognises her lifelong contribution to the education and welfare of Tibetan children, as well as her efforts to preserve Tibetan cultural identity within the exile community. The honour acknowledges Ama Jetsun Pema’s decades of dedicated service to Tibetan children and her pioneering role in creating educational opportunities that combine modern learning with Tibetan values, traditions and cultural heritage. Her work has been closely associated with the growth and development of TCV, which has since expanded into a network of more than ten branches. Speaking to media representatives after the ceremony, Ama Jetsun Pema emphasised the responsibility of Tibetan parents living in India and abroad to safeguard the cultural and spiritual heritage of younger generations. She noted that Tibetans living inside occupied Tibet continue to face the policies of the Chinese government, making it all the more important for Tibetan families living in free countries to ensure that their children remain connected to their religion, culture, traditions and way of life. She said the freedom enjoyed by Tibetans living outside occupied Tibet should be used constructively to nurture children with a strong sense of Tibetan identity. Through collective endeavour, responsible parenting and sustained efforts to transmit Tibetan values, she expressed confidence that the younger generation could grow up firmly rooted in their heritage. Reflecting on the award, she placed the recognition in a broader context, stressing that the development of TCV was not the achievement of one individual. She acknowledged the contributions of numerous colleagues, former staff members and others who worked tirelessly alongside her over the years. She said the institution’s accomplishments were the product of a collective commitment and the sustained efforts of many people who helped build and strengthen Tibetan education in exile. She also highlighted the pivotal role of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in the Tibetan community, noting that many major initiatives have emerged under his guidance and vision. With both herself and His Holiness now advancing in age, she said the responsibility of preserving and carrying forward his aspirations increasingly rests with the younger generation. The Christmas Humphreys Award is presented by the London-based Buddhist Society and is named after Christmas Humphreys, a prominent British barrister, judge and early advocate of Buddhism in the West. Humphreys founded the Buddhist Lodge in 1924, which later evolved into the Buddhist Society, one of Europe’s oldest Buddhist organisations. The award has previously been conferred on Tibetan spiritual leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama, who received the honour in England on May 28, 2005.

title: Tibetan theatre production ‘Phayul’ to premiere in Dharamshala ahead of international tour
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 7:Tibetan theatrical production ‘Phayul’ (Homeland), the prequel to the acclaimed play ‘Pah-Lak’ (Father), is set for world premiere on October 10, Saturday, at the Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts (TIPA) Hall in Dharamshala. The play revisits one of the most turbulent chapters in Tibet’s modern history—the emergence of resistance to Chinese rule in eastern Tibet during the 1950s. The two-hour production will officially premiere on Friday, October 9, at 6:30 p.m. at the TIPA Hall in Dharamshala, followed by a public performance on October 10 at the same time and venue. A special pre-premiere for schoolchildren is scheduled for October 8. Written by acclaimed Indian playwright Abhishek Majumdar and co-directed by Lhakpa Tsering and Harald (Harry) Fuhrmann, the play has been developed by Tibet Theatre in collaboration with local artists over more than three years. The production team said rehearsals for the production began on August 31, 2026. Set in Tibet’s Kham region in 1956, the play traces the formative stages of the Tibetan resistance to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). Rather than focusing solely on political leaders or military figures, the production turns the spotlight on ordinary Tibetans—including monks, nomadic families, women and relatives of resistance fighters—whose lives were profoundly altered by the conflict. At the heart of the play is the question of how scattered, largely regional resistance gradually evolved into a broader national struggle. The production explores the difficult choices confronting Tibetans at the time: whether to resist, whether resistance could succeed against a militarily superior force, and how different communities could overcome internal divisions to forge a collective movement. Speaking about the production toPhayul,co-director Harry said the play seeks to communicate a historical narrative in which Tibetans resisted what they regarded as an invasion, while also examining the human and social consequences of that resistance. A distinctive feature of the play is its exclusive use of the Tibetan language, accompanied by multilingual subtitles. Harry toldPhayulthat retaining Tibetan is both an artistic and cultural decision. The use of Tibetan, he said, allows performers to connect more intimately with their emotions while simultaneously presenting the richness of the language to international audiences. He also views the stage as a platform to highlight the growing concerns over the preservation of Tibetan language and culture, describing Tibetan as a language that the Chinese government is “trying to extinguish.” The emphasis on Tibetan women is another defining element of the production. Their experiences and contributions during the early years of the conflict have, according to the theatre group, received comparatively little attention in mainstream historical narratives. The play attempts to bring these overlooked voices to the foreground, portraying women not merely as witnesses to history but as individuals confronting displacement, uncertainty, courage and survival. The production follows Tibet Theatre’s acclaimed play ‘Pah-Lak’ (Father), also written by Majumdar and staged in 2022 and 2023. ‘Pah-Lak’ received considerable attention in India and internationally for bringing aspects of the Tibetan experience to wider audiences. ‘Phayul’ serves as a prequel, expanding the historical narrative and tracing the circumstances that preceded the events depicted in the earlier production. Harry said the play is intended not only for Tibetan audiences but also for Indian and international spectators. Following its Dharamshala performances, the play is expected to tour Tibetan settlements and schools across India before travelling to international theatre festivals in 2027. The production has already attracted invitations from prominent theatre platforms, including the Ruhrfestspiele Recklinghausen in Germany and the Theatre Winterthur Festival in Switzerland. The teams said further performances are planned in Germany, Switzerland, France and potentially Belgium.

title: CTA President to attend Forum 2000 conference in Prague
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 6:The President of the exile Tibetan government, officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), Penpa Tsering, departed Dharamshala on Monday for an official tour of Europe that will take him to Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, including participation in the upcoming 30th Forum 2000 Conference in Prague. The Tibetan political leader is scheduled to spend the first two days of his tour in Delhi before departing for Zurich, Switzerland, on October 8. He will undertake a series of official engagements in Zurich on October 9 and 10. On October 11, the CTA President will travel to Prague, Czech Republic, where he is scheduled to attend the 30th Forum 2000 Conference on October 12 and 13. He will then travel to Germany on October 15 for further official engagements, which are scheduled to continue until October 17, before returning to India. The Forum 2000 Conference is an annual international gathering held in Prague that brings together political leaders, diplomats, human rights advocates, academics, journalists, civil society representatives and other prominent figures to discuss major global challenges, including democracy, human rights, freedom and the international rules-based order. The 30th edition of the conference comes at a significant milestone for the organisation, coinciding with the 30th anniversary of the Forum 2000 Foundation and the 90th birth anniversary of its founder, former Czech President Václav Havel. Held under the theme “Reimagining the Power of the Powerless,” this year’s conference draws on Havel’s influential 1978 essayThe Power of the Powerlessand will explore how individuals and societies can respond to authoritarian pressures while strengthening democracy, human rights and civic participation. Forum 2000 traces its origins to 1996, when Havel, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Elie Wiesel and Japanese philanthropist Yohei Sasakawa established the Forum 2000 Foundation. The first conference was held in Prague in September 1997 under the theme “Concerns and Hopes on the Threshold of the New Millennium.” It brought together political leaders, religious figures, scholars, writers and artists to discuss the challenges facing humanity and possible paths towards a better future. Over the years, Forum 2000 has developed into a prominent platform for international dialogue on democracy, human rights, civil society, religious and ethnic tolerance, the rule of law and other global issues. According to the Forum 2000 Foundation, its mission is rooted in Havel’s legacy of promoting democratic values, respect for human rights and civil society while encouraging religious, cultural and ethnic tolerance. The conference also has a longstanding connection with the Tibetan issue. The exile Tibetan spiritual leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama has participated in Forum 2000 events on several occasions and is listed among the distinguished participants of the conference series. The 30th Forum 2000 Conference will be held at the Prague Congress Centre from October 11 to 13, with the main conference programme taking place on October 12 and 13. The organisers have said the programme will bring together international participants for discussions on democracy, political representation, technology and other challenges confronting democratic societies.

title: Chinese authorities continue to deny visits to family, lawyer of jailed Tibetan businessman
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 6:Fresh concerns have emerged over the condition of imprisoned Tibetan businessman and philanthropist Dorje Tashi, as his lawyer, Wang Fei, has questioned prison authorities over their continued refusal to allow him and Dorje Tashi’s family to meet with him. A recently leaked audio recording posted on X (formerly Twitter) under the account name Sakar Tashi captures a telephone conversation between Dorjee Tashi’s lawyer, Wang Fei, and a police official associated with the prison administration of the so-called Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), in which the lawyer seeks an explanation for the authorities’ continued refusal to allow him to meet his client. According to the recording, the official attributed the restriction to Wang Fei’s previous disclosure to Dorje Tashi’s family about an assault he had reportedly suffered in prison. The disclosure prompted family members to protest and submit appeals outside the prison, the official reportedly said. Wang Fei, however, questioned the legal basis for preventing prisoners from meeting their family members and asked the authorities to provide in writing the reasons for denying his access to Dorje Tashi. He also warned that continued restrictions could inevitably fuel further concern among the family about Dorje Tashi’s well-being. The latest development comes after the lawyer submitted requests in July and August this year to meet Dorje Tashi, but was reportedly denied access. His family has similarly faced prolonged restrictions. Tashi’s elder brother and sister Gonpo Kyi have not been permitted to see him since 2019, while his wife and children have reportedly been denied visits since 2024. The restrictions have also extended to online discussion of Dorje Tashi’s case. Chinese authorities have repeatedly removed social media posts calling for a fair trial and questioning the legality of his imprisonment. Authorities have also reportedly demanded that advocates remove online material about his case and apologise before they would consider visits. Wang Fei was reportedly able to meet Dorje Tashi for less than an hour in October 2025 after years without access. During that meeting, the lawyer learned that Tashi had been physically assaulted by other prisoners. In November 2025, he had sustained serious injuries in a prison assault. The reported assaults have intensified concerns over Dorje Tashi’s safety, particularly as his family and legal representatives have subsequently faced additional barriers to contact. Rights advocates have argued that regular access to family members and legal counsel is essential not only for a prisoner’s welfare but also for independent scrutiny of his treatment in custody. Dorje Tashi has been imprisoned since 2008, following his arrest amid the widespread protests that swept across Tibet that year. At the time, Chinese authorities reportedly accused him of supporting activities considered a threat to national security and alleged links to Tibetans in exile. He was subsequently tried behind closed doors and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2010. Although the case initially carried political allegations, his eventual conviction was based on charges relating to alleged loan fraud. His family and legal advocates have consistently rejected the allegations and sought a retrial. His case has been marked by repeated attempts to challenge the conviction. His lawyer filed an appeal in 2013, but reportedly received no response for several years before it was rejected in 2019. A further legal effort eventually enabled Wang Fei to meet Dorje Tashi in prison. His family has also mounted a persistent campaign for his release and for access to him. His sister Gonpo Kyi has repeatedly staged peaceful protests outside courts in Lhasa, demanding a retrial and visitation rights. Her activism has resulted in detention, physical assault and intimidation, according to rights groups and reports. In 2023, Gonpo Kyi and her husband were detained after protesting outside the Lhasa People’s Court with a request for a retrial and visitation rights. A year later, a Chinese court dismissed her lawsuit challenging her detention and upheld the authorities’ actions.

title: 42 days, 1000 kms: US Tibetan activist heads to UN for final leg of ‘Freedom March’
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 6:Tibetan activist and lone marcher Sonam Dorjee has covered more than 1,000 kilometres on foot in 42 days as part of his ongoing “Freedom March” across the United States, a journey he says is dedicated to raising awareness about the Tibetan issue and in solidarity with Tibetans who have self-immolated for freedom. Sonam began the march on August 24, 2026, from the Chinese Consulate in Chicago. Speaking to Phayul from Baltimore, he said he has walked through Indianapolis, Dayton, Columbus, Pittsburgh, parts of Maryland and Virginia, Washington D.C., and is currently in Baltimore. “I have covered more than 1,000 to 1,100 kilometres,” Sonam said, adding that the entire journey from Chicago to New York is expected to cover at least 1,400 to 1,500 kilometres over approximately 55 days. The final leg of the march will take him to New York, where he plans to conclude the journey on October 17 in front of the United Nations, at the site associated with the self-immolation of the late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen. He said the march is particularly dedicated to the late martyr, whom he described as the first Tibetan American to self-immolate on U.S. soil, as well as to more than 170 Tibetans who have self-immolated in occupied Tibet and elsewhere. Beyond raising public awareness, he said the march has also served as an advocacy campaign, allowing him to meet American lawmakers and their staff and lobby for greater U.S. support for Tibet. During the 42-day journey, he said he has interacted with more than 1,000 individuals and groups. He said public responses have varied, with many Americans initially unfamiliar with the Tibetan issue but expressing sympathy and solidarity after learning about self-immolation in occupied Tibet. Some members of the public have supported the march by sponsoring meals, providing accommodation or making donations, he said. Sonam said nine American restaurants or café owners provided him with food during the journey, while at least five Americans donated money towards his campaign. A major component of Sonam’s march has been lobbying U.S. lawmakers. He said he has met or sought to lobby with at least 10 members of Congress during the journey, including representatives or their offices in Indianapolis, Dayton, Columbus, Pittsburgh, Frederick, Rockville and Washington, D.C. He said he has urged lawmakers to support two Tibet-related bills already introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives, while also asking them to pressure Beijing over its policies toward Tibet, including the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” One of his most significant lobbying experiences came in Columbus, where he visited the office of U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty. According to him, the delegation met with the district director, district executive director and several staff members. “They listened to us very nicely, and they inquired about what is inside the bill and how we can support the Tibetan cause,” he said, describing the meeting as one of the most notable experiences of the journey. He said he also received particularly encouraging responses from meetings in Columbus and Pittsburgh. Sonam’s journey is now entering its final phase. From Baltimore, he expects to travel next to Wilmington, Delaware, where he plans to meet with members of Congress, followed by Philadelphia. He then plans to continue to New Jersey before making his way to New York. The march will culminate on October 17 outside the United Nations, marking the end of what he describes as a 55-day walk for freedom. By the time he reaches New York, Sonam expects to have walked more than 1,400 kilometres, with the possibility of reaching approximately 1,500 kilometres depending on the final route. “This whole journey is dedicated, especially to the self-immolation of the late martyr Lobga Rangzen,” he said. “My 55 days of walking from Chicago to New York will be dedicated to Pawo Lobga Rangzen.”

title: Chinese national arrested in US for spying on Taiwan President’s son
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 6:A Chinese national has been arrested in the United States for allegedly acting on behalf of Beijing to conduct surveillance on the son of Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te, according to US authorities. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as “Heather” Zhang, at Los Angeles International Airport on October 4, shortly before she was scheduled to travel to China. Zhang, 34, from Irvine, California, is accused of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. Prosecutors allege that Chinese officials directed her to monitor Lai Ting-yu, the US-based son of President Lai, as well as his family. According to the FBI complaint, Zhang and an alleged accomplice travelled to the Seattle area in September 2025, where they allegedly photographed and recorded the family’s residence, vehicles and other details. The information, including photographs, videos and vehicle licence-plate details, was allegedly shared with individuals linked to the Chinese government. US authorities further allege that Zhang maintained communications with people she believed to be Chinese government officials and used the micro-messaging platform WeChat to transmit information. The FBI complaint states that Zhang was introduced to a Chinese official through a former classmate at Beijing’s University of International Relations. US authorities say the institution has links to China’s Ministry of State Security. The case has drawn attention because it involves the family of Taiwan’s sitting president and raises concerns over transnational repression, a term used to describe efforts by governments to monitor, intimidate or pressure people beyond their own borders. Taiwan’s Presidential Office has reportedly described the alleged surveillance as an instance of transnational repression. The Office condemned the arrest of 34-year-old Wanying Zhang, calling her actions a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanking the U.S. government for protecting Taiwanese citizens. Presidential spokesperson Karen Kuo stated that Taiwan “expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations”. Chinese authorities, meanwhile, have said they were not familiar with the specific case and criticised what they described as US efforts to portray China as a source of espionage threats.

title: Tibetan activist concludes 600-km ‘Rangzen Yatra’ from Dharamshala to Delhi
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 2:Tibetan activist Lhodrak Tharchin on Thursday concluded his more than 600-kilometre “Rangzen March” or “Azad Yatra”, a solo march from Dharamshala to New Delhi advocating Tibetan independence. Lhodrak began the peaceful march on August 20 and completed the journey in 40 days, travelling across three states and two Union Territories. His route passed through towns and cities including Kangra, Amb, Una, Mohali, Chandigarh, Panchkula, Ambala, Karnal, Panipat, and Sonipat. During the journey, Lhodrak said he met with civil society organisations, media outlets, and political figures to discuss developments in occupied Tibet, regional geopolitical dynamics and the broader implications of China’s policies in occupied Tibet. After entering New Delhi on September 22, he continued the march through the capital, meeting representatives of media organisations, educational institutions, political parties, and other groups. He also visited areas around the diplomatic district to raise awareness about occupied Tibet and discuss developments inside occupied Tibet and their wider regional implications. The march concluded on October 1 at the Samyelling Tibetan Settlement in Majnu Ka Tilla, north Delhi, after passing through the University of Delhi’s North Campus. Lhodrak said he deliberately chose October 1—the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China—for the conclusion of the march, describing the final leg as a protest against what he characterised as China’s occupation and colonial rule in Tibet. According to Lhodrak, the march sought to raise international awareness about what he described as the Chinese government’s “genocidal policies” in occupied Tibet and to garner support for Tibetan independence. He said the journey was undertaken on behalf of his family members inside occupied Tibet, whom he said are unable to express their views under Chinese rule freely. Lhodrak also dedicated the march to late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2 in protest against Chinese policies in occupied Tibet. He said the journey was also a tribute to other Tibetans who have sacrificed their lives for what he described as the cause of Tibetan freedom and dignity. The completion of the Rangzen Yatra marks the end of Lhodrak’s 40-day overland journey to the Indian capital, during which he sought to bring discussions on occupied Tibet to Indian civil society, political and media platforms.

title: China expands drone surveillance network across occupied Tibet, report finds
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 1:China has built an extensive drone surveillance and counter-drone network across occupied Tibet, deploying unmanned aircraft, automated docking stations and drone-detection systems as part of its broader security apparatus, according to a new report by Tibet Watch. TitledEyes Above the Plateau: Drones, DJI, and the Aerial Architecture of Control in Tibet, the report, published on September 29 with research support from US-based non-profit C4ADS, traces the expansion of aerial surveillance in Tibet through Chinese government documents, including police tenders, procurement contracts, training records, flight restrictions and official bulletins published since 2017. The report describes what it calls an emerging “aerial architecture of control”, with security agencies ranging from regional anti-terror units to county-level police stations acquiring drones for surveillance and “stability maintenance”—a term used by the Chinese Communist Party to describe measures aimed at preventing and suppressing dissent. According to the research group, the procurement records indicate that drones have been deployed particularly in areas associated with protests, religious activity and resistance to government policies. Driru County in so-called the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), which witnessed a violent crackdown following protests in 2013, has the largest county-level police drone fleet identified in the records examined by the report, with 18 aircraft reportedly conducting daily patrols. In Derge, Kham, eastern Tibet, county police reportedly purchased four automated DJI drone docking stations for a checkpoint along the Sichuan-Tibet road 15 months after protests against a hydropower project that threatened villages and monasteries. The report also highlights the parallel expansion of counter-drone capabilities. In 2021, Lhasa police made one of the largest purchases identified in the research for equipment designed to detect and jam unauthorised drones. Airspace restrictions have accompanied the expansion of surveillance. Tibet Watch says that during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the occupied Tibet in August 2025, airspace over Lhasa and four other prefecture-level areas was closed to flights except those authorised by authorities. Chamdo authorities also warned that unauthorised drones could be shot down. Since May 2026, newly manufactured drones in China have also been required to be registered to their owners’ identities before they can operate, further tightening state oversight of civilian drone use, according to the report. A significant finding concerns the involvement of Chinese drone manufacturer DJI, whose equipment appears in 12 confirmed procurement contracts awarded to security and government agencies in Tibetan areas. The contracts, which collectively amount to approximately ¥24.8 million (around £2.8 million), include 15 aircraft for police operations covering central Lhasa and the Jokhang Temple. Tibet Watch notes that the equipment was procured through resellers and that the available records do not establish that DJI itself contracted directly with the Chinese security agencies. The report draws a parallel with the United Kingdom, where DJI drones have also been widely used by police forces. It cites 2023 disclosures showing that at least 230 of 337 drones reported by 37 UK police forces were manufactured by DJI. Tibet Watch contrasts this with the UK government’s decision in 2022 to remove Chinese-made surveillance cameras from sensitive government sites on national security grounds, arguing that similar scrutiny should be applied to drones. The report says the use of drones has become routine and extensive in some Tibetan areas. In one district of Shigatse, police records reportedly document more than 5,700 drone-related operations and over 22,700 kilometres of flight since May 2024. These activities included monitoring crowd movements during large public events in an area that is home to Tashilhunpo Monastery, the traditional seat of the Panchen Lamas. Tibet Watch also identifies Nyingtri, near the disputed India-China frontier, as a significant site of military-linked drone infrastructure. According to the report, a “low-altitude defence network” there incorporates radar detection and enforcement capabilities, making it the only city-level drone-control body identified in the records with military participation. The report further draws similarities between the use of drones in occupied Tibet and Xinjiang, where Chinese authorities have faced widespread international criticism over mass surveillance and repression of Uyghurs. Tibet Watch says a police drone-training programme in Tibet prepares pilots for “stability maintenance”, while DJI provided drone training to police in Xinjiang in 2017. The United States subsequently sanctioned DJI in 2020 and 2021 in connection with surveillance concerns involving Uyghurs. Shede Dawa of Tibet Watch said the Chinese government’s own procurement and regulatory records provide evidence of an expanding surveillance system over Tibetan areas.“China has published the evidence itself,” he said, describing the system as one in which police drones are positioned over places where Tibetans “protest, pray and try to leave”, while access to the airspace is increasingly restricted for others. Tibet Watch is calling on the UK government to extend its 2022 restrictions on Chinese-made surveillance cameras to drones, issue guidance to police forces and consider using proposed powers under the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to address equipment already in service. The group has also called on the United States, European Union and retailers to examine the use and sale of drone technology in light of the findings documented in Tibet.

title: TYC youth activists storm Chinese Embassy in New Delhi on China’s National Day
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 1:Around 30 youth activists from the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) staged a protest outside the Chinese Embassy in New Delhi on Thursday, coinciding with the 77th founding anniversary of the People’s Republic of China. The protesters attempted to approach the Chinese Embassy while raising slogans and displaying placards highlighting the Tibetan struggle for freedom and condemning China’s policies in Tibet. The demonstration was organised to draw attention to what the TYC described as the denial of fundamental rights and the suppression of Tibetan identity and culture under China’s colonial rule. In a statement issued following the protest, TYC President Tsering Choephel “unequivocally condemned” what the organisation described as China’s “continued assertion of sovereignty and political control” over Tibet, East Turkistan, Southern Mongolia, and Manchuria. The TYC reiterated that “Tibet is never part of China and will never be,” rejecting what it described as the forced invasion and subsequent incorporation of the erstwhile independent state of Tibet. It similarly described the incorporation of East Turkistan, Southern Mongolia and Manchuria as assaults on freedom and accused China of pursuing what it characterised as colonial and imperialist policies through territorial expansion and border incursions. The TYC further asserted that no Chinese laws or policies, including what it described as colonial laws, would succeed in erasing Tibetans’ “distinct national historical claims, identity and will to determine their own political future.” Following the protest, the activists were detained by Delhi Police and taken to Mandir Marg Police Station, where they were held for several hours. The organisation said the protesters were subsequently released later that evening. While China’s National Day celebrations unfolded across China, including a flag-raising ceremony at Beijing’s Tiananmen Square and an official reception attended by Chinese President Xi Jinping, independent reporting from Tibet on how the anniversary was observed remains limited amid restrictions on access and information. Previous reporting has documented heightened security and restrictions around National Day events in Lhasa and other Tibetan areas. The 70th anniversary in 2019 saw official celebrations in Lhasa taking place under heavy security, with restrictions affecting residents’ daily lives.

title: CTA unveils five-year roadmap on Middle Way, community sustainability and strengthening CTA
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Oct. 1:The exile Tibetan government, officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), under the 17th Cabinet led by President Penpa Tsering, on Wednesday unveiled its revised five-year “Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future.” The CTA President outlined its priorities for the 2026–31 term across three broad areas: advancing the just cause of Tibet, safeguarding the welfare and sustainability of Tibetans in exile, and strengthening the CTA’s institutional capacity. Released three years after the 16th Kashag (Cabinet) introduced its first Vision Paper under the guiding principles of Equitable Justice, Cooperative Effort and Moving Forward, the revised document retains the Middle Way Policy as the CTA’s existing political direction, seeking to resolve the Sino-Tibet conflict through non-violence and dialogue. At the same time, the 17th Cabinet introduces several new or more specifically defined priorities, including greater engagement with the Chinese public, a campaign for international recognition of Tibet’s historical status, preparation against possible Chinese interference in the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, the relocation of 1,855 households, phased consolidation of Tibetan schools, and the introduction of artificial intelligence and data-management systems within the CTA. Retaining the Middle Way Policy, the paper states that the current Chinese government’s policies offer no indication of an opening for a mutually agreed solution. Nevertheless, the Cabinet says it will continue pursuing a lasting settlement through non-violence and dialogue while adapting its strategy to changes in international politics and developments in China and Tibet. The 17th Cabinet is changing the machinery and scope of advocacy surrounding that policy. The revised Vision Paper proposes expanding the CTA’s engagement beyond governments and traditional international advocacy networks to include the Chinese public. The Cabinet says it will build on its previous engagement with overseas Chinese communities and strengthen joint activities with Mongols, Uyghurs, Manchus, Hongkongers, and Taiwanese. It also proposes developing approaches to inform Chinese people about Tibet and what it describes as Chinese government repression. The revised paper gives specific attention to what it describes as Chinese government attempts to weaken the Tibetan movement through infiltration, deception, and efforts to create divisions within the exile community. The Cabinet identifies regional, sectarian, and political divisions as areas of concern and says the CTA, particularly its Task Force on Political Crises, will respond to such activities. The Cabinet also proposes strengthening the Voluntary Tibet Advocacy Group (V-TAG) by providing members with advocacy materials and training and by expanding participation through V-TAG+, including greater involvement from non-Tibetans. It also seeks stronger cooperation among Tibet advocacy groups, parliamentary support groups, Tibetan associations, umbrella organisations, and NGOs operating within the jurisdictions of the Offices of Tibet. The 17th Cabinet retains the previous administration’s emphasis on strengthening compact Tibetan settlements to sustain the community in exile. One of the most concrete commitments in the new Vision Paper is relocating 1,855 households registered with the CTA’s Department of Home. The paper says the relocation has already begun and is being actively followed up, with housing for Tibetans without homes or land intended to strengthen compact Tibetan communities. The 17th Cabinet proposes the progressive consolidation of Tibetan schools in India, based on birth data, current student enrolment and the circumstances and needs of individual schools. The Department of Education is expected to consult educational bodies and develop a jointly agreed plan for phased consolidation. School integration was already identified by the 16th Cabinet as necessary in response to declining student numbers. The new Vision Paper, however, places greater emphasis on moving toward an organised, data-based, and phased consolidation process. The preservation of Tibetan language remains a longstanding priority, but the 17th Cabinet expands the scope of that policy. The CTA says its offices and associated bodies will prioritise Tibetan in correspondence, announcements and meetings. It also proposes support for Tibetan-language software for technological and artificial intelligence systems, as well as Tibetan films, animations and short-form social media content. The language policy is therefore no longer limited to schools and traditional cultural preservation; it explicitly includes digital technology and AI. On strengthening the capacity of the CTA, the Cabinet proposes establishing an Institutional Development Index–Data Management (IDI-DM) system to manage institutional databases and standalone software applications. It also proposes a dedicated Statistics Section serving the CTA. The Vision Paper proposes continuing the development of several AI-assisted administrative systems, including: rules database; personnel database; personal assistant; project tracking portal; and budget database. The CTA also proposes progressively sharing these systems across departments as they become operational. The Cabinet says civil servants will receive stronger practical training in artificial intelligence and information technology, alongside specialised training from experts and experience-sharing among officials. The Cabinet says it will strengthen data collection and analysis, improve monitoring of activities and evaluate results more systematically. The stated aim is to improve target achievement and ensure that programmes approved by the administration are properly implemented and followed up.

title: Bipartisan US delegation reaffirms support for Tibet, say Trump-Xi meeting does not alter Washington’s position
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 30:A bipartisan US congressional delegation that met with Tibetan leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama in Dharamshala on Wednesday reaffirmed Washington’s support for the Tibetan people, stressing that the recent meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping does not alter the US position on China’s treatment of Tibetans and other communities. The delegation comprising Congressmen Brian Mast, James Gallagher, Jimmy Patronis, Shri Thanedar, and Haley Stevens met with the exile Tibetan spiritual leader during their visit to Dharamshala. Speaking to media representatives after the audience, Congressman Brian Mast described his meeting with His Holiness as an experience he would “never forget,” saying the delegation held an extensive conversation with the Tibetan spiritual leader on a range of issues, including China, freedom in Tibet, and His Holiness’s advocacy for freedom around the world. Phayul asked whether President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to Washington DC and his meeting with President Trump could have implications for the US approach to Tibet and Tibetan issues. Mast said His Holiness believes that dialogue between world leaders is important. Mast said the meeting between the two leaders, however, should not be interpreted as diminishing US opposition to repression in China. “It doesn’t take away in any way from believing that China should not be repressing its people, should not be repressing the Tibetan people or the Uyghur people,” he said, adding that countries should instead work towards supporting freedom. When asked by a media representative how he viewed the recent Trump-Xi meeting in relation to ties between the CTA and the United States, Mast said he saw it having a “positive” effect. “I see it affecting it positively. Every time that world leaders get together, there is a positive outcome in part in that there has been communication,” he said. Mast acknowledged that such meetings do not necessarily produce an immediate or tangible outcome, but argued that communication allows governments to better understand one another. “It doesn’t always mean that there is an immediate, positive, tangible thing that you are taking away. But every time that we speak, we understand each other more,” he said. When pressed whether the United States considers China a friend, Mast said Washington has a relationship with Beijing as two of the world’s largest powers, but pointed to significant areas of disagreement. “We have a relationship with China as two of the world’s largest superpowers,” he said. “But China does not conduct friendly activities to the United States of America,” Mast said, citing what he described as intellectual property theft, espionage, and differences over fundamental rights and freedoms. “There are very big differences. And I think we can easily focus more on the acts that are counter to friendship than the acts that are synonymous with friendship,” he added. Phayul asked the delegation about its outlook on the recently introduced Assuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026 (AFTA), which seeks to strengthen US recognition of and engagement with the CTA in

title: Tibetan athlete Tenzin Choezom clinches gold medal at Asian Games
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 30: Tibetan athlete Tenzin Choezom has bagged a gold medal in the women’s marathon race walk at the 2026 Asian Games after Kazakhstan’s Yasmina Toxanbayeva, who initially crossed the finish line first, was disqualified over her footwear. Toxanbayeva completed the 42.195-kilometre race in 3:22:20, finishing ahead of Choezom and initially taking the top spot. However, following the race, an event official reportedly submitted photographs and relevant documentation concerning the shoes worn by the Kazakh athlete to the competition committee. Her result was subsequently invalidated after officials determined that the footwear she used was not among the models approved under World Athletics regulations. Choezom, who had initially finished second, was therefore elevated to first place and awarded the gold medal. China’s Ma Li was declared the silver medallist after finishing the race in 3:32:26, while Japan’s Umeno took bronze in 3:34:59. Choezom’s Asian Games gold adds to a series of notable results in race walking. In 2024, she won first place in the women’s half-marathon race walk in Lhasa. In 2026, she finished third at the Chinese National Women’s Race Walking Half Marathon Championship in Huangshan, Anhui, before securing second place at the Chinese National Women’s Race Walking Championship in Hefei, Anhui, in May.

title: Solo peace marcher reaches Dharamshala, urges for greater youth participation
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 29:After eight days on the road, 59-year-old Tibetan activist Tashi Thakchoe arrived in Dharamshala on September 28, completing a solo peace march from New Delhi aimed at raising awareness about the Tibetan cause and encouraging greater participation among Tibetan youth. A member of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) Hunsur chapter, Thakchoe began his journey from the Indian capital on September 20. He reached Dharamshala at around 8 p.m. on September 28, bringing to an end a physically demanding journey undertaken largely on foot. Upon reaching McLeod Ganj, Thakchoe was received by local Tibetans and members of the TYC Centrex at the McLeod Main Square. The gathering welcomed him at the conclusion of his journey, marking the completion of his eight-day march from Delhi to Dharamshala. Speaking about the journey, Thakchoe said he set a daily target of covering between 40 and 45 kilometres. The long distances, however, left little room for extended rest.
