When exhaustion became difficult to manage, he said, he would book a hotel during the afternoon and take a short break of one or two hours before resuming his journey. The march was not without difficulties. Recalling one incident in Panipat, Thakchoe said he encountered a group of Indians whom he described as being under the influence of drugs and who chased him during his journey. The encounter was among the challenges he faced while travelling alone over the long route from Delhi to Dharamshala. Beyond the physical demands of the journey, Thakchoe said the march was intended to draw attention to the Tibetan cause and serve as a reminder of the need for continued public engagement. He particularly emphasised the role of younger Tibetans in sustaining the movement, expressing concern that elderly Tibetans constitute a significant presence at many forms of activism, including peace marches and protests. Thakchoe urged Tibetan youth to take a more active role in the movement and participate in campaigns and public actions related to Tibet. For him, the journey was therefore not only a personal endurance test but also an effort to encourage a wider and more sustained participation in the Tibetan cause.

title: Tibetan activist urges Canada to raise late Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation at UN
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 29:Tibetan Canadian activist Youngdoung Tenzin has urged the Canadian government to raise the self-immolation of late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen at the United Nations and address Tibet-related human rights concerns in its engagement with China. He made the appeal after meeting with a policy adviser to Canada’s foreign minister in Ottawa, where he briefed Global Affairs Canada on late martyr Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2, 2026. In a petition submitted to Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, he called on Ottawa to pursue three key measures: raise Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation at the UN General Assembly and support a multilateral joint statement on human rights in occuTibet; bring the matter directly to Chinese counterparts during diplomatic engagements; and formally address China’s “Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress,” which he described as an illegal policy and an act of genocide against Tibetans. He also urged Canada to include Lobga Rangzen’s case and the broader human rights situation in Tibet in Global Affairs Canada’s annual human rights reporting. He said Lobga Rangzen self-immolated on July 2, 2026, outside the UN headquarters in New York, carrying the Tibetan national flag and calling for an end to Chinese colonial rule in occupied Tibet. He said the UN’s lack of an official response following the incident was deeply concerning and argued that Canada, as a UN member state with a history of supporting Tibetan human rights, should take the issue forward through international diplomatic channels. The petition also refers to Canada’s historical engagement with the question of Tibet, including its votes in favour of UN General Assembly Resolutions 1353 (1959), 1723 (1961), and 2079 (1965). It further cites the Canadian Parliament’s 2022 motion calling for the resumption of Sino-Tibetan dialogue and its 2024 motion concerning the Tibetan people’s right to self-determination. He additionally raised concerns about transnational repression, citing his own experience of being sanctioned by the Chinese government in December 2024 for his advocacy for Tibet in Canada. He said he had faced intimidation and death threats but remained committed to advocating for Tibetan rights. During the meeting, he formally submitted his petition along with an English transcript of Lobga Rangzen’s final live video message. He appealed to Tibetans living in democratic countries to make use of their civic rights and engage with their elected representatives. “Every single one of us has the responsibility to carry forward the aspiration of Pawo Lobga Rangzen,” he said, urging members of the Tibetan diaspora to approach their local members of parliament and foreign ministers and raise the case through democratic channels.

title: 7th peace rally marathon for Tibet underway in Canada
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 29:The 7th Peace Rally Marathon for Tibet reached its fifth day on Sunday, with a five-member team continuing its 450-kilometre journey from Ottawa to Toronto to raise international awareness of the situation in occupied Tibet and garner international support for the Tibetan cause. Organised by the Toronto Pemakoepa Youth Association, the peace run began on September 23 outside the Chinese Embassy in Ottawa. The campaign is scheduled to conclude on October 1 outside the Chinese Consulate General in Toronto, coinciding with China’s National Day. According to the organisers’ latest update, the fifth day of the run began in Kaladar and ended near Belleville. The runners were welcomed along the route by local Tibetan residents as well as non-Tibetan supporters. The five-member team comprises runners Pema Kunga, Dechen Wangdi and Gyurme Tsultrim, with Kalden Wangchuk serving as navigator. Dawa Norbu Dayab is serving in a triple capacity as driver, coordinator and runner. The campaign is centred on three demands. The organisers are calling for the repeal of China’s “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which they say threatens Tibet’s religion, culture and language; greater international awareness and protection of the Tibetan Plateau and its fragile environment, which they describe as the “Third Pole”; and the unconditional release of Tibetan political prisoners. The organisers have also been using the journey to engage members of the public and political representatives. Along the route, the participants have distributed informational leaflets on Tibet to raise awareness among foreign nationals and others. Before beginning the journey from Ottawa, the delegation held a demonstration outside the Chinese Embassy and met Canadian Members of Parliament James Maloney and Karim Bardeesy at Parliament Hill. The team presented its petition and urged the lawmakers to raise issues concerning Tibet in Parliament during the ongoing session. The organisers said the delegation also distributed more than 200 informational brochures across the national capital region. The peace run was first launched in 2020 and has been organised by young Tibetans from the Miao Choepheling Tibetan Settlement in Arunachal Pradesh, northeastern India. During the current campaign, the participants are also scheduled to meet Canadian parliamentarians and government officials in Ottawa to discuss possible support for the Tibetan cause. The runners are expected to continue towards Toronto over the next few days, with the 450-kilometre peace run set to conclude on October 1 outside the Chinese Consulate General, where they will join members of the local Tibetan community and Tibet supporters for a peaceful demonstration marking China’s National Day.

title: CTA rejects climate activist Sonam Wangchuk’s comparison of Ladakh situation with Tibet
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 25:The Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) on Friday rejected climate activist Sonam Wangchuk’s comparison between the situation in Ladakh and conditions inside Tibet, saying the comparison was “misplaced and inaccurate” and did not reflect the reality faced by Tibetans under China’s colonial rule. Wangchuk made the remarks on Thursday at NDS Ground in Leh while addressing a gathering marking the first anniversary of the September 24, 2025 violence in Ladakh, in which four protesters were killed in police firing. He said Ladakh had chosen to remain with India because of its democratic system and the expectation of living with dignity, but argued that the situation had since deteriorated. “Today, such oppression is being inflicted on Ladakh that, in my view, even China is not doing this to Tibet,” Wangchuk said. The CTA spokesperson, Tenzin Lekshay, in a statement issued Friday, pushed back against the comparison, highlighting what it described as the continuing repression of Tibetans under China’s colonial rule. “The Central Tibetan Administration expresses deep concern over remarks made by Sonam Wangchuk in his recent public speech in Ladakh, in which he compared the situation in Ladakh with that of inside Tibet,” the statement said. The CTA described the comparison as “misplaced and inaccurate,” adding that Wangchuk’s remarks “don’t reflect the real situation inside Tibet.” “Tibet continues to remain under China’s authoritarian rule, where Tibetans face systematic repression of their fundamental rights, religious freedom; and intensification of measures aimed at erasing its distinct cultural identity,” the statement said. The CTA’s statement was followed by criticism from Tibetan voices living and working in Ladakh, who argued that the suffering of Ladakhis and Tibetans should not be placed in a hierarchy or used to diminish either community’s experience. Tsering Wangmo, a Tibetan filmmaker based in Ladakh, acknowledged her personal connection to the region while challenging Wangchuk’s characterization of the situation in Tibet. “I was born and raised in Ladakh. Ladakh means a great deal to me. I love Ladakh and I care deeply for it,” Wangmo said, adding that she supports “Ladakh and its people’s wishes for political stability and self-determination.” She then contrasted her experience in Ladakh with her connection to Tibet, saying she lives in Ladakh as a stateless person because her homeland remains under Chinese control. “My grandparents, my father, and other members of my family passed away in exile without ever having the right to return to their homeland,” she said. She further pointed to restrictions faced by Tibetan artists, writers and singers, saying they have been imprisoned or silenced because of political expression. “Forget about any right to outright express our desires for freedom. The situation in Tibet is incomparable to any other,” she said. “Just as every form of oppression is unique and can never be compared with another.” Calling for solidarity rather than competition between communities facing hardship, Wangmo said: “Only through solidarity can we speak of shared experiences and find points of alignment, but we should never turn suffering into a competition over who has suffered more.” Addressing Wangchuk directly, she added: “I respect you. I never expected someone of your stature to make a remark like this.” Ladakhi singer Tenzin Shayan, who is based in Zanskar, Ladakh, similarly expressed support for Wangchuk’s broader advocacy for Ladakh while condemning his characterization of Tibet. “I totally agree with and respect what Ka Sonam Wangchuk said today at NDS Ground, and I sincerely thank him for standing up selflessly for the people and future of Ladakh,” Shayan said. However, he objected to the suggestion that Tibetans do not suffer significantly under Chinese rule, pointing to the imprisonment of Tibetans, self-immolations and restrictions on religious and cultural expression. Shayan also referred to restrictions surrounding images of the Dalai Lama and concerns over Tibetan language, culture and traditions under Chinese policies. “His Holiness had to leave his country behind with millions of Tibetans becoming refugees today separated from their loved ones for ages,” he said. While expressing hope that “the dreams and aspirations of Ladakh are achieved,” Shayan stressed that Ladakh’s struggle should not come at the expense of acknowledging the Tibetan experience. “Achieving our own aspirations should never require us to minimise or dismiss the suffering of another people,” he said. “I say this with respect, but also with the responsibility of speaking for the truth and dignity.”

title: Thousands of Tibetans and supporters rally on Capitol Hill to protest Xi’s state visit
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 25:Around 2,500 Tibetans and Tibet supporters, including Uyghurs, Hongkongers, Taiwanese, and Chinese dissidents, converged on Capitol Hill in Washington D.C. on Thursday under the banner of “Chalo DC” to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit. The rally, organised by the pro-independence group Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), also drew support from advocacy groups including the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT), Tibetan National Congress (TNC) and Students for a Free Tibet (SFT), among others. Longtime Tibet supporters, former U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), also joined the demonstration and addressed the gathering at the National Mall. Pelosi told demonstrators that political leaders needed to hear their voices, saying it was important for elected officials, as well as the presidents of the United States and China, to hear their concerns. “It’s really important for elected officials and for the president of the United States and the president of China to hear what you have to say,” Pelosi said, adding that the United States presents itself as a country that cares about “human rights” and “the dignity and worth of the people.” She also called for respect for Tibet’s distinct religious and cultural identity, saying, “We have to insist that the religion, the language, the faith, the sense of community in Tibet be respected. We must continue to fight for Tibet.” McGovern, meanwhile, used his address to press the U.S. administration to confront Beijing over its human rights record and policies affecting Tibetans. “We demand that President Trump get tough on the Chinese president’s abysmal human rights record,” McGovern said. He also called on the administration to oppose China’s newly enacted “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” address transnational repression of Tibetans and ensure that Tibetans in the United States are not deported to China. The congressman had already joined fellow lawmakers Jamie Raskin and Gregory Meeks in urging President Donald Trump to raise the law directly with Xi during the summit. In a September 23 letter, the lawmakers argued that the legislation gives Chinese authorities broad powers against Tibetans, Uyghurs and other minority communities, as well as critics living outside China. They called for the law to be repealed. McGovern has also specifically raised the case of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, recognised by the Dalai Lama as the 11th Panchen Lama, who disappeared after being taken into Chinese custody in 1995. At the rally, McGovern called for his release and for him to be allowed to communicate freely with the Tibetan people. However, the demonstrations were accompanied by disruptions from groups supporting Xi Jinping. Individuals carrying Chinese national flags used microphones and loudspeakers to repeatedly play the slogan “Welcome, welcome, a warm welcome,” along with loud recorded noise that protesters said was intended to cover or drown out Tibetan protest voices. Tibetan protesters also reported confrontations with individuals they identified as pro-Beijing supporters. Some people seen at the demonstrations wore matching gray bucket hats, face masks and sunglasses and were accused by protesters of photographing and recording the demonstrations. Protesters further alleged that some individuals carried pepper spray and tactical umbrellas and confronted people on the streets. The ‘Chalo DC’mobilisation formed part of a broader coalition of diaspora communities seeking to draw international attention to their concerns over Beijing’s policies. For Tibetan protesters, the rally focused on Tibet’s political, cultural, linguistic and religious rights, while Uyghur, Hong Kong, Taiwanese and Chinese dissident groups used the occasion to highlight their own grievances. Together, the demonstrations placed issues of human rights, cultural identity, political freedoms and the right to dissent alongside Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington.

title: Tibetans, Uyghurs, Hongkongers, Chinese dissidents protest against Xi in Washington
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 24:Tibetans, Uyghurs, Hongkongers, and Chinese dissidents gathered in Washington DC, on Wednesday and Thursday in a sustained mobilisation against Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit, bringing their concerns over Tibet and other rights issues to the streets as Xi arrived in the US capital on September 23. The mobilisation intensified on Thursday, September 24, when demonstrators assembled outside the Chinese Embassy carrying Tibetan national flags, placards, and banners and chanting slogans directed at Xi and the Chinese Communist Party. The protesters later marched towards the White House, where US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, during a state arrival ceremony on the South Lawn. The demonstrations unfolded amid heightened security and a series of confrontations between protesters and pro-China counter-demonstrators. On September 23, Tibetan protesters said pro-China demonstrators attempted to obscure their banners and Tibetan national flags by waving Chinese flags after they unfurled a banner protesting Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington DC. The counter-demonstrators were also seen pushing Tibetan activists during the demonstration. A similar confrontation was reported later that night outside the Waldorf Astoria, where Xi is staying during his Washington visit. Chinese pro-democracy activists holding a peaceful demonstration were confronted by individuals described by protesters as Chinese Communist Party supporters. The individuals, wearing hats, dark glasses and masks, allegedly attempted to disrupt the demonstration. Activists from Tibetan, Chinese, Uyghur, and Hong Kong diaspora communities have previously reported similar counter-protest tactics at demonstrations critical of Beijing. Protesters have described some of those involved as CCP supporters or “lackeys.” The demonstrations coincided with Xi’s meetings with Trump, as diaspora organisations and human rights groups sought to place issues concerning Tibet, East Turkestan (Xinjiang), Hong Kong, and broader human rights concerns alongside the principal agenda of the US-China engagement. For Tibetan protesters, the mobilisation has centred on opposition to Beijing’s assimilation policies in occupied Tibet and calls for greater international attention to Tibetan political, cultural, and religious rights. Uyghur and Hong Kong activists have likewise used the demonstrations to highlight their own concerns over policies they say have restricted political and civil freedoms. The protests have consequently brought together several diaspora communities with distinct political grievances but a shared opposition to aspects of Beijing’s policies. Their presence in Washington has created a parallel narrative around Xi’s state visit—one focused on human rights, cultural and political freedoms, and the right to dissent. As Trump welcomed Xi at the White House, protesters continued their mobilisation outside the venues associated with the Chinese president’s visit, seeking to keep Tibet, East Turkestan, Hong Kong, and other human rights concerns visible during the high-level US-China engagement.

title: Tibetans travelling to Tibet must not be tool for propaganda: Security Minister warns in Parliament
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 24:Concerns over Tibetans living abroad travelling to Tibet for family visits and tourism came under scrutiny on Thursday as members of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile fenced questions to the minister of Central Tibetan Administration’s Department of Security on the eighth day of the ongoing session. The discussion centred on the implications of such visits amid what parliamentarians described as heightened restrictions inside Tibet. Parliamentarian Lobsang Gyatso Sither said the issue warranted careful consideration, while acknowledging that travelling to Tibet can provide Tibetans living abroad with an opportunity to reunite with families, relatives, and visit their homeland. He pointed to China’s 2026–2030 Five-Year Plan, arguing that Beijing has given tourism development significant importance within its policy framework. He cautioned that Tibetans travelling to Tibet could, in certain circumstances, risk being perceived as lending support to or becoming part of such initiatives. He also referred to figures concerning tourism and visa arrangements, saying that China had set ambitious targets for international visitors and that a large proportion of foreign travellers were making use of visa-free or simplified entry arrangements. He linked these developments to the broader expansion of tourism in Tibet. The parliamentarian further recalled guidance issued by the previous Cabinet concerning travel to Tibet, saying that many Tibetans should follow the guidance and maintain contact with the Department of Security regarding their visits. He also questioned the lack of public disclosure surrounding some Tibet-related trips and highlighted what he described as a contradiction between seeking asylum abroad on the grounds of difficulties inside Tibet and subsequently returning to Tibet. Responding to concerns raised by members, Security Minister Kunga Tashi urged Tibetans travelling to Tibet to exercise caution and ensure that their visits do not turn them into instruments of Chinese propaganda. He said Tibetans who encounter transnational repression by Chinese authorities should report such incidents to the Department of Security. According to the Minister, documented cases would enable the department to raise the matter with relevant governments and pursue appropriate channels of action. The issue of Tibetans travelling to Tibet was also raised in connection with organised trips involving young Tibetans from Europe. Some parliamentarians expressed concern that Tibetan children were being taken to Tibet under programmes organised by particular groups and called for greater awareness among parents. Minister Kunga Tashi said the department was aware of the issue and maintained that some of the programmes were being organised with private financial interests in mind. He urged the Tibetan public to exercise vigilance and said the department had been taking measures in response. Members also raised concerns about Tibetans travelling to Tibet in connection with what they described as Chinese united-front activities, as well as the potential consequences faced by Tibetans who return and speak publicly about their experiences. He reiterated that Tibetans visiting Tibet should be particularly mindful of the possibility of being used for propaganda purposes and urged anyone subjected to pressure or repression beyond China’s borders to report it to the department. The parliamentary discussion also touched on the continuing decline in the number of Tibetans arriving in India from Tibet. In response to questions from parliamentarians on Wednesday, the Security Minister said the number of new arrivals from Tibet had generally declined since 2012, with only seven Tibetans arriving from Tibet so far this year.

title: CTA launches ‘Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week’ to counter China’s assimilation campaigns
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 23:The Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) President Penpa Tsering on Wednesday formally launched the observance of “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week,” an initiative aimed at reinforcing Tibetan language, culture, and national identity in response to what the exile administration describes as China’s state-driven assimilation policies in occupied Tibet. As the first public initiative marking this year’s “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week,” the Tibet Museum under the CTA’s Department of Information and International Relations (DIR) organised a screening of the animated film Man of Peace at Maximus Mall in Lower Dharamshala, followed by an evening play at the Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts (TIPA) depicting the implications of China’s so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” The CTA President said the week-long observance will be held during the fourth week of September, following a resolution adopted during the 11th session of the 17th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile designating the period as the “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week.” The initiative comes in response to China’s annual “Ethnic Unity and Progress Propaganda Week,” which, according to the CTA President, Chinese state institutions use to promote assimilation-oriented policies and campaigns centred on the dominance of the Chinese language and a unified national identity. President Tsering also referred to amendments made by the Chinese government on 27 December 2025 to the country’s “Law on the National Commonly Used Language and Script.” According to the CTA, the revised provisions further institutionalise Mandarin as the principal language of instruction from preschool through higher education, as well as in government offices and public spaces. He said the annual propaganda campaign forms part of a broader effort by Chinese authorities to consolidate the use of Mandarin and promote what Beijing describes as “ethnic unity.” Calling for collective participation in the observance, the CTA President urged Tibetans worldwide—including individuals, families, schools, community organisations and activists—as well as supporters of Tibet, to work under the guidance of Offices of Tibet representatives and Tibetan Settlement Officers. He also called on Tibetan communities to stand in solidarity with Tibetans inside Tibet and implement the activities outlined in the public announcement issued by the Cabinet on 21 August 2026, alongside the newly launched “Principles and Guidelines for the Preservation of Tibetan Language.” The comprehensive guidelines set out responsibilities for families, schools, Tibetan communities, and the CTA Department of Education, with measures ranging from making Tibetan the primary language of communication at home and strengthening Tibetan-medium education to establishing community language classes, immersion programmes and greater use of Tibetan in public spaces and social media. The guidelines also call for teacher training, scholarships, modern Tibetan-language educational resources and the development of Tibetan terminology for contemporary fields. The policy further calls for greater integration of Tibetan into digital technologies, including machine translation, speech recognition, artificial intelligence and optical character recognition, while reaffirming Tibetan as the official language of the CTA. A three-to-five-member Tibetan Language Preservation Committee is also to be established to monitor implementation and publish an annual assessment of the policy.

title: SFT activist scales Washington light pole, unfurls anti-Xi banners ahead of Xi’s US visit
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 23:A 20-year-old Tibetan activist with Students for a Free Tibet (SFT) climbed a light pole near the US Capitol in Washington D.C. and unfurled banners denouncing Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of his arrival in the US capital on September 23-25. The youth activist, identified as Tenzin Namgyal, carried out the action on September 22, drawing attention to Tibet as Xi prepared for his first visit to Washington in a decade. The banner read, “Dictator Xi, Your Empire Will Fall! Free Tibet.” Video footage released by SFT International showed the protester scaling a light pole along Pennsylvania Avenue NW, several blocks from the US Capitol. Police and emergency crews temporarily closed the roadway in both directions as authorities responded to the demonstration. After the activist descended, a fire department ladder truck was used to remove the banner from the pole. The youth activist was subsequently taken into police custody, according to SFT. Following his release, Namgyal said the action was carried out in memory of the late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, who died after self-immolating outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2. Namgyal said he first encountered the late martyr as a child during a protest and later drew inspiration from his activism and commitment to the Tibetan cause. In remarks released following the action, Namgyal also linked his protest to China’s policies of cultural assimilation and environmental exploitation in occupied Tibet. He raised concerns over restrictions affecting Tibetan language, religion and cultural identity, as well as dam construction, mining and other projects under the pretext of “development” on the Tibetan Plateau. The protest comes amid heightened Tibetan mobilisation surrounding Xi’s visit to Washington. Tibetan activists and supporters are expected to gather in the US capital as the visit gets underway, voicing opposition to Beijing’s policies in Tibet, East Turkestan (Xinjiang) and Hong Kong, as well as raising broader concerns over alleged human rights violations. Meanwhile, during a press conference in Dharamshala on Wednesday, a journalist asked Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) President Penpa Tsering about Xi Jinping’s scheduled visit to the United States. Responding to the question, President Tsering said, “We are watching every step the Chinese government is taking.” His remarks came ahead of Xi’s scheduled September 23 arrival in Washington for a three-day state visit to the United States at the invitation of US President Donald Trump. Xi’s three-day state visit to the United States comes as Washington and Beijing seek to manage tensions in their increasingly consequential bilateral relationship. The visit, Xi’s first to Washington in more than a decade, follows his meeting with US President Donald Trump in Beijing in May and is intended to sustain high-level dialogue on trade, economic ties, and wider global issues. China has said the two leaders will discuss China-US relations and international issues concerning peace and development. At their White House meeting, trade is expected to feature prominently, including tariffs, agricultural purchases and non-tariff barriers, alongside negotiations over critical minerals and rare-earth supplies. The leaders are also expected to address artificial intelligence, Taiwan and the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, although the precise scope of the discussions remains subject to negotiations. Reports suggest Taiwan remains a particularly sensitive issue for Beijing, while Washington and its allies have expressed concerns over the security implications of China’s growing role in critical technologies and mineral supply chains.

title: Tibetan educational sociologist Dr. Gyal Lo honoured with Tenzin Delek Rinpoche Medal of Courage
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 23:Dr. Gyal Lo, a Tibetan educational sociologist and prominent researcher who has documented and exposed China’s state-run residential school system across occupied Tibet, has been honoured by the International Tibet Network (ITN) with the Tenzin Delek Rinpoche Medal of Courage. The honour recognises his efforts to document and raise international awareness of the impact of China’s assimilation policies on Tibetan language, culture, and identity. “Dr Gyal Lo’s tireless work has helped to raise international awareness and push back against China’s assimilationist policies,” ITN stated. “For years, Dr Gyal Lo has carried out the monumental task of documenting China’s colonial boarding school system in Tibet. He visited schools, collected educational resources and witnessed for himself how Tibetan children have been affected by these boarding schools and boarding pre-schools. In recent years, he has travelled the world, addressing governments and the United Nations to warn about the devastating effects of this policy,” ITN added. Born in Tibet, Dr. Gyal Lo completed his early education in his home region before earning a master’s degree in Tibetan Language and Culture from Northwest Minzu University (formerly Northwestern University for Nationalities) in Lanzhou, China. In 1995, he was appointed Assistant Professor in the same department, where he taught for the next decade and conducted extensive academic research on Tibetan education. Dr. Gyal Lo later left China to pursue a Master of Education and a PhD in the Sociology of Education at the University of Toronto, Canada. Upon returning to China in 2015, he was denied reemployment at his former institution due to political sensitivities surrounding his time abroad and Western academic training. His return to Tibet also brought him into direct contact with the experiences of his two grandnieces, who had been enrolled in a newly developed mandatory pre-boarding school. These schools, introduced for Tibetan children as young as four to six years old, operated alongside residential boarding schools serving children aged six to eighteen. Concerned by the effects of the pre-boarding system on his grandnieces, Dr. Gyal Lo undertook five years of academic fieldwork, visiting more than 50 Tibetan boarding schools and documenting their impacts on children, families, and Tibetan communities. Alongside his research, Dr. Gyal Lo served as a Full Professor at the Institute for Studies in Education at Yunnan Normal University from 2017 to 2020. Three years into his five-year contract, however, his position was terminated amid a worsening political climate in China. He was dismissed on the grounds that he was a “foreign Tibetan with a Western background” and was considered a potential political risk. He left China on December 31, 2020, and has chosen not to return due to the risks associated with conducting independent research on Tibetan education and society. After resettling in Canada, Dr. Gyal Lo began speaking publicly about the threats facing Tibetan society and became an advocate for the preservation of Tibetan language, religion, culture, and rights. Drawing on his academic research and firsthand documentation of China’s colonial boarding-school system in Tibet, he has sought to raise international awareness of its impact on Tibetan children and communities. In February 2023, he testified before the Subcommittee on International Human Rights of the Canadian House of Commons, sharing his extensive knowledge and research on China’s boarding-school system in Tibet. Dr. Gyal Lo is the author of Social Structuration in Tibetan Society: Education, Society, and Spirituality (Lexington Books, 2016). The ‘Tenzin Delek Rinpoche Medal of Courage’, presented annually on the anniversary of his passing, honours the enduring legacy and moral courage of Tenzin Delek Rinpoche. The award recognises Tibetan human rights defenders who demonstrate an unwavering commitment to advancing the freedom and fundamental rights of the Tibetan people, often at great personal risk and sacrifice. Over the years, the medal has been awarded to individuals and groups who embody this spirit of courage, resilience and non-violent resistance. Recipients have included imprisoned retired physician Yeshi Choedron (2016); Tibetan language rights advocate Tashi Wangchuk (2017); filmmakers Dhondup Wangchen and Golog Jigme (2018); the 11th Panchen Lama, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima (2019); environmental activist A-Nya Sengdra (2022); imprisoned businessman Dorjee Tashi and his sister Gonpo Kyi (2023); Dege protesters who opposed the Kamtok hydropower project (2024); and thelate Tulku Hungkar Dorjee.

title: Gangjong Finance’s future remains uncertain as Finance Minister outlines closure review
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 22: The future of Gangjong Development Finance Private Limited, a banking system introduced by the Dr. Lobsang Sangya presidency, remained under discussion on the sixth day of the 18th Tibetan Parliament in Exile on Tuesday, with parliamentarians questioning whether the enterprise’s proposed closure adequately considers its long-term financial potential and possible benefits to the Tibetan community. Parliamentarian Kunchok Yarphel said Gangjong Finance had originally been established with a specific purpose and argued that any decision concerning its future should be based on a clear assessment of its financial performance rather than differences between successive Cabinets. He questioned whether the enterprise had ultimately incurred losses or generated returns since its establishment. He also cautioned against closing an enterprise that could potentially contribute to the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) and community in the future, saying such a decision could later be regretted. He called for the matter to be reconsidered from the beginning, with particular attention to the enterprise’s financial record and long-term viability. Responding to the concerns, Finance Minister Tsering Dhondup outlined the department’s efforts since the 17th Tibetan Parliament in Exile passed a resolution in March 2024 calling for Gangjong Finance to be transformed into an independent entity within two years, failing which its closure could be considered. According to the Finance Minister, the department subsequently explored various possibilities for transferring the enterprise into independent management and held discussions with relevant stakeholders. However, efforts to identify an organisations willing and capable of assuming responsibility for Gangjong Finance did not yield a concrete outcome. The minister said the enterprise’s operational capacity had also weakened considerably over the years. Although around 10 employees had remained at one stage and received training to strengthen their ability to manage its operations, most resigned in 2022, leaving only one employee from that period to continue maintaining the service with support from the Department of Finance. The department subsequently approached the Tibetan Chamber of Commerce in 2024, including its chairperson and executive members, to explore whether the Tibetan business community could take over and sustain the enterprise. The Finance Minister said the department viewed such a transition as potentially beneficial to the wider Tibetan economy, given the business community’s experience in financial and commercial management. However, the proposal did not materialise. The minister said further discussions were held this year, including renewed appeals in April, before the Tibetan Chamber of Commerce eventually communicated its response in August. Meanwhile, preparations for closure had already begun, following a resolution passed by the 17th TPiE designating 2026 as the year for Gangjong Finance to be wound up. The minister said, however, that subsequent expressions of interest from individuals willing to invest capital and continue the institution had led the Department of Finance to reconsider whether the closure should proceed immediately as planned. The minister clarified that no final decision has yet been taken. “As Gangjong Finance has 25 shareholders, the shareholders’ position remains central to determining its future,” he said. The Department of Finance has therefore contacted the shareholders to obtain their views before proceeding. Of the approximately 16 or 17 shareholders who had responded by Tuesday, the majority, according to the minister, had expressed support for closing the enterprise. The Finance Minister said the Department intends to consolidate the shareholders’ views before convening an Annual General Meeting by the end of September. The matter will then be placed before the shareholders’ meeting, where any decision reached will determine the subsequent course of action. The minister nevertheless acknowledged that, given recent developments and the enterprise’s potential value to the Tibetan community, the department considers it appropriate to examine the matter once more before proceeding with closure.

title: Tibetan-American entrepreneur Tenzin Seldon raises $63 million for climate fund
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 22:Tibetan-American entrepreneur and climate investor Tenzin Seldon has successfully raised $63 million for the inaugural fund of Pulse Fund, a climate-focused venture capital firm investing in early-stage companies working across energy, infrastructure, food and agriculture, and mobility. Founded in 2022, Pulse Fund was established by Seldon, who serves as its founder and managing partner. The fund’s close comes as Seldon’s career in climate policy, entrepreneurship, and investment continues to be shaped by her early experiences growing up in the Himalayan region. In a 2021 interview withTricycle, she recalled seeing ice-capped mountains around Dharamshala melting and said that climate change was not an abstract concept for her but something she experienced first-hand. Her early experiences eventually became the foundation of a career spanning climate policy, social entrepreneurship and venture capital. Seldon moved to the United States during her adolescence and graduated summa cum laude from Stanford University before becoming the first Tibetan-American Rhodes Scholar at the University of Oxford. She subsequently worked with the United Nations Environment Programme in Thailand, where her work included disaster-risk reduction policy. She later co-founded The Plant, a climate-focused initiative aimed at creating a hub for climate solutions through the redevelopment and adaptive reuse of historic buildings, before turning her focus toward climate investing. Through Pulse Fund, Seldon now backs early-stage companies developing solutions across energy transition, infrastructure, food and agriculture, and mobility. The firm’s investment thesis is built around the interconnected nature of these sectors rather than treating them as isolated areas of the climate economy. “We invest across energy, food and agriculture, infrastructure, and mobility, and we underwrite them together, because a breakthrough in one keeps turning up as the reason a company in another suddenly works,” Seldon said. “Investors who look at one sector at a time miss those companies, or they price them wrong.” The newly raised $63 million represents Pulse Fund’s inaugural fund, with the firm seeking to invest in companies developing scalable solutions to climate-related challenges. Its portfolio to date includes Mast Reforestation, a company focused on post-wildfire reforestation and carbon removal; Twelve, which develops fuels and other products using captured carbon dioxide; Endera Motors, an electric mobility solutions provider; and InventWood, a developer of engineered wood products designed to provide lower-carbon alternatives to conventional materials. Seldon has described the current period as a major transition in the global economy, with significant amounts of capital expected to move toward technologies and businesses addressing climate change. “We are at the beginning of the largest capital reallocation in history, and understanding how the energy transition, infrastructure, food and agriculture, and mobility move together will define where that capital lands,” she said. “We back the founders who see those connections before the market does and build companies at the center of them. This close is a mandate to go find more of them.”

title: Parliament adopts solidarity resolution on Tibet after prolonged debate
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 21:A six-point solidarity motion on the critical situation inside Tibet triggered an extensive and at times heated debate in the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile on Monday, with lawmakers divided over the wording as well as Central Tibetan Administration’s core positional implication due to a provision calling for continued efforts toward “Tibet’s freedom and independence”. The motion was tabled by Parliamentarian Gyaltsen Choekye Gagya and supported by Parliamentarian Gonpo Dhundup on the fifth day of the ongoing session of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile. The House ultimately adopted the resolution expressing solidarity with Tibetans inside Tibet, without the fifth point of the resolution which failed to secure the required majority, receiving 17 votes in favour and 24 against. The most contentious deliberation centred on the wording of the fifth point of the resolution, which called on Tibetans living in free countries to intensify efforts to raise international awareness of the Tibet issue, engage governments, and maintain unity while continuing efforts for “Tibet’s freedom and independence.” The Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) President Penpa Tsering raised a point of order, arguing that although the motion was presented as an official expression of solidarity and condolences, the wording of the fifth point of the resolution had implications for the CTA’s established policy position. He maintained that if the provision amounted to a substantive change in the CTA’s policy, the matter would have to be addressed under Article 56 of the Charter of Tibetans in Exile, which provides a mechanism for dealing with important policy matters concerning the fundamental interests of Tibet or the Tibetan people. Some parliamentarians proposed replacing the phrase “to continue efforts for Tibet’s freedom and independence” with wording along the lines of “to clarify the ultimate truth of the Tibet issue,” in keeping with terminology currently in use in the Charter. Others argued that language referring to the “struggle for the Tibet issue” should be retained. Several members also questioned whether the adoption of the contested wording could create ambiguity over the CTA’s policy in the future. They sought clarification from Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang on whether her assertion that the motion would not alter the CTA’s policy position would be formally recorded. The Speaker subsequently maintained that the motion had been introduced in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures. She said the matter had been discussed within the Standing Committee and that the resolution, as presented, would not constitute a change in the CTA’s policy. While some parliamentarians supported the motion in its entirety and stressed the importance of respecting the Middle Way Approach, others argued that calls for a review or reconsideration of policy were compatible with democratic processes. Some lawmakers also called for greater clarity over what pursuing Tibetan independence would entail in practical terms, including the strategies and mechanisms that would be required to translate the objective into concrete political action. The debate also brought renewed attention to the political significance of the late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation. Several parliamentarians said his death had resonated particularly strongly among Tibetan youth and argued that his sacrifice should not be allowed to fade without further action on the Tibet issue. The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile adopted five of the six points of a resolution expressing solidarity with Tibetans inside Tibet, calling for the protection of their human rights, religious, and cultural identity, and urging the Chinese government to address the Sino-Tibetan conflict through dialogue. The resolution condemned decades of what it describes as repression of Tibetans’ religious and national identity and paid tribute to those who have protested Chinese government policies, including Tibetan self-immolators. It specifically honoured Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, who died after self-immolating outside the United Nations Headquarters in New York on July 2, and expressed condolences to his family. It called on the United Nations’ leaders to raise the Tibetan issue with Chinese authorities, while seeking the release of arbitrarily detained Tibetans—including the 11th Panchen Lama—and urged an end to restrictions on Tibetan language, religion, and culture, as well as policies affecting Tibet’s environment. The resolution supported resolving the Sino-Tibetan conflict through dialogue, while rejecting China’s so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” It also expressed gratitude to India and acknowledged governments, parliaments, organisations, and individuals worldwide for their continued support of the Tibetan cause.

title: Anthropic report reveals China-based AI-enabled surveillance on CTA, ICT and SFT
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 19:A new threat intelligence report from Anthropic has revealed how China-based, government-aligned actors used artificial intelligence to conduct surveillance and intelligence gathering targeting Tibetan Buddhist civil society, the exile Tibetan government officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), and Tibetan advocacy organisations, including the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT), and Students for a Free Tibet (SFT). Anthropic’s report, “Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026,” covered malicious activity identified and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 involving its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models. Anthropic said the cases represent some of the most notable and novel misuse of its AI systems that it has identified. Among the cases documented is an operation identified as GTG-14020, which Anthropic described as a China-based, PRC government-aligned intelligence operation targeting Catholic, Tibetan Buddhist, Falun Gong and Taiwanese Christian communities. The operation used Claude as a substitute for a team of human analysts, generating Chinese-language intelligence dossiers, investigative reports and daily “situational awareness” briefings on individuals and organisations. According to Anthropic, the operation specifically targeted members of Tibetan Buddhist civil society and the administration in exile, with its target list explicitly including the CTA, ICT, and SFT. The operators gathered personal information including individuals’ birth dates, birthplaces, immigration dates, and social-media accounts. They also conducted reconnaissance of religious venues, collecting information such as floor plans, building facades, and structural diagrams. Their monitoring extended across both Chinese and international social-media platforms, including WeChat, Xiaohongshu, Douyin and Weibo, as well as LinkedIn, Instagram, Threads, X, and Facebook. Anthropic said the Tibetan-focused work stream produced daily and batch situational-awareness reports and an organisation dataset. Claude was used to ingest information in multiple languages and convert it into structured Chinese-language dossiers based on templates resembling internal security documents. One of the most significant findings concerned the use of AI not only for surveillance and information processing, but also for political narrative framing. Anthropic said operators explicitly instructed Claude to adopt “China’s standpoint” and to describe the Tibetan administration in exile as an “illegal separatist administration.” The report identified this terminology as part of a broader state-security lexicon observed in the operation. The finding indicated that the AI system was being incorporated into an intelligence workflow in which information about Tibetans and Tibetan organisations was not simply collected, translated and summarised, but processed according to terminology and framing preferred by the operators. Anthropic said the operation’s targeting priorities aligned with China’s United Front and religious-affairs apparatus, identifying the United Front Work Department, the Ministry of State Security and the former State Administration for Religious Affairs among the relevant state bodies. In one instance, a user reportedly identified themselves as an information-security officer for the Chinese state. The findings also form part of a wider case study in Anthropic’s report concerning China-based “stability maintenance” operations. Anthropic said actors linked to municipal public- and state-security organs used Claude to support surveillance and transnational repression, including monitoring overseas dissidents, advocacy organisations and civil-society groups. In a separate operation, Anthropic found AI being used to process open-source reporting, assess political sensitivity, standardise terminology and reframe foreign media coverage into government-style public-opinion briefings. The monitored targets included Tibetan and Uyghur communities, overseas dissidents, activists and international human-rights organisations. Anthropic said it banned the accounts associated with the Tibetan and religious-affairs intelligence operation and enhanced its detection systems to reduce the possibility of similar misuse in the future. The report therefore raised a broader question about the use of increasingly capable AI systems in surveillance: whether technologies designed to process information at unprecedented speed can also be turned into tools for profiling diaspora communities, monitoring religious institutions and amplifying state-preferred political narratives.

title: Dalai Lama to visit Tashi Lhunpo Monastery in South India this winter
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 19:The revered Tibetan spiritual leader, His Holiness the Dalai Lama, is scheduled to visit Tashi Lhunpo Monastery in Bylakuppe, Karnataka, South India, this winter, according to an official communication from the Office of His Holiness the Dalai Lama dated September 17, 2026. The letter addressed to the Khenpo Rinpoche and officials of Tashi Lhunpo Monastery states that the nonagenarian leader is expected to travel to South India during the winter and that his stay will, as in previous years, be at the monastery. The Office stated the exact dates and programme of the visit will be communicated later. The upcoming visit follows the Tibetan spiritual leader’s regular winter sojourns in southern India, where he meets devotees and monastic communities and takes part in religious ceremonies, teachings, and other spiritual engagements. During his most recent winter visit, His Holiness the Dalai Lama travelled to Mundgod in Karnataka on December 12, 2025, arriving at Drepung Gomang Monastery in the Doeguling Tibetan Settlement. He remained there for 60 days before departing for Delhi on February 9, 2026. His stay in Mundgod included several major religious engagements. On December 24, 2025, he attended an enthronement ceremony and long-life prayers offered by Drepung and Rato monasteries at Drepung Lachi Monastery. He also attended the annual winter debate at Drepung Gomang Debate Hall in January 2026. Tashi Lhunpo Monastery in Bylakuppe is one of the major Tibetan monastic institutions established in exile and serves as the traditional monastic seat of the Panchen Lamas. The monastery has previously hosted His Holiness for religious ceremonies and teachings, making the forthcoming winter visit significant for the monastic community and Tibetan settlements in southern India.

title: Opinion: Two Tibetans in August – China’s Dual Strategy of Attack and Propaganda
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: On 13 August, China Daily published an attack on Tibetan self-immolation protest. Five days later, on 18 August, another Chinese state media outlet, People’s Daily, published a tribute to a living Tibetan portrayed as loyally guarding China’s border in occupied Tibet. Read separately, the two articles may appear to be routine pieces of state propaganda. Read together—both centred on Tibetan loyalty—they reveal a single strategy executed in two acts: discredit the Tibetan who sacrificed his life in exile for Tibet, and manufacture the image of the Tibetan loyalist who serves the Chinese state. Act One: Discredit the Martyr On 2 July 2026, a Tibetan refugee named Lobga Rangzen left a video statement on his Facebook account calling for victory for Tibet’s independence and set himself on fire in front of the United Nations headquarters in New York. As his body burned, he scattered pamphlets into the air. Two phrases were legible: “Free Tibet” and “China out of Tibet.” In his final message, Rangzen urged fellow Tibetans to intensify the struggle to restore the independence of Tibet, a nation invaded by Chinese military forces in the 1950s. China Daily’s response, six weeks later, was to call his self-immolation protest a “stunt.” The state media outlet labelled him a separatist, described his act as anti-Buddhist, and alleged that it had been instigated by a separatist group associated with the 91-year-old exiled Tibetan leader, His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama. It ultimately sought to connect his protest to a U.S. conspiracy against China’s new ethnic law that took into effect one day before Rangzen’s death following the self-immolation protest. The anti-Buddhist charge against Rangzen is deeply ironic. It comes from the propaganda apparatus of an officially atheist one-party state that has repeatedly branded the 14th Dalai Lama a separatist and vilified him despite his international recognition as a symbol of peace, compassion, and humanitarianism. Such portrayals are part of a familiar political manoeuvre. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) routinely employs political narratives and defamatory characterizations against individuals and institutions whose positions contradict Beijing’s political stance, particularly on Tibet. The attack on Rangzen went further by attempting to transform his self-immolation into evidence of a foreign conspiracy. China Daily alleged that his protest was connected to the U.S. government’s campaign against China’s so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law. In doing so, it sought to replace Rangzen’s own stated political motivation with an external one. That serves an important propaganda purpose. If Tibetan dissent can be framed not as an expression of Tibetan political conviction but as the product of foreign manipulation, the Tibetan dissenter is denied political agency. Rangzen’s final testimony stated what he believed and why he acted. Recasting his protest as part of a foreign intelligence operation allows the state to divert attention from that message and from the political cause he sacrificed his life to highlight. Act Two: Manufacture the Loyalist Five days after the attack, as Tibetans around the world were mobilising against the Chinese Communist Party’s portrayal of Rangzen, another branch of the same state media outlet, People’s Daily, told a very different Tibetan story. On 18 August 2026, People’s Daily published a report titled “Three Generations Have Continuously Guarded the Borderlands of the ‘Snow Land’ for Fifty Years,” profiling Dargye, a 73-year-old Tibetan Communist Party member and former soldier from Puktsang Village in Zayu County, Nyingchi City, Tibet Autonomous Region. The area borders the north Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, where recent local reports have described increasing intrusions by Chinese soldiers. The report presents Dargye and his family as a model of multi-generational service to the Chinese state in a strategically sensitive border region. Their participation in border defence is held up as evidence of patriotism and loyalty, reinforcing Beijing’s broader propaganda narrative of Tibetan happiness, development, and support for state security objectives. According to the report, Dargye joined the People’s Liberation Army at the age of 21 and received four years of border-defence training under the Chamdo Military Sub-command. It states that he later returned to his hometown and became a local platoon commander responsible for border patrols, defence activities, and the transportation of military supplies across difficult mountainous terrain. The article traces three generations of his family serving in border defence—Dargye, his eldest son, and his grandson—with a great-grandson described as aspiring to join the military and “repay the motherland.” The significance of the story lies not only in Dargye’s biography but also in the strategic value of recruiting Tibetans from border communities into China’s border-security network. Local Tibetans possess intimate knowledge of the terrain, mountain routes, settlements, and surrounding communities. In difficult, high-altitude, and geographically isolated border environments, such knowledge can provide significant operational advantages to China’s border-security forces. The incorporation of Tibetans into the local security forces and other auxiliary roles therefore strengthens the state’s capacity to monitor and control sensitive border regions. It also draws local communities directly into the security apparatus, creating financial dependence on state subsidies, placing Tibetans themselves on the front line of implementing Beijing’s border-security policies. A Tibetan living in a border area, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confided to the author that all men in his village are required to join local civil-military groups and participate in border-guarding activities on a rotating basis, assisting regular border forces. He further stated that the local government had installed a fingerprint-scanning machine at the village entrance, requiring villagers to scan their fingerprints daily. According to him, the system enables officials to monitor villagers’ movements and identify absences. Those who have been away may subsequently be questioned about where they went and what they did. Another Tibetan from the same region of Dargye said, “My mother and my family were asked to patrol the border. China is spending a huge amount of money on people living in the border areas. They are spending money to buy people’s loyalty. My home village is at the border, so everyone is being paid to live there. People cannot refuse the payment either.” These testimonies, absent from state media, reveal the coercive reality behind China’s supposedly “voluntary” border patrols. Through payments, compulsory participation, and high-tech surveillance, Tibetans are drawn into the state’s security system, where coercion is repackaged as patriotism and an image of Tibetan loyalty is constructed to advance Beijing’s broader colonial strategy in Tibet. Two Tibetans, One Strategy Neither China Daily’s attack on Lobga Rangzen nor People’s Daily’s tribute to Dargye is primarily about the individual Tibetan at the centre of the story. Rangzen represents the Tibetan whom the state cannot accommodate. His explicitly stated political conviction must therefore be discredited, attributed to separatism, foreign manipulation, or conspiracy, and stripped of legitimacy. Dargye represents the Tibetan whom the state can celebrate. His purported life and family history are presented as evidence that Tibetans willingly identify with the Chinese state, defend its borders, and regard service to China as an expression of patriotism. Taken together, the two stories expose the dual logic of Beijing’s Tibet propaganda: delegitimize the Tibetan who dissents, glorify the Tibetan who purportedly serves, and present the manufactured contrast as proof that Tibetans freely accept China’s authority. (Views expressed are his own) The author is a Senior Researcher and Research Manager at Tibet Watch, where he leads research on human rights and contemporary developments in Tibet. His work focuses on analysing Chinese policies, governance, and their impact on Tibetan communities.http://tibet.people.com.cn/n4/2026/0818/c309795-20034349.html?utm_source=chatgpt.comhttps://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202608/13/WS6a7ddfbfa31073853ec53329.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com

title: Amendment seeking overseas MP to Standing Committee fails to secure majority
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 18:The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile on Friday rejected a proposed amendment that sought to revise the composition of its Standing Committee by introducing representation from parliamentarians representing Tibetans in North and South America; Europe; and Australasia and Asia, excluding India, Nepal, and Bhutan. The amendment sought to revise Article 42 of the Charter of the Tibetans in Exile, which governs the composition of the Standing Committee, the parliamentary body responsible for carrying out legislative functions when the house is not in session. Under the existing provision, the committee comprises parliamentarians drawn from Tibet’s three traditional provinces and its religious constituencies. The proposed amendment sought to extend this representation to overseas constituencies. The proposal was tabled by parliamentarian Kalsang Phuntsok Godruk and supported by parliamentarian Thupten Gyatso. It prompted an extensive debate among lawmakers, with proponents and opponents advancing divergent views on the institutional implications of incorporating overseas representation into the Standing Committee. Those opposing the amendment argued that the present composition of the parliament is based on symbolic representation of Tibetans and traditional set up of Tibet and not necessarily the exile Tibetan demographic, hence adding the representatives of overseas MP to the standing committee may suggest that the parliament is representative of only exile Tibetans. Some lawmakers also raised concerns over the institutional implications of such a change. Questions were also raised over whether a parliamentarian elected from one overseas constituency would be able to adequately represent Tibetans across other overseas regions. In particular, parliamentarians questioned whether a representative from the United States could effectively speak for overseas Tibetans in South America, Europe, and Australia. Another issue centred on the practical demands placed on members of the Standing Committee. As members are required to remain in Dharamshala for the duration of their one-year tenure, some parliamentarians expressed concern that the requirement could create difficulties for Tibetans living overseas, particularly younger and professionally productive and established Tibetans, and potentially discourage them from seeking election to the Parliament in the future. Supporters of the amendment, however, argued that overseas representation on the Standing Committee would provide greater geographical inclusivity and parity within the parliamentary structure. They maintained that the composition of Tibetan parliamentary representation has expanded historically and that the Standing Committee should evolve accordingly. They also pointed to the substantial Tibetan population living outside India, Nepal, and Bhutan, arguing that their concerns should have a direct channel into the Standing Committee. Including an overseas parliamentarian, they said, would enable issues affecting Tibetan communities abroad to receive greater institutional attention. During the clarification stage, MPs Kalsang Phuntsok Godruk and Thupten Gyatso, responded to concerns over the availability of young, educated Tibetans abroad to serve on the Standing Committee. They said there were individuals who had expressed their willingness to serve as parliamentarians and on the Standing Committee in the future. Addressing questions over the representational reach of an overseas member, they said that whichever overseas parliamentarian was elected to the Standing Committee could represent Tibetans across the wider overseas constituency through an appropriate decision of the committee. They also stated that the five overseas parliamentarians had discussed the proposal among themselves before it was formally introduced on the House floor. The amendment was subsequently put to a vote. It received 23 votes in support, but failed to obtain the required two-thirds majority of the 30-member House. The proposal was therefore not adopted, leaving the existing composition of the Standing Committee unchanged.

title: Parliament adopts resolution mandating CTA officials to use Tibetan in official duties
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 18:The Tibetan Parliament in Exile on Friday adopted a resolution mandating leaders, officials, and staff of the exile Tibetan government officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), to use Tibetan in their official duties without unnecessarily mixing it with other languages. The resolution, the second Private Member’s Resolution presented during the ongoing second session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament in Exile, was tabled by Parliamentarian Lhakpa Tsering and supported by Parliamentarian Gyaltsen Choekye Gagya. It was subsequently put to a vote and adopted by the House. Speaking on the resolution, MP Lhakpa Tsering said the three pillars of Tibetan democracy should lead by example by making greater use of the Tibetan language in their official work. He argued that language is not merely a means of communication but a fundamental vessel of a people’s identity, culture, and continuity. He recalled having previously called for greater use of Tibetan during a parliamentary visit to Varanasi, and said sustained efforts were needed to cultivate the habit of speaking Tibetan in official settings. He stressed that the change should begin with public servants themselves before being extended more broadly to the Tibetan public. Parliamentarian Rigzin Lhundup, who also spoke in support, described it as unfortunate that a parliamentary resolution was needed simply to encourage Tibetans to speak their own language. He said the use of Tibetan by officials when communicating with the public would not only make government institutions more accessible but also provide an important example for younger generations. He further maintained that the preservation of Tibetan should not be viewed merely as a reaction to language policies imposed in occupied Tibet. Rather, he said, speaking Tibetan is integral to affirming Tibetan identity. He urged Tibetans to communicate, ask questions and conduct everyday interactions in Tibetan wherever possible, saying there was no reason to delay such efforts. Parliamentarian Gowo Lobsang Phende similarly backed the resolution, while calling for greater attention to the distinction between speaking Tibetan and speaking pure Tibetan. He noted that although officials across the CTA’s three pillars generally use Tibetan, unnecessary English terms, and mixed expressions have increasingly entered official communication even when suitable Tibetan equivalents exist. He said the CTA employs more than 500 people across its three pillars and argued that consistent use of pure Tibetan by those in public service could have a wider ripple effect throughout the exile community. Referring to restrictions on Tibetan language and script in occupied Tibet, he said the exile administration has an added responsibility to safeguard and strengthen the language where it retains the freedom to do so. He also welcomed recent efforts by local Tibetan leadership in Dharamshala to encourage the use of Tibetan in official letters and statements. He called for such initiatives to be implemented consistently rather than remaining limited to formal announcements. The resolution was ultimately adopted by the House, highlighting renewed efforts to strengthen the use of Tibetan language within the exile administration. It comes amid concerns over China’s implementation of the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which Tibetan exile leaders have condemned as a legal framework aimed at accelerating the assimilation of Tibetans by eroding their distinct identity, language, culture, and way of life.

title: Resolution on Tibetan independence policy fails to secure majority for debate
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 18:A private member’s resolution seeking the adoption of a policy supporting Tibetan independence failed to secure the majority number after securing 15 votes in favour and 23 against, on Friday, during the second session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, The resolution was subsequently dropped from further discussion. The resolution, tabled by Parliamentarian Sangye Dorjee and supported by Gyaltsen Choekye Gagya, sought to establish Tibetan independence as a policy position, calling for the restoration of Tibet’s sovereignty and the continuation of the independence struggle until Tibetans inside and outside Tibet are reunited. The motion faced a series of points of order from parliamentarians during the proceedings, with Central Tibetan Administration President Penpa Tsering repeatedly questioning whether a private member’s motion could be used to alter the Administration’s established policy position. While tabling the resolution, MP Sangye Dorjee argued that since 1959, following what the resolution describes as the illegal occupation of the entire territory of Tibet by Communist China, Tibet’s environment, religious institutions, language, and cultural identity have faced sustained destruction and assimilation. The resolution alleged that hundreds of thousands of Tibetans had been killed, imprisoned, or subjected to torture, while Tibetan children had been placed in residential schools and access to monasteries restricted for those under 18. It further cited the removal of Tibetan-language instruction from schools and what it described as efforts to assimilate Tibetan customs, traditions, culture, and language. According to the resolution, these policies amount to an attempt to erase Tibet’s national identity and eliminate the Tibetan people as a distinct nation. It argued that, so long as Tibetans remain, the struggle for freedom must continue and efforts must be made to restore Tibet’s sovereignty as a historically independent nation. The resolution also paid tribute to Tibetans who had sacrificed their lives for the Tibetan nation and people, pledging to fulfil their aspirations. It called for the independence struggle to continue “even at the cost of one’s life” until Tibet is restored with freedom, religious prosperity, well-being, and the reunification of Tibetans inside and outside Tibet. The CTA President raised a procedural concern over the proposed resolution, arguing that because it could alter the Central Tibetan Administration’s existing policy, it should not be treated as an ordinary private motion. Citing Article 56 of the Charter in Exile, he said major policy changes concerning Tibet and Tibetans are subject to specific approval thresholds and, where applicable, a public referendum. He cautioned that allowing an individual parliamentarian to change the Administration’s policy through a private motion could set a precedent for altering major policy positions too readily in the future. “It cannot simply be introduced in this manner and then immediately taken up for discussion,” the CTA President said, stressing that the matter should either follow the relevant parliamentary procedure or be brought before the House under another appropriate agenda item. Speaking again during the proceedings, the CTA President urged the Speaker to review the procedural basis of the proposed private motion submitted by an individual member, arguing that if it could lead to a change in the Central Tibetan Administration’s official policy, Article 56 of the Charter may apply. He reiterated that his intervention was not a position for or against the independence proposal, saying, “I do not know whether I support or oppose it. My concern is solely with the procedure.” He argued that if the resolution were allowed to proceed and ultimately resulted in a change to the CTA’s policy, it would constitute a policy change of significant importance, making the application and interpretation of Article 56 particularly relevant. He warned that failing to properly observe parliamentary rules could create difficulties not only in future proceedings but also in how substantive issues are introduced, debated, and interpreted within the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile. Despite the procedural objections, the House ultimately rejected the motion at the threshold stage, with 15 members voting to allow discussion and 23 voting against, bringing the proposed independence policy resolution to an end without a substantive debate on its contents.

title: Rights coalition urges Xi to reopen dialogue, release Panchen Lama, repeal ethnic unity law ahead of US visit
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 17:A coalition of 30 human rights organisations has called on Chinese President Xi Jinping to take immediate and verifiable steps on human rights, including resuming dialogue with representatives of the Dalai Lama, releasing the 11th Panchen Lama Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, and repealing China’s newly enacted “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” ahead of Xi’s upcoming visit to the United States. The open letter, issued on September 16 ahead of Xi’s expected September 24 visit to Washington, also urged Beijing to release prisoners of conscience, end transnational repression, and reform laws and policies that criminalise peaceful expression, religious practice, association, and dissent. The signatories include the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT), Committee to Protect Journalists, Reporters Without Borders (RSF), Amnesty International USA, Freedom House, Human Rights Foundation, World Uyghur Congress, and International Tibet Network (ITN), among others. On Tibet, the coalition specifically called for the resumption of substantive and unconditional dialogue with representatives of His Holiness the Dalai Lama and the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). The organisations also demanded the immediate release of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, recognised by the Dalai Lama as the 11th Panchen Lama, who has not been publicly seen since his disappearance in 1995. The letter additionally calls for the release of other political prisoners and individuals it identifies as prisoners of conscience. The third Tibet-related demand centres on China’s “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which was passed by the National People’s Congress in March and came into force on July 1, 2026. The legislation has drawn criticism from ICT and other rights organisations, which argue that it provides a legal framework for the assimilation of Tibetans and other non-Chinese ethnic communities. Separately, the Washington-based advocacy group International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) urged US President Donald Trump to make Tibet and human rights a prominent part of his forthcoming talks with Xi. ICT called on Trump to press Beijing to restart substantive dialogue with the Dalai Lama and Tibetan representatives, secure the release of the Panchen Lama and oppose policies that, according to the organisation, seek to erode Tibet’s religious, linguistic, and cultural distinctiveness. ICT President Tencho Gyatso said existing US legislation, including the Tibetan Policy Act of 2002 and the Resolve Tibet Act of 2024, provides a policy framework for Washington to promote a negotiated resolution to the Tibet-China dispute through substantive dialogue without preconditions. The rights group also pointed to what it describes as increasing political interference in Tibetan Buddhist institutions, the demolition of monastic residences, the separation of Tibetan children from their families through state-run boarding schools, and the detention of Tibetans over peaceful expression. The new ethnic unity law has become a particular focus of international criticism. ICT stated the legislation codifies policies it characterises as forced assimilation and places greater emphasis on a unified national identity under Communist Party leadership. The organisation has also raised concerns about the law’s extraterritorial implications.
