The open letter, rights group said, frames the three Tibet-related demands within a broader appeal for human rights reforms across China, arguing that the forthcoming US-China engagement should be accompanied by concrete and verifiable measures rather than diplomatic commitments alone.

title: Lawmakers call for greater preparedness, relief for flood-hit Gegayling Tibetan settlement in Nepal
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 17:Members of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile on Thursday called for greater preparedness and contingency planning for Tibetans in Nepal following the devastating August flash flood that caused extensive destruction in Nepal’s Rasuwa bordering Tibet where the Tibetan community in Gegayling settlement was severely affected. Concerns were raised during the ongoing second session of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, as lawmakers discussed the disaster’s impact and the Central Tibetan Administration’s response. Parliamentarians extended condolences to families affected by the disaster and enquired about the CTA’s response, particularly plans for relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction. MP Tashi Dhondup specifically drew attention to what he described as a challenging political environment for Tibetans in Nepal, referring to discussions in the Nepalese Parliament and statements by former Nepalese home ministers that, according to him, included calls for the removal or expulsion of Tibetans from the country. Against this backdrop, he urged Tibetan representatives in Nepal to strengthen their preparedness and establish a coordinated mechanism for responding to future emergencies. He said local representatives of the CTA’s Department of Home had recently held meetings to assess the situation and sought updates and reports from the ground. Responding to the MP, CTA Home Minister Palden Dhondup said the Department of Home initiated an emergency response as soon as it received information about the disaster. The department contacted its local representatives in Nepal and instructed them to assess immediate requirements and submit a financial estimate for emergency assistance. The initial estimate stood at ₹5 lakh, but was subsequently revised upward, with ₹7 lakh eventually dispatched for emergency relief. The minister said the assistance was intended as an initial intervention, as the full scale of casualties and property damage could not be estimated immediately. “At this stage, we do not yet know exactly how many people have died or the extent of the damage to property and belongings,” he said. He added that a more comprehensive assessment would follow as information from the affected areas became available. The Home Minister also disclosed that 14 people connected to the Tibetan community were initially unaccounted for. Of these, 11 were under the jurisdiction of a local Tibetan representative, while two boys, approximately 19 and 13 years old, had travelled from Kathmandu towards the affected area and were also reported missing. Another young man from a Tibetan settlement in southern India, who had reportedly moved to Nepal and married a Nepali woman, was likewise among those whose whereabouts were unknown. The minister cautioned against prematurely assuming that those missing had died, stressing that confirmation could take considerable time amid the scale of destruction and disrupted communications. He said the Government of Nepal had extended rescue and relief assistance to Tibetans without discrimination, with necessary facilities made available to those affected. He said Tibetan representatives on the ground had been instructed to address immediate requirements while simultaneously developing longer-term plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction. They were also asked to identify needs for food and other essential supplies. Beyond preliminary assessments, the Department of Home plans to engage professionals to undertake a detailed evaluation of damaged houses, water-related destruction, infrastructure and other property before preparing a standardised reconstruction estimate, he said. Minister Dhondup further said the department had received reports that some children affected by the disaster may have lost one or both parents and could face difficulties continuing their education. However, he said most of the cases identified so far appeared to concern the local Nepali population, and the department did not yet have a verified figure for Tibetan children in such circumstances. He said the information would be further cross-checked before definitive figures were released. The minister also emphasised that reconstruction should not be based solely on preliminary estimates submitted by local representatives, but should follow a systematic and professional damage assessment. Beyond the immediate disaster response, the Home Minister’s intervention placed the flood within a wider discussion about the vulnerability of Tibetans living in Nepal. He said the CTA has been monitoring developments in Nepal closely while attempting to avoid actions that could further complicate the circumstances of Tibetans living there. The Home Minister said the Department’s approach was to continue supporting Tibetans in Nepal while recognising the political sensitivities surrounding their presence in the country.

title: China says PM Modi promised not to allow ‘anti-China activities’ on Indian territory
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 17:Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun has claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi assured Chinese President Xi Jinping that India would not allow its territory to be used for “anti-China activities,” following their bilateral meeting on September 12 on the side-lines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. “Prime Minister Modi said that India has an independent foreign policy, developing relations with China is not affected by any third party and that it will not allow any force to engage in anti-China activities on its territory,” Guo said at a press conference in Beijing on Monday. The Chinese account also said that India’s policy and position on issues concerning Tibet and Taiwan remained unchanged. The reference to Tibet is notable given India’s long-standing hosting of the Tibetan exile community and the space historically afforded to Tibetan organisations to conduct political advocacy, demonstrations and public events. However, India’s official readout of the Modi-Xi meeting does not mention any such assurance on “anti-China activities.” The Indian account instead said the two leaders agreed that bilateral ties should be viewed from a “strategic and long-term perspective” and that “differences should not become disputes.” Modi reiterated that India-China relations should be guided by “mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.” The Chinese claim comes days after the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) and Students for a Free Tibet (SFT) staged protests against Xi’s visit in New Delhi, during which dozens of Tibetan activists were detained by Delhi Police. The timing has drawn particular attention to the possible implications of Beijing’s characterization of “anti-China activities” for Tibetan political activity in India. The Modi-Xi meeting comes as New Delhi and Beijing seek to consolidate a gradual thaw in bilateral ties following years of tensions triggered by the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley clash along the disputed India-China border. Relations began to improve after the two sides reached an agreement in October 2024 that facilitated disengagement in the eastern Ladakh sector, although significant differences remain. During the September 12 meeting, Modi stressed that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remained an “essential basis” for the continued development of bilateral relations and called on both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings concerning the border. The two leaders also expressed commitment to pursuing a “fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable” resolution of the boundary question. The leaders also discussed expanding people-to-people ties, cultural exchanges, business linkages, and greater mobility between the two countries. On economic and trade relations, they agreed on the need to address concerns including the structural trade imbalance, supply-chain issues, and the facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access. The meeting was Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and marked another step in efforts to stabilise relations after the 2020 military confrontation. Bilateral trade has rebounded despite continued tensions, while institutional exchanges, flights and people-to-people contacts have gradually resumed. However, reports say, unresolved border issues, trade imbalances, and strategic mistrust continue to complicate the relationship. China has meanwhile sought to frame the renewed engagement in broader terms. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the two leaders reached a key consensus that India and China should regard each other as “partners rather than rivals,” reflecting Beijing’s push for a broader reset in bilateral relations.

title: Speaker of Parliament launches sweeping critique of China’s ‘Ethnic Unity Law’
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 16:The second session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile commenced in Dharamshala on Wednesday and is scheduled to continue through September 25. Speaker Tsering Dolma Tsering Teykhang used her opening address to launch a sweeping critique of Beijing’s recently enacted “Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law” and call for greater unity within the Tibetan exile community. In her opening address, Speaker Dolma Tsering characterised the legislation as the latest manifestation of what she described as a decades-long policy trajectory aimed at eroding the distinct identities of Tibetans and other minority communities. Tracing the evolution of China’s ethnic policies, she pointed to a succession of measures affecting the linguistic, educational, cultural and socioeconomic foundations of Tibetan society, including the displacement of nomadic communities from their ancestral lands and the proliferation of state-run boarding schools. She maintained that the new legislation should not be viewed in isolation, but understood within this broader continuum of policies. The Speaker argued that eroding a community’s religion, culture, and language cannot legitimately be presented as “development,” just as erasing one ethnic identity cannot be construed as “unity.” She asserted that such measures undermine the principles of genuine progress, cultural preservation, and peaceful coexistence. The Speaker situated the legislation within the broader trajectory of Beijing’s “second-generation ethnic unity” policy, rolled out in the Tibetan Autonomous Region around 2018–19 and subsequently drawing scrutiny from members of the US Congress, including Senator Marco Rubio. She further contended that the law’s accelerated passage was driven not merely by ethnic policy considerations, but also by internal political manoeuvring aimed at reinforcing President Xi Jinping’s authority. Turning to the Tibetan community in exile, Speaker Dolma Tsering stressed that unity and mutual respect are essential in confronting policies that, she said, seek to weaken the collective Tibetan identity. She emphasised that unity does not require uniformity and that individuals are entitled to differing political views and opinions. However, she said those entrusted with political responsibility bear a duty to pursue the resolution of the Sino-Tibet conflict under the Tibetan administration’s established Middle Way policy. She also called for greater tolerance and mutual respect, cautioning that internal divisions could undermine the Tibetan community’s collective efforts. The opening session subsequently turned to a series of official condolence and tribute resolutions, with five motions presented during the morning proceedings. MP Geshe Lharampa Atuk Tseten tabled a resolution honouring the sacrifice of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, who died on July 2, 2026, after self-immolating outside the United Nations headquarters. The Parliament also paid tribute to former minister Chope Paljor Tsering, who passed away in June this year, and Professor Robert A. F. Thurman, the renowned American scholar of Tibetan Buddhism and long-time friend of Tibet. A further obituary reference was made to former US Congressman Barney Frank, who died in May. Frank was among those who played a significant role in supporting the resettlement of Tibetans in the United States under the Immigration Act of 1990. The Parliament also adopted a resolution expressing condolences and solidarity with those affected by the devastating flash floods along the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26. The second session will primarily deliberate on the detailed annual reports of the Central Tibetan Administration’s departments and subordinate offices for the 2025–26 financial year. The reports will be considered alongside questions submitted by the Standing Committee of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, followed by responses from the Cabinet and presentations by the respective Ministers.

title: China’s new exit-and-entry regulations take effect, widening control over overseas travel
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 16:China on Tuesday brought into force a new set of regulations on Exit and Entry Administration, giving authorities broader powers to scrutinise and restrict the overseas travel of Chinese citizens while tightening requirements for foreign nationals entering the country. The regulations, issued as State Council Order No. 841, were approved by the State Council on June 29 and signed by Premier Li Qiang on July 22. Beijing says the framework is intended to standardize exit-and-entry administration, protect travelers lawful rights, and safeguard China’s sovereignty, national security, and development interests. Under the new rules, Chinese citizens subjected to administrative detention for fraudulently obtaining exit-entry documents or for illegally crossing borders can be prohibited from leaving China for six months to three years after completing their punishment. Similar restrictions can apply to citizens who engage in criminal activities overseas that are deemed to endanger China’s national security or interests. One of the most consequential changes concerns technology and industrial security. Article 4 gives authorities a basis to prohibit Chinese citizens from leaving the country when violations of export-control or technology import-and-export regulations are considered capable of endangering national industrial or technological security. Reports say the provision has drawn particular attention because it creates a clearer legal route for export-control violations to result in travel restrictions. The regulations also place greater scrutiny on people involved in sensitive sectors and on immigration intermediaries. Immigration-service providers are required to operate under a new regulatory framework, while authorities can require travellers to provide relevant documents and information during the application and verification process. For foreign nationals, the regulations introduce corresponding restrictions. Foreigners who submit false information or documents when applying for Chinese visas or seeking entry can face entry bans of one to five years, depending on the circumstances. According to reports, the new framework has prompted concern among Han Chinese citizens and communities abroad over the expanded discretion it gives authorities to regulate international travel. Reuters reported that the regulations formalise and broaden existing restrictions, including potential exit bans lasting between six months and three years in certain national-security cases. For Tibetans, Uyghurs, and residents of some Hui-populated areas, however, the September 15 regulations come more than a decade after Beijing imposed a particularly stringent passport regime that severely curtailed access to international travel. The roots of the policy can be traced to late 2011 and early 2012, when approximately 7,000 Tibetans from the so-called Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) travelled to India to attend the Kalachakra teachings. According to a report by Human Rights Watch (HRW), hundreds were detained upon their return and subjected to interrogation and political indoctrination. Some Tibetans who attempted to return through Nepal were also prevented from re-entering. In April 2012, authorities in the TAR ordered residents to surrender their valid ordinary passports, officially describing the measure as part of a transition to new electronic passports. Authorities subsequently imposed stringent procedures for obtaining replacements. HRW found no evidence that the confiscated passports were returned or replaced on a meaningful scale, effectively curtailing ordinary international travel for large numbers of Tibetans in the region. The policy established a pattern that human rights groups have characterised as a highly restrictive system of cross-border mobility, in which passports, border crossings and even family reunification can become subject to political and security considerations. Against this backdrop, observers say, the September 15 regulations do not mark the beginning of restrictions on Tibetan mobility. Rather, they represent the latest legal development in a much longer trajectory of increasingly securitised passport, exit and border controls.

title: Over 60 TYC activists detained after protesting Xi’s visit near BRICS venue in New Delhi
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: NEW DELHI, Sept. 13:At least 64 activists of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), including Vice President Tashi Targyal and Information and International Secretary Tenzin Dehsal, were detained by Delhi Police after staging a protest near the venue of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi late Saturday night. The protest began at around 9:45 p.m. on September 12 along Mandapam Bhairon Marg, close to the summit venue at Bharat Mandapam, with participation from at least 15 regional chapters of the TYC. The protesters denounced Chinese President Xi Jinping’s participation in the two-day summit and his presence in New Delhi. Xi, visiting India for the first time in nearly seven years, also held bilateral talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the summit on September 12. Speaking toPhayul, TYC General Secretary Tenzin Lobsang said the detained activists were being held at several police stations across Delhi. According to him, 19 men and 10 women were being held at Mandawali Police Station, three men and two women atAshok Vihar, 10people at Gokulpuri, and 16 at Gazipur. He added that there were four additional TYC members who were detained in New Delhi before they could join the protest were also taken into custody, although their whereabouts remained unknown at the time of publication. Lobsang said the organisation is in communication with senior police officials and other authorities seeking the release of the detained activists, and expressed hope that they would be released by Sunday evening. The latest detentions came amid heightened security and surveillance around Tibetan areas in the capital in the days surrounding Xi’s visit. Sources toldPhayulthat two members of the TYC Centrex—Joint Secretary Tenzin Dekyong and Culture Secretary Thupten Tsering—were placed under house arrest by Delhi Police shortly after Saturday night’s protest. The move reportedly came as authorities intensified preventive measures against possible demonstrations linked to Xi’s presence in the capital. Sources further said that the vicinity surrounding the Tibetan Samyelling Settlement in Majnu Ka Tila, where the TYC protest movement had been organised and mobilised, remained under close surveillance by Delhi Police and the Intelligence Bureau. Members of the TYC Centrex were also reportedly subjected to continuous monitoring, with their mobile phones being tracked by authorities. The reported surveillance and preventive detentions come against the backdrop of heightened security measures in New Delhi during the BRICS Summit, as Tibetans sought to use Xi’s visit to draw international attention to Tibet and reiterate their opposition to Chinese colonial rule in occupied Tibet. Phayulis continuing to follow developments, including efforts to ascertain the whereabouts of the four detained activists, whose current location remains unknown. Further updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

title: Tibetans protest against Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi, activists detained near summit venue
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: NEW DELHI, Sept. 11:Hundreds of Tibetans took to the streets of New Delhi on Friday to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s scheduled participation in the 18th BRICS Summit, calling for greater international attention to Tibet ahead of his arrival in the Indian capital. The protest march, organised by the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), began from the Samyelling Tibetan Settlement in Majnu Ka Tila and brought together Tibetans from more than 20 settlements across India. A heavy deployment of Delhi Police accompanied the march as protesters denounced Chinese regressive policies in occupied Tibet and Xi’s participation in the summit, scheduled to be held in New Delhi on September 12–13. Prominent Tibetan political figures attended the demonstration, including former Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) minister Gyari Dolma, former Tibetan Parliamentarian Acharya Yeshi Phuntsok, and sitting Tibetan MPs Wangdue Dorjee, Gyaltsen Choekyi, and Kunchok Rinchen. In a statement, the TYC condemned Xi’s participation in the BRICS Summit, accusing his administration of presiding over what it described as an ongoing campaign of cultural repression and forced assimilation in Tibet. “Xi Jinping is the primary architect of the ongoing cultural genocide in Tibet,” the organisation said, further alleging that Chinese policies had contributed to the erosion of Tibetan culture, language, religion, and identity. The TYC also urged India and other BRICS member states to raise the issue of Tibet with Chinese leadership during the summit, arguing that international cooperation should not come at the expense of human rights and cultural preservation. The organisation pointed to China’s recently enacted “Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress,” which came into effect on July 1, saying it would further accelerate the assimilation of Tibetans and marginalisation of their distinct cultural identity. The TYC also referenced the self-immolation of late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen outside the United Nations headquarters on July 2, describing it as a stark reminder of what it called continued repression in occupied Tibet. The organisation said nearly 170 Tibetans have self-immolated since 2009 in protest against Chinese colonial rule. Students for a Free Tibet (SFT) staged a protest near Bharat Mandapam at Pragati Maidan, the venue of the BRICS Summit, at around 7:30 a.m. on Thursday. Three Tibetan youth activists, along with a Tibetan journalist and an Indian college student working as a photographer, were later detained by Delhi Police after the protesters unfurled banners critical of Xi Jinping and displayed the Tibetan national flags. Speaking toPhayul,SFT India National Director Tenzin Passang said the three Tibetan activists—two girls and one boy—were detained for displaying anti-Xi banners and Tibetan flags near the summit venue. According to Passang, the three activists were subsequently taken from Mandir Marg Police Station to Tihar Jail, where they are being held under preventive detention until September 14. The actions by TYC and SFT come as security has been tightened across the Indian capital ahead of Xi’s scheduled arrival for the summit. The protests have placed Tibet once again in the spotlight as India prepares to host the Chinese president for the high-profile multilateral gathering. Xi’s high-profile diplomatic trip marks his first visit to Indian soil in nearly seven years, with his last visit being the informal summit in Mamallapuram in October 2019. Reports say the highly anticipated visit comes against the backdrop of a gradual diplomatic thaw between Asia’s two largest nations following years of severe military confrontation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), and is being viewed as a significant milestone in efforts to stabilise bilateral ties.

title: New visuals show China pressing ahead with demolitions at Tibetan Buddhist institute of Larung Gar
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Recent photographic evidence and satellite imagery show Chinese authorities are continuing their latest round of demolitions of monastic residences at the Serthar Larung Five Sciences Buddhist Academy, popularly known as Larung Gar, in Serthar (Chinese: Seda), Kardze (Ganzi) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan province in eastern Tibet. The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT)first reportedthe new demolition drive launched by authorities on July 13 at Larung Gar, one of the world’s largest Tibetan Buddhist academies. Images and video taken on August 13 and satellite images — from July 27, obtained by ICT and from August 14, obtained by Radio Free Asia (RFA) — reveal the systematic destruction of monastic residences at Larung Gar. ICT Research found that the physical destruction of monastic residences at Larung Gar is occurring alongside a sustained ideological campaign to “Sinicize” Tibetan Buddhism and erode Tibetan religious and cultural identity, while imposing a state-mandated national identity centered on loyalty to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Combined with sustained political indoctrination, these demolitions disrupt collective study and practice at Larung Gar and undermine the academy’s capacity to operate as an autonomous center of Tibetan Buddhist learning. “The destruction at Larung Gar is not simply the demolition of buildings; it is part of a wider systematic campaign to bring Tibetan Buddhism under the control of the CCP,” said Tencho Gyatso, President, International Campaign for Tibet. “By demolishing the residences that sustain collective Buddhist study while subjecting monastics to relentless political indoctrination, the Chinese government is attacking both the physical foundations of religious life and the Tibetan beliefs, identity, and community they support.” “ICT calls on the international community to intervene urgently by pressing for an immediate halt to the demolitions, independent access to Larung Gar and protection for its monastics and residents. ICT also urges global leaders to raise Larung Gar directly with Chinese authorities and hold them accountable for violations of religious freedom and Tibetan cultural rights,” Gyatso added. The August 13 photographs show demolition crews targeting monastic residences, while high-resolution satellite imagery from July 27 shows that the demolitions were concentrated around the center of the academy. The August 14 imagery obtained by RFA shows a demolished area around the center, with the curved road leading to the central structures cleared — further evidence that the demolitions continued after July 27. Sources told ICT that the current phase of demolitions was scheduled to conclude by August 20. ICT is concerned that another phase may follow, as the authorities’ stated target was the demolition of at least 1,060 residences. Despite intensified surveillance and restrictions on communications and movements, ICT will continue to monitor developments at Larung Gar. The following photographs of Larung Gar emerged a month after the demolitions began. Collectively, these images provide visual confirmation of large-scale, mechanized demolition involving multiple excavators and work crews. They show that the demolitions took place during both daytime and nighttime and affected residential areas in the center of the academy. An August 13-dated photograph shows Chinese authorities continuing their latest round of demolitions at Larung Gar, a month after they began on July 13, 2026. (ICT sources) One daytime photograph shows the demolition activity amid densely packed red monastic residences that are characteristic of Larung Gar. Multiple excavators stand on a slope amid large piles of rubble and debris from destroyed buildings. Workers wearing red hard hats and high-visibility yellow vests can be seen standing along a yellow-railed pathway and among the ruins. Another August 13-dated photograph shows proximity of the latest round of demolition work being carried out at Larung Gar to the center of the Buddhist academy. (ICT sources) Another photograph taken at night shows a large SANY excavator operating under bright lights on a steep, rubble-strewn incline amid piles of broken concrete, bricks, and other debris. In the background, a large structure with illuminated golden roofs, most likely the main assembly hall at the center of the academy, remains standing, highlighting the proximity of the demolition work to the center of the complex. A photograph showing the latest round of demolition of monastic residences at Larung Gar. (ICT sources) Another photograph shows a Zoomlion excavator high on a hillside, dismantling structures or clearing debris. Green safety netting covers part of a nearby building. In the foreground, a bilingual banner in Chinese and Tibetan reads “Forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation”. The background reveals the extensive spread of Larung Gar’s red wooden huts across the valley and hillsides, underscoring that the demolitions are taking place within the heart of the monastic complex. High-resolution satellite imagery from July 27 obtained by ICT shows that the demolitions are concentrated around the center of Serthar Academy. When compared with freely available Google Earth imagery from August 10, 2019, significant changes are visible around the academy’s central area. Later imagery from August 14, obtained by Radio Free Asia (RFA), shows a cleared area around the center, with the curved road leading to the central structures cleared and dump trucks and excavators visible. Overall, the satellite imagery and the photographs together confirm that Chinese authorities are continuing this latest round of demolitions at Serthar Buddhist Academy, which ICT first reported on July 17. Planet Labs satellite imagery of Larung Gar on July 27, obtained by ICT. Planet Labs satellite imagery of Larung Gar on August 14, obtained by RFA. Google Earth imagery of Larung Gar on August 10, 2019. These demolitions are occurring against the backdrop of the Chinese government’s new so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which took effect on July 1, 2026, and longstanding policies emphasizing the “Sinicization” of Tibetan Buddhism and its subjugation under the leadership of the CCP. Earlier demolition campaigns in 2001 and 2016 similarly involved work teams accompanied by security personnel, homes marked for destruction, residents forced to sign documents agreeing not to return, and monastics bused away from the academy. The cumulative impact of these successive rounds of demolition campaigns has been a substantial reduction in the physical footprint and population of Serthar Academy, transforming parts of what was once a densely inhabited religious valley that accommodated around 40,000 practitioners at its height. The current demolitions at Serthar Larung Gar are not merely administrative or logistical measures; they are a physical expression of a repressive Chinese state policy aimed at forging “a sense of Chinese national community” and ensuring the “Sinicization of religion.” The visual evidence documents the ongoing physical destruction, but these changes are inextricably linked to a parallel ideological campaign designed to transform the academy from an autonomous center of Buddhist learning into a tightly managed institution aligned with CCP priorities. The Chinese state’s physical intervention is driven by mandates requiring monastics to prioritize political reliability over traditional Buddhist study. This is framed through the Chinese party-state’s concept of the “sense of community for the Chinese nation,” a directive explicitly delivered to senior religious leaders. During a January 2022“tea reception”for Tibetan New Year celebrations, religious leaders — including Khenpo Tsultrim Lodro, the academy’s executive vice dean and Khenpo Sodargye, executive deputy director of its management committee — were instructed by Party officials to deepen the “Sinicization of religion” and play an active role in safeguarding national unity. Such public rituals serve a specific purpose: to enlist prominent Tibetan Buddhist figures to legitimize state policies. By demanding pledges of loyalty and broadcasting their compliance on state television, the authorities aim to project an image of harmony while reinforcing a strict hierarchy of subordination. Serthar Larung Gar’s two Khenpos were required to attend the then-Kardze (Ganzi) prefecture party secretary Shen Yang’s New Year “tea reception” in 2022. (State media Kardze TV broadcast screenshot, Jan. 2022) The physical dismantling of Larung Gar has consistently been preceded by political indoctrination, often referred to by the Chinese state as “patriotic re-education.” These sessions are designed to instill absolute loyalty to the Chinese state and the CCP. A key component of this indoctrination is the affirmation of the “five identifications,” which require monks and nuns to identify with “the great motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the CCP and socialism with Chinese characteristics,” as represented in thisMay 2021 reporton activities in the academy. This ideological framework seeks to ensure that the monastic community functions as a subset of the broader Chinese national identity rather than as part of a distinct Tibetan cultural or religious entity. Political indoctrination session at Serthar Buddhist Academy where monastics were required to affirm the “five identifications”. (State media handout, May 2021) In January 2026, the state-controlled Serthar County Buddhist Association intensified this campaign by launching adrivefocused on the “Three Consciousnesses”; national consciousness, citizen consciousness, and rule-of-law consciousness. Its primary goal is to force monastics to internalize the principle that “national law is greater than religious rules.” By embedding this hierarchy into the daily life of the academy, the state aims to align the thoughts and actions of religious practitioners with the decisions of central and provincial Party committees. A political meeting convened by the state-controlled Serthar County Buddhist Association in session. (State media handout, January 2026) Chinese authorities’ push to forge a national community is also framed as central to national security. Inmid April 2026, the academy was subjected to a series of “National Security Education” activities, including mandatory flag-raising ceremonies and oath-taking events. These sessions are designed to cultivate a “collective sense of responsibility” among both monks and cadres to ensure the state’s security. This campaign has also reached deep into monastics’ private lives through “outreach activities” that bring legal and political propaganda directly into their living quarters. By distributing handbooks on national security and anti-espionage laws, the state attempts to cultivate support for its Chinese national security agenda and effectively turn the monastic community into a monitored and self-monitoring unit of the state. Officials speaking about national security to a group of Serthar monks on China’s National Security Education Day. The red banner in Chinese reads “Serthar Larung Gar Buddhist Academy’s National Security Day Publicity Meeting, April 15”. (State media handout, April 2026) The physical demolitions of monastic residences and the sustained ideological indoctrination sessions are taking place in parallel at Larung Gar. The destruction of residential housing systematically dismantles the physical infrastructure that sustained it as an autonomous religious center, dispersing its community, disrupting collective monastic life, and making it far more difficult for the academy to function as an independent hub of Buddhist learning and practice. At the same time, the indoctrination sessions work to replace traditional religious identity with a state-mandated national identity, requiring monastics and residents to internalize party ideology, loyalty to the Chinese state, and a redefined sense of belonging that prioritizes political allegiance over spiritual lineage and Tibetan cultural identity. By forcing Larung Gar to “adapt” to a socialist society, the Chinese government is not merely changing an institution but is systematically eroding its autonomy. Material destruction and ideological indoctrination work together to significantly restrict the academy’s ability to operate according to its own religious and communal traditions. Instead, it is being reshaped to serve the singular goal of a unified, “sinicized” national community in which independent centers of Tibetan Buddhist authority are subordinated to state and Chinese Communist Party control. title: Family, lawyers of imprisoned Tibetan businessman denied visits, as authorities censor renewed calls for justice online
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Despite guarantees under China’s Prisons Law, Chinese authorities have repeatedly denied requests by lawyers of imprisoned Tibetan businessman Dorjee Tashi (Duoji Zhaxi) to visit him, including requests made as recently as July-August, according to an August 12, 2026-dated post on Chinese social media describing lawyers’ failed attempts to arrange such visits. Authorities have also been censoring information about the denial of Tashi’s visitation rights and have sought to silence any advocacy online on his behalf. Once a successful businessman and philanthropist in Tibet, Dorjee was first arrested in 2008, amid the wide-scale protests in Tibet that year, for allegedly “funding activities that endanger national security.” He is currently serving a life sentence in Lhasa’s Drapchi Prison, formally known as the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) Prison number 1, on politically motivated charges of “loan fraud.” In August 2021, ICT published Dorjee’stestimonydetailing the torture he suffered during his pre-trial detention. Advocacy by Chinese rights advocates, legal observers, and family members on behalf of Tashi on Chinese social media continues to be censored by authorities, ICT found. Shortly after an August 1 post argued that Tashi’s life imprisonment constitutes a “profound miscarriage of justice,” Chinese censors removed the post. It was reposted on August 12, but authorities took it down again shortly afterwards. The latest suppression of online advocacy on behalf of Dorjee Tashi has left the family, lawyers, and supporters even more frustrated with the Chinese legal system, as it follows years of authorities thwarting his family’s activism through sit-ins and lawyers’ challenges to his wrongful imprisonment and efforts to secure a retrial. When the previously taken-down August 1 post was reposted on August 12 on Chinese social media platform WeChat, the International Campaign for Tibet archived the page. The original WeChat link now displays a message in Chinese stating: “This content cannot be viewed due to violations. Following related complaints, this content violates the ‘Cybersecurity Law of the People’s Republic of China’”. The post’s repeated removal highlights the authorities’ persistent efforts to silence online discussion of the case after dismissing years of grassroots advocacy that called for due process and a retrial. Dorjee Tashi before his imprisonment in 2008. Tashi’s supporters lamented in the August 12 social media post that authorities had refused to grant a retrial, despite repeated appeals by family members and lawyers over ten years. This, they add, reflects authorities’ politically motivated violation of the legitimate rights and interests of prisoners and their families, as provided under China’s Prisons Law, and is not a case of the defense lacking evidence for a retrial. Supporters argue that the “loan fraud” conviction that Tashi was charged with has no real basis. They note that Tashi’s company had put up assets worth about 16.09 million yuan as collateral for a 1.5-million-yuan bank loan and that the principal and interest were repaid in full by 2013. They argue it was a civil loan dispute, not criminal fraud, as there was no intent to cheat the bank and the collateral far exceeded the loan. In addition to the broader legal issues surrounding his case, Tashi’s family and lawyers face severe restrictions on prison visits. In the initial years after his sentence began, family visits were allowed, but prison authorities began to limit the visits starting in 2019, without citing any clear legal reason. Dorjee Tashi’s elder brother and eldest sister have not seen him since their last visit in 2019 and his second sister since 2021. His wife and children have been denied visits for about two years since 2024. Defense lawyers Liu Zheng and Wang Fei have repeatedly submitted formal requests to meet Tashi but have faced delays, refusals, additional conditions or “retaliatory law enforcement” for exercising their right to demand justice through online channels. According to a social media post citing the lawyers, prison authorities denied lawyer Wang Fei his request to visit Tashi because he had informed the family that Tashi reported being beaten in prison during their last meeting which took place inOctober 2025, as reported by ICT. Prison officials also reportedly demanded that the family delete online posts about the case and issue an apology before authorities would consider allowing any visits. Tashi’s supporters say this turns a legal right into a bargaining chip and punishes people for speaking out. They demand that the TAR prison immediately stop linking visitation rights to online speech and allow the family and lawyers to visit. The supporters also urged prison officials, prosecutors, and disciplinary bodies to investigate the repeated denial of visits over the years and hold accountable those responsible. With Tashi having spent about 18 years in prison under a life sentence on spurious and politically motivated charges, his supporters have made renewed calls for a full retrial and the return of basic visitation rights that Chinese authorities have denied him for far too long, in clear violation of China’s own laws. title: Ahead of crucial 21st Party Congress, China cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Seventh-generation leadership in Tibet will be shaped by two guiding principles that institutionalize centralized Party control and accelerate Beijing’s forced assimilation of Tibetans: the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law and Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building. The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) released its 2026 Tibet Leadership Report, an annual report on the status of governance of Tibet, in which it states that Beijing is cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet, ahead of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) pivotal 21st Party Congress in 2027. Through leadership appointments, new legislation, and Party directives, China is deepening political control over Tibet and accelerating its policies of forced assimilation of Tibetans, amid a continued lack of any meaningful Tibetan representation in senior leadership positions, ICT said. The report finds that the “Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” and “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building” together form the legal and ideological foundations of a new governance model that prioritizes political loyalty, centralized Party authority, national security, and implementation of assimilation policies over meaningful Tibetan representation. Rather than replacing existing policies, these developments institutionalize them, embedding assimilation into the governance of education, language, religion, culture, and ethnic affairs. The report argues that the Ethnic Unity Law is Beijing’s most significant legal codification of assimilation policies to date, expanding Party authority over education, language, religion and culture while accelerating the shift toward Mandarin-medium education and restricting space for Tibetan identity. While leadership changes are expected across China and Tibet in 2026–2027, the report concludes that these changes are more likely to reinforce than alter existing policy. Drawing on new leadership data, the report finds that Tibetans remain largely excluded from positions of real political authority, with meaningful decision-making continuing to rest overwhelmingly in the hands of non-Tibetan Party leaders. As of July 31, 2026, Tibetans hold only 62 of 240 (25.8%) senior leadership positions across provincial, prefectural, and county levels, while non-Tibetans occupy 178 (74.2%). The absence of Tibetans is most pronounced in the Party, security, military, and judicial institutions that exercise the greatest political authority. The CCP’s 21st Party Congress in 2027 is expected to be a defining political moment for Xi Jinping’s next phase of leadership. Whether Xi Jinping chooses to elevate a potential successor or further consolidate his personal authority, the Congress will shape China’s senior leadership and policy direction for the next five years. The report argues that the leadership transition surrounding the 21st Party Congress is not simply about personnel changes, but about institutionalizing a new model of governance in Tibet. As leadership, ideology, and law become increasingly intertwined, Tibet offers an early indication of Xi Jinping’s governing vision for the post-2027 era – one that will guide the anticipated new seventh generation leadership of Tibet and have implications for the rights, identity and future of the Tibetan people. title: ICT 2026 Tibet Leadership Report: Ahead of 21st Party Congress, China cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet to enforce assimilationist agenda
