title: Tibet-Nepal floods reaffirm urgency of Tibetan stewardship of the plateau
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic chain of glacier collapse and debris flowsroared downfrom the high Himalayas, unleashing a wall of rock, ice, mud, and water that devastated valleys, villages, and infrastructure across western Tibet and northern Nepal while simultaneously obliterating the Kyidong (སྐྱིད་གྲོང་།) Port at the international border between Nepal and Tibet. Thedisaster left hundreds dead or missingin Nepal and Tibet, and reduced China’s primary trading port to South Asia to ruins in minutes. For decades, the Chinese slogan rendingshengtian人定胜天 (“human determination can conquer nature”) had justified large-scale engineering and development projects in Tibet and China that sought to overcome difficult terrain and assert mastery over the environment. Yet, the recent flooding in Tibet and Nepal demonstrated the limits and at times catastrophic failures of this development model. While the world debates whether the causal factor was climate change or a geological event, this disaster has made clear that nature can challenge and upend even the most ambitious and well-resourced development drives. In contrast to Beijing’s model, Tibetan communities across the plateau for centuries have recognized the importance of environmental stewardship and cultivating a symbiotic relationship with Tibet’s geography and resources. That resilient and sustainable model was overturned with China’s occupation of Tibet. With the occupation came the imposition of Beijing’s ideology that humans can control nature, and what closely followed was a relentless infrastructure push across the Tibetan highlands which in many respects destabilized the Tibetan plateau’s sensitive ecosystem and raised the probability of more frequent and severe natural disasters. The Nepal-Tibet floods are a tragic reminder of the Himalaya’s immense power to release the elements of nature and the importance of harnessing and working with these elements in a way that advances environmental resilience and sustainability. In contrast to Beijing’s top-down approach, centuries of Tibetan stewardship at the grassroots level offer an alternative and affirmative model of environmental risk management that China must urgently heed. Rooted in the Maoist slogan “man must conquer nature” (人定胜天), this worldview treats the Tibetan Plateau not as a sensitive high-altitude ecosystem or sacred landscape, but as a frontier to be subdued, engineered, and integrated into the modern Chinese state. Since the 1950s, and accelerating dramatically after 2000, Beijing has poured resources into transformative infrastructure projects. The Golmud-Lhasa Railway, completed in 2006 and later extended to Shigatse, pierced the plateau’s permafrost and high passes through 36 tunnels (7 between Golmud-Lhasa and 29 on the Lhasa-Shigatse stretch). Highways now crisscross the region, whilehundreds of hydropower damsharness the headwaters of Asia’s major rivers. Airports, high-voltage power lines, mining facilities, and urban sprawl have proliferated. These projects are framed officially as poverty alleviation, modernization, national security and ecology protection, yet in reality they serve to tighten political control, facilitate resource extraction, and alter traditional Tibetan ways of life. Additionally, they create significant environmental risks for downstream countries. Chinese state media propaganda handout featuring the CCP flag as the focal point of post-disaster road recovery efforts. The environmental costs of Beijing’s infrastructure building are significant. Construction disrupts sensitive alpine ecosystems, accelerates permafrost thaw, and increases the risk of landslides, glacier collapse and glacial lake outburst floods. Culturally, the scale of change has marginalized Tibetan wisdom that long emphasized harmony with nature. Unlike the traditional Tibetan knowledge systems, the Chinese party-state operates on the deep conviction that technology and state power can and should dominate nature. In Tibet, this ideology continues to shape one of the most intensive infrastructure campaigns on earth, leaving lasting marks on both the landscape and the Tibetans who inhabit it. The reach of China’s 人定胜天 ethos extends beyond its borders and exacerbates risks to the larger Himalayan ecosystem. The immediate vicinity of Langtang Lirung in Nepal is a prime example, having become an active hydropower development zone that contracts Chinese companies for their technical expertise. This area features multiple hydropower projects and extensive tunneling throughout the Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridor. The multi-billion-dollarChina–Nepal Railway(or Kyidong–Kathmandu Railway), proposed under China’s Belt and Road Initiative, is designed to slice through the Himalayan mountain ranges. According to the Nepali Times, citing a Chinese prefeasibility study, the route will run beneath Nepal’s Langtang National Park through a vast system of tunnels to connect Kyidong and Kathmandu. In the wake of the Nepal-Tibet flood, experts should raise questions as to the risks presented by such an ambitious and environmentally intrusive project, yet the dictates of Beijing’s development model may unfortunately override any concerns. While the world is still processing the shock of the recent Nepal-Tibet flood, Chinaannouncedon August 31 that it has officially commenced operations at the Shuangjiangkou Hydropower Station. Touted as the world’s tallest dam, the megaproject is built on the Gyalmo Ngulchu (Dadu) River in Barkham, Sichuan. The systemic risks of this infrastructure chain were dramatically highlighted on November 11, 2025, when the collapse of the 758-meter cantileverRed Flag (Hongqi) Bridgemade headlines worldwide. The collapse was caused by landslides triggered by water impoundment at the Shuangjiangkou reservoir—the fifth in a massive cascade of28 damsplanned along the Gyalmo Ngulchu. Traditionally, Tibetan stewardship of the plateau operated as a form of “living infrastructure”, a highly sophisticated, decentralized system of resource governance that managed the landscape without the need for disruptive physical barriers. For millennia, pastoral nomads and monastic communities maintained the delicate ecological balance of the plateau through fluid, mobile systems of rotational grazing rather than permanent divisions. By moving herds of yaks and sheep seasonally, they prevented soil compaction, aerated the earth, and allowed grasslands to naturally regenerate. Water sources and forests were protected through sacred designations asneri(sacred mountain), which functioned as culturally enforced conservation zones. This harmonious approach protected the headwaters of Asia’s major rivers and sustained the rangelands without the deployment of invasive concrete engineering, proving that ecological stability relies on working with natural geography rather than attempting to cage it. In stark contrast, the Chinese state-led approach treats the plateau as a canvas for rapid infrastructure projects that physically fracture this delicate ecosystem. Under the guise of modernization and “ecological migration,” Beijing has sought to conquer the landscape through mega-dams, extensive grid fencing, tunneling through mountains for roads and railways, and building static concrete border defense settlements dubbed as “Xiaokang villages”. By forcing nomadic herders off their traditional pasturelands and confining them to fixed housing colonies, the state has replaced a highly successful system of mobile land management with rigid physical and economic boundaries. The results have been ecologically disastrous:relocationof hundreds of thousands of pastoralists and restricting livestock movement with wire fencing has caused localized soil erosion and desertification, while massive engineering projects like the Shuangjiangkou Hydropower Station and the extensive tunneling for Himalayan railways disrupt hydrological flows and trigger devastating landslides, as exemplified by the dramatic collapse of the Red Flag Bridge. This heavy-handed reliance on construction over ecological wisdom demonstrates how top-down infrastructure projects can quickly destabilize a globally crucial environment. Amid global debate over the causality of the flood, China’sdeclarationthat the disaster was induced by global warming along with its commitment to “working with Nepal and the rest of the international community to strengthen cooperation and prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change” may have come as a surprise to many. However, this does not imply Beijing will halt the construction of dams and infrastructure on the Tibetan Plateau. Instead, it likely signals a shift toward framing these projects as necessary measures to combat climate change. Indeed, this climate-mitigation narrative serves as the raison d’être for building cascading dams on the eastern edge of the Tibetan plateau, ostensibly to protect mainland Chinese citizens living downstream, even while placing Tibetan communities on higher ground at risk. Looking ahead, even the proposed Medog Dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) River, which is slated to be the world’s largest, may be framed as a climate-resilience project under Beijing’s “community with a shared future for mankind” vision, supposedly designed to protect downstream countries. The alternative to China’s heavy-handed 人定胜天 model – Tibetan stewardship of the land at the grassroots level – has demonstrated success over centuries in increasing sustainability and environmental resilience, while still being able to harness the benefits of Tibet’s ecosystem and resources. The devastating flooding that occurred last week is a tragic reminder that the environmental risks are only growing in the Himalayan region. It also demonstrates the importance of China recalibrating its development approach across the plateau and throughout the region. Beijing only needs to look to the proven Tibetan model to reduce environmental risks and ensure the sustainable use of Tibet’s resources. The international community, and particularly countries in the region, must call on China to change their approach, increase transparency, and have the humility to engage with Tibetan communities and communities across the Himalayas who have the know-how to manage the incredible power of the Himalayan terrain. As the August 26 event demonstrate, this call has never been more urgent. title: ICT calls for timely, independent information and access to Tibet on humanitarian grounds after Nepal-Tibet disaster
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Families of the missing remain without answers as China restricts access, punishes at least 19 people for flood posts challenging official casualty figures and amplifies the state’s account of relief efforts. In the wake of the catastrophic floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, the International Campaign for Tibet has called for the immediate release of complete, timely and independently verifiable information on casualties, missing people and conditions in Kyirong (Chinese: Jilong; also referred to as Gyirong) County in Shigatse, Tibet, together with meaningful access for independent journalists and observers. These measures are urgently required on humanitarian grounds: to help families determine the fate and whereabouts of missing relatives, identify affected communities and unmet needs, and support an effective rescue and relief operation.ICT is also calling for unhindered accessfor international humanitarian organizations and for governments worldwide to press Beijing to provide information and access commensurate with the scale of the disaster. Those demands have become more urgent asChinese authorities impose severe information controls and punish people for online poststhat authorities characterize as “rumors,” including claims that the death toll in Tibet is considerably higher than official figures indicate. Official Chinese media reported on September 3 that seven additional people had been summoned, penalized or reprimanded for posting flood-related information. An August 31 statement by the Ministry of Public Security’s cybersecurity department said authorities had imposed “administrative penalties” on 10 people, which included seven who were punished for stating that the actual death toll was more than 1,000. ICT’s latest accounting indicates that at least 19 people have now been targeted or punished in connection with disaster-related posts. Chinese authorities reported 21 people dead and 541 missing in Tibet as of midday September 2 and had announced no further change in the toll by September 3. Their August 30 update said that 261 of those missing were foreign nationals from 23 countries, including 104 people from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the United States and 15 from the United Kingdom. None of these official figures can be independently verified while journalists, international humanitarian organizations and other independent observers remain barred from the affected area. For families of the missing, the resulting information vacuum has prolonged days of uncertainty and denied them credible, timely answers about the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones. Chinese officials said that, by noon on September 2, authorities had received 876 calls concerning people reported dead or missing — 448 domestic calls and 428 international calls — underscoring the scale of the demand for authoritative information. “ICT’s call for greater transparency and access to information arises first and foremost from humanitarian considerations,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “In a disaster of this scale, timely and reliable information can help save lives.” Sources told ICT that survivors and displaced residents have been evacuated to Kyirong town and are being kept under centralized supervision, with communications and visitors restricted. ICT sources on August 30 reported mandatory government-organized propaganda and “psychological counseling” sessions at these venues. According toChinese state media on September 3, authorities said a team of 70 professionals had been assigned to provide psychological counseling to families of people reported dead or missing and had delivered care 1,107 times. They added that 1,220 personnel had been organized to support these services. Sources told ICT that four villages, including Rizi, Sale, Serchung and Labi, were among the hardest-hit in Kyirong County, and reported that many remain unaccounted for. ICT also received reports that rescue workers did not reach some communities until roughly 50 hours after the flooding. Sources said around 140 survivors from Sale, including children from a local boarding school, were evacuated on the third day. Tibetans from other areas who sought to deliver relief directly were reportedly required to transfer funds and supplies to government authorities and barred from providing direct assistance, sources said. Chinese authorities have publicized the state’s response and rescue efforts via official state media. Officials said the regional government activated its highest natural-disaster emergency level; the central government allocated 220 million yuan for relief and emergency recovery; and 2,141 personnel, 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 pieces or sets of rescue equipment were mobilized. They also reported that 499 people from five high-risk villages were evacuated to five resettlement sites, 555 domestic tourists were transferred, and more than 57,000 relief items were distributed. The scale of the announced response underscores the gravity of the disaster, but official reporting cannot substitute for independent scrutiny of whether assistance has reached every affected community, whether the official casualty figures are complete or whether survivors can communicate their experiences and needs without restriction. Severe restrictions on speech and access have made ground-level information from Tibet exceptionally difficult to obtain. Local residents are afraid to share details even when contact can be established, with one source telling ICT that it was “extremely unsafe” to speak and another urging ICT not to make further contact because of the critical situation. These warnings illustrate how the crackdown is obstructing not only public reporting but also basic efforts to determine the condition of affected communities. Sources told ICT that WeChat groups and comment sections are closely moderated to amplify praise for the government response and remove criticism. State media have concentrated on leadership directives, road repairs, deployment figures and officially organized relief, while providing limited community-level information about casualties, missing people and survivors’ experiences. Foreign correspondents or independent media have not been permitted independent access to Tibet, while videos and other firsthand documentation posted to Chinese social-media platforms have disappeared. Under the ongoing “Clear and Bright: Cyberspace Cleanup” campaign, Chinese authorities have also penalized, summoned or reprimanded people who shared information about the Kyirong floods or questioned official statistics. An August 30 government notice disclosed administrative penalties were imposed on at least 10 individuals for spreading disaster “rumors” online; of these, seven posts claimed that more than 1,000 people had died. ICT also learned of separate case where two people in Lhokha were questioned, subjected to “criticism and education” and required to delete posts authorities described as false or exaggerated. On September 3, a local report said seven more people had been summoned, penalized or reprimanded for flood-related posts. ICT’s latest accounting indicates that at least 19 people have now faced some form of police or administrative action for allegedly spreading “rumors” about the disaster. The restrictions appear integral to the official disaster response. At a September 1 emergency-relief meeting, Wang Junzheng, Communist Party Secretary of the Tibet Autonomous Region, emphasized adherence to Xi Jinping’s directives and political thought. According to the official account of the meeting, Wang also prioritized control of online public opinion, “stability maintenance” and the safeguarding of long-term political stability. Penalizing the circulation of disaster information entrenches fear and self-censorship at the moment when accurate reporting is most consequential. Official images of rescue operations, however valuable, are no substitute for independent journalists interviewing survivors, unhindered humanitarian access, systematic updates to affected families and a credible village-by-village accounting of the dead and missing. Since the onset of the disaster, ICT along with other Tibetan and international Tibet-support groups, human rights organizations, advocacy networks, and activists have mobilized international media attention to ensure that conditions inside Tibet — and the consequences of Beijing’s restrictions — remain part of the global response. ICT President Tencho Gyatso highlighted the disparity between open reporting from Nepal and the controlled information environment in Tibet. “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet,” Gyatso toldThe Guardian. In television interviews withCNBC-TV18andSky News, and in separate interactions withLa Croix, AFP,Le Monde, and others, Gyatso emphasized that the outside world was being shown the Chinese Communist Party’s account of the response rather than a comprehensive picture of the disaster’s impact on Tibetan communities. ICT Executive Director Ryan Fioresi’s comments toThe New York Times,CNNandBBC Newshourfocused on the scarcity of verifiable information from Tibet, the exclusion of independent journalists and observers, and the international community’s dependence on Chinese state media. He stressed, in interviews with NPR,Radio Free Asia,ABC News Australiaand other outlets, that official coverage prioritized Xi Jinping’s directives and descriptions of state relief efforts over survivors’ experiences and the full extent of the casualties and destruction. In an Op-ed inThe Diplomat, Fioresi also argued that the disaster exposed a broader, CCP-imposed information vacuum in Tibet and called for open access, stronger regional sharing of disaster-risk information and an adequate response for missing foreign nationals. ICT EU Policy Director Vincent Matten’s op-ed in theLa Libre Belgiqueextended ICT’s public advocacy on the Nepal-Tibet disaster to Belgian and European audiences. ICT representatives also engagedDeutsche Welle,The Telegraph,ZDF Heute,Tagesschau,El País, NPR, theFrankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Süddeutsche Zeitung, Tagesspiegeland other media. ICT Germany Executive Director Kai Müller emphasized that information control prevents an independent assessment of both the death toll and whether relief is reaching Tibetan communities. “The people affected by this catastrophe deserve the fullest possible rescue and humanitarian response,” Gyatso said. “They also deserve the freedom to communicate what has happened to them. Transparency and independent access should strengthen the rescue effort, not threaten it.” ICT’s advocacy is directed both at Chinese authorities and at governments with the diplomatic leverage and responsibility to press Beijing for greater transparency. In its letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, ICT urged the State Department to publicly express condolences for those affected in Tibet, seek greater transparency regarding casualties and missing persons, and encourage access to affected areas for humanitarian assistance and independent reporting. The international dimensions of the disaster are already driving government engagement. The U.S. State Department hasissued information for U.S. citizensand reported Americans unaccounted for in China and Nepal.British authorities have coordinated with local authoritiesregarding missing UK nationals, whileLatvian and Canadian diplomatic missions have sought updates from Chinese authoritiesregarding their citizens. These consular efforts underscore the direct interest governments have in reliable information from Tibet. Publicly documented governmental demands for independent access and comprehensive disclosure, however, remain limited — reinforcing ICT’s call for governments to move beyond case-by-case consular coordination and press China collectively for transparency. ICT is calling on the international community, the United States, the European Union and other governments and institutions to: The Central Tibetan Administration has launched emergency relief efforts for Tibetan communities in Nepal andappealed to Tibetans in exile to contribute voluntarilythrough Offices of Tibet and Tibetan settlement offices. The CTA identified Shabru settlement and Timure, near the Kyirong border, as among the hardest-hit Tibetan communities on the Nepal side. Five Tibetan families in Timure were reported to have been swept away by the deluge. In the Rasuwa Geygheling Tibetan settlement, all 11 homes were swept away by the floods, CTA said. His Holiness the Dalai Lama expressed condolencesand called attention to the need to understand the disaster’s underlying causes. “Since this region has seen calamities in the past as well, these are certainly symptoms of a deeper underlying cause—whether climate change or other factors,” he said. “I hope that appropriate follow-up measures will be taken, wherever possible, to help ensure that such disasters do not recur.” The immediate priority is rescue and humanitarian support, but the disaster is also a warning for the wider Himalayan region. Kyirong has experienced repeated flood and disaster disruption in recent years. Extreme rainfall, rising temperatures, glacial and permafrost melt, earthquakes and unstable slopes create compound risks across a region where hazards do not stop at political borders. ICT urges Beijing to support a joint scientific investigation, with regional and international participation, into the causes of the August 26 event and the increasing frequency of destructive floods. The findings should be published openly, and glacial-lake risk assessments for Tibet should be made public. No dam or infrastructure project should be blamed for this event without evidence. ICT also calls for a permanent disaster-data-sharing arrangement between China and downstream Himalayan states; stronger high-altitude monitoring and early-warning systems; and meaningful participation by Tibetan communities in decisions affecting their land and safety. The postICT calls for timely, independent information and access to Tibet on humanitarian grounds after Nepal-Tibet disasterappeared first onInternational Campaign for Tibet.

title: ICT expresses solidarity with communities affected by Nepal-Tibet disaster; calls on authorities in Tibet to ensure transparency and unhindered humanitarian access
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) has been closely monitoring the humanitarian disaster following the devastating mudslides and flooding on Aug. 26, 2026 in Kyirong (Chinese: Jilong or Gyirong) County in Shigatse Prefecture, Tibet, and in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa and Nuwakot. ICT mourns the loss of life among local communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border, and we are deeply concerned about the fate of the many international tourists and pilgrims who remain missing. We hope for the swift and safe rescue of all those still trapped or unaccounted for, and we commend the brave first responders and local communities undertaking search and rescue efforts under extremely difficult circumstances. Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border — families who have lost loved ones, the many who remain injured or missing, and the communities confronting this unfolding disaster. On Thursday, His Holiness the Dalai Lama expressed his sadness over the loss of life and extensive structural damage caused by the floods in Nepal and Tibet. He offered prayers for those who have lost their lives and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and everyone affected by this tragedy. “Since this region has seen calamities in the past as well, these are certainly symptoms of a deeper underlying cause — whether climate change or other factors. I hope that appropriate follow-up measures will be taken, wherever possible, to help ensure that such disasters do not recur,”His Holiness said in a statement. Sikyong Penpa Tsering, the democratically elected head of the Central Tibetan Administration, also expressed his condolences and solidarity with all those affected. The CTA,said in a statement on Thursday, that it directed relevant officials and offices to begin emergency relief work without delay to help those affected in the five Tibetan settlements or communities within the jurisdiction of the Nepal-based Sha-Wa-Ra Sum Tibetan Settlement Office, of which Shabru settlement and Timure on the Kyirong border were the hardest hit. CTA appealed to Tibetans in exile to contribute voluntarily through their respective Offices of Tibet and Tibetan settlement offices to support relief efforts for Tibetan communities affected on the Nepal side. While Nepal is providing timely information and avenues for international humanitarian assistance, disaster relief efforts in Tibet must also be accompanied by timely and transparent information sharing and unhindered access for humanitarian support. Without independent access to the Tibetan side of the Nepal-Tibet border, it is impossible to determine the full scale of the losses or obtain a complete picture of the situation in Kyirong County. The international community, therefore, remains largely dependent on Chinese state media, whose coverage so far has focused primarily on Xi Jinping’s directives and official accounts of rescue and relief efforts, rather than on firsthand accounts of actual conditions on the ground, survivors’ experiences, or the full extent of the casualties and destruction. “ICT calls on the Chinese government to disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties, permit independent reporting, and allow unhindered access for humanitarian assistance,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “Authorities in Tibet must permit the free flow of information, unhindered humanitarian access, and the meaningful involvement of local communities in disaster relief efforts to help save lives and ensure that assistance reaches everyone in need,” she added. According to ICT sources on the ground, the Chinese government is already severely restricting detailed information about the situation inside Tibet. ICT sources inside Tibet have confirmed that videos and other firsthand documentation uploaded to Chinese social media platforms are being removed, raising serious concerns about deliberate information control. Another source from Kyirong told ICT that major flooding in the Kyirong border region completely destroyed Tibetan-owned shops, restaurants, and teahouses near the border crossing and reportedly caused numerous casualties on the Tibetan side of the border. During past disasters, including asrecently as the 2025 Dingri earthquake, restrictions on access and information have raised serious concerns about transparency, the accuracy of official reporting, and whether the needs and voices of affected Tibetan communities were being fully addressed. ICT calls on Chinese authorities to urgently implement an effective emergency response that includes timely and transparent information, independent scrutiny, unrestricted access for humanitarian aid, and the free flow of information from all affected areas. title: New European Parliament report calls for stronger EU action on human rights in China, reiterates concerns over forced assimilation in Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The European Parliament adopted a new report on EU-China political relations this week calling for a more coordinated and human rights-centered European policy towards China and reiterating concern over China’s assimilation policies in Tibet. While the report contains many welcome statements on Tibet, including a call on China not to interfere in the selection of the next Dalai Lama, ICT hopes to see these commitments translated into practical EU policy measures that make a meaningful difference to the Tibetan people. The report adopted at the European Parliament plenary session in Strasbourg on October 7, addresses a wide range of challenges in EU-China relations, from economic and security concerns to China’s support for Russia’s war against Ukraine and tensions in the Taiwan Strait. While stressing the importance of continued dialogue with Beijing, it reaffirms that the EU is required to pursue a “principled, coherent, and human rights-centered China policy” and urges the EU to “keep the pressure firmly on China with regard to the defense of human rights and to not ignore human rights in EU-China relations.” Screenshot from the European Parliament’s Plenary recording showing the result of the vote on the report on EU-China political relations on October 7, 2026. (Source: European Parliament webcast) Regarding Tibet specifically, the report expresses “deep concern” over China’s systemic repression and forced assimilation policies in Tibet,” including “attempts at forced Sinicization and destruction of cultural heritage.” It reiterates the Parliament’s previous calls for the abolition of the boarding-school system for Tibetan children and for China to refrain from interfering in the selection of Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leaders – describing such interference as a “politically calculated move” to undermine Tibetan spiritual authority, culture and identity. It also calls for information on the whereabouts of the Panchen Lama and demands the unconditional release of political prisoners, while urging that these concerns be raised during diplomatic meetings with Chinese counterparts. On the new Chinese “ethnic unity” law, the report raises concerns about its potential to further “undermine the linguistic, cultural and religious rights of ethnic minorities,” and calls for the repeal of Article 63, which allows China to exercise jurisdiction over individuals residing in third countries. The report also addresses the August floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, calling on Chinese authorities to provide full and verifiable casualty data and to allow independent observers, journalists and humanitarian organizations access to the affected Tibetan areas. ICT had previouslyreportedon the lack of independent access, restrictions on information and the need for greater transparency and accountability following the disaster. “With this report, the European Parliament has sent a clear message that China’s human rights violations in Tibet and elsewhere cannot be treated as a peripheral issue in EU-China relations,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “This clear stand against China’s assimilation policies in Tibet is particularly timely as the new Chinese law on “ethnic unity,” which entered into force on July 1, 2026, institutionalizes these policies and further undermines Tibetans’ human rights, language, culture, and identity.” During thedebate ahead of the vote on the report, several MEPs stressed that closer engagement with China cannot come at the expense of human rights. “Partnership cannot mean silence. Not on the Uyghurs, not on Tibet, not on Hong Kong,” said the Rapporteur for the report, Parliamentarian Hilde Vautmans. The European Commission, represented by EU Commissioner for Democracy, Justice, the Rule of Law and Consumer Protection Michael McGrath, similarly stressed the need to raise concerns over “systemic human rights violations in Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong” in the EU’s engagement with Beijing. Member of the European Parliament Hilde Vautmans, Rapporteur for the report on EU-China political relations, presents her report during the parliamentary debate on 6 October 2026. (Source: European Parliament webcast) The European Parliament’s position on Tibet has been consistent in recent years, with repeated calls for an end to policies that undermine Tibetan cultural and religious identity. In December 2023, Parliament notablycalledfor the immediate abolition of China’s state-run residential boarding-school system for Tibetan children. In May 2025, itopposedChinese government interference in the selection of Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leaders, including the Dalai Lama. In April 2026, the European Parliament also adopted aresolutionraising concerns about the ramifications of China’s new “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” for the languages, cultures and religious practices of Tibetans and other non-Chinese people, as well as its potential reach beyond China – concerns that were also set out in anICT analysis of the lawshared with Members of the European Parliament ahead of the resolution’s adoption. The new EU-China report now places these concerns within the broader framework of the EU’s relations with Beijing, signaling that human rights concerns over Tibet should remain central to the EU’s wider political engagement with China, rather than being addressed only in discussions specifically focused on human rights. In this context, the EU should also consider appointing an EU Special Coordinator for Tibet to improve coordination and coherence in EU policy on Tibet and ensure that Tibet remains effectively addressed across the EU’s engagement with China. The report also calls on the EU “to engage with China to reinforce and make more effective the EU-China Human Rights Dialogue in order to keep the pressure firmly on China” and stresses that human rights concerns should be raised “at every political meeting with Chinese counterparts.” This reflects longstanding concerns among civil society organizations, including the International Campaign for Tibet, about the limited impact of the Dialogue in addressing China’s deteriorating human rights record. In recent years, NGOs have called for the Dialogue to be substantially reformed, arguing that human rights should not be confined to a dedicated dialogue that has not delivered any concrete results, but should be systematically raised across the full range of EU-China political engagement. At this stage, no date has been confirmed for the next EU-China Human Rights Dialogue or for the next EU-China Summit.

title: ICT launches Tibet Journalism Lab to support independent reporting on Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet is pleased to announce the launch of the Tibet Journalism Lab, a new grant initiative supporting independent journalists and media organizations producing in-depth reporting on Tibet. A total of $24,000 will be awarded across approximately six projects that deepen public understanding of Tibet through original reporting, research and documentation. “For decades, a central part of ICT’s work has been to help close the information gap on Tibet by documenting developments on the ground, bringing credible information to the international community, and challenging misinformation about Tibet and the Tibetan people. The Tibet Journalism Lab builds on that commitment by investing directly in independent journalism on Tibet,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “We hope this initiative will enable important reporting that might otherwise go unfunded and underscore the urgent need for greater and sustained support for Tibetan journalists and media organizations,” she added. Projects supported by Tibet Journalism Lab will include investigative and in-depth articles, multimedia reporting, audio and visual journalism, and other reporting formats intended for publication or distribution in Tibetan or any other language, along with an English version. Selected journalists will also have access to a panel of mentors for editorial guidance and support, while preserving their editorial independence. This support will focus on reporting practices, editorial standards, digital security, news verification, source protection, and sensitive Tibet reporting practices, among others. “Access to reliable information from inside Tibet remains severely restricted. Journalists face extraordinary challenges in gathering and verifying information, while Tibetans who communicate with the outside world face significant risks. This makes independent, secure and credible reporting essential to ensuring that developments inside Tibet continue to reach global audiences. ICT’s Tibet Journalism Lab seeks to strengthen that vital work,” said Ryan Fioresi, Executive Director, International Campaign for Tibet. Tibetan journalists from any part of the world are eligible to apply for grants up to $5,000 for their proposed project. In the case of collaborative journalism projects, the primary applicant must be Tibetan. Projects will be selected based on the strength and relevance of their pitch, feasibility, journalistic rigor, potential impact and plans for publication or distribution. Applications for the inaugural grant cycle will be accepted from October 7 through November 15, 2026 and applicants will be notified of their selection by late December 2026. The Tibet Journalism Lab is part of ICT’sTibetan Empowerment Programs, which include theTibetan Youth Leadership Program, theWashington Internship Program for Tibetan Americans, theRowell Fund for Tibetand theSchrucker Fellowship for the Arts. You can read more about theprogram guidelines and access the online application form here.

title: ICT brings Tibetan children’s rights, enforced disappearances and political prisoners into focus at UN Human Rights Council
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet, in partnership with the Central Tibetan Administration, Tibet Action Institute, and other Tibetan and rights groups, raised the rights of Tibetan children, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention and the implications of China’s new “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” among other human rights concerns, during the ongoing 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva this month. The panel of the side event on children’s rights in Tibet, organized by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights on Sep. 24, 2026. (Source: FIDH) Opening the session with hisoral update to the Council, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk renewed his criticism of Beijing’s policies in Tibet. “In China, tightening restrictions on the rights of the Tibetan people, including their freedom of religion, are deeply troubling,” he said, while calling for an “urgent U-turn” on these policies. During the session, a number of states and theEuropean Unionechoed concerns about the human rights situation in Tibet, with several also raising the potential impact of China’s repressive new so-called “ethnic unity law.” States that specifically addressed Tibet included Australia, Denmark,Finland, Germany, Ireland,Japan, Sweden, Switzerland and theUnited Kingdom(see below for more details). Ahead of the upcoming review of China by the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, scheduled for 2027, ICT participated in a side event focused on the worsening human rights situation faced by Tibetan children and organized by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFHR) on Sept. 24. Speakers at the side event included Thinlay Chukki, Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in Geneva; Lhadon Tethong and Dr. Gyal Lo of the Tibet Action Institute (TAI); and Kai Müller of ICT. ICT’s Vincent Metten moderated the discussion on behalf of the HFHR. In his presentation, Müller, who serves as Executive Director of ICT Germany, highlighted how China’s recently adopted “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” further entrenches policies and practices that violate the rights of Tibetan children by Chinese authorities in Tibet,as documented by ICT. Müller also pointed to the increasingindoctrination and militarisationof Tibetan children, alongside systematic restrictions on their freedom to practice their religion. The side event was attended by representatives of states, observer delegations, and a number of civil society groups. ICT representatives also delivered three oral statements by video on behalf of the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights during the Council session, drawing attention to enforced disappearances, arbitrary detentions and the serious implications of China’s repressive new “ethnic unity law. A post shared by International Campaign for Tibet (@savetibetorg) “When Tibetans disappear into custody, many do not come back alive,” Kai Müller warned in hisstatementon Sep. 15 during the Interactive Dialogue with the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances. Müller highlighted the case of Tibetan Buddhist teacherChoktrul Dorje Ten Rinpoche, who was detained by Chinese authorities on Dec. 4, 2025 and whose whereabouts remain unknown. He also cited anICT reportdocumenting the cases of 16 Tibetans who died in custody or shortly after their release between 2014 and 2026. The following day, Vincent Metten highlighted the “systematic use of arbitrary and incommunicado detention in Tibet” in hisstatementduring the Interactive Dialogue with the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention. He drew attention to the arbitrary detentions of Tibetans for peacefully defending their language, culture, religion and environment. Metten called on China to release all those arbitrarily detained, disclose the fate and whereabouts of disappeared Tibetans, guarantee detainees access to lawyers and their families, and investigate allegations of torture and ill-treatment. On Sep. 22, during the General Debate under Item 4 — Human rights situations that require the Council’s attention — ICT President Tencho Gyatso delivered avideo statementin which she highlighted concerns over China’s new “Ethnic Unity Law,” which entered into force on July 1, 2026 and codifies China’s forced assimilation and Sinicization of Tibetans and other non-Chinese people. Gyatso welcomed Türk’s call for the law to be abolished, saying that his appeal reflected the absence of fundamental rights to which the Tibetan people are entitled. In another oralstatement, Phuntsok Topgyal of the Tibet Bureau in Geneva, speaking on behalf of the Society for Threatened Peoples, raised the case ofLobga Rangzen, who died on July 2, 2026 after self-immolating outside the UN Headquarters in New York, one day after China’s new ethnic unity law entered into force. The following states and observers specifically mentioned Tibet in their statements during the Sep. 22 General Debate on human rights situations requiring the Council’s attention: Australia:“We remain gravely concerned by ongoing human rights violations against Uyghurs and Tibetans. Consistent with international law and norms, governments should not interfere in the selection of religious leaders including the Dalai Lama.” Denmark:“We reiterate our serious concerns over the human rights situation in China, in particular in Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong” Finland:“Finland remains concerned about the erosion of civil and political rights in Xinjiang and Tibet as well as restrictions in Hong Kong.” Germany:“In China the space for freedom of speech and peaceful assembly is as restricted as ever. With great concern we note that the law on promoting ethnic unity and progress further reinforces existing restrictions on cultural and religious freedoms, particularly in the Tibet Autonomous Region and the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous region.” Ireland:“On China we remain concerned over restrictions on civic spaces in Hong Kong, the treatment of Tibetans, repression of Uyghur people in Xinjiang, and the potential impact of the new law on promoting ethnic unity and progress.” Japan:“On China, Japan is concerned about the recent trend of tightening restrictions on human rights defenders, intellectuals and other individuals. Freedom, respect for fundamental human rights and the rule of law must be ensured in China, including Hong Kong, Xinjiang and Tibet. We strongly urge China to take further constructive and concrete action including enhancing transparency.” Sweden:“We also remain seriously concerned about the situation in China, not least in Hong Kong, Tibet and Xinjiang. We urge China to implement the recommendations from the UPR, the OHCHR report on Xinjiang and Special Procedures.” Switzerland:“Switzerland expresses its concerns about the consequences of the new law on ethnic and progress in China. Implemented in its current form, it will seriously undermine linguistic, cultural and religious autonomy of ethnic minorities especially Tibetans Uyghurs and Mongols.” European Union (with Albania, Montenegro and Liechtenstein aligning):“We reiterate concerns about the situation in China including in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia and about the ethnic unity law.” In addition, the UK delivered the following statement during the Item 2 General debate on the oral update of the High Commissioner on Sept. 8: United Kingdom:“Evidence of violations in Xinjiang and Tibet persists, freedom of religion or belief is being further restricted, and the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress risks undermining the rights of individuals belonging to minorities. We welcome the High Commissioner’s continued engagement on these issues.”

title: Central Tibetan Administration and International Campaign for Tibet representatives visit Panama to educate public on Chinese Communist Party repression of Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Venerable Thubten Wangchen, Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama and the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) for Latin America, and Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. Panama City– Venerable Thubten Wangchen, Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama and the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) for Latin America, and Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT), will visit Panama from September 30 through October 2 to strengthen engagement with government officials, civil society, and other key stakeholders and raise awareness about the situation in Tibet and China’s efforts to destroy Tibet’s distinct cultural, religious, and linguistic identity and heritage. The visit will provide Panamanian audiences with opportunities to learn about the experiences of Tibetans who have been forced into exile after the Chinese occupation of Tibet. It will also offer them a space to engage directly with CTA and ICT representatives through discussions with elected officials, students, civil society organizations, journalists, and community leaders. During the visit, they will screen the documentariesFree Tibet: Voices in ExileandThe Sun Behind the Cloudsin Panama City andColón. Each screening will be followed by an opportunity for participants to speak with the Tibetan representatives about the documentary and explore the difficult issues it addresses. “What is happening in Tibet is not only a Tibetan issue; it is a question of whether a people can preserve their language, faith, culture and identity in the face of systematic efforts to assimilate them,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “Through this visit, we hope to build greater awareness of the situation inside Tibet and encourage meaningful conversations about human rights, religious freedom and the fundamental right of Tibetans to preserve their identity.” The Tibetan representatives will also seek to build support for the Tibetan people’s fundamental rights and democratic institutions and mobilize support for a resumption in dialogue between His Holiness the Dalai Lama or the democratically elected Tibetan leaders and the Chinese government. The Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) is the government-in-exile of Tibet, which was invaded by China in 1949. Based in Dharamsala, India, the CTA provides services to Tibetan refugees, including education, healthcare, cultural and religious preservation, and community support. As Tibet’s government-in-exile, the CTA advocates internationally for the political, religious, and cultural rights of the people of Tibet. The International Campaign for Tibet works to promote human rights and democratic freedoms for the Tibetan people, preserve Tibetan culture and identity, and support efforts to reach a peaceful resolution for Tibet through dialogue. Through its work with elected leaders, global governments, testimony at government hearings and advocacy for important legislation, ICT has helped mobilize the international community to take meaningful action on Tibet. Ciudad de Panamá, 29 de septiembre de 2026– El Venerable Thubten Wangchen, representante de Su Santidad el Dalái Lama y de la Administración Central Tibetana (CTA) para América Latina, y Tencho Gyatso, presidenta de la Campaña Internacional por el Tíbet (ICT), visitarán Panamá del 30 de septiembre al 2 de octubre con el objetivo de fortalecer el diálogo con funcionarios gubernamentales, representantes de la sociedad civil y otros actores clave, así como para crear conciencia sobre la situación en el Tíbet y los esfuerzos de China por destruir la identidad, el patrimonio cultural, religioso y lingüístico distintivos del Tíbet. La visita brindará al público panameño oportunidades para conocer las experiencias de los tibetanos que se han visto obligados a vivir en el exilio tras la ocupación china del Tíbet. Asimismo, ofrecerá un espacio para interactuar directamente con representantes de la CTA y de ICT mediante conversaciones con funcionarios electos, estudiantes, organizaciones de la sociedad civil, periodistas y líderes comunitarios. Durante la visita, se proyectarán en Ciudad de Panamá y Colón los documentalesFree Tibet: Voices in ExileyThe Sun Behind the Clouds. Después de cada proyección, los participantes tendrán la oportunidad de conversar con los representantes tibetanos sobre los documentales y profundizar los difíciles temas que abordan. “Lo que está ocurriendo en el Tíbet no es únicamente un asunto tibetano; se trata de determinar si un pueblo puede preservar su idioma, su fe, su cultura y su identidad frente a los esfuerzos sistemáticos por asimilarlo”, afirmó Tencho Gyatso, presidenta de la Campaña Internacional por el Tíbet. “A través de esta visita, esperamos generar una mayor conciencia sobre la situación dentro del Tíbet y fomentar conversaciones significativas sobre los derechos humanos, la libertad religiosa y el derecho fundamental de los tibetanos a preservar su identidad”. Los representantes tibetanos también buscarán generar apoyo a los derechos fundamentales y las instituciones democráticas del pueblo tibetano, así como promover la reanudación del diálogo entre Su Santidad el Dalái Lama, o sus líderes tibetanos elegidos democráticamente, y el Gobierno chino. Acerca de la Administración Central Tibetana La Administración Central Tibetana (CTA) es el gobierno tibetano en el exilio. El Tíbet fue invadido por China en 1949. Con sede en Dharamsala, India, la CTA presta servicios a los refugiados tibetanos, entre ellos educación, atención médica, preservación cultural y religiosa y apoyo comunitario. En su calidad de gobierno tibetano en el exilio, la CTA aboga internacionalmente por los derechos políticos, religiosos y culturales del pueblo tibetano. Acerca de la Campaña Internacional por el Tíbet La Campaña Internacional por el Tíbet trabaja para promover los derechos humanos y las libertades democráticas del pueblo tibetano, preservar la cultura y la identidad tibetanas y apoyar los esfuerzos encaminados hacia una solución pacífica para el Tíbet mediante el diálogo. A través de su trabajo con líderes electos y gobiernos de todo el mundo, su participación mediante testimonios en audiencias gubernamentales y su labor de incidencia en favor de legislación relevante, la ICT ha contribuido a movilizar a la comunidad internacional para adoptar medidas significativas en apoyo del Tíbet.

title: New Tibet Autonomous Region Party Secretary vows to prioritize national security and ‘stability,’ deepen ‘anti-separatist struggle’
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: China’s new party secretary of the so-called Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), Hu Changsheng, has vowed to “deepen the anti-separatist struggle” and “resolutely ensure long-term stability and security,” signaling a continuation of Beijing’s repressive policies in the region. A Chinese official, Hu replaced Wang Junzheng as TAR Party Secretary, according to anannouncementby the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) on Sep. 22, 2026. New TAR Party Secretary Hu Changsheng meets with TAR leader Phakpalha Gelek Namgyal on Sep. 23, 2026. Hu’s appointment as TAR Party Secretary reflects the CCP’s longstanding practice of excluding Tibetans from the most powerful administrative positions. To date, no Tibetan has ever been appointed as party secretary of the TAR.A native of Jiangxi Province, Hu is Chinese and has previous experience governing Tibetan areas in the traditional Kham and Amdo regions. He earlier served as Party Secretary of Kardze (Ganzi) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan from 2012 to 2015 and as a member of the Standing Committee of the Qinghai CCP from 2015 to 2017. More recently, Hu also served as Party Secretary of Gansu province from 2022 to 2026, during which time he oversaw the Kanlho (Gannan) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture. His remarks upon taking office underscored his intent to continue the CCP’s and Xi Jinping’s hardline policies in Tibet. Chinese state media quoted Hu as stating at an official announcement ceremony for the TAR’s leading cadres on September 22, 2026: “I will, adhere to the principle of coordinating development and security, fully implement the overall national security concept, deepen the anti-separatist struggle, strengthen the management of religious affairs according to law, take the strengthening of the sense of community of the Chinese nation as the main line, deepen the creation of a model area for ethnic unity and progress, strengthen and innovate social governance, and serve the national security with the stability of Tibet.” Additionally, ICT’s analysis of Hu’s career, particularly his record in Tibetan areas, together with his stated priorities upon taking office, indicates that he will likely continue to carry out restrictive and repressive measures against the Tibetan people. During his tenure in Kardze, Tibetans there facedsevere restrictions in their activities, including security forces firing on Tibetans who were calling for the release of arbitrarily detained Tibetans. Similarly, in July 2013, Kardze security forces were ordered to use tear gas and live ammunition to disperse a crowd of monks, nuns, and laypersons who had gathered in Daofu (Tawu) County to celebrate the 78th birthday of the Dalai Lama. Tsering Gyaltsen, a monk from Draggo Monastery in Draggo (Luhuo) County, died following a police beating for his participation in a protest in January 2012. Hu Changsheng, then Party Secretary of Kardze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, visited the monastery to prohibit senior monks from discussing the cases of four monks sentenced to five to seven years in prison for their participation in the January protest, according to the U.S. State Department’s2013 International Religious Freedom Report, which cited the exile media outlet Phayul.com. The repression continued after Hu’s departure as the prefecture’s party secretary, as evidenced by the CCP ordering a series of demolitions of structures of religious significance, including a 99-foot Buddha statue, a 45-foot Guru Padmasambhava statue at Channang Monastery, a 40-foot Maitreya statue housed inside Draggo Monastery, a row of 45 prayer wheels, and the Gaden Rabten Namgyal Ling monastic school. At least 11 known Tibetans who resisted the demolitions were detained between October 31 and December 31, 2021. During his most recent tenure as the party secretary of Gansu between December 2022 and September 2026, controls over Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in Kanlho (Gannan) prefecture and their religious activities intensified after Hu’s appointment, according to a Tibetan who escaped Tibet in 2024. In 2024, Gansuauthorities issued a stringent training manual to Buddhist clergypreventing monks from engaging in activities which the authorities labeled as threatening national unity or disrupting social stability. The restrictions included bans on any cooperation with Tibetan religious leaders and the exiled Tibetan community. A year earlier in 2023, Gansu officials initially cancelleda major Tibetan Buddhist festival from takingplace in Kanlho. When the festival was later allowed to proceed and rescheduled to later in the year, authorities imposed restrictions, including preventing devotees from gaining access to the lama, Gungthang Rinpoche. Under Hu’s provincial leadership, Kanlho Prefecture Party Secretary He Moubao made a major push to tighten ideological control in Tibetan areas. In November 2025, He summoned the heads of monasteries and nunneries in and around Sangchu (Xiahe) County and demanded absolute loyalty to the Chinese state and gratitude toward the CCP. In 2015, during his visit to the renowned Labrang Monastery in Kanlho, Hu emphasized the systematic “Sinicization” of Tibetan Buddhism and its complete integration into socialist society. The Party Secretary of Kardze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Hu Changsheng, is pictured in the official media visiting Larung Gar monastery on February 5, 2015. Management of monasteries by Party officials has been stepped up in line with the new ‘stability drive’ in Kham and Amdo. File photo of then Party Secretary of Kardze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture Hu Changsheng visiting Larung Gar Monastery on February 5, 2015 to step up management of monasteries as part of the Party’s “stability drive.” (State media propaganda handout) Hu Changsheng’s most recenthigh-profile meetingwith a senior American official took place in October 2024, when he met then-U.S. Ambassador to China Nicholas Burns. Their discussions centered almost exclusively on Gansu–U.S. relations, economic cooperation, and people-to-people exchanges. During the meeting, Hu projected a pragmatic and relatively measured image, emphasizing soft power, culture, tourism, and subnational exchanges while remaining aligned with central government policy. This engagement indicates Hu’s capability to conduct constructive external outreach—an approach he may also apply to Tibet, notwithstanding his concerning human rights record in Tibet. U.S. ambassador Nicholas Burns meeting with Hu Changsheng, then the Gansu provincial party secretary, in October 2024 (State media handout) Hu’s appointment is part of the expected regional leadership changes ahead of China’s 21st Party Congress in 2027, when Beijing will see broader leadership reshuffles under what is very likely to be Xi Jinping’s continued leadership of the CCP. Luo Dongchuan and Wu Xiaojun, party secretaries of Qinghai and Gansu. Along with Hu’s appointment, China also announced Luo Dongchuan and Wu Xiaojun as party secretaries of Qinghai and Gansu, respectively; both these provinces have significant Tibetan areas. Previously, while serving asGovernor of Qinghai, Luo led a delegation to meet the officials in Lhasain October 2025 during which they discussed “safeguarding national security and social stability,” and “signed a strategic cooperation framework.” Dechen Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture Acting Governor Li Yanlan. At the prefectural level, China announced in August that Li Yanlan, who is identified as being a Tibetan, had been appointed acting governor of the Dechen (Diqing) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Yunnan. Born in 1972, she has spent her entire career in Dechen, where she became the prefecture’s vice governor in 2016 and deputy party secretary in 2022. Born December 1963, Hu Changsheng is from Gao’an, Jiangxi Province. He joined the Communist Party of China in 1986 and graduated from an in-service postgraduate program of Ancient Chinese History at Shandong University. He holds a doctorate in history and is an associate professor. He is currently a member of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China. February 2012 – April 2012:Served as Deputy Secretary of the CPC Kardze Prefecture Committee, Sichuan Province (at the ministerial level) April 2012 – June 2015:Served as Secretary of the CPC Kardze Prefecture Committee June 2015 – July 2017:Served as member of the Standing Committee of the Qinghai Provincial Party Committee and Minister of the Organization Department December 2022–September 2026:Served as Party Secretary of Gansu. September 2026:Appointed Party Secretary of the Tibet Autonomous Region Born October 1965, Luo Dongchuan is from Chongqing. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in June 1986. He is currently an alternate member of the 20th CCP Central Committee and governor of Qinghai Province.
