title: ICT joins Tibetans, rights groups, Congressional partners in urging Trump to put Tibet and human rights on the agenda during Xi visit
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: As Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Washington for a state visit Sep. 23-25, the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) joined Tibetan organizations, Tibet supporters, human rights groups and members of the U.S. Congress in a coordinated campaign calling for Tibet and human rights to be prioritized both during Xi’s visit and in the broader U.S.-China relationship. Through advocacy with policymakers, coalition initiatives and participation in protests, rallies, press conferences and other public actions, ICT worked alongside partners to highlight Tibetan political prisoners, the disappearance of the 11th Panchen Lama, Chinese government interference in Tibetan Buddhist succession, coercive assimilation, transnational repression and China’s repressive new so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” Hundreds of Tibetans from across North America gathered at Washington D.C. on Sep. 24 to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit. (ICT) The campaigns culminated in a day-long mobilization on Sep. 24 by Tibetans and Tibet supporters that brought together over 2,000 Tibetan Americans from across North America, including Toronto, Minnesota, New York, Indiana, and many other locales. ICT joined the Tibetan-led protests outside the Chinese embassy and the peaceful march to the U.S. Capitol, where protestors were joined by congressional and human rights supporters. The Tibetan Youth Congress and Capital Area Tibetan Association led the Tibetan American mobilization, with participation and support from ICT, Students for a Free Tibet, Tibetan National Congress and other Tibetan organizations. ICT also participated alongside Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, Taiwanese, Southern Mongolians and Chinese democracy activists and dissidents in broader coalition protests during Xi’s visit, with a candlelight vigil at Franklin Park. The public mobilization was part of a broader advocacy effort before and during Xi’s visit. Ahead of Xi’s arrival on September 23,ICT called on President Donald Trump to make Tibet and human rights central to his discussions with Xiand to raise these issues both privately and publicly. ICT urged renewed substantive dialogue between Chinese authorities and Tibetan representatives, the release of the Panchen Lama, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, and a repeal of the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” (EUPL) and other policies threatening Tibetan religion, language, culture and identity. On Sep. 24, Rep. Jim McGovern addresses hundreds of Tibetans gathered outside the U.S. Capitol to protest Xi’s visit to Washington. (ICT) ICT simultaneously worked through broader coalitions.On Sep. 16, it joined a coalition of 30 human rights, democracy and religious-freedom organizations in an open letter calling on Xito release prisoners of conscience, end transnational repression and undertake legal reforms. The coalition included International Tibet Network, Campaign for Uyghurs, Uyghur Human Rights Project, Human Rights Foundation, Freedom House, Amnesty International USA, Hong Kong Watch, ChinaAid, Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists, among others. ICT also participated in aReligious Freedom Institute and International Religious Freedom Summit event on CCP repression. ICT Executive Director Ryan Fioresi and Head of Research and Monitoring Bhuchung K. Tsering spoke alongside former U.S. Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom Sam Brownback and representatives of other affected communities. Speakers addressed imprisonment, surveillance, forced labor, family retaliation and pressure reaching people outside China. Fioresi focused on restrictions on Tibetan Buddhism, and said restrictions have entered “the most intimate spaces of religious conviction,” affecting who may pursue monastic life, how teachings are transmitted and how Tibetan communities practice their faith. Fioresi also addressed Chinese government interference in religious succession, citing the case of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, who was disappeared by the Chinese authorities after he was recognized by the Dalai Lama as the 11th Panchen Lama. Fioresi argued that the case offers a warning about how Chinese authorities could seek to influence the eventual succession of the Dalai Lama. “Those decisions belong to Tibetan Buddhists themselves,” he said. At the U.S. Capitol grounds on Sep. 24, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and Rep. Jim McGovern join hundreds of Tibetan protesting Xi’s visit to Washington. (ICT) ICT Head of Research and Monitoring Bhuchung K. Tsering focused on the concerns around the new EUPL and emphasized that the legislation codifies Sinicization and coercive assimilation and “further undermines Tibetans’ fundamental freedom to preserve their unique culture, religion and way of life.” Tsering said policies implemented in Tibetan areas over more than a decade helped test an approach later incorporated into national legislation. His remarks highlighted four areas of concern: increased emphasis on a single Chinese national identity and Mandarin-language education; the treatment of ethnic affairs through a national-security framework; ideological influence extending into family life; and the law’s reach beyond China’s borders through Article 63. Tsering called on Trump to urge Xi to repeal the new law, protect Tibetan cultural and religious rights and seek the release of, or independent access to, the Panchen Lama. As Xi arrived in Washington, ICT President Tencho Gyatso also participated in a campaign organized by the Human Rights Foundation to call for the release of the 11the Panchen Lama. The campaign formed part of the broader human rights mobilization surrounding the visit and followed the joint call by ICT and other organizations for the release of prisoners of conscience, including Gedhun Choekyi Nyima. Members of Congress amplified these concerns as Xi arrived in Washington. Ajoint congressional letter signed by 37 members of the House of Representativesurged President Trump to raise the EUPL directly with Xi during their meetings and to press for its repeal. In the Sep. 23 letter — led by Jamie Raskin (D-MD), Jim McGovern (D-MA) and Gregory Meeks (D-NY) — lawmakers cited concerns about theEUPL’s implications for Tibetans, Uyghurs, other ethnic and religious communities, human rights advocates and critics of the Chinese government living outside China. On Sep. 23, Rep. Jim McGovern also convened a press conference with representatives of Tibetan, Uyghur, Hong Kong and Chinese communities. McGovern called on the administration to raise political prisoners, fundamental freedoms and other human rights issues directly with Xi and specifically criticized the EUPL, arguing that it threatens the distinct cultural and linguistic identities of non-Chinese communities. “Our call today is ‘no Xi in DC without human rights’,” McGovern said. “Our call must also be ‘no US foreign policy without human rights’.” Tibetans protest Xi visit to Washington on Sep. 24 (ICT) ICT President Tencho Gyatso joined McGovern at the press conference, urging the administration to raise Tibetan political prisoners, the Panchen Lama, the forced assimilation of Tibetan children and the need to resume meaningful dialogue on Tibet. Her message ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting was direct: “Put human rights on the agenda. Put Tibet on the agenda and ask where is the Panchen Lama?” Gyatso also spoke personally about carrying a connection to Tibet despite never having seen her homeland, saying the issues at stake concern whether Tibetan language, religion, culture and identity will survive. Gyatso connected the Panchen Lama’s disappearance to the broader question of who has the right to determine Tibetan Buddhist leadership, including the eventual succession of the Dalai Lama. She also warned that repression increasingly reaches beyond China through technology, surveillance and transnational pressure against people exercising their rights in the United States. Congressional support was also visible at the Sep. 24 Capitol rally, where Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and Congressman McGovern stood with Tibetan leaders, activists and representatives of other communities. Pelosi emphasized the preservation of Tibetan identity, religion, language and culture, and on following the message and example of His Holiness the Dalai Lama to continue striving for Tibet. “We have to demand and insist,” she said, “that the religion, the language, the faith, the community, the sense of community, in Tibet be respected.” Rep. McGovern reiterated four priorities: freeing prisoners of conscience, countering transnational repression, rejecting the EUPL, and ensuring that Tibetans, Uyghurs and others are not deported to China. The Sep. 24 mobilization extended across Washington. After gathering outside the Chinese Embassy, Tibetan protesters marched toward the Capitol for the afternoon rally. Participants in the Rangzen Walk, organized by Tibetan National Congress New York/New Jersey, joined the mobilization after walking from New York to Washington. Students for a Free Tibet organized additional protest actions, including demonstrations outside the Waldorf Astoria and at Joint Base Andrews, ensuring that Tibetan voices were visible at multiple locations associated with Xi’s visit. On Sep. 24, ICT President Tencho Gyatso addresses hundreds of Tibetans gathered outside the U.S. Capitol to protest Xi’s visit to Washington. (ICT) At the Capitol rally, Capital Area Tibetan Association President Tenzing Norbu emphasized both Tibetan resilience and solidarity with other affected communities. Uyghur Human Rights Project Executive Director Omer Kanat highlighted parallels between Tibetan and Uyghur experiences and the transnational pressure faced by diaspora communities, while Hong Kong democracy advocate Frances Hui urged policymakers not to allow political prisoners and human rights to disappear behind discussions of trade. Together, the speeches underscored one of the central themes of this week’s mobilization: Tibetans were not advocating in isolation, but in solidarity with other communities who have been impacted by Beijing’s repression. Through all of the actions this week, these collective voices highlighted the urgency of placing human rights and fundamental freedoms at the center of the U.S.-China relationship.

title: Dozens of House Representatives urge Trump to press Xi to repeal China’s repressive “ethnic unity” law
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Jamie Raskin (D-MD), Reps. Jim McGovern (D-MA) and Gregory Meeks (D-NY). On Wednesday, Sep. 23, as Chinese Communist Party leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington DC for a state visit, 37 members of U.S. Congressjoined togetherto call on U.S. President Donald Trump to condemn China’s“Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” (EUPL)and press Xi for its repeal. The congressional letter — written by human rights stalwart Jamie Raskin (D-MD) and led by Raskin, Tibet champion Jim McGovern (D-MA) and House Foreign Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-NY) — raises concerns about theEUPL’s implications for Tibetans, Uyghurs, other ethnic and religious communities, human rights advocates and critics of the Chinese government living outside China. It decries the EUPL as an “insidious declaration of China’s intent to further repress religious freedom and the freedom of group association.” The lawmakers sent the letter on the day of Xi’s arrival and urged President Trump to raise the EUPL directly with the Chinese leader during their meetings in Washington. Xi’s visit concludes today, Friday, following meetings with President Trump and a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening. Focusing on Tibet, the Representatives warn that the EUPL grants Beijing sweeping authority to prosecute Tibetans, expedite further transnational repression against Tibetan communities, escalate the systemic persecution of Tibetan Buddhists, and further entrench Chinese government forced assimilation policies aimed at suppressing Tibetan religious, cultural and linguistic identity. “During your meeting with Xi Jinping, it is imperative that you continue to voice your administration’s disapproval of this affront to the fundamental freedoms of minority communities, human rights advocates and U.S. citizens,” the lawmakers wrote. The letter concludes with a request for Trump to personally ask Xi for the repeal of the EUPL, warning that “our national security, sovereignty and basic human rights all over the world” are at stake. The International Campaign for Tibet welcomed the congressional intervention and thanked the lawmakers for acting as Xi arrived in Washington and ahead of his meetings with President Trump. “We are deeply grateful to Representatives Raskin, McGovern and Meeks and all the members of Congress who joined this important call for the repeal of the so-called ‘Ethnic Unity and Progress Law’,” said Ryan Fioresi, Executive Director, International Campaign for Tibet. “By sending this letter as Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, they ensured that the rights of Tibetans and other communities targeted by the Chinese government were part of the conversation surrounding this state visit. We thank them for standing with Tibetans, for drawing attention to the dangers posed by this law, and for urging President Trump to press Xi directly for its repeal,” he added. Led by Raskin, McGovern, and Meeks, the letter was also signed by Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (CA-11) and Representatives Jake Auchincloss (MA-04), Ami Bera (CA-06), André Carson (IN-07), Kathy Castor (FL-14), Steve Cohen (TN-09), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Madeleine Dean (PA-04), Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10), Lloyd Doggett (TX-10), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Al Green (TX-09), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), George Latimer (NY-16), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), Grace Meng (NY-06), Jerry Nadler (NY-12), Richard Neal (MA-01), Eleanor Norton (DC-AL), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Mark Pocan (WI-02), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Brad Schneider (IL-10), Brad Sherman (CA-32), Tom Suozzi (NY-03), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Dina Titus (NV-01), James Walkinshaw (VA-11) , Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25) and Maxine Waters (CA-43). Notably, Tibet Lobby Day 2026 participants met with many of these offices and asked them to oppose the EUPL. The letter was endorsed by the International Campaign for Tibet, and can beread here.

title: “Baptism of youth”: China continues to subject Tibetan children to military –style training and political indoctrination
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: A recentChinese state-media reportshows Tibetan children in the eastern Tibetan town of Dartsedo (Chinese: Kangding), Kardze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan province being subjected to a five-day training program combining instruction on “school rules and behavioral norms” with military-style drills and political indoctrination sessions. Tibetan children being subjected to military-style drills under “development education” program. (Source: Chinese State Media) Images published with the report show Tibetan middle school students dressed in military-style uniforms and participating in marching and formation drills and other training. The children were also subjected to ideological education which included sessions on “fostering ethnic unity.” The students appear to be middle school students who had only recently completed elementary school. The Chinese state media report described the activities carried out in this program as “moral education courses” aimed at cultivating a strong sense of “patriotism” and “ethnic unity”. It reported that children sang political songs such as “Without the Communist Party, There Would Be No New China”, and internalized the ideals of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and ethnic unity. The images and accompanying account provide another disturbing example of the increasing incorporation of military-style discipline and Chinese Communist Party (CCP) ideology into the education of Tibetan children. ICT is deeply concerned by the Chinese government’s accelerated deployment of military education and political indoctrination involving Tibetan children and condemns these practices. Middle school children perform military formation drills supervised by a Chinese officer. (Source: Chinese State Media) Tibetan children being subjected to military training in what the state media describes as the “baptism of youth.” (Source: Chinese State Media) “This is not simply children learning ‘school rules’. Tibetan children are being put in military uniforms, drilled in formation and immersed in CCP ideology at an age when they should be free to learn their own language and practice their own religion, culture, and traditions,” said Tencho Gyatso, President, International Campaign for Tibet. “When the CCP boasts of ‘baptizing’ Tibetan children through this kind of training, it reveals the disturbing purpose behind it: turning education into an instrument of forced assimilation and as a means to erase Tibetan identity. Such abuses must end,” she added. ICT has previouslyreportedon the CCP’s systematic militarization and indoctrination of Tibetan children. Similar images showed Tibetan kindergarten children marching in military uniforms and carrying imitation rifles. This latest report and the images with it is further evidence of how the CCP is forcefully introducing and subjecting Tibetan children to military training and intensive ideological programming. China has long pursued the erasure of Tibetan culture through forced assimilation policies and its vast state-runboarding schools, forcibly separating Tibetan children from their families and preventing them from learning or speaking Tibetan. This violates Tibetan children’s basic rights and threatens the very survival of Tibetan culture and identity. Tibetan children receive military training from a Chinese officer and perform songs like the “Strong Military Battle Song.” (Source: Chinese State Media) The treatment of Tibetan children will receive renewed international scrutiny as China enters its next reporting cycle before the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. The Committee is scheduled to consider a list of issues concerning China during its pre-sessional working group from Sept. 29 to Oct. 2, 2026, in which ICT will be participating. The upcoming review of states’ compliance with the UN Child Rights Convention is, therefore, an opportunity for the international community to hold China accountable for the human rights abuses committed against Tibetan children. The CCP’s systematic oppression of Tibetan children’s rights to freedom of speech, information, religion, culture and family unity is a direct violation of the Convention. The Committee on the Rights of the Child already found in2013that China’s education policies discriminated against Tibetan children. However, China has made no changes and continues to institutionalize violations of Tibetan children’s rights. To uphold the strength of international law, these abuses against children must be addressed and prevented. ICT calls on the Chinese government to end coercive political indoctrination and military-style training of Tibetan children and to ensure that Tibetan children can fully exercise their rights to their own language, religion, culture, education and way of life. The international community, including the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, should press Chinese authorities to provide transparent information about the scope and content of military-style and political education in Tibetan schools and to bring education policies in Tibetan areas into compliance with international human rights standards.

title: Nine months after his detention, prominent Tibetan Buddhist leader Choktrul Dorje Ten’s whereabouts, well-being remain unknown
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Family members and students of the detained Tibetan lama and educator have made seven separate formal appeals to Chinese authorities which have gone unanswered. Tibetan Buddhist leader Choktrul Dorje Ten in an undated photo (ICT sources) More thannine months after Tibetan Buddhist leader and educator Choktrul Dorje Ten Rinpochewas arbitrarily detained by Chinese authorities in December 2025, his whereabouts and well-being continue to remain unknown despite repeated formal appeals made to officials by his family members and students. A respected and influential leader and a firm proponent of Tibetan language and cultural preservation, Choktrul Dorje Ten was the head of Minthang Osel Thegchok Chokhorling Monastery in Minthang Township, Chikdril (Chinese: Jiuzhi) County, Golog (Guoluo) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Qinghai. He was also the founder of the Dorje Ten Ethnic Vocational School, a Tibetan-medium instruction school that was forcibly closed after his detention on or around December 4, 2025. Since then, his family members and students have submitted seven separate formal appeals to Chinese authorities requesting information about his whereabouts and physical well-being, sources told the International Campaign for Tibet. Chinese authorities have not provided any response to those appeals. A relative of Choktrul Dorje Ten who is based in exile told ICT that the complete lack of any verifiable information about the Buddhist lama’s whereabouts and well-being over the past nine months has sparked grave concern among his family members and students about whether he is even alive. In aresolution adopted on April 30, the European Parliament called for the immediate release of Choktrul Dorje Ten. Also in April, Amnesty International launched anUrgent Actioncampaign for the Tibetan lama’s release. In the wake of his detention, Chinese authorities have systematically shut down several educational and cultural institutions founded by Choktrul Dorje Ten. These include the Nyenpo Yutse Primary School, the Mayang Lhakhar Chukmo Gesar Cultural Propagation Center, and the Gesar Cultural Heritage Base and Mayang Chugmo Gesar Culture Training Center. Local authorities have also banned members from discussing organizational matters, permanently closed related WeChat groups, and placed the community under heightened surveillance and strict restrictions. Born on October 25, 1967, in Akyong Khangsar, Choktrul Dorje Ten (also known as Choktrul Thubten Yeshe Nyima) studied Buddhist teachings in the Nyingma tradition under revered masters including Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok. He earned the title of Khenpo, or abbot, at the Larung Gar Buddhist Academy in Sertar, one of the world’s largest Tibetan Buddhist learning institutes, which has long been a target of the Chinese government’s campaign of demolitions, expulsions of monastics, and severe restrictions on the free exercise of Buddhist traditions. A revered local community leader, Choktrul Dorje Ten Rinpoche was previously celebrated by Chinese authorities for his promotion of education and vocational training.

author: International Campaign for Tibet

title: New report reveals Chinese AI-enabled surveillance on Tibetan exile government, Buddhist members, ICT and SFT
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Anthropic findings show China-based threat actors instructing Claude AI to adopt the Chinese state’s political narrative on Tibet A new Anthropic threat intelligence report titled‘Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026’provides disturbing evidence of China-based, government-aligned actors targeting the Tibetan exile government or the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), members of the Tibetan Buddhist civil society and advocacy organizations, including the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) and Students for a Free Tibet (SFT). The findings — which were based on malicious activity identified on Anthropic’s Claude using Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models between December 2025 and August 2026 — provide independent evidence of the artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled surveillance of Tibetans, Uyghurs, Taiwanese and other religious groups by threat actors aligned with China’s United Front Work Department, the Ministry of State Security, and the former State Administration for Religious Affairs. ICT finds the report particularly disturbing because it also shows AI tools being used to advance the Chinese government’s political narrative on Tibet — potentially giving Beijing a powerful new mechanism to amplify and normalize that narrative at digital scale — and the deep integration of AI models into the daily work of the PRC municipal and state security bureau for “stability maintenance” and transnational repression. “When Tibetan Buddhist civil society, the Tibetan government-in-exile and organizations peacefully advocating for Tibetan rights are subjected to AI-assisted surveillance, this cannot be treated simply as the misuse of a new technology. It is the modernization of transnational repression,” ICT President Tencho Gyatso said. “Governments and AI companies must ensure that technologies built to expand human knowledge do not become instruments for authoritarian governments to monitor people, intimidate communities and impose their version of history on the digital world,” she added. Anthropic reports that the operation targeting members of Tibetan Buddhist civil society, the CTA and Tibetan advocacy groups, explicitly naming ICT and SFT, used Claude to transform multilingual information into Chinese-language intelligence dossiers, organizational datasets and daily “situational awareness” reports. They collected personal information, monitored Chinese and international social-media platforms and conducted physical reconnaissance of religious venues, including gathering floor plans and structural information. Anthropic also found operators instructing Claude to adopt “China’s standpoint” and characterize the Tibetan administration in exile as an “illegal separatist administration.” Anthropic also uncovered a separate China-based operation in which AI was used to impose PRC-preferred terminology and reframe foreign reporting critical of China for government intelligence briefings. “For decades, Beijing has tried to control Tibet by controlling our institutions, our religion, our language and the story the world hears about Tibet. What Beijing has sought to impose in Tibet’s physical spaces must not become the default version of Tibet in the world’s digital spaces,” Gyatso said. “Artificial intelligence should expand access to knowledge — not accelerate surveillance, intimidation and the erasure of a people’s history and identity.” Chinese authorities have long sought to reshape Tibetan identity and historical understanding through restrictions on Tibetan-language education, political education, controls over Tibetan Buddhism and efforts to replace the internationally recognized name “Tibet” with Beijing-preferred terminology. Anthropic’s findings point toward a digital extension of that effort, where AI can reproduce Beijing’s political framing of Tibet at speed and scale. The findings reinforce patterns documented separately by OpenAI, which has reported PRC-linked actors seeking assistance with large-scale social-media monitoring, profiling critics and identifying ethnic, religious and political content. OpenAI also reported a proposed “early warning” system combining transportation and police data to identify movements of people classified as “Uyghur-related” and “high-risk;” it was not able to establish whether the system was deployed. title: ICT calls on President Trump to publicly press Xi on Tibet, the Panchen Lama and human rights
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Ahead of the Chinese President’s US visit, ICT joins human rights groups in demanding Xi take immediate, verifiable steps to address China’s human rights record As U.S. President Donald Trump prepares to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., the International Campaign for Tibet urges him to make Tibet and human rights central to their bilateral discussions, and to press Xi, both privately and publicly, to resume substantive dialogue without preconditions with His Holiness the Dalai Lama and democratically elected Tibetan leaders; immediately release the 11th Panchen Lama; and end policies that institutionalize the forced assimilation of Tibetans. On Wednesday, ICT, representing more than 50,000 members and supporters and standing with Tibetan Americans across the United States, also joineddozens of human rights organizations in callingon the Chinese government to take immediate, verifiable steps to address its human rights record. Those steps include releasing prisoners of conscience, ending transnational repression, and reforming laws and policies used to criminalize peaceful expression, religious practice, association, and dissent. “Since you assumed power in late 2012, our organizations have documented—and some have lived—your government’s widespread, systematic human rights crimes, which violate domestic and international legal obligations. Tibetans, Uyghurs, and other communities continue to face your government’s atrocity crimes designed to erase their culture, identity, and language, and their rights to free speech and fair trials,” the29 rights groups wrote in their joint letter to Xi. Nowhere are the consequences of these policies more evident than in occupied Tibet. China calls Tibet “autonomous.” In reality, Xi’s policies have sought to eliminate any semblance of meaningful autonomy for the Tibetan people. That lack of meaningful autonomy is reinforced by Xi Jinping’s and the Chinese Communist Party’s tightening control over Tibetan society and their increasingly draconian efforts to forcibly assimilate the Tibetan population, including through the recently implemented so-called“Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” Buddhist institutions face political interference, monastic residences are being demolished, Tibetan children are separated from their families through state-run boarding schools, and Tibetans continue to be imprisoned for peaceful expression, including mere possession of images of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. With China’s forced assimilation policies intensifying since Xi assumed power in 2012, the importance of implementing established U.S. policy on Tibet in support of a negotiated solution has become increasingly urgent. “U.S. policy on Tibet is clear.The Tibetan Policy Act of 2002and theResolve Tibet Act of 2024establish that the Tibet-China dispute should be resolved peacefully through substantive dialogue without preconditions. They direct the U.S. government to promote dialogue between Chinese authorities and His Holiness the Dalai Lama or his representatives, or democratically elected Tibetan leaders,” ICT President Tencho Gyatso said. “President Trump must therefore uphold this policy and use his meeting with Xi to press for the resumption of Sino-Tibetan dialogue — especially at this critical juncture, when China’s new, so-called ‘Ethnic Unity and Progress Law’ threatens the very foundations of Tibetan identity,” she added. author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet is now accepting applications for the Rowell Fund for Tibet’s 2027 grant cycle. This fund supports Tibetans who can make a significant impact in their communities or reach an international audience in the fields of visual arts, media, literature, environmental conservation, and women’s empowerment. TheRowell Fund for Tibetwas established in memory of Galen and Barbara Rowell, devoted friends of the Tibetan people. title: ICT welcomes Senate introduction of Assuring the Future of Tibet Act
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet welcomes the introduction of theAssuring the Future of Tibet Act (AFTA)(S.5362) in the US Senate, bringing important bipartisan legislation to both chambers of Congress and building momentum to secure enduring US support for the Tibetan people, their democratic institutions and democratically elected leadership. Introduced bySenators Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Jim Risch (R-ID), and co-sponsored by Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA) Todd Young (R-IN), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), and Rick Scott (R-FL), the legislation is the Senate companion to the bill (H.R. 8982) introduced in May 22, 2026 in the House of Representatives by Reps. Jim McGovern (D-MA) and Michael McCaul (R-TX). The Assuring the Future of Tibet Act recognizes a fundamental principle: Tibet’s future cannot be decided without the Tibetan people themselves. AFTA will make it US policy to maintain direct engagement with the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), the democratically elected representatives of the Tibetan people inside Tibet and in the global diaspora. “Human rights and basic dignity for the people of Tibet cannot be ignored. Our bipartisan bill sends a clear message that the United States will stand with Tibet in its fight for these fundamental freedoms and the promise of tomorrow,” said Merkley. “As long as the People’s Republic of China continues to ignore the rights of Tibet under international law, America will not abandon the Tibetan people.” “The Chinese Communist Party has sought to erase Tibetan culture, religion, and language, among other grievous actions. What Beijing has done to Tibet, they want to do elsewhere to anyone who defies the CCP,” said Risch. “This bill supports the Tibetan people, key partners in pushing back against China’s authoritarianism, and counters China’s malign influence at the United Nations.” Sens. James Risch, R-Idaho and Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. “I thank Senators Merkley and Risch for introducing this vital bill and Senators Kaine, Young, Rosen, and Scott for serving as its original co-sponsors. The International Campaign for Tibet looks forward to working with Congress towards its swift passage,” said ICT President Tencho Gyatso. “At a time when China is accelerating its campaign to erase Tibetan identity, this bill sends a powerful message – that America’s support for the Tibetan people, their democratic institutions, and the Tibetan people’s right to determine their own future is unwavering,” she added. The group of original co-sponsors of the Senate bill underscores the broad and bipartisan support for Tibet within the United States Congress. This support has been pivotal in advancing and passing major legislation on Tibet over the past decade, including the Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act, the Tibetan Policy and Support Act, and the Resolve Tibet Act. The introduction of companion legislation in the Senate marks another important step in that record and demonstrates enduring bipartisan and bicameral support for ensuring that US policy toward Tibet remains strong and prepared for the future, including by elevating and strengthening the democratic institutions of the Tibetan people. “For decades, His Holiness the Dalai Lama has worked to build democratic institutions that give Tibetans a voice and preserve their aspirations for freedom and dignity. The Central Tibetan Administration is the democratic expression of that vision. By deepening the US government’s relationship with the CTA, this legislation helps ensure that Tibetans and their democratically elected leaders have the decisive voice in Tibet’s future,” Gyatso said.
