title: At Times Square tribute, ICT Chairman Richard Gere calls on Tibetans to honor Lobga Rangzen’s legacy, carry forward his final message: “I am Tibetan”
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Longtime Tibet advocate and International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) Board Chair Richard Gere urged Tibetans to carry forward the legacy of Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen by embracing the message he asked the world never to forget: “ང་བོད་པ་ཡིན། I am Tibetan.” Speaking to around 2,000 people gathered in New York’s Times Square on Aug. 1, one month after Lobga Rangzen self-immolated outside the United Nations, Gere called on Tibetans to make His Holiness the Dalai Lama proud by taking action for Tibet; standing up for their identity; and continuing the Tibetan struggle with unity, courage and purpose. ICT Chairman Richard Gere addresses Tibetans and Tibet supporters at Times Square, New York during the vigil to honor Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen on Aug. 1, 2026. (Source: ICT) The August 1 vigil, organized by a coalition of eight Tibetan organizations led by the Tibetan National Congress, brought together Lobga Rangzen’s family, prominent Tibetan leaders and activists, elected officials, and representatives of the Uyghur, Southern Mongolian, Hong Kong and Taiwanese communities in a powerful tribute to the life and sacrifice of the longtime Tibetan activist. The evening combined remembrance with renewed calls for international action in response to China’s escalating repression in Tibet and its implementation of the so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, which codifies the forced assimilation of Tibetans by targeting their language, religion and culture. Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation, the first Tibetan self-immolation on US soil, took place a day after China’s repressive new law came into effect on July 1, 2026. Tibetan community members of all ages gathered in Times Square to honor Pawo Lobga Rangzen on Aug. 1, 2026. (Source: ICT) Standing before a sea of Tibetan national flags and hundreds of candles in the heart of Times Square, Gere described Lobga Rangzen as a man “whose message now asks something of every one of us: to stand together for Tibet and be a voice for those inside Tibet.” “He loved Tibet so deeply he refused to let its suffering remain invisible. He wanted the world to understand that Tibet is not simply occupied. It is a civilization at risk,” Gere said. Warning that China’s policies threaten the very survival of one of the world’s oldest civilizations, Gere said the Tibetan language, Buddhist religion and centuries-old culture are living traditions that survive only if someone is free to pass them on. “When a civilization loses the freedom to teach its children, humanity loses something it can never replace,” he added. Quoting His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s teaching that “my religion is kindness,” Gere reminded the crowd that kindness is never passive and instead demands action. “Real kindness is standing beside those punished for speaking their language or practicing their faith,” he said. “Real kindness is our refusal to look away when China’s injustice seeks to dismantle Tibetans’ centuries-old culture and push an entire civilization toward extinction.” ICT Chair Gere and President Tencho Gyatso urge the gathering to call on Congress to take action for Tibet by supporting pro-Tibet legislation and demanding the repeal of China’s ethnic unity law. Gere, along with ICT President Tencho Gyatso, urged participants to take meaningful action for Tibet, asking them to record videos calling on members of Congress to support theAssuring the Future of Tibet Act(AFTA), bipartisan legislation that seeks to strengthen US support for the Tibetan people and the Central Tibetan Administration and demand the repeal of China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, using the hashtags #SupportAFTA and #RepealEthnicUnityLaw on social media. Making their first public appearance since Lobga Rangzen’s funeral, members of his family delivered emotional tributes to the activist whose advocacy and final message has galvanized Tibetans around the world. His niece, Sonam Choedon, described her uncle as a man who devoted every day of his life to Tibet’s freedom. “For my uncle, Tibet was not a cause; it was his life’s purpose,” she said. “He lived for Tibet every single day, and in the end, he gave his life for Tibet.” She recalled how Lobga Rangzen walked to the United Nations carrying the Tibetan national flag before planting it firmly in the ground and throwing into the air leaflets that said “Free Tibet” and “China out of Tibet” as flames engulfed his body. “Through his final act, my uncle awakened something powerful. He reminded Tibetans everywhere that we share one homeland, one history, and one responsibility,” she said. Calling on the international community not to remain silent, she said more than 170 Tibetans had self-immolated crying out for freedom and begging the world to witness what is happening inside Tibet. Turning to Tibetans gathered in Times Square, she urged them to continue protecting their identity and carrying forward the struggle “to bring His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama back to the Potala Palace in a free and independent Tibet.” Speaking before the crowd gathered at Times Square, Tashi Palmo, friend of late Lobga Rangzen and member of the Tibetan National Congress, read the final message Lobga Rangzen posted on Facebook in which he called for Tibetans to be united in their struggle for Tibet and to heed His Holiness’s guidance to serve as the voice for Tibetans inside Tibet. (Read thefull translated text message hereor watch thevideo message here.) Around 2000 Tibetans gathered at Times Square, New York on Aug. 1, 2026 to honor Lobga Rangzen at a vigil organized by a coalition of eight Tibetan organizations led by Tibetan National Congress. (Source: ICT) ICT President Tencho Gyatso said Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice must become a rallying point for renewed unity among Tibetans worldwide. “When we remember him today, we also remember the message he left us,” she said. “He called on Tibetans to stand together in unity, to do what each of us can, in whatever way we can, for Tibet.” Warning that China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Law seeks to dismantle Tibetan identity by targeting language, culture and history, she said, “A people, a nation cannot survive if they are separated from their language, their history, and who they are.” “The greatest way we can honor Pawo Lobga Rangzen is not only by remembering his sacrifice,” she said, “but by answering his call.” A post shared by International Campaign for Tibet (@savetibetorg) ICT Executive Director Ryan Fioresi said Lobga Rangzen had left behind not a message of despair but of determination. “He did not want our mourning,” Fioresi said. “He wanted us to redouble our effort, strengthen our unity, and raise our voices to the international community to proclaim that Tibet can no longer be ignored.” Noting that Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation came one day after China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Law took effect, Fioresi called on the United Nations and governments around the world to condemn the legislation, demand its repeal and press Beijing to resume dialogue with His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s representatives. Fioresi said Tibet’s struggle cannot be viewed in isolation. “The Tibetan struggle is bound to the Uyghurs, the Hong Kongers, the Southern Mongolians, the Taiwanese, and to every person of conscience who refuses to accept that a government may erase a people,” he said. Jigme Ugen, president of the Tibetan National Congress, praised the Tibetan youth organizers for bringing Tibet’s message to “the loudest and busiest pedestrian crossing in the world.” “For more than 70 years, Tibetans have been told to accept the unacceptable,” he said. “We waited. And while we waited, China used that time to kill over 1.5 million Tibetans, separate more than one million children from their language, identity and families, control our monasteries, rewrite our history, erase our language and every foundation of the Tibetan way of life.” He said Lobga Rangzen believed that “the loss of independence was the root of Tibet’s suffering,” and sacrificed his life to restore Tibet’s freedom. NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) Commissioner Midori Valdivia also paid tribute to Lobga Rangzen, a beloved member of the TLC driver community, by lighting an honorary candle in his memory. Tibetan community member in the audience. Paying tribute to his longtime friend, Tibetan National Congress Founder Jamyang Norbu readI Will Burn Myself Again and Againby the Tibetan Amdo poet Zung Chu Kyi. Written during the wave of Tibetan self-immolations that began in 2011, the poem mourned the destruction of Tibet’s land, language and culture while affirming an unwavering commitment to freedom and dignity. Its words echoed across Times Square as hundreds stood in silence while Norbu read the poem: This is my last testament written with my bloodBecause of necessity it is my goal to burn myself foreverSo let me accomplish this!” Representatives from other communities facing repression under the Chinese government emphasized that Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice resonated far beyond Tibet. Uyghur activist Rushan Abbas said Tibetans had inspired oppressed peoples around the world through their resilience and refusal to surrender their identity. “Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice must not be forgotten,” she said. “His message was not only for Tibetans; it was for every person who believes that human dignity is worth defending.” Enghebatu Togochog, Director of the Southern Mongolian Human Rights Information Center, remembered Lobga Rangzen as “a man of unwavering courage, compassion and conviction” who had stood beside other oppressed peoples at protests and demonstrations for years. Calling his self-immolation “a desperate call for humanity not to look away,” he expressed hope that the world would eventually confront Chinese colonialism and authoritarian expansion before it is too late. Hong Kong democracy activist Alex Chow, Tibet Action Institute founder Lhadon Tethong, son of late Taktser Rinpoche Kunga Norbu, and New York Assemblymembers Steven Raga and Catalina Cruz also called on supporters to continue Lobga Rangzen’s struggle by fighting for Tibet and ensuring that the sacrifices of Tibet’s self-immolators are never forgotten. The evening’s vigil included acts of devotion and nonviolent protest that transformed New York City into a powerful expression of solidarity with Tibet. Tibetan youth volunteers performing full-body prostrations from Brooklyn Bridge arrive in Times Square to honor Pawo Lobga Rangzen on Aug. 1, 2026. Throughout the day, Tibetan youth volunteers performed full-body prostrations from the Brooklyn Bridge to Times Square, while Tibetan students staged a performative die-in representing the more than 170 Tibetans who have self-immolated in protest against China’s occupation of Tibet. Tibetan children from the DC Capital Area Tibetan Association also paid tribute by reading the names of the over 170 Tibetan activists who had self-immolated in protest against China’s rule of Tibet. Following the vigil, hundreds of participants marched peacefully from Times Square to United Nations Headquarters – the site where Lobga Rangzen tragically self-immolated on July 2. Wearing white ceremonial scarves over their mouths, the marchers created a striking visual symbol of both the voices silenced inside Tibet and the silence of the international community in the face of China’s repression. ICT leadership speaks with local Tibetan community members at the memorial site outside UN, New York on Aug. 1, 2026. ICT Chair Gere, President Gyatso, and Executive Director Fioresi also visited the memorial outside UN Headquarters, where Tibetans have maintained a continuous, round-the-clock vigil at the site where Lobga Rangzen self-immolated one month earlier. There, the ICT leadership honored the late activist by offering flowers,katag, and butter lamps. As they met with Tibetans keeping vigil at the memorial, Gere and the ICT leadership reaffirmed their commitment to the Tibetan cause. The vigil participants expressed their gratitude to Gere for his decades of steadfast support and advocacy for Tibet. A young community member offers a candle at the memorial site. As thousands walked toward the United Nations carrying candles and Tibetan flags, the message that echoed throughout the evening – from Richard Gere, Lobga Rangzen’s family, Tibetan leaders and allied human rights defenders – was unmistakable: the greatest tribute to Lobga Rangzen would be carrying forward his life’s work together, united in ensuring that every Tibetan can proudly say, “ང་བོད་པ་ཡིན། I am Tibetan.”

title: Tibetan monk remains in critical condition two years after suffering abuse by Chinese authorities over Derge dam protest, reflecting broader pattern of torture in custody
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Two years after his detention for opposing China’s controversial hydropower dam project in eastern Tibet, a Tibetan monk from Yena Monastery remains in critical condition at a hospital in Chengdu after being tortured by Chinese authorities while in custody, sources told the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT). Gonpo Tsering’s case reflects a broader pattern of torture and abuse of Tibetans in Chinese custody. As documented in a recent ICT report titled ‘Justice Denied: The Patterns of Deaths In and After Custody in Tibet,’ torture, denial of medical care and the absence of accountability are systemic features of China’s detention system in Tibet, with detainees released only after their health had deteriorated beyond recovery. Tibetan monk Gonpo Tsering of Yena Monastery, Derge county remains in critical condition two years after suffering abuse by Chinese authorities over Derge dam protest. Gonpo Tsering, 46, among the administrators of Yena Monastery in Derge (Chinese: Dege) county in Sichuan province, was detained after Chinese authorities accused him of helping lead theFebruary 2024 protests againstChina’s planned construction of the Kamtok (Gangtuo) hydropower dam. Local Tibetans and monks opposed the project, which threatened to destroy centuries-old monasteries, including the Yena and Wonto Monasteries, and inundate several villages and sacred religious sites. Following his arrest, Chinese authorities subjected Gonpo Tsering to severe physical abuse and torture while in custody. Because of this, he was rushed to West China (Huaxi) Hospital in Chengdu, where he has remained in critical condition for two years, sources said. Sources also told ICT that Gonpo Tsering is currently bedridden, unable to stand or speak, and is fed through tubes. He is unresponsive to family members and unable to recognize people around him. Devastated by his son’s detention and condition, his father, Lobsang Dorjee, passed away on Sep. 21, 2025. Despite the severity of his injuries, the Chinese government has provided no financial assistance for his medical care, said sources. Instead, authorities maintain strict and constant surveillance at the hospital, restricting visitors, monitoring those caring for him, and prohibiting photos or videos from being taken or shared, sources told ICT. Gonpo Tsering’s condition reflects key findings in ICT’s “Justice Denied” report: that detention in Tibet can itself become life-threatening and that the Chinese authorities’ abuse of Tibetans in custody does not end with their torture but extends well beyond their detention. Families are frequently denied information about the injuries sustained by detained relatives, independent investigations are absent, and those seeking answers face intimidation and surveillance. His case also illustrates the continuing impunity enjoyed by those responsible for torture and other forms of abuse in custody. “Gonpo Tsering’s case is not an isolated incident. It is proof of a systemic pattern of arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearance, and impunity in Tibet that demands a coordinated international response,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “ICT urges governments to move beyond expressions of concern and press China to release all Tibetans arbitrarily detained for exercising their fundamental rights, account for those who have been disappeared, investigate allegations of torture, and grant independent UN experts meaningful access to Tibet,” she added. In mid-2024, Chinese courts sentenced Jamyang Lekshe, the head of Yena Monastery, to four years’ imprisonment at Ya’an Prison on charges of “gathering a crowd to disrupt public order.” (ICT sources) Chinese authorities had responded with a sweeping crackdown to the widespread protests against the dam construction in February 2024,arresting over 100 Tibetansat the time, including Gonpo Tsering. In mid-2024, Chinese courts sentenced Jamyang Lekshe, the head of Yena Monastery, to four years’ imprisonment at Ya’an Prison on charges of “gathering a crowd to disrupt public order.”Gonpo Tsering was sentenced to three yearson similar charges, although his severe injuries from police abuse required him to seek emergency medical hospitalization. While reports indicate that construction on the Kamtok Dam and forced relocations have been paused, Chinese authorities are actively intimidating and imposing political demands on local monastic communities, sources told ICT. Monks at both Yena and Wonto monasteries are routinely forced to sign written pledges agreeing not to disrupt government construction projects and to strictly obey official directives. These campaigns reflect a broader effort by Chinese authorities to tighten political control over Tibetan Buddhist institutions and suppress peaceful expressions of environmental, religious, and cultural concern. Landscape view of Yena monastery, Derge (Chinese: Dege) county, Kardze (Ganzi) Tibet Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan. (ICT sources) The proposed Kamtok Dam ispart of a larger plan by the Chinese governmentto build 13 hydroelectric dams along the upper reaches of the Drichu (Yangtze) River. Nine of these border the Tibet Autonomous Region and Sichuan Province. The project bordering Derge and Jomda counties is primarily led by China Huadian Corp through a consortium of several state-backed entities, including China Huadian Group Co. Ltd. (48%), Tibet Development and Investment Group Co. Ltd. (20%), Sichuan Tietou Kangba Investment Co. Ltd. (20%), and Huadian International Power Co. Ltd. (12%). For Tibetans, opposition to these projects has extendedbeyond concerns about displacementand the threat to sacred sites that hold profound religious, cultural, and historical significance. The detention and torture of peaceful protesters such as Gonpo Tsering highlight the severe measures Chinese authorities employ to suppress opposition to development projects in Tibet and reinforce concerns about the broader pattern of human rights violations documented in ICT’sJustice Deniedreport.

title: China pressures Nepal over Tibetan studies conference as it expands control over Tibetology under new ethnic unity law
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: China has quietly pressed Nepal over an upcoming Tibetan studies conference in Kathmandu, just weeks after its new“Ethnic Unity and Progress Law”came into effect. This development is the latest sign that Beijing is expanding its campaign of transnational repression into academic discourse as part of its broader efforts to turn Tibetology into an ideological tool that reinforces the state’s vision of a unified Chinese national identity, while silencing scholarship that challenges its official narrative. According to media reports, the Dharamshala-based Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) has decided not to send its researchers in an official capacity to the17th Seminarof the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS), scheduled to be held August 23-29 in Kathmandu, to avoid jeopardizing the conference and to ease Chinese pressure on Nepal. The CTA had initially planned to send representatives from its think tank, the Tibet Policy Institute, but later decided towithdrawformal participation, following the concerns conveyed by Chinese officials to the Nepalese government. Inauguration of the Thrangu Rinpoche Academia Industry Block at Kathmandu University, April 15, 2026. (Image via Kathmandu University) In a meeting on July 21 with Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai, Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming raised China’s concerns about presumed statements critical of China. Citing a senior Nepalese foreign ministry official, theKathmandu Poston July 22 reported that the Chinese Ambassador raised concerns that “some individuals could speak against China and in support of Tibet and urged officials to make sure that no such things happen.” Although no formal diplomatic protest or written demand for cancellation was submitted, China’s démarche led to the withdrawal of CTA researchers. “The significance of this incident extends well beyond a single academic conference. Beijing is institutionalizing a system in which diplomacy, repressive domestic legislation implemented outside China’s borders, and state-directed academic scholarship reinforce one another,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “The newEthnic Unity and Progress Law, together with China’s efforts to recast Tibetology as a vehicle for ‘forging a strong sense of the Chinese national community,’ is designed to advance the forced assimilation of Tibetans while reshaping international understanding of Tibet. Global governments and academic institutions must recognize this as part of Beijing’s broader pattern to eliminate Tibetan identity and expand its transnational repression and call for therepeal of this repressive law,” she added. Nepal hosts a sizeable Tibetan refugee community, but more importantly, most of the Nepali citizens who hail from its northern region bordering Tibet share a common cultural and religious tradition with the Tibetan people. Historically, Tibetan Buddhist studies were central to the lives of these Nepali citizens. At the same time, Beijing has been exerting enormous pressure on Nepal to curb any activities it deems and characterizes as “pro-Tibet,” including Tibetan cultural and religious ceremonies, even to the point of denying the rights of Nepali citizens who follow Tibetan Buddhism. Even though it is an independent academic conference to which China itself sends delegates, Beijing’s latest intervention over the IATS seminar, therefore, fits a broader pattern of Chinese pressure on Nepal and efforts to control all international discussions on matters relating to Tibet. The International Association of Tibetan Studies (IATS) is a non-political academic associationformally foundedat the University of Oxford in 1979 after the first seminar at the Ethnographic Museum of the University of Zurich in June 1977. The association is dedicated to promoting research on Tibetan history, religion, linguistics, and arts. Its seminars, mostly held every three years, are widely regarded as the leading global forum on Tibetology. The 2026 seminar will be hosted for the first time in Nepal by Kathmandu University’s Himalaya Centre for Asian Studies (HiCAS) and the KU Centre for Buddhist Studies at Rangjung Yeshe Institute. Kathmandu University Center for Buddhist Studies at Rangjung Yeshe Institute. (Source: IATS) More than 700 scholars from about 39 countries, with a large delegation of around 100 from China, including from the China Tibetology Research Center, are expected to participate in the 17th seminar in Nepal, according toIndia Today. The opening is scheduled at Kathmandu University’s Dhulikhel campus, with main panels at Hotel Soaltee in Kathmandu. The reported participation of the state-controlled China Tibetology Research Center at an independent academic forum is a cause of major concern as the center has been mandated by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to drive a narrative that advances its forced assimilation agenda. This is consistent with Beijing’s efforts to use Tibetan studies as an instrument to advance CCP ideology, boost political legitimacy, and shape global narratives about Tibet. This shift was particularly evident last month when senior Chinese officials and state-controlled Tibetology scholars marked the40th anniversaryof the China Tibetology Research Center in Beijing on June 3, during which they cast state-led research as a key instrument in building “an independent knowledge system of Tibetan studies with Chinese characteristics.” Speakers repeatedly highlighted the need to “influence on Tibet-related matters” and boost China’s “international discourse power” on Tibet, underscoring how Tibetology is being positioned as a political and ideological tool rather than an arena for independent scholarship. At the symposium, United Front Work Department cadres and state-controlled academics stressed that Tibetan studies must be guided by “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era” and tasked with “forging a strong sense of the Chinese national community,” a central mission in China’s new “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law.” The new legislation, which came into effect on July 1, requires government agencies, educational institutions, religious organizations, enterprises and society at large to promote a unified Chinese national identity. Although framed as a milestone in academic development, the anniversary event showcased the extent to which Tibet-related research in China now functions primarily to reinforce official narratives and tighten state control over representations of Tibet. That same trend was on display earlier at the7th Beijing International Symposium on Tibetology, themed “Prosperity and Development of Tibetology and an Open Tibet,” held on Aug. 14, 2023, which revealed China’s manipulation of academic platforms to legitimize the CCP’s approach in Tibet. While presented as a scholarly exchange co-hosted by entities like the China Association for the Preservation and Development of Tibetan Culture, the 7th Beijing International Symposium on Tibetology masked its real objective of pushing forward a state-centric narrative under the guise of academic discourse. Speaking at the opening ceremony, Chinese state media quoted Chen Zongrong, Party Secretary and Deputy Director-General of the China Tibetology Research Center, as instructing Tibetan studies research institutions at home and abroad to establish academic platforms in various forms, carry out extensive exchanges and cooperation, and “contribute to building a community with a shared future for humankind,” mirroring language associated with the CCP’s key foreign policy messaging. At the same event, Li Decheng, Deputy Director-General of the China Tibetology Research Center, pushed forward thestate narrativeon Tibetan Buddhism’s reincarnation practice, stating that the recognition of the Dalai Lama is a prerogative of the Chinese government and not the 14th Dalai Lama and arguing that religious affairs are part of state affairs, and the management of religious affairs should be in accordance with state-promulgated laws. China’s reported pressure on Nepal over the IATS conference therefore represents more than a diplomatic objection to potential criticism. It illustrates the convergence of three parallel developments: Beijing’s growing willingness to project influence over any Tibet discourse abroad; the transformation of Tibetology into an instrument of Party ideology; and the institutionalization of Xi Jinping’s ethnic policy through the new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress. As Article 63 asserts jurisdiction over individuals outside of China deemed to undermine ethnic unity, and as state-directed Tibetology is increasingly tasked with strengthening China’s international discourse power, Beijing is attempting to extend its domestic governance framework into international academic spaces.

title: Rare Tibet visit by top CCP official Wang Huning signals push to enforce China’s new ethnic unity law, deepen forced assimilation policies
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Wang Huning, one of the most senior Chinese Communist Party leaders, made a rare visit to Tibet, just weeks after Beijing’s newEthnic Unity and Progress Lawcame into effect on July 1, signaling China’s determination to accelerate implementation of the law that provides the legal framework for deeper assimilation, ideological control, and security governance across Tibet. Wang Huning made a rare visit to Tibet from July 19-22, 2026. Wang is seen here on July 21during his visit to a village in Tsamdha (Zanda) County in Ngari Prefecture. (Source: Chinese state media) Wang Huning, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee and Chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), made the visit to Tibet from July 19-22, 2026, conducting inspections at the capital city of Lhasa and surrounding areas like Ngari. During his visit, according to Chinese state media, Wang emphasized that the core governance priorities in Tibet must focus on the implementation of the new ethnic unity law and on accelerating efforts toSinicize Tibetan Buddhismas well on ensuring “social stability maintenance,” a term Beijing uses to refer to a system of policies and security measures established to suppress dissent. “We must ensure the effective implementation of theLaw on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, improve the ability and level of governing ethnic affairs according to law, and promote the meaning of ethnic unity and progress in all development. In accordance with the requirements of systematically promoting the Sinicization of religion in my country and strengthening the rule of law in religious affairs, we must continuously guide Tibetan Buddhism to adapt to socialist society,” Wang repeatedly emphasized during his tour, according to Chinese state media. Wang’s visit comes mere weeks after Tibetan activistLobga Rangzen self-immolatedoutside the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2, a day after China’s enactment of the new ethnic unity law. As the Party’s chief ideologue and one of Xi Jinping’s political advisers, Wang’s inspections are closely watched as they indicate the Party leadership’s highest policy priorities. “Wang Huning’s visit underscores Beijing’s continued reliance on increasingly sophisticated legal and political mechanisms to accelerate its forced assimilation policies in Tibet. Coming just weeks after theEthnic Unity and Progress Lawtook effect, this high-level inspection and Wang’s repeated emphasis on ‘ethnic unity’ throughout his visit demonstrates the high priority the Chinese government places on institutionalizing policies aimed at erasing Tibetan identity under the guise of ethnic unity,” said International Campaign for Tibet President Tencho Gyatso. “The international community and governments should recognize this law for what it is — a dangerous legal framework designed to undermine and ultimately erase Tibet’s distinct language, religion, culture and identity — andmust call on China to repeal it,” she added. Wang Huning during his July 19-22, 2026 visit to Tibet, where he conducted inspections in Lhasa and other surrounding areas in Ngari. (Source: Chinese state media) During Wang’s latest July 2026 visit — which included inspections of Sera Monastery in Lhasa and Tholing Monastery, one of the oldest monasteries in Ngari Prefecture — authorities imposed severe security restrictions, sources told ICT. Wang also inspected a ‘xiaokang’ or border village, and other villages in surrounding counties of Purang, Tsamdha (Zanda), and Gar. Main roads were cordoned off, public movement was strictly limited, and security checkpoints were heavily reinforced across Lhasa and Ngari, sources told ICT. In Ngari, local authorities went so far as to ban pilgrims from visiting the sacred Mount Kailash during the visit, they added. During this visit, Wang stressed on the need to secure and develop the border regions, where China has prioritized building ‘dual purpose’ (civilian-military) villages to advance its expansionist objectives in the region. In line with the CCP’s ongoing efforts to reshape historical narratives and portray Tibet as an integral part of China ‘since ancient times,’ he called on local authorities to “… strengthen the protection and utilization of Tibetan historical documents, archaeological artifacts, and cultural relics, showcasing the historical process of exchanges, interactions, and integration among ethnic groups and demonstrating the vastness and brilliance of Chinese civilization.” Wang — who was accompanied by United Work Front Department Head Li Ganjie — also called for intensified propaganda aimed at “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation,” promoting the construction of “a national model area for ethnic unity and progress,” and deepening the creation of such model areas. His directives reflect another requirement under the new ethnic unity law, particularly Article 56, which mandates publicity about the law and designates the fourth week of September every year as the national propaganda week for the new law. Visits to Tibet by members of the Politburo Standing Committee generally occur when Beijing is reinforcing major political initiatives or strategic priorities in the region. For example, during Wang’s priorTibet visits in 2023 and 2024, he promoted Xi Jinping’s “new era” strategy for governing Tibet and emphasized ethnic unity, border security, and the Sinicization of Tibetan Buddhism.

title: Tibetan American students put leadership into action through ICT’s Tibetan Youth Leadership Program
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Fourteen Tibetan American students put their newly acquired advocacy and leadership skills into practice as they met with congressional offices on Capitol Hill to advocate for theAssuring the Future of Tibet Act (H.R. 8982)during the International Campaign for Tibet’s (ICT) 2026 Tibetan Youth Leadership Program, held July 11–18 in Washington, DC. The 2026 cohort of ICT’s Tibetan Youth Leadership Program. Following advocacy training, lobbying simulations, and communications workshops as part of ICT’s program, the 14 Tibetan American undergraduate and graduate students advocated at the offices of their elected representatives for the bipartisan legislation, introduced in the House of Representatives by Representatives Jim McGovern (D-MA) and Michael McCaul (R-TX), which would elevate the US government’s engagement with the Central Tibetan Administration and strengthen long-term US support for Tibet. By the end of the week, participants left Washington with a deeper understanding of the American political process, stronger advocacy and communication skills, and firsthand experience engaging with policymakers and advocates who help shape US policy on Tibet. “ICT’s Tibetan Youth Leadership Program gave me the confidence to step into leadership in ways I hadn’t before,” said Tenzin Rigden, a member of the 2026 Tibetan Youth Leadership Program cohort and a student at Penn State University. “Working alongside other Tibetan students challenged me to take initiative, whether it was helping organize our group or speaking up during discussions. I hope to use what I’ve learned to mentor younger Tibetans, encourage civic engagement, and help others better understand the policies and issues that affect our community.” ICT’s 2026 TYLP cohort at the Human Rights Watch office in Washington, DC. Established in 2001, ICT’s Tibetan Youth Leadership Program brings emerging leaders into direct conversation with policymakers, advocates, scholars, journalists and Tibetan community leaders while building practical skills in communications, civic engagement and public service. “One of the most powerful aspects of the Tibetan Youth Leadership Program is witnessing young Tibetan American students discover how their identities and lived experiences can become a powerful source of leadership and advocacy,” said ICT Executive Director Ryan Fioresi. “Leadership takes many forms, and each of these students have a meaningful role to play in contributing to and advancing the Tibetan cause.” The week began with foundational conversations on the history of the Tibetan movement, particularly in the United States, and the challenges facing Tibet today. At the Office of Tibet, students met with Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama to North America Dr. Namgyal Choedup and staff to learn about the work of the Central Tibetan Administration and its engagement with Tibetan communities across North America. Former ICT President John Ackerly shares his photos from the 1987 protests in Tibet. Sessions with ICT founding President Tenzin Namgyal Tethong, ICT’s Head of Research and Monitoring Unit Bhuchung K. Tsering, and educational sociologist and Tibet expert Dr. Gyal Lo deepened participants’ understanding of the evolution of the Tibetan movement, encouraged them to explore the power of their own identities as Tibetan Americans, and examined the impact of China’s policies on Tibetan language, education, and the larger Tibetan society. Throughout the week, participants met with individuals whose careers have advanced the cause of Tibet through human rights advocacy, grassroots activism, journalism, and diplomacy. Former ICT President John Ackerly reflected on his introduction to Tibet during the 1987 protests in Lhasa and his decades-long of advocacy for Tibet, while American student activist Thomas King Jackson, who is completing a‘1,000 Miles for Tibet’ walking initiative to create awareness about Tibet, shared how his grassroots activism has introduced new audiences to the Tibetan cause, even as he strives to find the right balance between being an activist and a student. Students exploring the Tibetan collection at the US Library of Congress. Students also explored broader human rights challenges through discussions with rights advocates and experts such as Chinese Human Rights Defenders Co-Executive Director Sophie Richardson, Hong Kong activist Joey Siu, and Chinese activist Sophie Luo. At Human Rights Watch, participants explored the organization’s work documenting and responding to human rights violations across Asia. A visit to the Library of Congress introduced students to one of the world’s largest collections of Tibetan materials, where Tibetan and Mongolian specialist Susan Meinheit highlighted the Library’s efforts tohelp preserve Tibetan language and history. The program also featured engagements with Tibetan media professionals, journalists, and Tibetans working in public service, offering participants insight into the many ways they can contribute to their communities and the larger Tibetan movement. One of the defining features of TYLP is the opportunity for participants to gain practical real-world advocacy experience. Groups present findings during a workshop. Following a workshop on communications and media led by ICT Director of Strategic Communications Tenzin Pema, students also completed advocacy training and lobbying simulations before taking those skills to Capitol Hill for constituent meetings with congressional offices. For many participants, these meetings marked their first experience in engaging directly with the offices of their elected representatives. In these meetings, they discussed the importance of continued bipartisan support for Tibet and urged members of Congress to support theAssuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026, and call for the repeal of China’s recently implemented Ethnic Unity and Progress Law. TYLP participants prepare for their next meeting. The week concluded with a visit to the US Department of State, where participants met with officials covering Tibet, Nepal, and Bhutan to discuss US policy on Tibet, and share their own perspectives as Tibetan Americans. A diplomacy simulation facilitated by the National Museum of American Diplomacy challenged the young Tibetan leaders to negotiate, build consensus, and navigate competing priorities in a realistic diplomatic environment. From congressional offices and the US State Department to discussions with advocates and trainings and workshops, ICT’s TYLP program offered the participants a firsthand experience of how civic engagement, public service, and advocacy intersect in shaping US policy on Tibet. The Tibetan Youth Leadership Program is part of ICT’sLodi Gyari Tibetan Empowerment Program, which includes a suite of initiatives designed to strengthen Tibetan leadership and empower Tibetans to protect Tibetan culture and identity and advocate for their rights and future. AsChina continues to intensify its repression in Tibet, Tibetan American advocacy has become crucial to advancing US support for the Tibetan movement. Thanks in part to the sustained advocacy by Tibetan Americans, the US government has responded to China’s rights violations in Tibet by signing into law the Resolve Tibet Act in 2024, which reinforces US policy on Tibet and directs the State Department to counter the Chinese government’s disinformation campaign on Tibet. The US also passed theReciprocal Access to Tibet Act in 2018, which authorized the State Department todeny entry to Chinese officials responsible for restricting accessto Tibet for American diplomats, journalists, and ordinary citizens. The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) is a nonprofit organization that promotes human rights and democratic freedoms for the people of Tibet. Through advocacy, education, and outreach, ICT works to safeguard the unique culture and identity of the Tibetan people. For more information, visitwww.savetibet.orgor contactinfo@savetibet.org.

title: During Captive Nations Week, ICT urges US Congress to pass the ‘Assuring the Future of Tibet Act’ and call for the repeal of China’s ethnic unity law
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: As the US commemorates Captive Nations Week from July 19-25, the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) calls on the US Congress to reaffirm the United States’s longstanding bipartisan support to the Tibetan people by passing the‘Assuring the Future of Tibet Act’ (AFTA). ICT also calls on the US government to publicly condemn China’s repressivenew ‘Ethnic Unity and Progress Law’ (EUPL), a sweeping measure that seeks to institutionalize the forced assimilation of Tibetans and other non-Chinese peoples. Captive Nations Week was established by the US Congress in 1959 and proclaimed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower to recognize nations living under communist and authoritarian regimes and to reaffirm America’s support for their aspirations for freedom, self-determination, and human dignity. Tibet was among the original captive nations recognized by Congress in July 1959 in a declaration made only months after China’s brutal suppression of the Tibetan National Uprising on March 10, 1959 and His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s escape into exile. More than six decades later, Tibet remains one of the world’s longest-running struggles, making the principles behind Captive Nations Week as relevant today as they were in 1959. “Captive Nations Week reminds us that freedom cannot be taken for granted and calls on America to stand consistently with people who are denied their fundamental rights and act in solidarity with those who continue to defend it,” said Tencho Gyatso, President of the International Campaign for Tibet. “For more than sixty years, Tibet has symbolized the resilience of a people determined to preserve their identity and the cost of the world’s failure to confront authoritarian repression. Passing the‘Assuring the Future of Tibet Act’would reaffirm America’s enduring support for the Tibetan people’s democratically elected leadership, while a clear condemnation of China’s ‘Ethnic Unity and Progress Law’ would send an unmistakable message to Beijing that forced assimilation has no place in the twenty-first century,” she added. This year’s Captive Nations Week observance comes just weeks after Beijing’s new“Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” (EUPL)came into force on July 1. The law codifies and expands China’s longstanding policies of forced assimilation targeting Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, and other non-Chinese peoples. The EUPL promotes Chinese-language education and dominance, ideological conformity, restrictions on religious practice, and expanded state authority over education and culture while extending Beijing’s reach beyond its borders through provisions that raise concerns about transnational repression. The US Congress has already demonstratedstrong bipartisan leadership in condemning this lawand calling for its repeal. Lawmakers have introduced bipartisan Senate legislation condemning the EUPL and warning of its impact on not just Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, Hong Kongers, Taiwanese, and Chinese dissidents, but also on American citizens and organizations for actions deemed by the Chinese government to be harming “ethnic unity.” In addition, abipartisan group of House members recently urged US Secretary of State Marco Rubioto publicly condemn the law as a tool of forced assimilation, ideological control, and transnational repression while coordinating with allies to challenge it internationally. ICT welcomes these important Congressional measures but stresses that additional action remains urgently needed. ICT calls on the US administration to publicly condemn the EUPL, raise it in bilateral engagements with Beijing, coordinate multilateral opposition through the United Nations and like-minded governments, strengthen protections against transnational repression, and expand support for Tibetan language, religion, education, and cultural preservation. This year’s Captive Nations Week also provides a reminder that at a time when Beijing continues to intensify its campaign to erase Tibetan identity, bipartisan leaders in the US Congress have responded with important bipartisan initiatives that deserve swift action. TheAssuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026, (H.R. 8982), introduced in the House of Representatives by Representatives James P. McGovern (D-MA) and Michael McCaul (R-TX), would empower the US government to elevate its engagement with and recognition of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) as the democratically elected representative of the Tibetan people and to ensure that US policy supporting Tibet continues beyond the lifetime of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama. “At a time when Beijing has abandoned any pretense of offering autonomy for Tibetans and refuses to engage in dialogue with the Tibetan side, the United States needs to take a bold step forward in defense of freedom and democracy for the Tibetan people. This bill answers that call,” said ICT President Gyatso when AFTA was introduced. The legislation reflects the bipartisan consensus that America’s support for Tibet must continue across generations by recognizing and supporting the Tibetan people’s democratic institutions, aspirations, and internationally recognized human rights. ICT urges both chambers of Congress to advance and pass the legislation without delay and encourages lawmakers to support its Senate companion legislation. This year’s Captive Nations Week also carries profound significance as it comes just weeks after the death of Tibetan activistLobsang Palden, widely known as Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2, one day after the EUPL went into effect. Lobga Rangzen’s tragic passing marked the first Tibetan self-immolation on US soil. Since 2009, there have been over170 Tibetan self-immolations both inside Tibet and in exilethat reflect the extraordinary lengths to which Tibetans have gone to defend their identity, religion, language, and homeland in the face of relentless repression. title: Famed Larung Gar Buddhist academy in eastern Tibet faces new round of demolitions
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: A2016 file photoof Larung Gar Buddhist Academy at night. A new round of demolitions that will impact at least 1060 residences of monks and nuns has begun atSerthar Larung Five Sciences Buddhist Academy, popularly known as Larung Gar, in eastern Tibet in Serthar (Chinese: Seda), Kardze (Ganzi) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, in Sichuan province, a source with knowledge of the matter told the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT). ICT is concerned that this latest round of demolitions at one of the largest Tibetan Buddhist centers in the world represents a further tightening of restrictions of religious practice and comes amid an escalation in the Chinese government’s coercive assimilation policies in Tibet after China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Law went into effect on July 1. The demolitions began around July 13, 2026 and are being carried out at nighttime, the source said, in what is seen as a move by authorities to evade public documentation, reporting, and satellite surveillance. As of July 15, 2026, six residences have been demolished, said the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals. Authorities have earmarked at least 1,060 residences of monks and nuns for demolition as part of this latest round of demolitions, the source told ICT. Given the strict control of information, the source could not provide more details, including on the reasoning given by authorities for the demolitions. Earlier this year, a traveler to Serthar, where Larung Gar is located, confirmed this in a vlog in Chinese saying, “Let me briefly summarize the biggest changes in Serthar in 2026. The one word that stands out to me is restrictions. There are restrictions everywhere: restrictions on where you can go, restrictions on how long you can stay, and even restrictions on the operating hours of the shuttle buses. Altogether, these measures don’t make the experience particularly visitor friendly.” Screenshot of a video posted by a traveler to Larung Gar in 2026, in which he confirmed the tight restrictions in Serthar. Since 2001,Chinese authorities have repeatedly targeted Larung Gar for demolitions, forcing monks, nuns, and lay practitioners to leave and destroying vast swaths of living quarters in an effort to severely reduce the size of the center, which wasfounded by the late charismatic Tibetan Buddhist master, Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok. Founded in 1980 to revive Buddhist scholarship and meditation in the wake of Mao Zedong’s turbulent Cultural Revolution, Larung Gar grew in size and reputation over the decades as one of the most influential centers for the study of Tibetan language, culture and religion, attracting thousands of Chinese Buddhist practitioners in addition to Tibetans. An undated photo of Larung Garwith large empty space made vertically by demolitions carried out by Chinese authorities. In 2001, Chinese authorities forcibly downsized Larung Gar by half through demolishing the dwellings of the then estimated 8,000 monks and nuns, including Chinese practitioners. Thereafter, the Academy was able to recover from the demolitions and undertake some of its activities, despite continued restrictions imposed in the movement of Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok. However, in 2016 and 2017, close to 5,000 dwellings were demolished again, with the then-10,000 resident population halved in accordance with a central government order, a copy of which was obtained and translated by Human Rights Watch. About 5,000 monks and nuns were evicted at the time. InFebruary 2017, six UN experts reported that they had made a joint submission to China stating that the developments at Larung Gar violate international human rights law and “seem to be concerted attacks on tangible and intangible cultural heritage, which constitute serious violations of cultural rights of current and future generations.” This map is intended to show the location of Larung Gar and does not equate Tibet with only the Tibet Autonomous Region as Tibet includes Tibetan areas in Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu, and Yunnan as well. Sincemid-2019, Chinese authorities have also resorted to measures aimed at mitigating the influence of Tibetan religious leaders and restricting activitiesof Larung Gar by imposing restrictions on the participation of Chinese students in the academy. As a result, the once-burgeoning Chinese practitioner population has trickled to a minuscule number. This campaign was further bolstered in November 2021, withcoercive separations of Chinese Buddhist practitioners from others. Witharound 30 to 40 Han Chinese with semi-permanent residencesat Larung Gar in 1991, the number grew to an informal quota of around 2,000 Han Chinese monks and nuns in residence among the academy’s roughly 5,000 practitioners — after the government’s ceiling to halve the earlier 10,000 practitioners — in recent years. In addition to imparting Buddhist teachings to the Chinese practitioners in Larung Gar, Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok had been giving teachings in many cities across China. The Khenpo had also traveled abroad in the early 1990s, including to India where he met with His Holiness the Dalai Lama. However, since the mid-1990s, Chineseauthorities had denied him permission to travel abroad until he passedon January 7, 2004 in Chengdu, Sichuan province at the age of 70. “Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok worked very hard for the preservation and promotion of the unique religious faith of all Tibetans,”Lodi Gyari, then Special Envoy of the Dalai Lama, said at the time.

title: ICT remembers and honors Sigrid Joss-Arnd, a lifelong friend of the Tibetan people
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: The International Campaign for Tibet extends its heartfelt condolences to the family and friends of Ms. Sigrid Joss-Arnd, whose recent passing marks the loss of a lifelong friend of the Tibetan people who dedicated her life to providing critical support for Tibetans in exile and leading humanitarian projects inside Tibet. Arecipient of ICT’s 2013 Light of Truth Award, Ms. Joss-Arnd dedicated more than six decades to supporting Tibetan refugees, helping transform the lives of generations of Tibetan children and families. Ms. Sigrid Joss-Arnd receiving ICT’s 2013 Light of Truth Award from His Holiness the Dalai Lama, in recognition of the contribution of her organization, the Swiss Red Cross, in providing critical support to Tibetans in exile as for its humanitarian projects in Tibet. In recognition of her exceptional service, His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama presented Ms. Joss-Arnd withICT’s Light of Truth Awardin 2013. Accepting the award with much humility, she concluded her remarks with words that captured her enduring devotion to Tibet: “May His Holiness be blessed. May the Tibetans in Tibet be blessed. May the Tibetans in exile be blessed. And may they all be reunited soon.” Those heartfelt words continue to resonate today, reflecting the compassion, hope, and solidarity that defined her life and work. ICT honors Ms. Joss-Arnd’s extraordinary legacy and extends our deepest condolences to her family, loved ones, colleagues, and all who were privileged to know her. Her kindness, generosity, and steadfast friendship and support of the Tibetan people will never be forgotten.

title: Lhasa conference signals escalation in China’s efforts to institutionalize AI-enabled narrative control on Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: China’sSecond Tibet International Communication Conference, convened in Lhasa on June 16, 2026, represents a significant escalation in the Chinese state’s efforts to institutionalize and technologize its official narrative on Tibet, as provisioned in the new Ethnic Unity and Progress Law. The conference outlined an integrated system that combines the use of emotional storytelling, artificial intelligence, historical revisionism, and institutional coordination to “proactively” shape the global narrative on Tibet, operationalizing several provisions of the new law. While framed under the benign theme of “Understanding and Support, Empathy and Connection,” the conference advanced a sophisticated framework, designed to stage a highly managed, “proactive” propaganda system that seeks not merely to defend official positions but to dominate the global conversation and hide China’s human rights abuses in Tibet. The second Tibet International Communication Conference in session at Lhasa on June 16, 2026. A central focus of the conference was the move toward “narrative innovation,” specifically through the use of “cross-cultural empathy.” Li Yafang, president of the Academy of Contemporary China and World Studies, explicitly argued that effective communication requires illustrating developments through “ordinary people’s experiences”. By focusing on curated “authentic details” and individual anecdotes of “solidarity,” the Chinese state seeks to create an emotionally persuasive alternative reality of Tibet that resonates with the international community while bypassing scrutiny. This approach is legally provisioned under Article 19 of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law (EUPL), which stipulates that “News media such as newspapers, radio, and television, as well as publishing units and online providers, shall carry out work such as publicity reporting and presentations of the accomplishments of forging a strong sense of the community of the Chinese people and advancing the establishment of the community of the Chinese people”. This approach aligns withParty Secretary Wang Junzheng’s directive, issued in adherence with Article 2 of the EUPL, that “the Tibet International Communication Conference is an important measure to implement Xi Jinping’s thought on culture, his important instructions on Tibet-related work, and the Party’s strategy for governing Tibet in the new era.” Wang’s instruction reveals that “empathy” is intended not as a means of achieving mutual understanding, but as a propaganda tool to create favorable international sentiment for the Chinese state’s governance strategy. Yang Dezhi, editor-in-chief of China’s Tibet magazine, stated that the responsibility of the current era is to “break through false narratives” by grounding communication in “historical and legal reasoning”. This strategy aims to move beyond “passive responses” to external criticism by proactively using state manufactured “historical facts and evidence” to shape international public opinion around the official CCP narrative. For instance, in mid-May, Sonam Nyima, the Minister of the United Front Work Department of the Tibet Autonomous Region, during aninspection tourof four Tibetan counties in Ngari (Ali) near the India-Tibet boundary, called for archaeological research to be used to promote a history of Tibet’s integration with the “motherland.” Similarly, Li Ganjie, the head of the CCP Central Committee’s United Front Work Department, during the40th anniversary of the China Tibetology Research Centerheld in Beijing on June 2, instructed the state-controlled “Tibetologists” to produce research that would “prove” the state’s official narrative that “Tibet is an integral part of China” and that Tibetan “folk culture” is part of Chinese culture. To provide a veneer of international objectivity, the recent Tibet International Communication conference highlighted “foreign experts” who validated the state’s narrative. For instance, Chinese state mediaGlobal Timescarried visuals of Indian Professor Manukonda Rabindranath stating that his observations of Tibet were “completely different” from Western media reports. Similarly, Nepali Professor Kundan Aryal said that “Xizang Province [sic] is not less than any modern city of the world,” while Sri Lankan academic Gayan Madushanka said “some western countries make narratives to push down Asian countries.” Such testimonials are integral to Beijing’s strategy of using international voices to lend credibility to a system that is, at its core, a top-down implementation of national diplomatic goals. Perhaps the most significant aspect of the conference was its focus on “technological empowerment,” which is provided for in Article 31 of the EUPL. Participants explored how emerging technologies can be leveraged to improve effectiveness of communication in an “algorithm-driven era”. This includes the use of “AI and new means” to reshape the communication landscape and establish “scientific mechanisms” for evaluating how well state messages are being received. This focus on technology suggests a shift toward targeted audience segmentation which utilizes foreign content creators. Officials called for “regionalized, segmented, and precise expression” to meet the specific needs of diverse overseas audiences. By utilizing “new media technologies” and “international content co-creation,” most likely with foreign propagandist hires like Daniel Dumbrill, Andy Boreham, Jason Smith, the state aims to saturate global digital spaces with its preferred narratives, effectively using algorithms to amplify state-approved voices while marginalizing authentic Tibetan voices. The conference also served to formalize a network of “coordinated participation” and consolidation of the propaganda platforms spreading misinformation on Tibet. The signing of the “Framework Agreement on Coordinated Cooperation for International Communication on Xizang” by ten organizations which includes the China International Communications Group (CICG), as provisioned in Article 17 of the EUPL, signals a move toward a centralized propaganda industry. This institutional consolidation is bolstered by the appointment of seven “Think Tank” experts and the formal unveiling of the “China Today Xizang Salon,” creating a self-reinforcing echo chamber of compliant academics and regime-friendly media operatives. The “Salon,” presented as a “dedicated platform for regular international cultural exchanges,” has already been launched in nine cities in China and abroad, including in Cairo, Egypt and Madrid, Spain. With this formal unveiling of the “China Today Xizang Salon” in Lhasa, a proliferation of similar “salons” is expected in the coming years. The Second Tibet International Communication Conference serves as a blueprint for a new era of narrative management. By combining “human-centric” storytelling with aggressive historical revisionism and leveraging Chinese techno-feudalism, the Chinese state is attempting to construct an emotionally persuasive “Xizang story” in line with President Xi Jinping’s directive to “tell a good Chinese story.” However, the party-state’s efforts to shape international public opinion on Tibet has thus far fallen short of their objectives. Acknowledging this, Ye Hailin of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences lamented in his keynote speech that, “International communication efforts regarding Xizang have faced a challenge. Even with plenty of facts and figures to share, we still find it hard to shake deep-rooted stereotypes and show the world the real picture.” The fact remains that ultimately, no amount of financial investment, narrative engineering, or propaganda sophistication has succeeded in obscuring the reality and truth of Tibet. In an age of global connectivity, facts prove far more resilient than lies. Timeline of the Development of China’s organized external propaganda system on Tibet:

title: UPDATE: Tibetan Activists Released After Arrest at UN Headquarters
author: tselhamo26
content: New York, NY—Three Tibetan youth activists were released from New York City’s 17th precinct. They were arrested yesterday on charges of “disorderly conduct” and “refusal to disperse” after chaining themselves to the vehicular entrances and exits of the United Nations (UN) headquarters on First Avenue. The three activists, Tsela Zoksang, Tenzin Kunchok, and Tenzin Tseten, are demanding the UN take action after the self-immolation of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen. The activists successfully blocked the UN entrance and exit, forcing official UN vehicles to wait on the street as activists chanted for a free Tibet. After around 45 minutes, the activists were arrested and taken into custody. Their action was accompanied by a peaceful protest outside the UN by hundreds of Tibetans and allied New Yorkers. A week after Lobga Rangzen’s death, the UN still has not taken any significant steps to honor Lobga’s life or tackle human rights abuses in Tibet. In response, Tibetan activists and Tibetans around the world have stepped up efforts to press UN leaders to confront an issue they are attempting to ignore. Tsela Zoksang, the 22-year-old Tibetan activist arrested today, said: “One week ago today, Lobga Rangzen self-immolated to spread the message he dedicated his life to: that a free and independent Tibet is not only a possibility but a moral imperative for the global community. The Chinese government is doing everything in its power to silence people like Lobga. The newly-enacted “Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” is the latest example of China’s decades-long quest to eradicate Tibet’s people and culture. By refusing to condemn this law and taking no meaningful action to honor Lobga’s sacrifice, the United Nations is complicit in China’s severe human rights violations. We took action today to ensure that this complicity is broadcast to the world.”

title: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Tibetan Activists Arrested After Blockade at New York UN Headquarters Vehicular Gates
author: tselhamo26
content: New York, NY—At 3:25 p.m. EST, three Tibetan youth activists chained themselves to the vehicular exits and entrances of the United Nations (UN) headquarters gates on First Avenue, demanding action after the self-immolation of Tibetan independence activist, Lobga Rangzen. After 47 minutes chained to the UN vehicular entrance, all three activists have been arrested and are currently detained. As they were being taken into police custody, Tenzin Tseten said: “Lobga Rangzen loved Tibetan culture, and he believed our people had the right to be free. He did not give up his life, his family, and his community because he wanted Tibetans to be a well-behaved “minority” inside a Chinese empire. He did it to sound the alarm on China’s new so-called “Ethnic Unity” law—a law designed to legally erase Tibetan national identity. The United Nations has failed Lobga Rangzen, the United Nations has failed the Tibetan people, time and time again.” Even after the activists were taken away, a growing protest of Tibetan community members remained on site, calling on the UN to take action for Tibet.

title: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Tibetan Activists Blockade at UN Vehicular Gates, Seeking Justice for Lobga Rangzen
author: tselhamo26
content: New York, NY—At 3:25 p.m. EST, three Tibetan youth activists chained themselves to the vehicular exits and entrances of the United Nations (UN) headquarters gates on First Avenue, demanding action after the self-immolation of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen. One week after his death, the UN has yet to take any meaningful action to honor Lobga’s life and address human rights violations in Tibet. These activists have therefore taken action to pressure UN leaders to address an issue they are trying to sweep under the rug. The young protestors blocked the UN vehicular exits and entrances while holding signs reading “Volker Türk break your silence on Tibet,” and “Lobga Rangzen Lives, Free Tibet.” The activists, ranging in age from 19 to 28, were all Students for a Free Tibet activists or friends of Lobga; some are Tibetans born in the United States and others were born inside occupied Tibet. As of 4:05 p.m., the activists are still chained to UN entrance and police have not yet arrived on scene. All official UN vehicles are unable to gain access to the main headquarters building and UN security is on site. Police have been called to the site. As the chained activists continued to block traffic into and out of the UN, Tibetan community members began arriving at the scene for the daily protest since his self-immolation. Waving the Tibetan national flag and chanting “Free Tibet,” the protesters came to support the youth activists and honor Lobga’s life. While UN diplomats inside attempt to conduct “business as usual,” Tibetan activists and protesters are outside demanding that they end their silence on Tibet and censure Beijing’s genocidal new “Ethnic Unity” law. Tenzin Kunchok, Students for a Free Tibet Activist and friend of Lobga Rangzen, said: “My generation is completely done waiting for international bodies to find a backbone. If Volker Türk is too compromised to speak the truth, then we will be the ones to scream it. We refuse to let the UN use the vocabulary of the colonizer to keep its hands clean. The silence ends with us.” Tenzin Myinlek, Executive Director of Students for a Free Tibet, said: “Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice was a direct warning against China’s newly enacted “Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” a legislative death sentence, aiming for the extinction of the Tibetan people. We demand the UN and Volker Türk break their silence on Tibet. For young Tibetans around the world, this is the ultimate call to action. In this critical moment, the UN has failed Tibetans once again. We are taking matters into our own hands as Lobga Rangzen’s spirit lives on in every single one of us.”

title: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Hundred of Tibetans interrupt “BUSINESS AS USUAL” at United Nations Headquarters following Tibetan activist’s self immolation
author: tselhamo26
content: NEW YORK, NY—Hundreds of Tibetans staged a large-scale demonstration outside of the United Nations Headquarters, disrupting normal operations at UN Plaza, as the United Nations opened its doors for the first time since the self-immolation of 52-year-old Tibetan independence activist, Lobsang Palden, known widely as Lobga Rangzen. The demonstration featured a coordinated car procession that occupied First Avenue directly alongside the UN complex. Vehicles draped in Tibetan flags and “Free Tibet” banners lined the street, creating a continuous cacophony of honking that drew the attention of arriving diplomats, UN employees, and passersby. At the center of the demonstration was Lobga Rangzen’s hearse. Demonstrators, dressed inchubas(traditional Tibetan dress), lined the streets to pay their respects. On the evening of July 2, 2026, Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters, in protest of China’s occupation of Tibet. He is one of over 170 Tibetans to self-immolate against Chinese occupation. This act came one day after the July 1implementation of Beijing’s draconian new “Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” codifying China’s assimilation policies and criminalizing Tibetan identity. In a six-minute video message recorded hours before his death, Rangzen explicitly stated: “I don’t want you to mourn for me, I want you to continue the struggle for Tibetan independence, because the lack of independence is the root of all our problems.”“The historic turnout of the Tibetan community today shows that Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice has galvanized generations of Tibetans. While diplomats walk into these air-conditioned rooms to conduct routine bureaucracy, hundreds of us are standing on their doorstep to wake the world up. For 67 years, the Chinese government has tried to crush Tibetan identity, and they have failed time and time again. Now, they are trying to criminalize our existence entirely through the newly enacted “Ethnic Unity” law. We will not allow the UN to look the other way while Beijing legalizes the total erasure of our people. ” says Tenzin Myinlek, Executive Director of Students for a Free Tibet.
