title: Chinese Democracy Groups Hold Conference Condemning China’s “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”
author: OOT - DC
content: Flushing, N.Y., 6 Oct 2026: Overseas Chinese pro-democracy organisations held a forum in Flushing on Tuesday condemning Beijing’s recently implemented “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.” Coinciding with celebrations for the 115th anniversary of the Republic of China’s (Taiwan) “Double Ten” National Day, the event was organised by Beijing Spring magazine, the Chinese Alliance for Democracy, and the Executive Committee of the China Democracy Party. Organisers brought together overseas Chinese scholars, democracy activists, and independent journalists. Dr. Yu Dahai, publisher of Beijing Spring , hosted and opened the conference, followed by a keynote speech from Hu Ping, the magazine’s honorary editor-in-chief. More than 20 Chinese scholars and democracy activists spoke across five panel sessions. Prominent speakers included commentator Chen Pokong, lawyer Gao Guangjun, Xue Wei (president of the Tibet-China Friendship Group), and Chen Liqun (president of the Chinese Alliance for Democracy). Tsultrim Gyatso, Chinese liaison officer at the Office of Tibet in Washington, D.C., was also an invited speaker. In his keynote address, Hu Ping noted that while the law does not explicitly mention His Holiness the Dalai Lama or Tibetan Buddhism, its implications directly harm Tibetan identity by stripping Tibetans of core rights. He also highlighted a letter sent to Xi Jinping by a group of Chinese “princeling” leaders condemning the regime’s harsh policies toward ethnic minorities. Chen Liqun offered an apology to the communities directly affected by the law and denounced the Chinese Communist Party’s ruthless policies against Tibetans and other ethnic groups. Additional speakers argued that despite being framed as a measure to promote unity, the law instead reinforces the official narrative of mandatory “ethnic identity” and “national unification,” escalating political pressure and severely restricting the religious, cultural, and political activities of minority groups. They warned that non-Han individuals are in risk of being labeled separatists or terrorists simply for voicing grievances. Tsultrim Gyatso argued that the law achieves the exact opposite of its stated name. Rather than fostering unity, he stated, it strips ethnic minorities of their constitutional rights and codifies a Han-centered assimilation policy around the slogan “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” He traced the roots of assimilation in Tibet to the 1950 military invasion, noting that the “second-generation ethnic policy” advocated in the early 2000s by Chinese scholars such as Ma Rong, Hu Angang, and Hu Lianhe paved the way for this legislation, which took effect on July 1. Tsultrim Gyatso highlighted the dire circumstances facing over one million Tibetan children currently placed in state boarding schools, many of whom are systematically losing their mother tongue. He cited the 2 July self-immolation of Lobga Rangzen outside the United Nations—following approximately 170 previous cases—as a tragic act that drew renewed global attention to the crisis. He further stated that the law violates international human rights norms, the Chinese Constitution, and the Law on Regional Ethnic Autonomy, warning that Article 63 could be weaponised against Tibetans abroad and their supporters. Finally, he noted that in response to Article 56’s mandated “ethnic unity publicity week,” the Tibetan administration declared the last week of September as “Tibetan National Identity Observance Week,” which officially launched in 23 Sept 2026. The forum concluded with a unified condemnation of the law and an urgent call for the Chinese Communist Party to repeal it. World Journal , a major Chinese-language newspaper distributed across North America, subsequently published a report on the event. -Report filed by Office of Tibet, Washington DC

title: Sikyong Penpa Tsering Engages with Tibetan Youth and Students in Switzerland
author: OOT - DC
content: Zurich, Switzerland: Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) addressed and engaged with Tibetan youth and students residing in and around Switzerland during an interactive meeting held in the afternoon of 8 October 2026 at the Hilton Zurich Hotel. The event was organised by the Tibet Bureau Geneva, led by Representative Thinlay Chukki, in close collaboration and cooperation with the Tibetan Community of Switzerland and Liechtenstein. During the address, Sikyong provided an in-depth overview of the organisational framework, historical evolution, and key responsibilities of the Central Tibetan Administration. He detailed the distinct mandates of each CTA department, highlighting ongoing initiatives and welfare, educational, and digital programs designed to sustain the exile community and preserve Tibetan culture and identity. Turning to global developments, Sikyong underscored the critical geostrategic and ecological significance of the Tibetan plateau, discussing how current shifts in world geopolitics directly affect the Tibetan cause. He highlighted China’s expanding economic footprints and strategic influence in global markets, urging the younger generation to remain informed and vigilant in navigating these complex international dynamics. Emphasising youth-led international engagement, Sikyong stressed the vital importance of the Voluntary Tibet Advocacy Group (V-TAG). He noted that V-TAG serves as a primary, structured platform enabling young Tibetans in the diaspora to leverage their linguistic skills, professional expertise, and local network integration to advocate effectively for Tibet in host countries. The hour-and-a-half-long session concluded with an open Q&A interaction, where students and young professionals raised questions on policy direction, diaspora engagement, and future advocacy strategies. The interactive dialogue offered the young attendees renewed clarity and inspiration, reinforcing their shared commitment and responsibility toward the collective struggle for Tibet. ‘

title: The European Parliament’s New China Report Rebukes Beijing Over Tibet
author: OOT - DC
content: Brussels, 7 October 2026: In a highly significant report on EU-China relations, adopted on Wednesday by a landslide majority of 454 votes in favour, Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) have delivered a stinging rebuke of Beijing’s policies. Drafted by Rapporteur Hilde Vautmans on behalf of the European Parliament’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the comprehensive document strongly condemns China’s intensifying campaign of mandatory “Sinicisation” and forced assimilation in Tibet. The newly adopted text expresses deep concern over the systematic erosion of Tibet’s linguistic, cultural, and religious identity. Lawmakers sharply criticised Beijing’s systemic human rights violations, denouncing the demolition of cultural heritage, the implementation of mass surveillance, and the widespread use of forced labor. Of particular concern is directed at the state-run residential school system where nearly one million Tibetan children have been forcibly separated from their families and subjected to forced assimilation into the Han majority culture. Citing the alarming trauma of family separation and its devastating impact on traditional Tibetan language and customs, the report calls for the immediate abolition of this system. Furthermore, the European Parliament fiercely condemned Chinese state interference in Tibetan Buddhist religious affairs. The text explicitly opposes Beijing’s calculated political manoeuvres to control the succession and reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, emphasising that protecting religious autonomy is non-negotiable. Lawmakers also demanded immediate information regarding the whereabouts of the missing Panchen Lama. These targeted violations are framed within a broader, deeply concerning pattern of restrictions on religious freedom affecting communities operating outside state-controlled organisations across mainland China The severe extent of Beijing’s domestic information control was starkly illustrated following the deadly flash floods that struck the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August 2026. While the disaster caused mass casualties, Chinese authorities heavily underreported the death toll, scrubbed survivor accounts from social media, and penalised citizens for sharing information. The report highlights how this tight pattern of censorship directly obstructs accountability, fuelling urgent demands for Beijing to grant independent journalists and humanitarian groups immediate, unimpeded access to the affected areas. To counter China’s expanding reach of transnational repression, the report urges the European Union to consistently raise these human rights concerns at every political meeting with Chinese counterparts. Beyond economic diplomacy, the European Parliament insists that the protection of minority rights must become a central, binding element of future EU-China relations. Concurrently, the text calls for the immediate closure of all illegal, undercover “Chinese overseas police stations” operating within EU member states. The adoption of this report marks a decisive step in the European Parliament’s sustained scrutiny of Beijing, signalling a unified demand for the EU to maintain maximum pressure over the protection of Tibetan cultural and religious rights. Welcoming this timely report, Representative Rigzin Genkhang expressed deep gratitude to the European Parliament for consistently championing Tibetan rights. The final document closely reflects specific priorities put forward during the preparatory process, conveying the gravity of the situation on the ground. The full report is available here . – Report filed by Office of Tibet, Brussels

title: Sikyong Penpa Tsering Arrives in Zurich for Official Visit to Three European Countries
author: OOT - DC
content: Zurich, Switzerland, 8 October 2026: Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) arrived at Zurich Airport today, marking the beginning of an official visit to Switzerland, the Czech Republic, and Germany. Upon arrival, Sikyong was warmly received by the Representative and staff of the Tibet Bureau, Geneva, the President of the Tibetan Community of Switzerland, and representatives of local Tibetan associations and community members. During his visit to Switzerland, Sikyong is scheduled to hold a series of official meetings with various stakeholders, interact with members of the Tibetan community, and lead an interactive session with Tibetan youth. Following his engagements in Switzerland, Sikyong will travel to Prague, Czech Republic, to participate in the 30th Forum 2000 Conference, before proceeding to Germany for further high-level engagements. The three-nation visit forms part of the CTA’s ongoing international outreach to strengthen dialogue, raise awareness of the Sino-Tibet conflict among political leaders, policymakers, civil society organisations, and European stakeholders, and consolidate engagement with the Tibetan diaspora.

title: Kasur Jetsun Pema Honours with Prestigious Christmas Humphreys Award by The Buddhist Society, London
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: In recognition of her lifelong and transformative contribution to Tibetan education and child welfare, Kasur (former Minister) Jetsun Pema was conferred with the prestigious Christmas Humphreys Award by The Buddhist Society, UK , on the morning of 7 October 2026. The award was presented at a formal ceremony held at Hermann Gmeiner Hall, Upper TCV, Dharamshala, Himachal Pradesh. Among the gathering were Chief Justice of the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission, Yeshi Wangmo, along Justice Commissioners Dawa Phunkyi and Phagpa Tsering; Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile (TPiE) and Deputy Speaker Khenpo Sonam Tenphel; Kalon Kunga Tashi of the Department of Security, Kalon Tsering Dhondup Gyangser of the Department of Finance, Kalon Pema Tso of the Department of Health; and Secretary Lobsang Jinpa of the Office of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Also present were members of the Standing Committee of the Tibetan Parliament in Exile, secretaries and staff of the Central Tibetan Administration, representatives of local government and non-government organisations, TCV President Sonam Sichoe, as well as administrators, staff and school students. The school’s Ngoenpa Group presented a traditional ceremonial performance, followed by a welcome address by TCV President Sonam Sichoe, who highlighted the significance of the occasion for the Tibetan community and paid tribute to Kasur Jetsun Pema’s decades of dedicated service to TCV and her lifelong commitment to the welfare of Tibetan children in exile. He particularly acknowledged her contributions to the holistic development of children, including their academic, emotional, and social wellbeing, while nurturing a sense of love, dignity, and compassion. Representing the voice of the student, two students share brief account of extraordinary life and legacy of Ama Jetsun Pema, presented in English and Tibetan. As the award was presented, a group of students from the Junior Section performed a special tribute song in honour of Kasur Jetsun Pema. At the same time, representatives from various TCV schools came forward to offer traditional Tibetan khatas (scarf), joined by the school’s faculty and staff, in recognition of her lifelong dedication and service to Tibetan education and the welfare of Tibetan children. Addressing the gathering, Dr Desmond Biddulph CBE, President of The Buddhist Society, UK, spoke about the historical origins of the Christmas Humphreys Award and the significance of his presence in Dharamshala to present the honour to Kasur Jetsun Pema. He also highlighted the history and contribution of The Buddhist Society in the United Kingdom, founded by Christmas Humphreys in 1924, and its longstanding commitment to promoting the study and understanding of Buddhism. Following that, Chief Guest Kasur Jetsun Pema delivered her speech on the occasion, expressing her gratitude to The Buddhist Society, UK, for conferring the prestigious Christmas Humphreys Award in recognition of her lifelong commitment to Tibetan education and child welfare. She reflected on her decades of work in the field of education and her enduring dedication to the welfare and development of Tibetan children. Kasur Jetsun Pema also spoke about the importance of education in shaping the future of Tibetan children and preserving their cultural and linguistic heritage. She expressed her appreciation to the teachers, staff, students, and supporters who have contributed to the development of Tibetan education over the years, and acknowledged the continued support of institutions and individuals committed to the wellbeing and education of Tibetan children. Distinguished Guest of Honour, Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile , addressed the gathering, followed by Guest of Honour Kalon Kunga Tashi of the Department of Security, representing the Kashag delivered its address. In his remarks, Kalon Kunga Tashi highlighted the longstanding service and contributions of Kasur Jetsun Pema to the Tibetan people, particularly in the fields of education and healthcare. Kalon Kunga Tashi recalled Kasur Jetsun Pema has been formally honoured as the “Mother of Tibet” by the CTA and the TPiE, following a parliamentary resolution passed in 1991. He noted that the title reflects the deep respect and affection she has earned from the Tibetan community for her decades of dedicated service, particularly her tireless efforts for the welfare, education, and upbringing of Tibetan children in exile. He further praised Kasur Jetsun Pema’s lifelong dedication to strengthening the foundations of Tibetan education and healthcare, noting that her contributions have extended beyond the Tibetan community and earned recognition and respect among wider communities internationally. Kalon Kunga Tashi described the occasion as a significant and proud day for Tibetans, noting that the presentation of the prestigious Christmas Humphreys Award to Kasur Jetsun Pema serves as an important recognition of her extraordinary contribution and lifelong service. Before concluding his address, Kalon Kunga Tashi expressed his appreciation to The Buddhist Society, UK, for recognising Kasur Jetsun Pema’s lifelong service and honouring a distinguished Tibetan figure whose dedication and contributions continue to inspire generations of Tibetans. The programme featured heartfelt tributes from student representatives, a commemorative performance of the musical piece ‘Ama Jetsun Pema’ , and cultural performances by the TCV Cultural Troupe, paying tribute to Kasur Jetsun Pema’s lifelong service and contributions to Tibetan education and child welfare. The ceremony concluded with a formal vote of thanks delivered by Principal Tenzin Choekyi, who expressed appreciation to the distinguished guests, The Buddhist Society, UK, and all those who contributed to the successful organisation of the commemorative event. Kasur Jetsun Pema, younger sister of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, was born in Lhasa on 7 July 1940. She came to India in 1950 and later pursued her education in India, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom before returning to India in 1964. At the request of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, she took charge of the Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV) in Dharamshala in 1964 and went on to lead the institution for more than four decades, dedicating her life to the education, welfare, and holistic development of Tibetan children in exile. In 1990, Kasur Jetsun Pema became the first Tibetan woman to serve as a Kalon of the Central Tibetan Administration and was subsequently entrusted with the Department of Education. In recognition of her decades of service to Tibetan children, the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile conferred upon her the title “Mother of Tibet”. Her distinguished service has also received international recognition, including the UNESCO Medal in 1999, the World’s Children’s Honorary Award in 2000 and 2006, the Human Rights Hero Award in 2010, an Honorary Doctorate from the University of San Francisco in 2012, and India’s Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018.

title: Central Tibetan Administration Celebrates 157th Birth Anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: To commemorate Gandhi Jayanti, which marks the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, the Father of the Nation of India, the leadership and staff of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) gathered in front of the T-building at Gangchen Kyishong to join their Indian brothers and sisters in observing this significant occasion. The gathering was attended by Chief Justice Commissioner Yeshi Wangmo, Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang, Sikyong Penpa Tsering, Deputy Speaker Khenpo Sonam Tenphel, Justice Commissioners Dawa Phunkyi and Phagpa Tsering, Kalon Tsegyal Chukya Dranyi, Kalon Palden Dhondup, Kalon Tsering Dhondup Gyangser, Kalon Kunga Tashi and Kalon Pema Tso, Chief Election Commissioner Lobsang Yeshi, Public Service Commission Chairman Karma Yeshi, Auditor General Tashi Topgyal, members of the Standing Committee of the Tibetan Parliament in Exile, as well as secretaries and staff of the Central Tibetan Administration. Reaffirming their commitment to pursuing the Tibetan struggle for freedom and justice through non-violence and dialogue, the Tibetan leadership paid homage to Mahatma Gandhi, the revered apostle of non-violence and a celebrated champion of civil rights and India’s independence, on this occasion. Mahatma Gandhi’s principles and path have long been deeply admired by His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama. His Holiness’ lifelong commitment to non-violence and peaceful dialogue reflects the values and ideals embodied by Mahatma Gandhi. During the celebration, Sikyong Penpa Tsering addressed the media, noting that Mahatma Gandhi’s philosophy and practice of nonviolent resistance had profoundly influenced subsequent movements and leaders, including Nelson Mandela, Martin Luther King Jr., and His Holiness the Dalai Lama, in their respective struggles for justice, equality, and freedom.

title: U.S. Congressional Delegation Raises Concerns Over China’s “Ethnic Unity Law” During Media Address in Dharamshala
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: A five-member bipartisan delegation from the United States House of Representatives addressed the media in Dharamshala on 30 September 2026, following an audience with His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama at his official residence. The delegation comprised Representatives Brian Mast (Republican–Florida), James Gallagher (Republican–California), Jimmy Patronis (Republican–Florida), Haley Stevens (Democrat–Michigan), and Shri Thanedar (Democrat–Michigan). The delegation was accompanied by Sikyong Penpa Tsering and Representative Jigme Tsering of the Bureau of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in New Delhi. Upon arriving at Kangra Airport the previous day, the delegation received a warm reception from senior leadership of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), led by Tsegyal Choekya Dranyi, Kalon of the Department of Religion and Culture; Tashi Gyatso Shadrong, Interim Cabinet Secretary and Political Secretary; Jigme Tsering, Representative of the Bureau of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in New Delhi; Tempa Gyaltsen Zamlha, Joint Secretary of the Department of Information and International Relations (DIIR); and Ngawang Choedhar, Protocol Officer of the DIIR. Later that evening, Sikyong Penpa Tsering accompanied the congressional delegation on a guided tour of The Tibet Museum. Thereafter, the CTA hosted a welcome dinner reception in honour of the visiting delegation at the Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts. After receiving a special audience with His Holiness the following day, the delegation briefly spoke to the media waiting outside His Holiness’ residence. The delegation’s chair, Representative Brian Mast, reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to human rights, religious freedom, and the democratic aspirations of the Tibetan people. He also highlighted growing concerns over China’s transnational repression and said that support for Tibet remains a bipartisan issue in the U.S. Congress. Reflecting on his meeting with His Holiness the Dalai Lama, Congressman Mast said it was an experience he would “never forget.” He said the two discussed a wide range of issues, including China, the freedom of the Tibetan people, and His Holiness’ representation of freedom across the globe. Referring to the China’s so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”, Congressman Mast expressed concern about its potential impact beyond China. He highlighted that freedom and basic rights are inherent to every individual and that a government’s true purpose is to safeguard those rights rather than grant them. He added that these core principles mark a fundamental distinction between the Chinese regime, the United States, and the peaceful struggle of the Tibetan people. Responding to a media question about the recent meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Congressman Mast said that, in his understanding, His Holiness the Dalai Lama considers engagement between world leaders important. He said His Holiness had expressed the view that it was important for President Trump to meet President Xi, given their positions as leaders of two of the world’s major powers. Answering media inquiries regarding U.S.–China diplomatic relations, Congressman Mast stated that high-level international meetings would not weaken concerns about human rights violations in Tibet and other countries. Reaffirming the U.S. Congress’s firm opposition to Chinese state coercion, he called on China to stop its repression of Tibetans and Uyghurs. He added that China should instead “embrace freedom and support freedom across the globe.” He also addressed a range of other topics, including changing U.S. geopolitical priorities and relations with China; the American role in defending rights and democracy and the extent to which these values remain central to U.S. foreign policy; the delegation’s expectations regarding the passage of the Resolve Tibet Act ; the recent self-immolation of Martyr Lobga Rangzen; China’s interference in the reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama; and the PRC’s dialogue with representatives of the Tibetan people.

title: 17th Kashag Unveils Revised “Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future,” Focusing on Advocacy, Community Welfare and CTA Strengthening
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: Three years after the launch of the first Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future by the 16th Kashag of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), the 17th Kashag launched a revised version of the paper earlier this morning at Sikyong Hall in Gangchen Kyishong. Guided by the principles of Equitable Justice, Cooperative Effort, and Moving Forward, the revised paper aims to provide clear direction and guidance to the staff and leadership of the Central Tibetan Administration. It seeks to further strengthen institutional efficiency, enhance productivity, foster cohesive collaboration, promote sustainability, and ensure greater self-reliance in the face of emerging challenges. Sikyong Penpa Tsering, using a PowerPoint presentation, introduced the key issues outlined in the paper to a gathering of all CTA staff. The Kalons (Ministers) of the 17th Kashag, with the exception of one, also accompanied Sikyong on the dais during the presentation. The presentation was conducted with the aim of fostering strong leadership–bureaucratic alignment in fulfilling the CTA’s two key responsibilities: seeking an early resolution to the Sino-Tibet conflict and promoting the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile, while also ensuring efficient and effective administrative functioning of the CTA through strengthening its capacity. The session was also joined by Representatives of the Offices of Tibet and Tibetan Settlement Officers virtually and was aired online for the general public on Tibet TV. According to the Sikyong’s message in the paper, “The 16th Kashag published the Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future to help officials, the public, and all concerned understand the importance of Tibet and the Tibetan people; strategies for realising the just cause of Tibet; policies for the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile; and plans to strengthen the Central Tibetan Administration. It sought to bring everyone’s collective efforts together and has yielded positive results. Building on that foundation, we now present a revised paper setting out the 17th Kashag’s overall position, working approaches, and long-term vision for the attention of all relevant stakeholders.” The highlights in this revised version have been compartmentalised into three sections. The first encompasses the realisation of the just cause of Tibet through strengthening the existing Permanent Strategy Committee; engaging with Chinese people and affected groups; securing recognition of Tibet’s historical status; countering the Chinese government’s interference in the reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama; countering the Chinese government’s infiltration and deception; and strengthening Tibetan advocacy. Pertaining to the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile, the second section addresses the reinforcement of social cohesion through safeguarding and sustaining democratic practices, ensuring transparency in administration, strengthening relations between the administration and the public, providing additional care for those in need, empowering women and youth, and strengthening relations with organisations and other bodies. This section also discusses protecting Tibetan identity and sustaining the community by building and sustaining compact Tibetan communities, supporting monastic and religious institutions, promoting healthy settlements, and creating opportunities for sustainable livelihoods. In the face of Beijing’s systematic efforts to eradicate Tibetan linguistic and cultural heritage, including the coercive enrolment of more than one million Tibetan children in state-run boarding schools and the enactment of the so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”, the paper underscores the promotion of Tibetan education and language through consolidating Tibetan schools in India, sustaining the Basic Education Policy for Tibetans-in-Exile, and promoting the use and development of the Tibetan language and script. To fulfil these objectives and realise the policies, the final section emphasises strengthening the capacity of the CTA. This section addresses programme planning, implementation, and follow-up in accordance with the laws of the host country, with the aim of ensuring financial transparency and a sound system of accountability. It further highlights the strengthening of institutional capacity through the controlled and appropriate use of artificial intelligence, the establishment of an Institutional Development Index Data Management (IDI-DM) system, and the timely delivery of staff capacity-building training. Along with the revised Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future , two additional documents outlining the 17th Kashag’s position and providing guidelines for the working approach of CTA departments were also presented to the gathering. title: Education Council and Advisory Committee Holds its 14th Meeting in Dharamshala
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: The two-day 14th meeting of the Central Tibetan Administration’s Education Council and Advisory Committee began earlier this morning at the Department of Education’s conference hall. The meeting focused on reviewing previous resolution, improving educational curricula, strengthen efforts to preserve the Tibetan language and culture in exile. Presided over by Sikyong Penpa Tsering, the inaugural session of the conference was attended by Education Education Kalon (Minister) Urgen Tenzin, Chair of Education Council Thupten Lungrig (former Education Kalon and former parliamentarian), Education Secretary Karma Choeying, and members of the Education Council and Advisory Committee, namely Additional Secretary Tenzin Pema (DoE), Joint Secretary Jamyang Wangyal (Head of the Academic Section), Deputy Secretary Ngodup Tenpa (Traditional Education Officer), Professor Sonam Gyaltsen (CHTS, Sarah), Principal Nyima Dhondup (Palkhang Academy), Geshe Lharampa Lodoe Sangpo, Education Director Ngawang Lhamo (TCV), Education Director Rinzin Dawa (THS Mussoorie), and Deputy Director Tenzin Ngadon (STSS). The session began with a welcome address and introduced the programme of the joint meeting by Executive Director of the Education Council, Additional Secretary Tenzin Pema. She further introduced the new Chair of the Education Council Thupten Lungrig, new members Geshe Lharampa Lodoe Sangpo, and THS Mussoorie Education Director Rinzin Dawa. Chair of Education Council Thupten Lungrig, addressed the gathering stating that the Education Council and Advisory Committee’s was established following the introduction of Basic Education Policy (BEP) as well as the importance of knowing BEP, and its background. Highlighting the historical foundations of Tibetan education in exile, he detailed how the Charter of the Tibetans-in-Exile mandates the establishment of a standardised educational framework. This constitutional directive subsequently led the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) to formulate and enact the Basic Education Policy for Tibetans in Exile in 2004. He elucidated that the mandate formalised in the Charter and the subsequent formulation of the BEP are deeply intertwined with the vision of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama. His Holiness served both as the primary conceptual architect of the exile educational system and the supreme authority who historically brought it into law. Later when BEP was passed in 2004, and later as a result the Mewoen Tsuglag Petoen School was explicitly established by the CTA to serve as the official model school for implementing the core principles of BEP. He further emphasised the importance of understanding the historical and key objectives of the BEP when implementing its guidelines, noting educators and administrators must align their daily teaching practices with the core vision to ensure the long-term preservation of Tibetan language and values. Addressing the gathering, Education Kalon Ugen Tenzin briefed on the significance of the 2004 Basic Education Policy and traced its evolution since the founding of the Gangkyi Petoen School. He noted that the initiative received overwhelmingly positive feedback, paving the way for the progressive implementation of BEP guidelines across various other Tibetan schools in exile. Kalon Ugen Tenzin highlighted the transformative impact of the BEP within the Tibetan community, drawing a parallel to how India’s National Education Policy (NEP) seeks to foster independent, and holistic learning for future generations. Education Kalon called upon all schools, parents, and the broader society to recognise the importance and long-term benefits of the BEP in shaping the future of the younger generation. He also stressed the indispensable role of parents in understanding and upholding the policy at home, emphasising that family engagement is crucial to nurturing native language proficiency and traditional ethical values. Addressing broader geopolitical challenges, Education Kalon noted that among the key proposals presented, one specifically focused on strategies to counter the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.” He highlighted the urgent need to challenge forced assimilation policies and protect Tibetan cultural and linguistic identity against China’s systematic erasure. Education Kalon also highlighted Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week, designated by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) to be observed annually during the fourth week of September. In conclusion, Kalon urged educators, administrators, and community members alike to thoroughly understand the background and fundamental objectives of the BEP, calling unified efforts to safeguard Tibetan identity and heritage for generations to come. Addressing the gathering, Chief Guest Sikyong Penpa Tsering also spoke about Education Council Chair Thupten Lungrig, who has been associated with the development and implementation of the BEP since its early stages. Sikyong acknowledged his longstanding contribution and involvement in the formulation of the policy. Sikyong also discussed the potential benefits of making the Education Council and its Advisory Committee more autonomous that greater institutional independence could benefit both bodies as well as the Department of Education and contribute to positive outcomes in the future. He emphasised that this should be kept in mind when considering the future development and functioning of the education system. In his address, Sikyong Penpa Tsering also spoke about the declining number of students enrolling in Tibetan schools, identifying the low birth rate within the Tibetan community as one of the major factors contributing to the decline in school enrolment. He noted that the issue presents a growing challenge for the Department of Education and requires more than simply offering advice or raising awareness. He emphasised the need to understand the underlying demographic and social factors and to develop practical and sustainable measures to address the changing circumstances of Tibetan schools and communities. Sikyong further emphasised the need to take into account the current challenges faced by major Tibetan settlements and communities while planning for the future of Tibetan education. He called for forward-looking strategies, clear implementation plans and concrete proposals that respond to changing needs and circumstances. Sikyong stressed that future policies and programmes should be developed through careful assessment of existing challenges, with a focus on practical implementation and achieving positive outcomes for Tibetan students and the education system as a whole. Sikyong also highlighted the financial challenges faced by Tibetan schools in Nepal to suggest that sustainability of these institutions requires close coordination between the Department of Education and the Department of Finance. He particularly drew attention to the eight Tibetan schools currently operating in Nepal, including those in Kathmandu, and stressed the need to assess their present circumstances and consider their long-term sustainability. Sikyong underscored that the future of these schools should be carefully considered in light of changing student enrolment, financial constraints and the evolving needs of Tibetan communities. He called for both departments to work together in developing appropriate strategies, proposals and implementation plans to ensure the continued functioning and effectiveness of Tibetan schools in the years ahead to exile Tibetan communities. Sikyong also addressed the challenges faced by Tibetans in exile, particularly among the younger generation living abroad. He highlighted concerns over the declining use of the Tibetan language and the difficulties faced in maintaining language proficiency among younger Tibetans. He emphasised the need to strengthen Tibetan language education and improve teaching methods. Before concluding, Chief Guest Sikyong Penpa Tsering emphasised the urgent need to ensure that younger generations of Tibetans remain informed about the prevailing situation inside Tibet. He expressed concern over policies and laws being implemented by PRC that are increasingly undermining the use and preservation of the Tibetan language. He stressed that the erosion of the Tibetan language poses a serious challenge to the preservation of Tibetan identity, culture and heritage, and called on the younger generation to recognise the importance of safeguarding their language and maintaining their connection to Tibet. The two-day joint meeting will feature ten session covering various topics. The first and second agenda centred on reviewing resolutions and follow-up actions from the 13th Education Council and Advisory Committee Joint Meetings held on February, along with other matters deemed necessary by the committee.

title: Second Session of 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile Concludes
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala, 25 September 2026: The 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile successfully concluded its second session after deliberating on the reports of the seven departments of the Central Tibetan Administration, amendments to the Rules of the Public Service Commission (PSC), passing resolution on the constitution of the 13th Public Accounts Committee, the passage of three obituary references, an official solidarity resolution concerning the critical situation inside Tibet, and a resolution mandating the use of the Tibetan language, without mixing it with other languages, by the leaders, officials, and staff of the Central Tibetan Administration in carrying out their official duties. Chaired by Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang, the ninth day of the second session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile commenced with deliberation on the DIIR’s annual report with DIIR Kalon Penpa Tsering providing clarifications in response to questions raised in the House. The discussion highlighted the importance of imparting accurate and relevant information about Tibet to a wider audience. Particular emphasis was placed on the need to produce concise and engaging short videos on Tibet-related issues and share them through social media platforms, in order to reach a broader audience, especially younger generations. The discussion also underscored the importance of strengthening unity and solidarity among Tibetans and encouraging the collective efforts of every Tibetan toward the common cause of Tibet. In this context, the final message of Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen was recalled as a powerful reminder of the responsibility and collective commitment required from Tibetans. The research articles and publications produced by the Tibet Policy Institute were also appreciated for their contribution to generating greater awareness and understanding of Tibet-related issues. There was further discussion on the need to expand the Institute’s research and outreach activities so that its work can reach a wider audience and contribute more effectively to informed discourse on Tibet. The précis report for 2025–2026 of the Department of Health (DoHe) was then presented by its Kalon, Pema Tso. Parliamentarian Gyaltsen Choekye Gagya subsequently presented the Standing Committee’s reviewed report on the DoHe’s detailed annual report for 2025–2026. A motion to deliberate on the DoHe’s annual report was moved by Parliamentarian Lobsang Thupten Pontsang and seconded by Parliamentarian Choedak Gyatso. The DoHe Kalon then presented the Kashag’s clarifications on the matters raised during the deliberation. The House discussed the importance of the health and well-being of the Tibetan diaspora in sustaining the just cause of Tibet. The discussion covered improving accessibility and providing necessary support and assistance for differently abled members of the community, concerns regarding the increasing number of autism cases, strengthening healthcare facilities and ensuring regular health check-ups, the need to establish emergency health funds, and initiatives to promote mental health awareness across Tibetan communities. Kalon Pema Tso responded to and addressed the questions and concerns raised by the members of the House. The session proceeded with the presentation of the Interim Budget of the Department of Home (DoH), comprising Interim Budget Nos. 205, 206, and 207, by DoH Kalon Palden Dhondup. A motion to deliberate on the DoH’s Interim Budget was moved by DoH Kalon Palden Dhondup and seconded by DoF Kalon Tsering Dhondup. Following discussion, the Interim Budget for the renovation of offices and quarters, as well as the procurement of necessary items for the quarters, was approved with a majority vote. An official motion to constitute the 13th Public Accounts Committee was moved by parliamentarian Lobsang Thupten Pontsang and supported by parliamentarian Choedak Gyatso. The official motion was passed unanimously. Continuing with legislative procedures, third reading and adoption of the Rule of Public Service Commission (PSC), followed by reading of leave of absence of the members by Secretary-General Sonam Dorjee. The Speaker then gave her concluding address before announcing the conclusion of the second session of the 18thTibetan Parliament-in-Exile. In her conclusion address, the Speaker provided an overview of the agenda discussed in this session and noted that the average participation of MPs in the deliberation was 29 parliamentarians. Speaking about the Sinicization policies implemented in Tibet under the rule of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the Speaker expressed concern over the declining birth rate among Tibetans in the diaspora. She underscored the importance of quality upbringing and called for greater efforts to ensure that younger generations remain deeply connected to and grounded in the rich cultural heritage, traditions, and values of the Tibetan people. Calling for the collective efforts of Tibetans across the world, the Speaker appealed to Tibetans from all walks of life to contribute meaningfully to the Tibetan cause and to the preservation and promotion of Tibet’s rich cultural and traditional heritage. In conclusion, the Speaker expressed her sincere gratitude to the staff of the Parliamentary Secretariat, the Department of Information and International Relations, the Department of Security, and the electrician from the Department of Home for their dedicated service and assistance throughout the session. She concluded by offering prayers for the long life and continued well-being of His Holiness the Dalai Lama and for the swift and peaceful resolution of the Sino-Tibetan conflict. The session adjourned sine die at 7:40 pm. – Report filed by Tibetan Parliamentary Secretariat

title: Sikyong Penpa Tsering Proclaims Observance of ‘Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week’ Amid Beijing Crackdown
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala: This morning, Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), at a press meet, officially proclaimed the annual observance of “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week”, to be observed from the fourth Wednesday of September through the following Wednesday. The proclamation formally launches a global campaign to confront and counter the various methods and systematic policies implemented by the Chinese Communist Government to eradicate Tibetan identity, particularly its recently enacted so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” which, under the guise of law, further intensifies the assimilation and eradication of national identities. A Proclamation on the Observance of Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week By resolution approved at the 11th session of the 17th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile designating the fourth week of every September as “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week”, I hereby proclaim the commencement of this observance effective 23 September 2026. Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week will be observed annually, from the fourth Wednesday of September through the following Wednesday. The proclamation formally launches a global campaign to confront and counter the Chinese Communist Government’s implementation of various methods and systematic policies aimed at eradicating Tibetan identity—specifically, its recently implemented so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” which escalate eradication of nationalities under the guise of law. Our campaign must effectively counter the Chinese Communist Government’s observance of the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Propaganda Week,” during which the state organs are directed to execute various forms of state-sponsored assimilation propaganda and re-education campaigns. The contents and the serious threats posed by the Chinese Communist government’s so-called law have been extensively detailed across key forums and appeals, including: The preamble of the resolution adopted during the First Session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile; The official statement of the Kashag (Cabinet) on the auspicious occasion of the Birthday celebration of His Holiness the Dalai Lama; The official statement on Tibetan Democracy Day; The urgent diplomatic appeal dispatched by the Sikyong to foreign governments in June 2026; The Kashag’s statement delivered at the 49th-day memorial service for the late martyr Lobga Rangzen; and Comprehensive short video awareness campaigns. On the global stage, governments—including those of the United States, Germany, Belgium, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, the Czech Republic, Japan, and the European Union— along with the eight UN Special Rapporteurs and UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk, have issued official statements declaring that the Chinese Communist government’s so-called law violates international law, serves as a tool for forced assimilation, and poses a risk of transnational repression. The United States Congress, the European Union, and the Parliament of the Czech Republic have adopted resolutions confronting this so-called law. In addition, members of Parliament in over twenty free countries have expressed grave concern and strong opposition, while dozens of international human rights organisations and research institutions have released articles and reports exposing the grave dangers of this so-called law in the eradication of nationalities. We take this opportunity to express our heartfelt gratitude to all our international supporters, and we call for sustained, resolute action against the measures of the Chinese government that run against the progress of human society. On 27 December 2025, the Chinese Communist Government revised the so-called “Law on the National Commonly Used Language and Script,” which mandates Chinese as the primary medium of instruction from pre-school through university, as well as the primary language used in all government offices and public gathering places, while enforcing an annual national propaganda week to promote Mandarin dominance. I call upon all Tibetan individuals, families, schools, community associations, activists, and Tibet supporters—under the leadership of the respective Representatives of the Offices of Tibet and Tibetan Settlement Officers—to unite in solidarity with the Tibetans inside Tibet with unyielding dedication and fulfil the responsibilities and activities set forth in the public announcement regarding the observance of the “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week” issued by the Kashag on 21 August 2026. Today, I am proud to announce the launch of the Principles and Guidelines for the Preservation of the Tibetan Language, recently adopted by the Kashag. To help the public better understand and apply these guidelines, an awareness video will be released shortly. I urge every Tibetan to take ownership of this vital cause and actively fulfil the responsibilities outlined in the guidelines. I appeal to our youth in particular not to view the observance of the “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week” as a temporary campaign to be observed for just one week, but as an enduring pledge, and to remember your responsibility as representatives of over seven million Tibetans inside Tibet. I urge you to unite your strength in the struggle for the just cause of Tibet with an unwavering commitment to preserving our Tibetan national identity, and cultivate the courage to become Tibetans who lead on the path of non-violence and compassion, and are capable of taking responsibility for the greater welfare of the world in accordance with the vision of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Penpa Tsering Sikyong 23 September 2026 ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………… Principles and Guidelines for the Preservation of Tibetan Language “If Tibetans neglect treasures such as the Tibetan language—which uniquely defines our distinct national identity—and if educated leaders fail to guide the youth, who in turn ignore their elders’ warnings about irreparable loss, our language risks extinction. If Tibetans across China, India, Nepal, and Western countries prioritise Chinese, Hindi, Nepali, and English solely for temporary survival, relying on foreign languages to speak among themselves, it would be both tragic and embarrassing. Therefore, I appeal to every Tibetan to take personal responsibility and make dedicated efforts to cherish and preserve our Tibetan religion, culture, and language.” – An excerpt from His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s message delivered on 11 March 2026. 1. Preface The Tibetan language is the backbone of Tibetan culture and history and a mirror of the Tibetan people’s unique identity and traditions. It is the primary medium for expressing the Five Major Sciences—arts, medicine, grammar, epistemology, and Buddhist philosophy—and the Five Minor Sciences—poetry, lexicography, prosody, drama, and astrology. It is also a vast treasury for passing down Tibet’s history, politics, economy, military, society, and geography to future generations. It serves as a vital core for safeguarding social unity, collective rights, and the capacity to self-govern. According to research by modern historians and linguists, the Tibetan script was created in the 7th century, modelled after the Gupta or Brahmi scripts prevalent in Northern India. With a history spanning over 1,300 years, it is recognised as one of the world’s ancient languages with uninterrupted use. The largest and most complete collections of Buddha’s teachings, Buddhist philosophy, epistemology, and psychology transmitted from India are found in the Tibetan language. Enriched by tens of thousands of volumes of treatises and commentaries, it has become a vital treasury housing crucial components of ancient Indian wisdom. Studying the Tibetan language helps preserve and promote Tibet’s unique cultural heritage, benefiting all sentient beings. In line with the vision of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, it helps us nurture individuals who can guide others along the path of non-violence and compassion and shoulder responsibility for the greater good of this world. According to research by UNESCO, UNICEF, and numerous internationally renowned research institutions, implementing mother-tongue education during at least the lower primary school years has been shown to boost students’ self-confidence, foster awareness, and build a solid foundation for learning other languages. It has also proven to significantly enhance cognitive skills, classroom engagement, and overall academic performance. Findings show the method yields clear advantages over forcibly instructing students in a foreign language. The Chinese Communist government has placed nearly one million Tibetan children in residential schools in Tibet, shifting the medium of instruction to Chinese. It has imposed Chinese-language education in preschools and restricted the use of the Tibetan language in administrative offices. Furthermore, by introducing legal tools under the so-called ‘Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,’ it has intensified policies aimed at identity eradication. Speaking Chinese has become increasingly common in homes in villages and towns in Tibet today, making communication breakdowns between grandparents and grandchildren a widespread concern. This reflects a central aim of the Chinese Communist government’s policy, placing this generation at risk of losing their distinct Tibetan identity. Within the Tibetan exile community, the rapid emigration to Western countries has outpaced the setup of Tibetan-medium preschools, while birth rates across India, Nepal, and Bhutan continue to decline. Strengthening practical strategies for studying and using the Tibetan language—both inside Tibet and in exile—has therefore become an urgent policy priority focused on education and everyday use. 2. Responsibilities Concerning Learning and Usage of Tibetan Language a) Responsibilities of Families: Building the Foundation The cornerstone of the Tibetan language’s sustainability is maintaining uninterrupted transmission of the mother tongue across generations. To do so, parents must embrace their role as a child’s first teacher—teaching their mother tongue from early childhood to ensure the new generation continues to speak Tibetan. To bring this about, each family must; Establish a home rule of speaking exclusively in Tibetan during family gatherings, striving to speak pure Tibetan without mixing foreign words whenever Tibetans interact. Tell their children Tibetan folktales, history, and culturally relevant stories to foster interest in and affection for the language. Create an engaging learning environment by using Tibetan-language children’s stories, films, animations, and nursery rhymes. Observe traditional Tibetan festivals to instil religious practices, culture, and customs and traditions in children. Participate in community cultural and artistic gatherings to expand opportunities for young generations to use the language in social settings. Such practices are doable and essential duty for every household. b) Responsibilities of Schools: Ensuring Proficiency in the Tibetan Language Maintain the policy of making Tibetan language the primary official language of schools, except where foreign languages are specifically required, so that school practice clearly serves Tibetan language preservation. Build a firm foundation to enable children to think and express themselves in their mother tongue during the golden period of cognition; focus on teaching in the mother tongue at the preschool level. Tibetan shall serve as the primary medium of instruction through the primary level, with all middle school textbooks in Tibetan, while secondary languages are introduced contextually as appropriate. Organise regular debate and public speaking contests, calligraphy competitions, essay contests, art and drama performances, and poetry recitations within and between schools to foster a vibrant Tibetan language environment. Create opportunities for philosophy teachers to introduce students to Buddhism, Buddhist logic, and traditional cultural studies. Invite scholars in Tibetan language, culture, and arts to inspire students and unlock their latent talents. c) Responsibilities of the Community: Creating an Ideal Environment for Students to Study and Use the Tibetan Language Establish dedicated Tibetan language classes on weekends and during academic holidays, tailored for students attending non-Tibetan schools. Provide teachers with modern pedagogical training and expert guidance to deliver high-quality instruction in reading, writing, listening, and speaking for students learning Tibetan as a second language. Organise dedicated language immersion programs in areas with significant Tibetan populations, pairing Tibetan children who speak Tibetan as a second language with elders proficient in pure Tibetan for designated periods of language study. Provide diverse educational resources for students by creating conditions where activities extend beyond formal classroom instruction, ensuring breaks, entertainment, and recreational play are conducted entirely in Tibetan. Display Tibetan as the primary language on signboards, street signs, public announcements, and in community spaces in settlements and Tibetan residential areas. Encourage speaking pure Tibetan and learning Tibetan song lyrics during gatherings, such as circle dances ( Gorshey ), in alignment with White Wednesday ( Lhakar ) observances. Encourage Tibetan social media users to use Tibetan as the primary language in their posts and account handles. Encourage social media influencers to prioritise speaking pure Tibetan as well as write in Tibetan. Ensure Tibetan language is featured prominently on backdrops and banners for sports events and cultural nights, using Tibetan as the primary language for hosting events. Encourage Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) to launch effective campaigns supporting Tibetan language study and usage. d) Responsibilities of the Department of Education, CTA: Ensuring Language Mastery and Nurturing Capable Individuals Based on the benchmark of ensuring independent proficiency in the Tibetan language upon completion of basic education, the Department shall structure textbook compilation and curriculum scheduling accordingly, while monitoring, evaluating, and providing encouragement to ensure full, ongoing implementation across all educational systems in support of Tibetan language preservation. Develop comprehensive implementation plans to provide higher education scholarships, dedicated academic seats, and competitive teacher remuneration to nurture teachers capable of instructing secondary school subjects in the Tibetan language. Through standardised research, introduce a curriculum for teaching dialectics and logic ( Riglam ) at the upper primary or middle school level. Provide training for teachers to enable the instruction of other academic subjects through dialectical methods. Develop interactive multimedia educational tools and digital learning software that reflect curriculum content in contemporary real-world contexts, rather than relying solely on teacher-led instruction. Create Tibetan language learning opportunities for students residing in university hostels. Provide learning support and facilities for Tibetan students dispersed across various higher education institutions. Formally recognise and support higher education institutions that offer Tibetan language courses. Provide special scholarship facilities to nurture individuals specialising in traditional Tibetan fields of knowledge whether they are enrolled in formal programs or informal ones. Plan and organise annual regional student competitions dedicated to preserving the Tibetan language. Formulate and standardise modern social science and natural science terminology aligned with Tibetan grammar and linguistic conventions and ensure its widespread adoption. Support research community workforce needs and provide career counselling to students entering higher education accordingly. Offer recognition and assistance to individuals and organisations actively promoting effective Tibetan language learning and usage programs. e) Official policy of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) Sustain the continued implementation of the Basic Education Policy for Tibetans in Exile. Uphold Tibetan as the official language of the Central Tibetan Administration. Strengthen measures to prioritise Tibetan in official correspondence, policy documents, public notifications, and related materials. Encourage non-governmental organisations and civil society bodies to actively use Tibetan in their operations. Support higher education institutions that teach in Tibetan and incentivise the development of experts in Tibetan culture wherever possible. Support the establishment of specialised schools for Tibetan children residing in Western countries. Assist programs offering summer camps and online courses focused on Tibetan language, religion, and culture. Continue to provide equal basic education facilities and resources for students from the Himalayan region as per the guidance of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Establish expert committees to assist with recognition awards for writers, translators, educators, activists, and parents who make outstanding contributions to the preservation and promotion of the Tibetan language. Develop a standardised, comprehensive Tibetan language portal showcasing the Ten Traditional Sciences, culture, and customs of Tibet. Lead and encourage measures to expand the use of the Tibetan language across modern media and digital technologies, while supporting intelligent software tools—including Tibetan input methods, machine translation, speech recognition, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR)—to improve access to Tibetan language use. f) Policy Implementation and Conclusion A Tibetan Language Preservation Committee comprising three to five experts with deep knowledge and experience in Tibetan religion, culture, education, and language will be established. The Committee will publish an annual report evaluating the implementation outcomes of this language policy in collaboration with the Education Council of the Department of Education, Central Tibetan Administration Whether the Chinese Communist government’s policy of restricting Tibetan language study and usage achieves its intended outcomes in a specific period depends on how effectively Tibetans inside and outside Tibet respond to and counter these plans, and how strongly the international community supports our just cause. Therefore, every individual Tibetan must recognise the inherent value of the Tibetan language, take active responsibility for its preservation, and amplify the Tibetan people’s truthful voice across the international arena. The Kashag 23 September, 2026.

title: EU Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Calls for Greater Clarity and Transparency on Humanitarian Situation in Tibet Following Devastating Flash Floods
author: OOT - DC
content: Strasbourg, 17 September 2026: Expressing gratitude for the EU’s rapid response following the devastating flash floods that struck the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August 2026, leaving hundreds dead and thousands still unaccounted for, the Office of Tibet Brussels has urged the EU authorities not to overlook the suffering of the Tibetans in Tibet affected by the same disaster. Immediately following the disaster, the Office of Tibet Brussels reached out to Members of the European Parliament (MEPs), urging them to raise concerns over the lack of reliable information from the Tibetan side of the border and to ensure that Tibet was included in discussions surrounding the humanitarian crisis. Unlike Nepal, where information about the disaster and rescue efforts has been widely available, information from Tibet has been severely restricted. This has made it difficult to assess the full extent of the devastation, determine the full scale of the humanitarian needs, and to establish what assistance, if any, has reached affected communities on the Tibetan side. The issue was raised in a restricted format in the European Parliament during its plenary session in Strasbourg, held from 14 to 17 September 2026, where only one round of interventions by speakers representing the political groups was permitted to take the floor. MEP Tomáš Zdechovský MEP Tomáš Zdechovský, a longstanding supporter of Tibet and a member of the European Parliament’s largest political group, the European People’s Party (EPP), called for Tibet not to be overlooked in discussions about the disaster. “We must not overlook Tibet, which is under Chinese occupation, while discussing this devastating flash flood in Nepal. No information is available on whether any aid has reached that part of the region.” MEP Zdechovský also underscored the importance of stronger regional cooperation, particularly in view of the European Union’s investment and engagement in the region. He called for greater attention to early-warning systems, data sharing, monitoring of the affected areas, and cross-border communication, particularly in responding to natural disasters that affect communities on both sides of the border. European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib stressed the need for greater clarity and transparency regarding the situation in Tibet, emphasising that reliable and timely information is essential to enable authorities and humanitarian actors to support affected communities and respond effectively. “Thank you for underlining the specific situation where Tibet is in. We must not overlook the situation in Tibet, I totally agree. We need to have reliable and timely information. It is essential, it supports search and rescue, enables families to obtain information and allows also responders to identify the needs. We would like to see more clarity and transparency on what is happening there.” Alongside its advocacy efforts, the Office of Tibet Brussels has mobilised Tibetan communities and friends, raising significant contributions towards CTA’s flood-relief efforts. – Report filed by Office of Tibet, Brussels

title: His Holiness the Dalai Lama Extends Warmest Birthday Greetings and Prayers for Good Health to Prime Minister Narendra Modi
author: OOT - DC
content: Thekchen Chöling, Dharamshala, HP, India: Today, on Prime Minister Modi’s birthday, His Holiness the Dalai Lama has written to him to offer his warmest greetings and prayers for his continued good health. “May I congratulate you on India’s emergence as a confident and strong nation,” he wrote. “This great country’s success also contributes significantly to global peace, stability and development. “I consider myself a proud messenger of India, which presents to the world an example of Ahimsa and Karuna — peace and harmony born from India’s ancient wisdom. “Once again, I would like to extend my deep gratitude to the Government and people of India for the warm and generous hospitality shown to me and my fellow Tibetans for well over 67 years now.” His Holiness concluded by offering prayers and good wishes once more. Source: dalailama.com

title: Second Session of 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile Convenes
author: OOT - DC
content: Dharamshala, 16 September 2026: The general session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, scheduled from 16 to 25 September 2026, commenced today at 9:30 a.m. Following the commencement announcement by Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang, the Speaker, Sikyong Penpa Tsering, Deputy Speaker Khenpo Sonam Tenphel, Kalons (Ministers), and Members of Parliament gathered in the Parliament Hall sang the Tibetan national anthem. After ascertaining the requisite quorum of the House, the Speaker, in her opening address, congratulated the newly appointed Kalons who were nominated by the Sikyong and approved by the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile during its first session. She then introduced the day’s brief agenda, which included obituary references, legislative amendments, resolutions, bills, and motions. The Speaker informed the House of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile’s strong opposition to the so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress” adopted by the People’s Republic of China, which came into effect on 1 June 2026. She stated that the legislation threatens the Tibetan people’s language, religion, culture, identity, and fundamental human rights, before outlining its background and implications in detail. She further informed the House that the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile had dispatched 837 official open letters to governments, parliaments, the United Nations, the European Union, and other international bodies around the world, and briefed Members on the responses received to those letters. The House was also informed about a parliamentary delegation led by the Deputy Speaker that met with Indian Union Cabinet Ministers, Members of Parliament, and other key dignitaries in late July, coinciding with the Monsoon Session of the Indian Parliament. The delegation advocated for Tibet and submitted official appeal documents concerning the sacrifice of the late Lobga Rangzen and the Chinese government’s “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.” Finally, the Speaker spoke about the inaugural visitation program of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, noting the appreciation, grievances, suggestions, and feedback shared by members of the general public during the program. Thereafter, in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, a Panel of Chairpersons and an Ad Hoc Committee were appointed. Following the list of business, obituary references were paid to Tibetan Patriotic Martyr Lobsang Palden, also known as Rangzen Lobga, who self-immolated in front of the United Nations headquarters, as well as to the passing of Kasur Chope Paljor Tsering, American Buddhist scholar Professor Robert A. F. Thurman, and former U.S. Congressman Barney Frank. The obituary references were presented by Parliamentarians Geshe Lharampa Atuk Tseten, Geshe Atong Rinchen Gyaltsen, Kunchok Chodon Juchen, and Lopon Thupten Gyaltsen. A resolution of condolence and solidarity to the victims of the devastating floods along the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August 2026 was presented by Sikyong Penpa Tsering and supported by Kalon Kunga Tashi of the Department of Security. A minute of silence was then duly observed in the House in mourning those named in the obituary references. Thereafter, Kalon Tsegyal Chukya Dranyi of the Department of Religion and Culture presented a précis of the ministry’s 2025–26 annual report. Parliamentarian Geshe Lharampa Atuk presented the Standing Committee’s review of the detailed 2025–26 annual report of the Department of Religion and Culture. Parliamentarian Tenpa Yarphel tabled a motion for debate on the report of the Department of Religion and Culture, which was supported by Parliamentarian Lopon Thupten Gyaltsen. Clarification to the questions from the Standing Committee’s review of the detailed 2025–26 annual report of the Department of Religion and Culture was presented by Kalon Tsegyal Chukya Dranyi. Members of Parliament subsequently participated in deliberations on the functioning of the Department of Religion and Culture, raising questions on Jang Gun Choe (Non-Sectarian Nun’s Annual Winter Debate), scholarship programs, regarding the return of Gyalwang Karmapa to India, Tibetan Digital Library Initiative, and other related matters which were duly clarified by the DoR&C Kalon. The deliberations on the undertaking of the Department of Religion and Culture will continue in tomorrow’s session.
