title: Tibetan monk remains in critical condition after being tortured by Chinese authorities
content: Dharamshala — A Tibetan monk has been bedridden for two years, unable to stand or speak, and is being fed through a feeding tube, after suffering torture and abuse at the hands of Chinese authorities while in Chinese detention. He had been arrested by the authorities for opposing China’s construction of the Kamtok (Gangtuo) hydroelectric dam, which threatened to destroy centuries-old monasteries in Gege County, Kham, in eastern Tibet. Gonpo Tsering, Tibetan monk and the head of Yena Monastery in Shiba Village, was among the more than 100 Tibetan monks from the Wonto and Yena monasteries who were arrested by Chinese armed forces on February 22, 2024. Many of them were beaten and injured and were subsequently admitted to Dege County Hospital for treatment. Following Gonpo Tsering’s arrest, Chinese authorities subjected him to severe physical abuse and torture while in custody. As a result, he was urgently transported to West China (Huaxi) Hospital in Chengdu, where he has been in critical condition for the past two years. "Gonpo Tsering is currently bedridden, unable to stand or speak, and is fed through tubes. He is unresponsive to family members and unable to recognize people around him. Devastated by his son’s detention and condition, his father, Lobsang Dorjee, passed away on Sep. 21, 2025," the source told ICT. Around 300 Tibetans gathered in front of the Dege county government building on February 14, 2024, and protested against the construction of the largest hydroelectric power plant in their region and the forced displacement of their homes and monasteries. They called on the county authorities to cancel the plan to build the power station and the order to move their homes and monasteries. The Chinese authorities plan to build a 2,240 megawatt hydropower station on the Drichu River (Jinsha River in Chinese) without the Tibetans' consent to dam construction and resettlement, and have ordered Tibetans and monks from six monasteries and two villages in two townships of Dege County, Kham, eastern Tibet, to resettle in other villages. Therefore, hundreds of Tibetans gathered in front of the Dege county government building on February 14, 2024 and protested against this action and to ask the concerned authorities to put an end to it. The Chinese authorities brought a specially trained police force to the Wonto village area on February 22, 2024 and arrested more than 100 Tibetan monks from the Wonto and Yena monasteries, as well as local residents, many of whom were beaten and injured before being admitted to Dege County Hospital for treatment. After peaceful protests by Tibetans and Tibetan monks continued from 14 to 22 February, 2024, the Chinese government sent in trained special forces to arrest the demonstrators. Tibetans working outside their villages returned home and asked the Chinese police to release the detained Tibetans. Unfortunately, the Chinese police arrested those who had made this request and detained more than 1,000 Tibetans on February 23, 2024, including Tibetan monks, local Tibetans and Tibetans from outside the villages. The police have asked family members to bring Tsampa-Tibetan food and blankets to the detention centres, as they do not have enough food for large numbers of detainees. Tibetans around the world, from the United States to Canada, Europe and India, have protested against the Chinese government's beating and arrest of Tibetans in Dege, Kham,Tibet, for their peaceful protest against the construction of a mega-dam and for forcibly ordering the relocation of six Tibetan monasteries and two villages in Dege County. Tibetans in exile expressed their deep concern about the unfair treatment of detained Tibetans. They also expressed their solidarity with Tibetans detained in Chinese-occupied Tibet. China-Tibet: The one-thing you need to know Over the past 70 decades, there has been ongoing political repression, social discrimination, economic marginalization, environmental destruction, and cultural assimilation, particularly due to Chinese migration to Tibet which is fueling intense resentment among the people of occupied Tibet. The communist-totalitarian state of China began its invasion of Tibet in 1949, reaching complete occupation of the country in 1959. Since that time, more than 1.2 million people, 20% of the nation's population of six million, have died as a direct result of China's invasion and occupation. In addition, over 99% of Tibet's six thousand religious monasteries, temples, and shrines, have been looted or decimated resulting in the destruction of hundreds of thousands of sacred Buddhist scriptures. Until 1949, Tibet was an independent Buddhist nation in the Himalayas which had little contact with the rest of the world. It existed as a rich cultural storehouse of the Mahayana and Vajrayana teachings of Buddhism. Religion was a unifying theme among the Tibetans -- as was their own language, literature, art, and world view developed by living at high altitudes, under harsh conditions, in a balance with their environment. title: Tibetans call on Switzerland and UN to hold China accountable for its human rights violations in Tibet
content: Bern, Switzerland — More than 200 Tibetans and supporters gathered near the Swiss Parliament in Bern on Friday and held a peaceful demonstration protesting China’s increasingly intense assimilation policies in Tibet, including the “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.” The rally also marked the 44th day since Tibetan martyr Lhoba Langzan died by self-immolation; his sacrifice has once again drawn international attention to the human rights situation in Tibet. They called on Switzerland government and the UN to hold China accountable for its human rights violations in Tibet. According to the Office of Tibet, Geneva, the demonstration was organised by the Tibetan Community in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, the Swiss Tibetan Friendship Association (GSTF), the Swiss Tibetan Women’s Association, the European Tibetan Youth Association, and Swiss V-TAG. More than 200 Tibetans and supporters gathered near the Swiss Parliament in Bern on August 14, 2026, for the peaceful demonstration. Among the participants were leaders of the Tibetan community, former Tibetan parliamentarians, former representatives of the Tibet Office, as well as representatives of the Tibet Office in Geneva, including Thinlay Chukki, representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, and Phuntsok Topgyal, UN Advocacy Officer. The gathering featured a series of solidarity activities, including the chanting of slogans, a scarf-presentation ceremony in front of a portrait of Pawo Lobga Rangzen, the singing of the Tibetan national anthem, a one-minute silence in memory of Tibetan martyrs, and prayers for peace. Representatives of each organising organisation addressed the gathering, highlighting the ongoing human rights concerns in Tibet and honouring the sacrifice of Lobga Rangzen. They called on Switzerland, the United Nations, and the international community to take stronger and more concrete action in response to the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet. Representative Thinlay Chukki expressed her gratitude to the Tibetan community and supporters who had gathered in Bern to honour the memory of Lobga Rangzen and raise international awareness of the continuing human rights violations in Tibet. She said, "Today, as we commemorate the 44th day since the self-immolation of Lobga Rangzen, I would like to sincerely thank all my fellow Tibetans who have gathered here in Bern, not only to remember his sacrifice, but also to remind the international community of the atrocities that Tibetans in Tibet continue to face." Chukki also thanked representatives of the Swiss Tibetan Friendship Association, the Tibetan Women’s Association, the Tibetan Youth Association, and other non-governmental organisations for their participation in the demonstration. Speaking about the self-immolation of Lobga Rangzen, representative Chukki said his sacrifice should serve as a powerful call for the international community to pay greater attention to the human rights situation inside Tibet. “Since 2009, we have seen 157 known cases of self-immolation inside Tibet, and each of these self-immolators has called for freedom in Tibet and the return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama,” she said. On behalf of His Holiness the Dalai Lama and the Central Tibetan Administration, she expressed profound gratitude to those who had sacrificed their lives and offered reassurance to their families that Tibetans in exile would continue working towards the restoration of freedom in Tibet. In her speech, the representative focused on the “Ethnic Unity and Progress law,” which was adopted by China on March 12, 2026, and took effect on July 1, 2026. She strongly criticised the legislation, arguing that it further institutionalises policies that threaten Tibet’s distinct cultural, linguistic, religious, and national identity. “It is unfathomable that the Chinese government has the audacity not only to egregiously violate Tibetans’ fundamental freedoms and human rights, but also to legalise such assimilation through legislation,” she stated. Chukki warned that the policies went beyond cultural assimilation and described the situation in Tibet as cultural genocide. She highlighted provisions relating to the prioritisation of Mandarin Chinese, increased state control over Tibetan monasteries, and measures that, she said, could also affect people outside China who support the Tibetan cause. “This law not only impacts Tibetans inside Tibet, but also every supporter who has stood with us and supported our struggle for freedom in Tibet,” she said. She called on the international community to take urgent and concrete action to ensure that the human rights of Tibetans are respected and protected in accordance with international law. Chukki also urged the United Nations to take concrete steps to investigate the human rights situation in Tibet. “The United Nations [must] take it upon itself to ensure that it sends a delegation to China, to Tibet, to document and record the human rights violations on the ground,” she said. The representative further appealed to the Swiss Government to increase diplomatic pressure on China to comply with international law and the treaties to which it is a party. On behalf of the Tibetan community, she expressed appreciation to Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs for acknowledging Tibetan appeals and responding with serious concern regarding the situation in Tibet. She also thanked members of the Swiss Parliamentary Group for Tibet for their continued support and urged Swiss parliamentarians to consider appropriate resolutions to ensure that the human rights situation in Tibet remains firmly on Switzerland’s political agenda. Concluding her address, Chukki posed a direct question to the international community: “Today, we have gathered here because one Tibetan self-immolated in New York. How many more Tibetans need to make this ultimate sacrifice before the international community truly opens its eyes and looks into the matter?” Her remarks resonated with demonstrators gathered in solidarity with Tibetans inside Tibet and in remembrance of those who have sacrificed their lives for freedom and the preservation of Tibet’s identity. The peaceful demonstration concluded with continued calls for international solidarity, human rights, religious freedom, and the preservation of Tibetan culture, language, and identity. Chukki concluded by expressing her hope that one day His Holiness the Dalai Lama will return to the Potala Palace in Lhasa and once again give teachings there. The gathering in Bern served as a powerful reminder that, despite decades of repression, Tibetans and their supporters continue to raise their voices on the international stage in defence of human rights, freedom, justice, and the preservation of Tibet’s distinct identity.། Tibet Human Rights UNO

title: UN expresses deep concern over China's tightening restrictions on Tibetans
content: Dharamshala — Addressing the opening of the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, on September 7, 2026, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk expressed deep concern over the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet, particularly restrictions affecting the Tibetan people’s freedom of religion. UN Human Rights chief said, 'China is tightening restrictions on the rights of the Tibetan people, including their freedom of religion, are deeply troubling. I appeal for an urgent U-turn on these policies.' The UN Human Rights chief said, "We live in an age of extremes. Raging wars, painful polarization, climate chaos, and head-spinning technological change make people feel disoriented and even powerless." Regarding the protection of people against disasters such as the recent glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet border, he stated: "We must keep our focus on limiting global warming to 1.5°C, as set out in the Paris Agreement, by ensuring the current overshoot is as small and short as possible." "What drives us is the belief that human rights will help the people of all our societies to realise their hopes and aspirations, in the spirit of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which affirmed that everyone, everywhere is born free and equal in dignity and rights," the UN Human Rights chief said. Office of Tibet, Geneva stated, "the statement is particularly significant as concerns continue to grow over restrictions on the exercise of religious and cultural rights in Tibet. The High Commissioner’s call underscores the importance of respecting fundamental human rights and ensuring that Tibetans are able to exercise their rights and freedoms without undue restrictions." The Tibet Bureau, Geneva, welcomes the explicit attention given to the human rights situation in Tibet and reiterates the importance of sustained international engagement on the protection of Tibetan religious, cultural and fundamental rights. "The Bureau will continue to engage with UN mechanisms, diplomatic missions and international partners to ensure that developments in Tibet remain part of the international human rights discourse," they said. On April 16, 2026, United Nations special rapporteurs expressed serious concerns regarding the “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress” adopted by the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The United Nations special rapporteurs said, “We observe that the Law could unduly restrict the right to freedom of expression. Article 10 limits engagement on issues related to ethnic unity and progress by prohibiting perceived “foreign forces” from interfering, and it suggests that human rights cannot be invoked to challenge China’s efforts in this regard. We observe a risk that any human rights-based analysis of the Law could be negatively framed and mischaracterized as foreign interference." The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk also said at the 62nd session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland, on June 15, 2026, "We face very serious human rights challenges. An unprecedented, shameless onslaught against international law is causing appalling human suffering. We must call it out, every time and everywhere, and work to contain and end it." "I am very concerned about China’s counterterrorism and assimilation policies, particularly as they affect minorities in the Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Tibetan regions. The new law on ethnic unity risks deepening restrictions on freedoms of language, education, practice of religion, culture, expression and assembly; and penalizing the peaceful exercise of minority rights in general. I call for the law to be repealed and for these practices to end," said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Tibet Human Rights China

title: His Holiness the Dalai Lama expresses condolences over devastating flood in Tibet and Nepal
content: Dharamshala — His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, the Spiritual leader of Tibet, expressed his condolences over devastating floods along the Tibet and Nepal Border. The massive floods in Nepal and Tibet has claimed at least 335 people, while more than 1,400 individuals remain missing as now and destroyed homes, villages, roads, and bridges. His Holiness wrote,"I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy." His Holiness the Dalai Lama wrote on August 27, 2026, “I am saddened to learn of the devastating floods in the Rasuwa region of Nepal and Kyirong in Tibet, resulting in loss of life and heavy structural damage. I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy. “Since this region has seen calamities in the past as well, these are certainly symptoms of a deeper underlying cause — whether climate change or other factors. I hope that appropriate follow-up measures will be taken, wherever possible, to help ensure that such disasters do not recur,” His Holiness concluded with prayers. The devastating flood and mudslide occurred suddenly, without warning in Kyirong County and Rasuwa District, on August 26, 2026. They originated in the Bhote Koshi River, which rises near Kyirong in the Shigatse region of Tibet, and reached Kyirong County and Rasuwa District in Bagmati Province, Nepal. These widespread floods have claimed at least 335 lives, while more than 1,400 people are still missing; it also destroyed homes, villages, roads, and bridges. The first wave severely affected the port of Kyirong before sweeping through the Nepalese district of Rasuwa. Mountain villages such as Timure and Syapru Besi were completely devastated. Since this region is very popular with hikers and pilgrims, hundreds of those reported missing are foreign nationals. In particular, there are numerous reports of missing persons among Indian (178), American (65), China (100), Malaysia (51) Australian (34), British (33), Canada (24) and Ukrainian (53) citizens. According to the latest figures released by the Nepal Tourism Board and regional authorities, at least 777 tourists (including 517 foreign nationals and 260 people en route to Tibet) are missing in the disaster-stricken area. At least 19 major bridges have been swept away, and several sites of large hydroelectric projects located along rivers have been completely destroyed and flooded. Due to the disruption of power grids and the total destruction of communication lines, authorities estimate that it will take several more days to identify and confirm the exact number of communities that have been destroyed. According to available information, this catastrophic flash flood struck Tibet at 8:37 a.m. (Tibet time) and reached the Nepalese district of Rasuwa around 9:15 a.m. (Nepal time). The debris flow crossed the border and struck the Nepalese district of Rasuwa. It completely submerged the border posts at Timure and Rasuwagadhi before rushing down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The Central Tibetan Administration held a prayer service at the main Tibetan temple in Dharamsala on August 27, 2026, for the victims and those who lost their lives in the devastating floods that occurred on August 26, 2026, in Kyirong (Tibet) and Rasuwa (Nepal). title: Unity cannot be built by erasing identity: Tibetan Parliament condemns China's Ethnic Unity Law
content: Dharamshala — The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile condemned China’s so-called “Law on Ethnic Unity and Progress” and stated: “Lasting peace cannot be achieved through forced assimilation. Lasting unity cannot be built by erasing identity. ” It further urged the international community to closely monitor this law, express concerns about it, and pressure China to engage in peaceful dialogue to resolve the Sino-Tibetan issue, adding: “Tibet’s future must be built through dialogue, not assimilation; through justice, not coercion.” On August 3, 2026, the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile issued a global appeal—an open letter addressed to heads of state and government, parliamentary leaders and members, the United Nations, human rights organisations, religious and interfaith leaders, and friends of Tibet. The letter states, "The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile the democratically elected legislative institution representing the Tibetan people across the globe calls to act with urgency in response to the People’s Republic of China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, which came into force on 1 July 2026. Presented as a measure to promote “national unity,” this law deepens policies that threaten the Tibetan people’s language, religion, culture, identity, and fundamental human rights. "The gravity of this moment was tragically underscored by the sacrifice of Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen, who died after setting himself on fire outside the United Nations Headquarters in New York on 2nd July 2026. His final appeal was for a free Tibet where Tibetans can live with dignity, freedom, and the protection of their fundamental rights. "We respectfully call upon governments, parliaments, the United Nations, and the international community to: Closely monitor the implementation and human rights implications of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law and ensure sustained international scrutiny. Support independent investigations through United Nations human rights mechanisms, including the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, Special Rapporteurs, Treaty Bodies, and the Universal Periodic Review process. Publicly express concern regarding the implementation and consequences of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law. Raise the issue in bilateral engagements and multilateral forums, including the United Nations and other international institutions. Support the protection of the cultural, linguistic, religious, and human rights of Tibetans and other affected nationalities. Strengthen measures to counter transnational repression and protect Tibetan communities, human rights defenders, and advocates living within your country. Oppose all forms of transnational repression that threaten democratic freedoms in the world. Recognise that Tibet was historically an independent nation, prior to the forceful invasion and occupation of Tibet. Impress upon the leadership of PRC to engage in peaceful dialogue to resolve the conflict between Tibet and China supporting the peaceful, non-violent aspirations of the Tibetan people in accordance with the vision of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. A Defining Test of the International Human Rights System "The implementation of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law is not solely a Tibetan concern. It is a test of the international community’s commitment to protecting cultural diversity, freedom of religion or belief, linguistic rights, minority protections, and the rule of international human rights law. "When the identity of a people is threatened, the principles upon which the international human rights system is built are also put at risk. "The Tibetan people’s struggle has always been guided by truth, compassion, and non-violence. We believe that silence in the face of injustice only emboldens oppression. We therefore urge the international community to stand with the Tibetan people in defending human dignity, religious freedom, cultural diversity, and the universal values that unite us all. "Lasting peace cannot be achieved through forced assimilation. Lasting unity cannot be built by erasing identity. A stable and harmonious future can only be founded on respect for human dignity, cultural diversity, religious freedom, and meaningful dialogue "The future of Tibet should be shaped through dialogue—not assimilation; through justice—not coercion." title: Tibetans Protest with Photos of 171 Self-Immolators, Condemn UN Failure to deliver justice for Tibet
content: New York — Hundreds of Tibetans held a large-scale protest in front of the United Nations headquarters, in New York, on August 6, 2026, holding photographs of 171 Tibetan self-immolators including the latest Tibetan self-immolator Lobga Rangzen. They demanded justice for Lobga Rangzen and 170 Tibetan self-immolators. They further condemned the United Nations for failing to uphold justice for Tibet. The protest titled "Flames for Independence," organised by the Tibetan Youth Congress, aimed to mark the 5th week of the self-immolation of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, which took place on July 2, 2026, in front of the United Nations headquarters in New York. The protesters stood in front of the UN building and the site where the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen had self-immolated, shouted powerful slogans: “UN, are you deaf? UN, we want justice, we want human rights, we want a free Tibet, we want China out of Tibet now, shame on the Chinese government, China is guilty, guilty of genocide, wake up, world leaders, world leaders, are you deaf? We want justice, justice for Lobga Rangzen, Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire for a free Tibet, Tibet belongs to the Tibetans, Tibet has never been part of China, long live the Dalai Lama, China lies, people die, China lies, Tibetans die, China lies, the UN is missing, shame on the UN, UN, we want justice—justice for Lobga Rangzen.” The Vice President of the Regional Tibetan Youth New York and New Jersey said: “Two years ago, when I first met Pawo Lobga Rangzen, he told me that there were two important things in his life: the first was to fight for Tibet’s independence, and the second was to bring His Holiness the Dalai Lama back to Tibet. This moved me deeply. One day, the RTYC organised a hunger strike in front of UN headquarters in New York; he was among the participants. He said there wasn’t much hope left to place in the UN, as it had already become an institution serving the Chinese government. In my view, it is precisely because the UN has failed to do justice to Tibet that he chose to protest in front of its headquarters in New York.” The former President of the RTYC stated: “Pawo Lobga Rangzen self-immolated in front of UN headquarters in New York, representing the 158 Tibetans who have self-immolated in Tibet, because the Chinese government spread false information about them and conceals the reality of their situation as well as their true aspirations; these cases are, in fact, little known to the UN and the rest of the world. Lobga Rangzen wanted to make known the true aspirations of Tibetans living in Tibet, which are: they demanded a free and independent Tibet, as well as called for the return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama to Tibet.” Another former President of the Tibetan Youth Congress of New York and New Jersey stated: “All the Tibetans who have self-immolated both inside and outside Tibet, demanded for a free and independent Tibet and called for the return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. What we who remain must do is continue to uphold the final statements of our martyrs and the hope of the Tibetan people, to fight for Tibet’s independence, and to bring His Holiness the Dalai Lama back to Tibet. We must organise more protests and events than before, and more people should participate in them.” Tibet Justice UNHRC UNO

title: Activists meet with UNHRC, US Representatives for UN and urge them raise Tibet at the UN
content: New York — A Tibetan delegation including family members of the late Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated in front of the UN headquarters in New York, met with representatives of the U.S. Mission to the UN, the Special Representative of the UN Human Rights Council, and the U.S. Special Coordinator for Tibetan Issues in August. The delegation urged them to shed light on the true cause of Lobga Rangzen's self-immolation and condemn the Chinese government's genocidal law aimed at eradicating Tibetan identity. Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen self-immolated in front of UN headquarters in New York, on July 2,2026. He protested against the Chinese government’s repressive policies in Tibet including so-called the China’s new “Ethnic Unity Law” and demanded an Independence for Tibet, as well as preservation of Tibetan culture and language. The President of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) Tsering Chomphel, together with members of the family of Pawo Lobga Rangzen, former TYC President and MP Tenzing Jigme and Rtyc NYNJ President Jamphel Choesang, met with representatives of the U.S. Mission to the United Nations, on August 27, 2026 and briefed them on the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet as well as Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen’s extraordinary sacrifice. According to Tibetan Youth Congress, the delegation met with Yaryna Ferencevych, Deputy Representative U.S Mission to United Nations and Maria Macarena Apud, Adviser, U.S. Mission to the United Nations on Human Right Desk. The delegation briefed U.S. officials on the circumstances surrounding Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation in front of United Nations headquarters on July 2, 2026, as well as his final message calling for attention to the struggle for Tibet’s freedom and the urgent need for international action. The delegation emphasized that his sacrifice reflected the deep despair caused by the persistent denial of fundamental rights in Tibet. The delegation also raised serious concerns regarding China’s recently enacted "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress", which further institutionalizes policies that threaten Tibet’s distinct national, cultural, linguistic, and religious identity. "The meeting underscored the importance of continued U.S. and international attention to Tibet at the United Nations, particularly through the General Assembly and its human rights mechanisms," TYC said. The delegation further urged the United States Mission to continue raising Tibet’s human rights situation at the United Nations and ensure that the issue of Tibet is raised with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the upcoming meeting with President Trump. Sonam Choedon, niece of Tibetan Martyr Lobga Rangzen, Tsering Chomphel, the President of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), Jamphel Chosang, President of Regional Tibetan Youth Congress (New York and Nwe Jersey), Yeshi Tenzin, Former TYC centrex member, Tenzin Youdon, President Washingtong Area RTYC and former TYC President Chisur Tenzing Jigme, met with Riley Barnes, U.S Special Coordinator for Tibetan issue, on August 19, 2026, in Washingtong D.C. The delegation outlined the Special Coordinator about the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen's sacrifice, his final message, and the circumstances surrounding his death. "The meeting provided an opportunity for Lobga’s family to share their concerns and to urge continued U.S. attention to the human rights situation in Tibet and the issues that motivated his final act," TYC said. According to the TYC, The TYC President also presented several points for continued U.S. support for the Tibetan cause and for greater international attention to Tibet and urged the U.S. government to raise the issue of Tibet with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his upcoming visit. "The meeting underscored the importance of ensuring that Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice and his call for justice, unity, and action are not forgotten. The participants expressed appreciation for the U.S. government’s willingness to hear directly from Lobga’s family and representatives of the Tibetan Youth Congress," the President of TYC said. Two Family members of the Lobga Rangzen and Tsewang Rigzen, former President of TYC and former Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, met with UN Human Rights Council Special Representative Anne Siyota at the United Nations in New York, on August 12, 2026. During a one-hour meeting, they informed Siyota of the circumstances surrounding Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation in front of United Nations headquarters on July 2, 2026, as well as his final message calling for attention to be drawn to the struggle for Tibet’s freedom and the urgent need for international action. They also presented six demands to the UNHRC representative, in which they urged him to take more effective action in response to the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet. Another demand concerned the United Nations’ implementation of its previous resolutions on Tibet, adopted in 1959, 1961, and 1965. Those resolutions had expressed concern about violations of the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Tibetan people and called for an end to policies that infringed upon the human rights of Tibetans, including their right to self-determination. The Tibetan delegation also called on the UN to pressure Beijing to dismantle the Chinese boarding school system in Tibet, which aims to systematically erase Tibetan identity, language, and religion by separating children from their parents and homes. The delegation further urged the United Nations to publicly oppose the so-called China's "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress" recently adopted, and called for the immediate repeal of that law. title: Tibetans begin “Peace Walk for a Free Tibet”  to carry on Lobga Rangzen’s final call
content: Dharamshala — Tibetan-Americans including 82-year-old Dorjee Gyalpo began their "Peace Walk for a Free Tibet" from Saint Paul, the Capital city of Minnesota to Chicago, on August 5, 2026. They will arrive at the Chicago Chinese Consulate on the 49th day after Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen 's self-immolation outside the United Nations, NY. The Peace walk is to honor Pawo Lobga Rangzen and amplify his final call for Tibetan independence and raise awareness on critical situation in Tibet. Tibetan-Americans organised an event to launch “Peace Walk for a Free Tibet” at University of Minnesota Regent in Saint Paul, the Capital city of Minnesota, on August 5, 2026 and community members, Tibetan Buddhist monks, supporters, and elected leaders gathered at the State Capitol to send off the walkers. Minnesota State Senator Robyn Gulley and Jigme Ugen, President of the Tibetan National Congress, Tenzing Jigme, former MP of Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile and others delivered their speeches at the gathering. "Today, among the participants in the "Peaceful Walk for a Free Tibet," the oldest is 82 and the youngest is 20,” said Lhathok Mayong Nyima, leader of the “Peaceful Walk for a Free Tibet” campaign and President of the regional Chushi Gandruk regional. "More than 171 Tibetans have sacrificed their lives through self-immolation in the struggle for Tibet’s freedom and independence, calling for the return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Therefore, we must continue to redouble our efforts to fulfill their wishes, transform the ‘R’ (refugee) on our foreheads into an ‘R’ (for “Rangzen”—independence), and bring His Holiness back to Tibet." Jigme Ugen, President of the Tibetan National Congress, stated at the launch ceremony: “The Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen did not suddenly self-immolate. Day after day, he fought for the Tibetan cause, organised the Tibetan freedom movement, participated in protests against the Chinese government, ran marathons for Tibet, took part in hunger strikes, and devoted himself entirely to the Tibetan cause and Tibetan independence. Why did he self-immolate in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York?, it is because, even though the United Nations is well aware of what is happening in Tibet, no action has been taken to seek justice for Tibet.” Senator Robyn Gulley, said, "They are walking for Pawo Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated outside United Nations Headquarters in New York, and for the 170 other Tibetans who have self-immolated in protest against China’s occupation and destruction of Tibet. We must stand with the Tibetan people in their struggle for freedom, dignity, justice, and the right to determine their own future." The organiser said, "On July 2, Lobga Rangzen, stood outside the UN Headquarters with the Tibetan flag and calling for Tibet's independence, then self-immolated. He was the first known Tibetan to self-immolate in the United States, and the 171st known Tibetan to self-immolate against Chinese rule. The walk comes as China intensifies efforts to erase Tibetan identity suppressing the Tibetan language, controlling religious institutions, separating children into colonial boarding schools, and criminalizing dissent at home and across the diaspora." Tibet Justice Self-immolation

title: Tibetan Generation Z committed to fight for a free and independent Tibet
content: New York — Hundreds of Tibetans, particular Tibetan youth (Gen Z) gathered outside of UN Headquarters in New York on Thursday and protested against Chinese government's ongoing occupation of Tibet, it's repressive policies and genocidal policies, paid tribute to the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, and given powerful speeches by over 10 Tibetan youth and pledged to continue their struggle for a free and independent Tibet and bring His Holiness the Dalai Lama back to Tibet. Hundreds of Tibetans from various places in USA and Canada gathered outside of UN headquarters in New York, on August 12, 2026, to commemorate Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who passed away following self-immolating outside the UN, to protest against the Chinese government’s oppressive regime in Tibet and demand restoration of Tibetan independence. Then they marched toward Chinese consulate from UN headquarters in New York, and shouted slogans: “Free Tibet, China out of Tibet now, we want human rights in Tibet, we want a free Tibet, shame on the Chinese government, China is guilty, guilty of genocide, wake up, world leaders, world leaders, are you deaf? We want justice, justice for Lobga Rangzen, Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire for a free Tibet, Tibet belongs to the Tibetans, Tibet has never been part of China, long live the Dalai Lama, China lies, people die, China lies, Tibetans die." The Tibetan Gen Z movement was organised by the Regional Tibetan Youth Congress (NYNJ); total 12 young Tibetans spoke candidly, sharing their feelings with tears in their eyes, they spoke about the current situation in Tibet and the final words of the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, spoken outside UN headquarters in New York on August 12 (local time), 2026, and pledged to continue their struggle for a free and independent Tibet. On August 13, 2026, marking the sixth week since Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen self-immolated, in protest against Chinese government's ongoing occupation of Tibet, its repressive policies and genocidal policies in Tibet and demanded for a free and independence Tibet. At the event, young Tibetan Tenzin Tashi passionately spoke about remembering Pawo Lobga Rangzen and the impact he had on him. He said, “Today I wanted to talk about someone who had a big impact on my life; Uncle Lobga Rangzen (weeping). I have to look at him more than 10 years since I was little child and he was part of my life, he is like teacher to me, he told me why he believe in freedom and independence of Tibet, he cares about Tibetan people. He always spoke with kindness and wanted us to understand his beliefs. He was just a very kind person. And whenever he traveled, he would always bring back small gifts, those gifts made me happy. What I remember most is that he's a man who did not give up on what he fought for. His decisions always stayed the same. He always brought attention to the struggles of the Tibetan people. While many people have different views about his actions, I remember this as a caring, selfless person who gave everything for the Tibet to be free. I feel grateful that I had the chance to know him, and I will always remember his kindness and the lessons he taught me, the way he cared for others. “He and other Tibetans, who took the act of protesting by self-immolation, not only do this for their freedom and their nation, but they also did it for the younger Tibetan generation, so that in the future, they can have a place to call home. The sacrifice is a direct call to action for all of us. As the youth, we hold the future of Tibet in our hands and we must find the courage to stand up, speak out, and proudly preserve our language and keep our rich culture alive every single day. And continue the fight for our country's freedom. We will never forget where we come from and will never stop fighting for our homeland. Free Tibet, victory for Tibet.” Tsewang Dolma (13), said, "Today, I am standing here outside the United Nations because I am a Tibetan child. And I have something important to say. The day before Lobga Rangzen passed away, I was fortunate enough to have met him casually outside my house along with my mother. He told me to be kind. He told me to respect others. He told me to listen to my mother. But there was one thing he told me that I will never forget. He told me, "Never forget that you are Tibetan." Those words have stayed with me. I am only 13 years old, but I understand that being Tibetan is more than just having a Tibetan name. It is our language. It is our culture. It is our history. It is our identity. And today, Tibetan children inside Tibet are facing a future where that identity is being taken away from them. Children my age are being separated from their families and placed in boarding schools under policies described as promoting ethnic unity and progress law. But I have a simple question. What kind of progress makes a child lose their language and culture? What kind of unity requires children to grow up away from their families and communities? “I am lucky that I can speak Tibetan. I am lucky that I can learn about my culture. I am lucky that I can stand here today and say proudly that, I am Tibetan. But Tibetan children in Tibet deserve that same right. They deserve to speak their own language. To preserve their own history, they deserve to know their culture and they deserve to grow up with their families. This is why Lobga Rangzen's word means so much to me. Some people have called him crazy or stupid. Even the New York Post called him a "lunatic". But before judging him, I want people to ask: Why did he feel that he had to sacrifice everything just to make the world listen to Tibet? I am not here to say that losing a life is the answer. I want to live. I want to grow up. I want to go to school, laugh with my friends, and have a future. And I want Tibetan children in Tibet to have that same future. A future where they can be Tibetan without fear. A future where they can speak their own language. A future where they can learn their own history and culture. A future where children do not have to lose their lives for the world to listen. “Lobga Rangzen wanted the world to hear about Tibet. And today, we are here because we heard him. We must not let his voice disappear. We must not forget him. And we must not forget the more than one hundred Tibetan individuals who have lost their lives through self-immolation while calling attention to the situation in Tibet. Every child deserves the right to know who they are. And no policy called unity or progress should erase a child's language, culture, or identity. So today, standing here outside the United Nations, I ask the world: Please listen to Tibet. Please listen to Tibetan children. Please protect our language, our culture, and our identity. And most importantly, please do not forget Lobga Rangzen. He told me, "Never forget you are Tibetan." I promise, I will remember. And I hope all of you will remember too. Free Tibet, Victory for Tibet." Tenzin Minkyi said, “I have seen this with my own eyes, but I have been attending protests ever since I can remember and I will continue to do so. I knew Lobga Rangzen personally as he was a good family friend and was very kind to me growing up. He has always been a freedom fighter and his sacrifice would not go in vain. And to the United Nations, you have a responsibility to humanity. You have a responsibility to protect the people in this world and defend human rights. How can you turn a blind eye when the world once said, "Never again" after the Holocaust? We must not allow history to repeat itself. When human rights are violated, the international community has a responsibility to speak up. We need to wake up, you need to wake up, and hold China accountable for the mountains upon mountains of human rights violations inflicted upon the Tibetan people. We cannot remain silent. We cannot look away. Tibet deserves freedom, dignity, and the right to determine its own future." Tenzin Dolkar said, “Since 2009, more than 170 Tibetans have self-immolated, giving up their lives to free Tibet. Tibetans are being silenced in Tibet, how can the CCP and their supporters remain indifferent to our existence? So why can't we, the people who are living in countries where immigration is permitted, speak up a bit of our time to contribute to a free Tibet? In Tibet, the CCP has set up colonial boarding schools where cultural erasure is enforced. The recent implementation of the ethnic unity law has made cultural genocide even more vast and prominent across Tibet. Once we lose our culture, we lose our history, and all the sacrifices previously made go to vain. We have to make sure that we uphold our culture and traditions, because we have the freedom to do so, unlike those in Tibet. We should be held accountable, as Tibetans living in countries where we can use our voices, to utilize these rights and fight for the freedom of our country. As we get older, it is our responsibility as the youth to start to take initiative and fight for Tibet's independence. “Pawo Lobga Rangzen has achieved the freedom that every Tibetan is still fighting for. He moved to America where he was free from CCP oppression and could have lived a peaceful life. But he decided to sacrifice his life, right here, to fight for Tibet's freedom. Before he had sacrificed his life, he had told us to unite and understand that we have one common goal, a free Tibet. We need to fight now more than ever, with the sacrifice that our Pawo Lobga Rangzen has made, because we are responsible for fighting for our free Tibet. Victory for Tibetan independence.” Tenzin (young woman) said, “Do not mourns for me. But we should truly mourn is the loss of our country. Do not remain in grief. If you must grieve, then I ask each one of you to continue fighting for the just cause of the Tibetan independence movement. These were the dying wishes of Lobga Rangzen (crying)... these were the super requests he made of us. Six weeks later, we stand here, not just to remember him, but to ask: When will the world hear our pleas? When will they acknowledge our call to justice? How long will they turn a blind eye to our suffering? We stand before the United Nations. The very institution created to defend all human rights and our human dignity. And yet, six weeks later, after Lobga Rangzen’s protest here, we are still demanding for Tibet to be heard. Our struggle did not begin six weeks ago. For generations, Tibetans have watched their political freedoms, religious freedoms, language, and culture be threatened under Chinese rule. Tibetan language and education faces increasing restrictions. Tibetan borders are tightly controlled. Expressions of support for His Holiness the Dalai Lama, can invite punishment. Peaceful expressions can resort into tension. "So, if Tibetans inside in Tibet cannot decide, cannot speak freely, we must. If they cannot protest freely, we must. And if they cannot stand here, in front of the United Nations, then we must stand here for them. My generation, Gen Z, this is our responsibility. Our parents, our grandparents, carried this movement for decades. They marched; they organized, they taught our language, the justice in our traditional clothing. Brought us to protest and refused to allow Tibet to disappear from our hearts. But they cannot carry this movement forever. So, we will be the organisers. We will march into government offices, demanding action. We will teach the next generation what Tibet means. Our time is now, use your phones to amplify this voice; educate people, share the valuable information,attend protests, learn about Tibetan history, preserve our culture, contact elected officials and this is a support group and organisations. Talk about Tibet, even if Tibet is not trending, into the leaders who can hear us. Make Tibet a serious part of your foreign policy. Hold the Chinese government accountable for human rights abuses. Do not allow economic interests from them to ignore Tibet's suffering. The United Nations, right behind me, do not stay silent. If you stand for human rights, then Tibetan human rights must matter. If you stand for the right to speak, then Tibetan religious freedom must matter. And if you stand for the protection of culture, then Tibetan culture must matter. And if you stand for people whose voices are unheard, and then listen to Tibet. I have got on the ask us to not remain in grief, but to continue the cause he believed in. We honor that message by choosing to live, organise, educate, advocate, preserve Tibetan culture and refuse to be silent. To every young Tibetan in here, this is our generation now. To everyone else, you do not have to be Tibetan to stand against injustice. And to every leader who can hear us, how many more voices must cry out before you listen? We are here, we are speaking and we are not giving up. And we will continue to stand for the Tibet and fight the Tibetan freedom. I have lived my whole life in Chicago. And I have no longer fear in my life, for those whose voices have been silenced. My Tibetans may not be perfect. I still have my unconditional love, my language, my culture, and my freedom. I am here. I am showing up. And I am learning. And I am ready to fight for Tibetan independence and for the future of my people. My whole life, I questioned whether I was Tibetan enough. I don't question that anymore. I am proud of where I come from. I am proud to carry Tibet with me. And I will never, ever be afraid to say, "I am Tibetan.” Free Tibet and Victory for Tibet.” Tenzin Wangyal said, “Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s love for his nation, his desire for Tibetan independence was stronger than anything you could imagine. Our parents fled Tibet across the freezing dangerous terrain. Our parents built lives in strange countries, working odd jobs so that we could get this education, we could get these opportunities. And we could continue their fight. To our older generation, because of them, we have immense gratitude. My generation has learned a lot from our parents about Lobga Rangzen. But first to truly fight for our nation, our cause, we must, we must know the real facts about our history. Pawo Lobga Ranzgen said it was the best; the only path forward is independence. The only way to secure our future, our religious freedom, is independence. With the unified support of our community, I know we will win. So that we will all soon be reunited in a free and an independent Tibet.” Tenzin Desang (16) said, "I am opening my phone to see that someone I used to see at every single rally, someone who was there when I gave my very first speech for Tibet, has set himself on fire. Pawo Lobga Rangzen was so much to so many people. If you have ever lived in New York, you knew him. He was always there, at every rally, every prayer, and every candle vigil. He was standing in the crowd right alongside us. He showed up for everyone, every time. Standing here today, the strangest hardest part is looking out at the crowd, realizing he isn't in it. There's a photo of him sitting in the exact spot where he used to stand. I still find it difficult to believe that this actually happened. For me, Pawo Lobga Rangzen's self-immolation was a wakeup call. Everywhere we look, we see Tibetans coming together. We have seen weekly protests, peace walks, hunger strikes, head-shavings, and Tibetan youth dropping everything to be there. And we must. As Tibetan youth living in exile, we have freedoms that Tibetans and Tibetans in Tibet do not. I can speak Tibetan on the street without looking over my shoulder. I can learn about my culture and Tibetan Buddhism without being afraid of getting punished for it. Every right we enjoy hearing in exile, from the flags we wave to the images of His Holiness the Dalai Lama we see, is a privilege that Tibetans inside Tibet are punished for. “Tibet remains one of the least free places in the world. And now the Chinese government has enacted a law, "the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law," which criminalizes every aspect of Tibetan identity. Pawo Lobga Rangzen's self-immolation came just one day after the law was enacted. Every time the Chinese government talks about unity, Tibetans lose something. We lose another school that teaches our language. We lose another monastery to surveillance or the blade of a bulldozer. We lose another child forced into a colonial boarding school. We lose another Tibetan's life. And yet, against all odds, Tibetans inside Tibet are still resisting. It is our responsibility to stand behind them. Before his self-immolation, Pawo Lobga Rangzen left a final message. He said, "I don't want you to mourn me. I want you to continue the struggle for Tibetan independence." That is a call to action. Pawo Lobga Rangzen gave his life for Tibetan freedom, right here on the doorstep of the United Nations. And yet, the UN remains silent on Tibet. After his sacrifice, the only response from the United Nations was that "it's absolutely tragic and it's important that minorities are respected" and made to feel as part of a whole. It is absolutely tragic that this is all the UN has to say. Tibetans are not asking to be made to feel like part of a whole. We are asking to have our identity, our rights, our existence as a people recognized and protected. Because we are still here, we call on UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, to break his silence on Tibet. Establish an independent UN investigation into China's genocidal policies in Tibet, and demand the abolition of China's colonial boarding school system, which has torn one million Tibetan children from their families. “Here in exile, we are proud of a generation who have never stepped foot in Tibet. Many people don't remember or were not even alive for the 2008 uprisings. But we are the generation who has to watch Tibetan children online, who cannot pronounce their own names. We are the ones with more access, tools, and exposure than ever before. So we have no excuse, no right to turn even a blind eye. Freedom is our birthright, and yet we have learned the hard way that freedom will never be handed to us. It must be fought for. So when this protest ends, don't leave this energy on the sidewalk. Step out of your comfort zone. Join a Tibetan organisation or an event. Talk to one person about Tibet every day. Use your voice. Make the choice to fight back until we achieve what Pawo Lobga Rangzen lived and gave his life for. Free Tibet! Free Tibet!” Tenzin Tsekyi said, "When I think about Tibet. I don't think about the mountains or our culture. I think about our identity. I think about our language, our traditions, and the people who worked so hard to keep them alive (weeping). To me, Rangzen means freedom. It means being able to speak to them, practice our culture, and be proud of who we are without being afraid. One of the hardest things about learning about Tibet is hearing about Tibetans who have sacrificed their lives to make the world listen. Every person who self-immolates is a real person. They have families, friends, dreams, and people who love them (weeping). Recently, we lost our Pawo Lobga Rangzen and his sacrifice has been very difficult for many Tibetans. For me, Lobga Rangzen was not just a name heard on the news. He was a Tibetan who felt strongly enough about our people's struggle to make the ultimate sacrifice. His death reminds us that the struggle for Tibet is still happening. And also reminds us that we cannot let his message disappear. We should remember him, not only through sadness, but by learning from his courage and continuing to speak about Tibet. The way Lobga Rangzen sacrificed also makes me think about what our generation can do. We can... we may not be able to change everything overnight. But we can keep his message alive. We can talk about Tibet, educate others, and make sure people know why Tibetans continue to fight for their identity and freedom. "As young Tibetans, and as Gen Z, I think we have the responsibility to take action. We have social media, phones, and the ability to contact people from across the world. We can use these things to talk about Tibet and help other people understand what is happening. We also need to learn about things like the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, and how it can affect Tibetan language, culture, and identity. Even though we are young, we should still care about these things because they will affect our future. Sometimes I ask myself, what will Tibet be like when our generation gets older? Will Tibetan kids still speak Tibetan? Will they know our history? And will they still be proud to say "I am Tibetan." I think that depends partly on us. We might be young, but that doesn't mean our voices don't matter. We can learn our language, learn our history, speak up, and keep Tibet in people's lives. We can honor people like Lobga Rangzen. We can make sure that their sacrifices are not forgotten. We can carry their stories forward and make sure the next generation knows why we continue to stand for Tibet. Our culture matters, our identity matters, and Tibet matters. We will remember those who sacrificed for Tibet, and we will continue to raise our voices. Free Tibet, Victory for Tibetan independence, and Victory for Pawo Lobga Rangzen.” Tenzin Namdon said,"I remember when I first heard about all over Pawo Lobga Ranzen... I didn't know him personally (weeping), but there was a prayer for him in Minnesota. And it was only like an hour after he self-immolated, and so many people went inthe the room. And there were so many emotions that we all felt. And it made me realise that Tibetan community is so strong when we all truly together. He self-immolation is for many reasons; to spread awareness on Tibetan religion, cuture, which repressed by the Chinese government, and demand for independence of Tibet. And especially to bring awareness to the Chinese ethnic unity law. A new law which promotes all of China to make a singular Chinese national identity that aligns with the Chinese Communist Party. illegally enforces the Mandarin language as the primary language of teaching from preschool to high school, which destroys our language education. It is not only is it a way to brainwash many young Tibetans living in Tibet, it also poses a large threat to the extinction of our language, religion and culture. Without our language, Tibetans lose a vital form of communication and connection with each other, especially between the older and younger generations. Our religion, culture need to be protected so that we can connect with each other. Pass down generations worth of knowledge, experience. And most importantly, it gives us something worth fighting for. Lobga Rangzen is an inspiration for everyone here. We need to look at his lifelong actions of advocating and fighting for Tibet. And the lessons that we have to learn from. "There have been over 171 acts of self-immolation. The first one occurring in 1998 by Thubten Ngodup, who was a Tibetan activist living in New Delhi. And the youngest having been Dorjee Tsering, a 16-year-old. younger that almost everyone here (weeping)... These people are so brave to sacrifice their lives for their country. So it should be the bare minimum for all of us to protest as much as we can and speak up against the Chinese government and their actions, no matter where we are. I believe that if we keep fighting for our rights and our independence, one day we will all be able to go back to Tibet, not China. I believe that we can go and meet our families without worrying about getting sent back. And I believe that we will be able to freely and openly express our culture and identity everywhere we go. Free Tibet, Victory Tibet and independence." Tibet Independence Youth

title: Thousands join top officials in peace march honouring those who sacrificed for Tibet freedom
content: Dharamshala — Thousands of Tibetan exiles, and Tibet supporters flooded the streets of Dharamshala in a massive peace march organised by the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile and the Kashag. They gathered to fiercely condemn Beijing’s cultral genocidal law and honor the profound sacrifice of Tibetan independent activist Lobga Rangzen. The demonstrations transformed into a powerful unified front against China's relentless cultural assimilation polices. Protesters explicitly targeted Beijing’s controversial new "Ethnic Unity and Progress Law"—a policy widely denounced by Tibetan leadership as an authoritarian mechanism engineered to systematically erase Tibetan language, identity, and Buddhist heritage. Global wave of defiance across major international capitals in more than 20 countries. From mass rallies in Delhi—where emotional protesters shaved their heads at Jantar Mantar—to large-scale marches through Geneva, Paris, Toronto, Minnesota,Dharamshala, Darjeeling, Kolkata and New York, the diaspora unified to reject China's new "Ethnic Unity and Progress Law". Tibetan leadership explicitly slammed the policy as an authoritarian weapon engineered to systematically erase Tibetan language, identity, and Buddhist heritage, vowing that the global demand for a free Tibet will not be silenced. The 17th Kashag and the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile jointly organised a mass prayer service in honor of the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen and all Tibetans who have sacrificed their lives for the cause of Tibet, at the main Tibetan temple (Thekchen Choeling Tsuglakhang) on August 20, 2026. The prayer service joined by Top officials and all staff of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) and thousands of Tibetans around the Dharamshala. The prayer ceremony, which took place from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. at the temple, was followed by a peace march that began at the temple site. All shops and hotels in McLeod Ganj closed for the whole day as a sign of solidarity with our brothers and sisters who sacrificed themselves for a common cause: a free and independent Tibet. They then organised a peaceful march from the temple to the Dharamsala police ground to honor the sacrifice of the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen and pay tribute to all Tibetans who have sacrificed their lives for the justice cause of Tibet, and to denounce the repressive laws that China continues to enact in order to eradicate Tibet’s unique identity, culture, and way of life, including the recently enacted “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress". Peace protesters marched through the streets waving vibrant Tibetan national flags and holding signs that read: "United Nations, Break Your Silence", Lobga died for free Tibet -Justice for Lobga Rangzen", "No More Silence", "People of the World, Stand for Tibet", Tibet is belongs to Tibetans, China out of Tibet now", "Save Tibetan culture", "Rise Up Tibetans", "Unity is our Strength", and chanted slogans such as “Free Tibet,” “Save Tibet,” “Lobga Rangzen died for a free Tibet,” “Justice for Lobga Rangzen,” “Tibet’s independence is India’s security.” "Upon reaching the Police Ground in Dharamshala, the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) organized a concluding event, where Sikyong Penpa Tsering, Speaker Dolma Tsering, Shri Ajit Nehria (President of the Indo-Tibetan Friendship Association), and Shamsher Singh Nehria (Mayor of Dharamshala) addressed the gathering. Sikyong read out the Statement of the Kashag on the 49th-day of the Passing of the Late Martyr Lobga Rangzen,"Today marks the Seventh Week (49th-day) of the self-immolation and passing of the martyr Lobsang Palden, popularly known as Lobga Rangzen. He sacrificed his life on July 2, 2026, in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York City, United States, leaving behind a final testament stating that his action was undertaken in protest against the Chinese Communist Party’s policies and its systematic eradication of the Tibetan identity in Tibet, while calling on all Tibetans to unite and campaign for Tibet’s independence. "In observance of the 49th-Day, the Kashag and the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile today, are jointly organising this official solidarity prayer service and peace march to express our deep condolences and respect to the late Lobga Rangzen and all those Tibetans who have sacrificed their lives for the cause of Tibet. We express our strong opposition to the Chinese Communist Party’s implementation of repressive policies in Tibet, particularly the so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”. "To draw international attention to the Chinese government’s ongoing policy of eradicating the Tibetan identity, 157 Tibetans inside Tibet have been known to have self-immolated since 2009, out of which 136 died, 9 have survived, and the status of 12 remains unknown. In exile, including the late Lobga Rangzen, 11 Tibetans have self-immolated, of which 9 died and 2 survived. "Not a single brave Tibetan who self-immolated—whether inside Tibet or in exile—ever harmed the lives or property of others. Rather, they sacrificed their own precious lives with the sole motivation of drawing the attention of the Chinese government and the international community to the plight of the Tibetan people. "We appeal to Governments and Parliaments of free nations around the world to confront the Chinese government’s implementation of genocidal policies in Tibet through its blatant violation of international law and global order. We urge the international community to recognise the Sino-Tibetan conflict as an unresolved international legal issue and not an internal matter of China. And we seek your support in the resumption of Sino-Tibetan dialogue based on the mutually beneficial Middle-Way Approach policy without preconditions. We also request the think tanks and media organisations to conduct fair, objective analyses and accurate reporting. "We also urge the authorities of the Chinese government to stop acting against the progress of human society, cease clinging solely to the perpetuation of their power, and immediately halt policies aimed at eradicating the identities of other non-Chinese nationalities." Speaker of Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile read out its statement , " The sacrifice of patriotic hero Lobga Rangzen through his act of self-immolation highlighted the suffering of Tibetans to the United Nations, governments, and people around the world. By directly confronting and protesting Chinese policies, his action has opened a new chapter in the history of the Tibetan struggle for truth. "We express our deep appreciation to Tibetans and Tibet supporters worldwide who have continuously organized diverse and large-scale campaigns following the sacrifice of patriotic hero Rangzen Lobga—especially the Tibetans and non-governmental organizations in New York. We urge everyone, both publicly and individually, to maintain strong resolve in their hearts and intensify efforts for the common Tibetan cause until truth prevails. "During this critical and urgent time, we strongly appeal the international community to take a moral and just responsibility through the following actions: Closely monitor the implementation and human rights implications of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law and ensure sustained international scrutiny. Support independent investigations through United Nations human rights mechanisms, including the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, Special Rapporteurs, Treaty Bodies, and the Universal Periodic Review process. Publicly express concern regarding the implementation and consequences of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law. Raise the issue in bilateral engagements and multilateral forums, including the United Nations and other international institutions. Support the protection of the cultural, linguistic, religious, and human rights of Tibetans and other affected nationalities. Strengthen measures to counter transnational repression and protect Tibetan communities, human rights defenders, and advocates living within your country. Oppose all forms of transnational repression that threaten democratic freedoms in the world. Recognize that Tibet was historically an independent nation, prior to the forceful invasion and occupation of Tibet. Impress upon the leadership of PRC to engage in peaceful dialogue to resolve the conflict between Tibet and China supporting the peaceful, non-violent aspirations of the Tibetan people in accordance with the vision of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Tibet China Protests CTA
