The amended law introduces a new Article 3, stating that lawyers must adhere to CCP leadership and implement the policies and decisions of the Party and the state. The provision places Communist leadership directly within the statutory framework governing legal practice in China, the commentary noted. The rules have already required law firms with three or more CCP members to establish Communist Party organisations. Firms with fewer CCP members were required to conduct Party work through joint organisations or Party-building instructors. Law firms have been further required to create mechanisms to allow Party organisations to participate in decision-making and management, while providing space, personnel and funding for Party activities. The Aug 28 amendment moves all these requirements into national legislation. The law’s guarantees of protecting “lawyers’ lawful practice”, and the requirement for courts, prosecutors, police, state-security agencies and judicial-administration departments to establish systems protecting lawyers’ professional right are, therefore, subject to the overriding requirement of fealty to the governing CCP regime. The changes in the rules and now the law followed the so-called “709 Crackdown” which began on Jul 9, 2015 under which more than 300 lawyers, legal assistants and rights advocates were detained, questioned or otherwise swept up. Some lawyers were held incommunicado or subsequently prosecuted on national-security charges, while others lost their law licences. The pressure also extended to their families. Spouses and children reported surveillance, movement restrictions, pressure on landlords and interference with schooling, the commentary noted. Wang Yu, a rights lawyer detained during the “709 Crackdown”, has described her assessment of China’s legal system in an interview in Jun 2018: “Now I believe there is no law in China.” She argued that the essence of the rule of law is limiting government power, while the CCP was using the rule of law to reinforce its own rule, the commentary said.

title: The Dilemma of the Democratic System of the Tibetan Government-in-Exile
author: tibetanreview
content: Prof. Thomas Kell* dissects the exile Tibetan democracy, examines its fundamental shortcomings, practical dilemmas. and hidden dangers, and wonders whether the existing structure can independently maintain political continuity and the legitimacy of the movement in the post-Dalai Lama scenario without adequately adapting the institutional design to the realities of a shrinking, dispersed exile population and the generational change. As a researcher in Tibetan studies, I have interviewed many Tibetans in exile, including former Sikyong Lobsang Sangay, and heard numerous views on the “democratic system” of the Tibetan government-in-exile (referred to as Central Tibetan Administration, or CTA). In my opinion, the democratic system of the Tibetan government-in-exile suffers from multiple structural defects and practical dilemmas. The following represents only my personal views and is offered for discussion. The democratic system of the Tibetan government-in-exile began in the 1960s. The Charter of the Tibetans-in-Exile of 1991 established a three-branch framework, and after the Dalai Lama formally transferred political power in 2011, it was further “democratized,” with the election of a Sikyong (political leader) and a parliament. However, it is not the democracy of a mature sovereign state, but a limited experiment of a refugee community in exile. Its problems are particularly evident in inadequate representation, institutional fragility, the entanglement of religion and politics, and low governance effectiveness. I. Lack of a sovereign foundation: democracy remains largely formal The CTA has no territory, no army, and no coercive enforcement powers; it operates entirely under the legal frameworks of host countries such as India. Its “judicial institution” (the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission) is in essence closer to an arbitration body and cannot exercise genuine judicial independence or coercive authority. Voter eligibility depends on registration through the “Green Book,” and voting is dispersed across settlements and diaspora communities worldwide. Participation is severely constrained by geography, resources, and the policies of host countries. This “stateless democracy” makes the system inherently fragile: its budget relies on diaspora donations and external aid (for example, U.S. assistance has faced the risk of being frozen), and its core functions focus on refugee services and cultural preservation rather than effective political decision-making. Should the attitude of a host country change or aid diminish, the entire system faces an operational crisis. II. Clear unfairness and distortions in the electoral and representational mechanisms The parliament has 45 seats and uses a mixed model based on the three traditional regions (U-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo) with 10 seats each (including women’s quotas) + 10 seats for religious schools (Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug, and Bön) + a limited number of seats for overseas Tibetans, rather than pure one-person-one-vote or allocation according to the current population. Tibetans overseas (especially those outside South Asia) have very few seats, creating a de facto hierarchy of citizenship rights. The allocation of religious representatives directly grants the monastic community disproportionate political weight, contradicting the principle of equality proclaimed in the Charter and reinforcing residual theocratic elements. In addition, electoral rules restrict regional associations, religious schools, and NGOs from openly nominating or campaigning for candidates, effectively suppressing the development of party politics. Although there is democracy in name, there is a lack of mature opposition parties and competition based on programmatic platforms. Elections often devolve into contests of personal image and negative mudslinging. The limited and dispersed voter base, further subject to external interference (such as voting being obstructed in parts of Nepal), further undermines the fairness and credibility of the process. III. Repeated institutional deadlock and excessive reliance on personal authority After 2011, although the Dalai Lama withdrew from politics, his moral and spiritual influence continues to dominate. In 2021, the parliament’s impeachment of the justice commissioners triggered a constitutional crisis: the newly elected parliament could not be sworn in, the Sikyong could not form a cabinet, and the budget could not be approved. The stalemate lasted for months and was ultimately resolved only through the Dalai Lama’s intervention. Since then, the parliament has repeatedly adjourned or postponed sessions due to walkouts and lack of quorum, while judicial positions have remained vacant for long periods because of qualification requirements that are difficult to meet. These crises expose the failure of checks and balances: the boundaries between the legislative, executive, and judicial branches are blurred, and effective conflict-resolution mechanisms are lacking. In the exile environment, the logic of “unity first” is inherently in conflict with the pluralism and competition required by democracy, leading to intensified polarization and deepening rifts within the community. Divisions based on regional identity, religious background, and the “Middle Way” versus independence lines frequently turn into parliamentary internal strife rather than policy debate. IV. Incomplete disentanglement of religion and politics limits the quality of democracy Although secularized in form, the Charter still retains the concept of the “coexistence of religion and politics.” Religious representative seats, the influence of monastics in the community, and residual elements of historical familial and theocratic politics make it difficult for the system to fully escape the shadow of traditional theocracy. The Dalai Lama’s personal authority remains the ultimate arbiter at critical moments, indicating that the democratic system has not yet achieved genuine self-sustainability and secularization. At the same time, the absence of genuine multi-party competition and open public debate means that public opinion and organizational activities are constrained by internal community pressures, making it difficult to achieve adequate supervision and accountability. V. Insufficient governance effectiveness and long-term sustainability The CTA’s administrative focus has long remained on settlement services and cultural maintenance, with limited substantive impact on the situation inside Tibet. Internal polarization, crises of trust after leadership transitions, and a sense of alienation among the younger generation are all weakening cohesion. Facing the Dalai Lama’s advanced age and the uncertainties surrounding the question of reincarnation, whether the existing democratic structure can independently maintain political continuity and the legitimacy of the movement remains a major hidden danger. The institutional design has not adequately adapted to the realities of a shrinking, dispersed exile population and generational change. — * Thomas Kell, a Professor at Georgetown University Law Center, primarily focuses his research on the application of international law to geopolitical disputes in South Asia. Influenced by this work, he also developed a particular interest in Tibet and the Tibetan government-in-exile. After recently reading the statement issued by the Tibetan government-in-exile on the 66th Tibetan Democracy Day, he seeks to discuss with the Tibetan exile community, from a legal perspective, the shortcomings existing in the Tibetan democratic system.

title: China suppressing information, silencing victims, even as it takes a foreign media group to flood-ravaged Kyirong
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep06’26) – As families of pilgrims visiting Tibet from abroad who went missing after the devastating flash floods of ice, rock, and mud on Aug 26 morning demand answers on what was being done to find out about their fate or whereabouts, China has, for the first time, opened Gyirong (Tibetan: Kyirong) County in Tibet to a select group of foreign journalists, including the CNN and PTI , on Sep 6 . However, it is a carefully arranged visit in an effort to show the rescue operations going on at the Gyirong Port, said edition.cnn.com Sep 6. The visit to Kyirong County – which was jointly organized by China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and State Council Information Office, with the itinerary planned by the officials to access this restricted area – was aimed only at showing the destruction caused by the floods and the relief and reconstruction work now under way, said the PTI report Sep 6. China’s official Xinhua news agency said Sep 6 that the number of the dead in the Kyirong border area now stood at 43 as of Sep 6 at 6pm, with 519 missing. It did not say how many of either of these two figures include foreigners. It previously said the missing figure included 261 foreigners from 23 countries. China claims transparency and cooperation with other countries, but diplomats report no clear plan for DNA identification or sharing of vital data like video or facial recognition, reported Reuters Sep 5. The report said families accuse China of an information blackout, with no updates on missing persons or victim identification efforts, increasing their frustration and uncertainty. “There is no update from China about what is happening at Ground Zero, what is the situation over there,” Tarun, brother of a missing pilgrim has said. His sister, Priyanka Choudhary, an Indian-born Finnish citizen, was returning from a Hindu pilgrimage in Tibet, and was at a border crossing with Nepal when a catastrophic mudslide hit, the report said. Likewise, Naresh Goyal, brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, a 51-year-old British national, has said, “We are not getting anything from China, whether my sister is safe or alive or dead.” The report said China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the accusations, the timeline for victim identification, or DNA collection protocols being used on the Tibetan side. In Nepal, authorities, including the police, regularly share information on those missing and dead on social media, while search efforts have been accompanied by active DNA testing, the report noted. In addition, China has not offered to provide video from its side of the land port, including facial-recognition images, that could be shared with families or used in identifying the dead, the report cited diplomats in contact with China’s foreign ministry as saying. * * * Chinese authorities said they have been rebuilding roads to restore access to the cut-off border post and have also sent relief materials to Nepal. The journalists’ visit to Kyirong County was aimed at showing both the destruction caused by the floods and the relief and reconstruction work now under way, said the PTI report. Likewise, the CNN report said, “Information about who was impacted here has been slow to emerge from the port, cutting a contrast with Nepal where there have been frequent updates on the numbers of rescued or confirmed dead.” Chinese authorities have yet to publicly release a list of names of those who were at the port at the time or who are believed to be missing on this side of the border. That’s prompted questions about transparency – especially from families who are desperate for news of missing loved ones, the report said. The report continued, “Beijing has defended its release of information from its remote disaster area as open and timely. Its invitation to a group of around a dozen reporters from international news outlets – including CNN – for Sunday’s carefully arranged visit to the area is part of an effort to show the rescue operations going on at the port.” “We’re mainly focused on intensive search and rescue operations at this stage,” Zhang, who had been working at the site since access opened on Sep 2, has said. “Our approach is to dig one layer, search that layer, and then clear it before moving on to the next. We’re digging very carefully, searching thoroughly and clearing the debris layer by layer to see if we can find any of the deceased.” But there is still total lack of information on how the disaster hit the local area on the Tibetan side of the border on Aug 26 morning and its effects on people, their homes and families. Human Rights Watch said some Chinese journalists had been instructed not to interview relatives of people killed or missing and to rely only on material provided by Xinhua , noted the timesofindia.com Sep 5.

title: Human-induced heating, including climbers’ urinating, contributing to rapid melting of Himalayan glaciers
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep05’26) – China and Nepal may have to seriously consider curtailing or, otherwise, better managing their Mt Everest economy if they are to slow the pace of the already rapidly melting glaciers around the world’s tallest peak under the effects of global warming, according to a recent study. On the Nepali side, the quest to conquer Mt Everest is melting the Khumbu glacier on top of which a base camp is set up every season. The study has shown that human activities here, including urination, are melting this glacier rapidly, with the ground temperature rising every year, reported wionews.com Sep 4, citing the study. On the Tibetan side, the North Everest Base Camp is set up near the historic Rongbuk Monastery at an altitude of about 5,150 to 5,200 meters (16,900 feet) every climbing season. It is not clear whether there has been a similar study on that side of Mt Everest. The study on the Khumbu glacier base camp, published by a group of Nepali and American scientists in the journal Regional Environmental Change, shows how this human activity is driving the glacier to melt, setting the stage for an imminent disaster, the report said. Image courtesy: Google Earth/BBC It was stated to be a glacial lake outburst which shook the Kyirong-Rasuwa, Tibet-Nepal border port crossing with a massive flash flood on Aug 26, 2026 morning, washing away villages and marketplaces, and killing, potential, thousands of people. Information on the disaster on the Tibetan side of the border has been severely restricted or curtailed by China, with nothing available about victims and damages, but just numbers of the officially reported dead and missing, and a great deal about how the authorities are coping with the aftermath of the disaster. The new study is stated to focus on how, along with global warming and fossil fuel consumption, human urinary discharge is also causing the glacier to melt. The higher altitude requires climbers to drink more water, in turn leading them to pee more. According to the researchers, in the 2023 season, nearly 6,766 litres of urine were produced per day. Khim Lal Gautam and his colleagues have said that urine alone carries a lot of heat and is enough to cause considerable melting of the glacier, although it is far from being the main contributing factor. Estimating how much ice that amount of heat could melt, the researchers have said the glacier lost 154 tons of ice in that climbing season alone. However, human urine is not the biggest factor. After exiting the body at around 37 degrees Celsius, it cools down as well. Researchers have calculated how much ice it could melt in this state. And they have noted that only a little of that heat reaches the ice, as the rest either escapes into the air or rocks. The bigger problem has been found to be all the fuel consumption linked to the Base Camp. In the 2023 season alone, 824 cylinders of LPG, 18,935 litres of kerosene and 5,130 litres of gasoline were used for cooking, heating and electricity. It accounted for about 94 per cent of the melting caused by humans, while urine made up the other 6 per cent, the study has found. Scientists have been warning that the Himalayas are warming faster than other regions. Ice loss nearly doubled after 2000, compared to the previous quarter, as per a 2019 study published in Science Advances . The team has said that the surface temperatures at Base Camp are increasing faster than other parts of the Khumbu Glacier, rising at about 0.28 degrees Celsius per year. The scientists have called for better waste management and reliance on solar power.

title: Global press watchdog condemns China’s Tibet-blackout on Aug 26 flash flood crisis
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep05’26) – One of the world’s top press freedom organisations has on Sep 2 strongly condemned China for imposing sweeping restrictions on media professionals from accessing vital information on the Tibetan side of the border following the devastating glacier-avalanche triggered Tibet-Nepal flash floods of Aug 26 morning. Expressing grave concern, Paris-based Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said that no independent Tibetan media outlet or international news organisation had been granted access to the disaster-stricken Kyirong area of Tibet. This “reflects a long-standing practice of the Chinese regime, which exercises some of the strictest control in the world over media professionals,” the group said. In its report, titled as Floods in Nepal and Tibet: restrictions and disinformation are impeding vital news , the group noted that the Chinese authorities had only authorised state media to cover the floods in Tibetan areas, with reports highlighting Beijing’s achievements and successes in relief efforts rather than providing a comprehensive account of the scale and impact of the devastation. Tibet has become a “de facto information black hole” in recent years under Chinese President Xi Jinping’s leadership, Aleksandra Bielakowska, Head of Advocacy, RSF Asia-Pacific, has said. “No independent Tibetan media, nor any international media, are permitted to freely cover news from this autonomous region. The only outlets allowed to operate are those controlled by the state and its propaganda organs, which report on events in accordance with the guidelines approved by the Chinese Communist Party’s Propaganda Department. Under these circumstances, it is virtually impossible to gauge the true scale of the tragedy, as the regime seeks to whitewash its international image and stifle any information that might cast it in an unfavourable light,” Bielakowska has stated. “I noticed a very high level of censorship and information control inside Tibet. I also tried to reach Tibetans in exile whose families are in the flood-affected areas. Many have been reluctant to share information because they fear that speaking publicly could put their families inside Tibet at risk,” Kalsang Jigme, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Tibet Radio, has told RSF. Tibet Radio has said it independently confirmed the Tibetan death toll in Kyirong was at least 29 at a time when Chinese state media cited 16 deaths. RSF has also highlighted widespread censorship on Chinese social media, particularly on the platform WeChat , where references to the floods have been censored or deleted by the authorities. It cited Chinese state media to note that at least 10 internet users had been punished for allegedly “spreading rumours” related to the disaster. While the glacier-avalanche may have occurred on the Nepali side of the border, the flash flood it triggered first hit the Kyirong County’s border in Chinese ruled Tibet.

title: Dalai Lama back in D’shala after over two months in Ladakh
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep04’26) – The Dalai Lama returned to his exile home in Dharamshala, India, on Sep 4 morning to a rousing yet solemn welcome by the Tibetan and local host community after a knee surgery in Delhi followed by over two month’s summer stay in Ladakh, during which he gave audiences to more than 21,500 devotees, said the Central Tibetan Administration on its Tibet.net website Sep 4. While in Ladakh, the Dalai Lama attended celebrations marking his 91 st birthday on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground in capital Leh, located near his Shewatsel residence. He also attended prayer ceremonies at the Buddha statue in Stok and at the Buddha statue and stupa in Gonpa Village, besides visiting the Buddha Garden at the Mahabodhi International Meditation Centre. The Dalai Lama also attended the final session of the Yarchos Chenmo (Great Summer Debate) at the Matho Teaching Ground, as well as a long-life prayer offering on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground. The latter event, attended by more than 15,000 devotees, was jointly organised by the Ladakh Buddhist Association, Ladakh Gonpa Association, and the Tibetan Community in Ladakh. He topped his Ladakh stay by attending a thanksgiving and farewell cultural programme on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground on Sep 1, organized by the above groups and the Union Territory’s Muslim community. All in all, the Dalai Lama gave audiences to a total of 21,572 devotees. The Dalai Lama initially travelled to Delhi where he underwent surgery on his left knee on Jun 8, having previously had surgery on his right knee in Jun 2024 in New York City. He then flew to Ladakh on Jun 28 where he has spent much of his summer months in past many years. A widely anticipated meeting in Ladakh with the visiting US ambassador to India, Mr Sergio Gor, who is known to be close to President Donald Trump, eventually did not materialise. Gor was in Ladakh over Aug 20-21.

title: China warns of more Tibet glacier collapses, disasters after the deadly Aug 26 floods
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep04’26) – Referring to the devastating glacier-avalanche triggered Tibet-Nepal flash floods of Aug 26 morning that wiped out villages and markets while claiming what may amount to several thousand lives, China said Sep 2 that such disasters may become more frequent as a result of global warming. Many will argue that China’s infrastructure, mining, and resettlement devastation of the Himalayan environment plays big role in this worsening situation. Glacier disasters could become more frequent as global warming further weakens glacier stability on the Tibetan Plateau (now being referred to by China as “Qinghai-Xizang” Plateau after previously calling it “Qinghai-Tibet” Plateau), potentially triggering cascading effects that amplify damage and widen their impact, reported China’s Party mouthpiece globaltimes.cn Sep 2, citing an announcement that day by the country’s National Climate Centre. After analyzing remote-sensing monitoring data and information transmitted from the Tibet-Nepal disaster site, and combining these findings with on-site inspections and field visits, the cryosphere emergency response and disaster mitigation team of the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, concluded that at around 10:52 am on Aug 26, a glacier on the northern slope of Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal broke off at an elevation of approximately 5,200 metres, triggering an ice-and-rock avalanche, the report said. After explaining how the Aug 26 disaster played out, giving no room for immediate counteraction, the report cited Gao Rong, deputy director of China’s National Climate Centre, as saying during a press conference held by the China Meteorological Administration on Sep 2 that global warming is accelerating the melting of mountain glaciers worldwide. Climate warming has altered the dynamic characteristics of glaciers, leading to rising ice temperatures, faster glacier flow and more frequent surges. Since the beginning of the 21st century, particularly since 2010, ice avalanche events in high-altitude mountainous regions around the world have been on the rise. Against the backdrop of a warmer and wetter climate on the Tibetan Plateau, glaciers across the region are generally undergoing accelerated melting, Gao has said. SOURCE Google Earth Citing the Glacier Inventory of what constitutes the People’s Republic of China, Gao has said that glacier coverage on the Tibetan Plateau has shrunk by about 24 percent over the past 60 years, with some 7,000 small glaciers disappearing entirely. Rapid warming on the Tibetan Plateau is driving accelerated melting of the cryosphere, leading to an increase in the number of glacial lakes and rapid expansion of their area, while glaciers are becoming dynamically unstable, Gao has added. The cryosphere is the frozen water part of the Earth system, covering all regions where water exists in solid form like ice, snow, and permafrost. It is expected that the internal structural stability of glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau will decline further in the future. Glacier-related disasters may become more frequent and could also trigger cascading disaster effects, amplifying the scale of destruction and expanding their impact, Gao has said. * * * Meanwhile, in Nepal, confirmed deaths from the Aug 26 morning flash floods has risen to 1,287 as of Sep 4 at 12:30pm, with the number of missing persons climbing to 5,083, reported the kathmandupost.com Sep 4, citing the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The report said the toll included 140 bodies recovered in Rasuwa, 184 in Nuwakot, 63 in Dhading, 72 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 219 in Nawalparasi East, 212 in Nawalparasi West and 359 in Chitwan. Most of the missing are from Rasuwa (2,130) and Nuwakot (2,340). The official tally also lists 583 foreign nationals as missing. On the Tibetan side of the border, in Kyirong, the number of deaths has risen to 31 as of today at 6pm, with 531 still listed as missing, as reported by China’s official Xinhua news agency Sep 4.

title: China hurls vituperative invectives on Real Madrid for mourning for ‘Tibet-Nepal’ flash flood victims
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep03’26) – China has on Sep 2 strongly attacked the Spanish football club Real Madrid after it published a post on its official overseas social media account featuring a photo of the team observing a moment of silence for the Tibet-Nepal avalanche-triggered flash floods on Aug 26 morning, alongside the caption: “Moment of silence… in memory of the victims of the devastating flood that affected the border between Nepal and Tibet.” Real Madrid published the message on Instagram ahead of its match against Malaga at the Bernabéu stadium in Madrid. China’s official media expressed outrage in several online attacks targetting the club for allegedly placing Nepal and Tibet on an equal footing and, also, for failing to call “Tibet” by its colonial Chinese name “Xizang”. “The condolence message was supposed to be extending sympathy. But the Spanish football club was negligent, or political, in its wording, as it placed Xizang, an autonomous region of China, that is nearly 2.5 times the size of Spain, on the same footing as Nepal, a sovereign country,” railed China’s official English-language news outlet chinadaily.com.cn Sep 2 in a report headlined “Real Madrid scores own goal”. “Real Madrid’s wording was particularly conspicuous because several of its La Liga peers used the straightforward formulation ‘Nepal-China’ in their condolences,” the outlet said. La Liga is the top professional men’s football division in the Spanish football league system. The club should understand why Chinese supporters noticed the difference, the report said, referring to nationalist Chinese netizens’ criticisms of the top Spanish football club over the matter. A global institution with tens of millions of followers should know that every caption can travel farther than intended, the outlet said. It also noted, “A lot of Chinese fans and some media outlets have already contacted Real Madrid to call out the problem and voice their displeasure, demanding a change in wording. Yet, as of Wednesday (Sep 2), the club has remained tight-lipped. This is hardly a smart PR strategy.” The news outlet also posted another item, which was headlined as “Real Madrid faces backlash from Chinese netizens over listing Xizang alongside Nepal”. China’s Party mouthpiece globaltimes.cn Sep 1 also ran a piece titled “Real Madrid, please use ‘China’s Xizang’.” And it said: “The post placed ‘Tibet’ and ‘Nepal’ on an equal footing as two parallel entities, whereas several other La Liga clubs used ‘Nepal and China’ in similar memorial copy. After many Chinese netizens expressed their dissatisfaction, Real Madrid chose neither to delete the post nor to offer an explanation.” It then ran China’s propaganda bulldozer-narrative on Tibet, saying: “Xizang is an integral part of the Chinese territory. This is a universally recognized fact in the international community, a conclusion deeply rooted in history, jurisprudence, and culture, leaving no room for ambiguity. Placing China’s Xizang on par with the sovereign state of Nepal and deliberately stripping away Xizang’s attribute as part of China is, in essence, pandering to separatist narratives in disguise.” * * * Meanwhile, China has – six days after the devastating fast-moving chain mudslide – updated the number of the dead on the Tibetan side to 21, as against 16 updated earlier on Aug 28, with 541 still missing. Local authorities had received 876 phone calls from the relatives of the victims and missing people, said China’s official Xinhua news agency Sep 3. On the Nepali side, the death toll has risen to 1,252, with at least 4,216 people remaining unaccounted for as of Sep 3 noon, reported the kathmandupost.com , citing figures compiled by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). It said bodies have also been recovered in Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahun. Only 95 of the 1,252 bodies recovered so far have been identified and handed over to families, the report said. The missing-person figures are expected to change as authorities verify reports from affected communities and receive further information from the field. While hopes of finding more survivors among the thousands still missing in Nepal were fading on Sept 2, the authorities believed that dozens of workers trapped in the tunnels of hydropower projects hit by the Himalayan catastrophe could still be alive, Reuters Sep 2 cited authorities as saying.

title: 1989 Tiananmen Square protest leader addresses 66th Tibetan democracy anniversary
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep02’26) – Wang Dan, a prominent Chinese political activist, history scholar, and one of the primary student leaders of the 1989 Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement, visited Dharamshala as distinguished guest at the 66 th Tibetan democracy day which was commemorated by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) on the Thekchen Choeling Tsuglakhang courtyard on Sep 2 morning. Wang has accused the Communist Party of China of using violence and lies as means to control the country’s population whereas the Dalai Lama had employed democracy to unite the Tibetan people. “The Chinese Communist Party relies on violence, lies, and control. The Tibetan community in exile, in contrast, relies on the recognition of its people, democratic legitimacy, and a coalition of its institutions. It is obvious that this democratic system has brought together the Tibetan people across the world,” he has said. Wang, 57, and the founder of Dialogue China, has said Chinese democracy activists in exile were currently preparing to establish a China Congress, with more than a thousand founding electors already participating in the move. “We hope to bring democratic practices belonging to the Chinese people, accumulate experience for China’s future democratic transition, and contribute to constitutional development,” he has said. He felt that the Tibetan Parliament in Exile could serve as a valuable model for this endeavour. Wang has commended the CTA’s Middle Way Policy of seeking autonomy for Tibet under Chinese sovereignty while emphasising that a future democratic China should never repeat the repressive and assimilative policies of the Communist Chinese government. The 66th Tibetan Democracy Day, commemorated by the Central Tibetan Administration at the Thekchen Choeling Tsuglakhang courtyard on the morning of 2 September. (Photo courtesy: CTA/Tenzin Phende) Wang was placed on a list of the 21 most wanted student leaders of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and jailed twice for his role in it, accused of spreading counterrevolutionary propaganda and incitement. He later went into exile in the United States in 1998 and, after earning a PhD from Harvard University, divided his time between Taiwan, where he taught at several universities, and the United States. Before Wang, Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the CTA and Speaker Dolma Tsering Teykhang of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile have delivered their customary addresses to the gathering of CTA leaders and officials as well as the Tibetan public. The English translation of A Chronicle of Tibet’s Foreign Relations and Policy (7th–21st Century ), written by former TPiE member and CTA’s former New Delhi Representative Mr Lobsang Shastri was released, as also a publication by the Tibet Policy Institute documenting the history of relations between Tibet and its neighbouring nations. Also released was a publication refuting any role for the Chinese government in any matter concerned with the recognition of the reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, and the third volume of The Evolution of Tibetan Democracy in Exile , which is a compilation of His Holiness’s speeches delivered to the TPiE over the decades. Awards were also presented to seven Tibetans who had completed their PhD degrees and others for outstanding performances during the recent high school board exams in India. ( Based on tibet.net report Sep 2, 2026 and other sources )

title: Another former top Chinese leader in Tibet sacked for corruption
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct11’26) – Ding Yexian, who last served as deputy head of the standing committee of the People’s Congress of Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) from 2021 has been expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), reported China’s state news agency Xinhua Sep 9, citing both the top party and state anti-corruption bodies. He was earlier put under investigation on suspicion of “serious violations of laws and regulations” in Apr 2026. A native of Yanggu County, Shandong province, where he was born in 1960, Ding spent over 20 years of his party and government career in TAR’s Lhokha (Chinese: Shannan) Prefecture, before moving to TAR-level posts. Upon the approval of the CPC Central Committee, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision (NCS) had conducted an investigation into Ding’s case, the report said, citing a statement from both of them on Oct 9. The investigation was stated to have found that Ding had lost his ideals and convictions, and resisted an official inquiry and investigation of his case. Ding was also found to have used his position and influence to benefit others in matters concerning company public listing, project contracting and business operations. In return, he accepted huge sums of money and valuables, the statement was cited as saying. He is accused, as per the statement, of having violated the political, organizational and integrity discipline of the CPC and committed serious duty-related crimes, and is suspected of bribery. The report concluded that in line with Party regulations and laws, a decision has been made to expel him from the Party, revoke his entitlements, terminate his capacity as a delegate to the 10th Party congress of TAR, confiscate his illicit gains, and hand over his case for judicial proceedings. * * * Ding began as an electric utility operator in Lhokha Prefecture in Jan 1978. He graduated from the Shandong Electronics Professional College (now Shandong College of Electronic Technology) in Sep 1985 with a bachelor’s degree in computer science. He was promoted as the head of the economic and trade reform commission of the prefecture in Dec 1996, and named the head of the prefecture’s department of finance in Nov 1998. He was further promoted as the TAR department of finance in Apr 2000, and assumed the post of director of the regional finance bureau in Jan 2003. In Jan 2009, Ding was made assistant to the Chairman of the TAR, and promoted to Vice Chairman of the TAR in Sep 2010. He was named a member of the TAR Party Standing Committee member as well as deputy party secretary of TAR in Jun 2013. In Nov 2016, he was named Executive Vice Chairman of the TAR, and in Jun 2017, named as the Executive Deputy Party Secretary of TAR. Also holding a part-time Master’s degree in Business Administration from Sichuan Business School, Ding was, in Jan 2021, made the vice chairperson of the Standing Committee of the TAR People’s Congress. Ding’s downfall began on Apr 12, 2026, when he was suspected of “serious violations of laws and regulations” by the CCDI, the party’s internal disciplinary body, and NSC, the highest anti-corruption agency of China, leading to his expulsion on Oct 9.

title: China’s Panchen for aligning all religious work in Tibet with China’s national assimilation law
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct11’26) – The Chinese government-appointed Panchen Lama Gyaltsen Norbu has on Sep 30 called for all religious and other work in Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) to remain aligned with the overall work of the Party and the Party-state, including with the recently enacted Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law. The law is condemned in the outside world as a tool for the Sinicization and assimilation of Tibet. Presiding over a meeting of the TAR branch of the Buddhist Association of China, Gyaltsen Norbu called for in-depth study and publicity regarding relevant laws and regulations, including the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law and TAR’s regulations on religious affairs, to ensure that all work will remain aligned with the overall work of the Party and the country, reported China’s state news agency Xinhua Oct 10. The event took place in Shigatse City where he also presided over the 5th council meeting and a chairperson’s office meeting of the Shigatse Development Fund. In addition, he attended events hosted by the fund, the report said. The report said that after he arrived in Tibet’s capital Lhasa by air from his state-assigned home in Beijing on Jul 30, Gyaltsen Norbu travelled by road to Shigatse, home to Tashilhunpo Monastery, the traditional seat of the successive Panchen Lamas, on Aug 24. While in Shigatse, he was stated to have “carried out a series of religious activities and visited Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in Kangmar, Sagya, Xaitongmoin, and Bainang counties, and Sangzhuzi District, to pay homage to the Buddha, expound Buddhist teachings and conduct relevant social research.” On Sep 17, he has visited a quinoa planting and processing base in Sagya County and inspected quinoa growth in the fields. Quinoa was first grown in Tibet in 1988, when the Tibet Agriculture and Animal Husbandry University introduced three varieties from Bolivia. The 10th Panchen Lama brought quinoa seeds presented to him as a gift from Bolivia following a visit there in 1985, which eventually catalyzed research and cultivation trials in the region, China’s official chinadaily.com.cn previously reported Oct 8, 2021.

title: Dalai Lama congratulates 2026 Nobel Peace laureate, recalls her raising of Tibet concerns with China
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct10’26) – The Dalai Lama has on Oct 10 recalled global human rights jurist Navi Pillay’s call on China to address the underlying issues in Tibet while congratulating her on being awarded the Nobel Peace prize for 2026 the day before by the Norwegian Nobel Committee. Expressing admiration for having devoted her life “to the cause of people around the world who are denied their rights,” the 1989 Nobel Peace laureate has written: “I have long believed that a country governed by the rule of law, with an independent judiciary and a free press, is best placed to serve its own people and, in turn, the wider global community. Where the rule of law is absent, injustice and suffering inevitably follow.” He has further said, “As a Tibetan, I deeply appreciate your efforts, during your tenure as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, to call on China to address the underlying issues in Tibet.” In its announcement, the Nobel Committee said it decided to award the 2026 award to the 85-year-old Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a South African of Tamil-Indian origin, for her efforts to promote peace and international law. It called her a person with exceptional courage and integrity who led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order and who has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. In her long legal career, Pillay has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (2008-2014) and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide, the award announcement noted. Calling her “one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” the announcement said “her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law, and that her “commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.” The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when “the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right , it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence.”

title: European Parliament’s China-policy report condemns forced assimilation drive in Tibet
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct09’26) – The European Parliament has on Oct 7 adopted a set of policy recommendations on EU-China political relations drafted by its Committee on Foreign Affairs which among numerous other things strongly condemns China’s intensifying campaign of mandatory “Sinicisation” and forced assimilation in Tibet. China’s official media on Oct 8 severely condemned the report and warned of dire consequences, but with focus on the report’s labelling of the country’s industrial policy as an “existential threat” to the EU’s industrial base and as a “decisive enabler” of Russia in its Ukraine war. The European Parliament report – which is a set of Recommendation for the European Council, the Commission and the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy on EU-China political relations – demands a stronger and principled EU-China policy that combines dialogue with more protection of European interests. The MEPs have called for urgent action against the weaponisation of EU’s economic overreliance on China, alongside a rigorous de-risking strategy focused on critical raw materials, medicines, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, semiconductors and other strategic sectors. The MEPs have also demanded reciprocity and a level playing field in trade and investment and expressed support for proportionate EU action where China fails to open its internal markets. It also calls for stronger Global Gateway partnerships providing a credible alternative to China’s belt and road initiative, particularly in Africa and Latin America. The report reaffirms the EU’s One China policy while opposing any unilateral change to the status quo in Taiwan by force or coercion. The MEPs have not only called for stronger resilience against cyberattacks, foreign interference, espionage and hybrid threats, but also demanded reinforced human rights dialogue and pressure on China over repression, forced labour and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang. In particular, the Parliament has expressed deep concern over China’s adoption of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which came into force on Jul 1, 2026, and its potential to further institutionalise assimilationist policies. They have also called for unconditional release of political prisoners. In specific terms, the European Parliament has criticised Beijing’s calculated political manoeuvres to control the succession and reincarnation of the Dalai Lama, emphasising that protecting religious autonomy is non-negotiable. The MEPs have also demanded immediate information regarding the whereabouts of Tibet’s decades-long missing religious leader Panchen Lama Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, whom Beijing replaced with Gyaltsen Norbu back in 1995. To counter China’s expanding reach of transnational repression, the report urges the EU to consistently raise these human rights concerns at every political meeting with Chinese counterparts. Beyond economic diplomacy, the European Parliament insists that the protection of minority rights must become a central, binding element of future EU-China relations. The report also calls for the immediate closure of all illegal, undercover “Chinese overseas police stations” operating within EU member states. China condemned the report, saying it risks harming the foundation of China-European Union relations and warned of dire consequences. The European Parliament report overlooks the fact that China and the EU have no fundamental conflicts of interest or geopolitical contradictions; nevertheless, it is advocating a confrontational approach, including a continuous European naval “presence” in and around the Taiwan Strait, said a chinadaily.com.cn editorial piece Oct 8. It accused the European Parliament of “mistaking a partner for a rival — a misjudgment whose cost would be enormous for either side.”

title: Seminar discusses upgrading China’s first Tibetan-language AI model to promote ‘ethnic integration’
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct08’26) – China held a seminar on Sep 5 in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, to discuss issues such as improving Tibetan artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and expanding the application of its Tibetan large language model (LLM) into multilingual simultaneous interpretation. And the creators of China’s first Tibetan-language AI mode, DeepZang, have pledged to speed up upgrades aimed at promoting ethnic integration, reported the scmp.com Oct 7, citing the state-run portal Chinanews.com . Tenzin Norbu, founder of CHOKNOR, which developed DeepZang, has said his research team will continue to upgrade Tibetan-language AI and expand its applications, using technology to support interethnic exchanges and promote digital and intelligent development in ethnic minority regions. DeepZang was launched in March, roughly three years after the unveiling of Monlam AI, a Tibetan-language LLM developed by Monlam Tibetan IT Research Centre, a non-profit organisation based in Dharamsala – the Indian hillside town that has hosted the 14th Dalai Lama and the Tibetan administration-in-exile since 1960. The report noted that Tibet remained a top priority in ethnic and religious affairs for Beijing, which has consistently bolstered domestic Tibetan studies to regain control of international discourse on the issue. DeepZang is part of this broader effort to reshape global narratives around Tibet with its own authoritative data and technology. These efforts are also stated to be reflected in Beijing’s push since 2023 to use the romanised Pinyin name “Xizang” instead of “Tibet” in English articles, projecting its sovereign narrative globally. The legal basis for all this is the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which lays the legal foundation for assimilating minority groups and took effect on Jul 1, 2026. DeepZang has been trained on nearly 70 million Tibetan texts and over 30,500 hours of audio covering the language’s three main dialects. It powers AI chat, real-time translation and speech-to-text features across Tibetan, Chinese and English. The seminar was also stated to have outlined future plans to integrate DeepZang into sectors including public services, education, healthcare and local governance, while “empowering the digital transmission of fine traditional Tibetan culture and ensuring that all ethnic groups equitably share the benefits of technological progress”. Since its launch, DeepZang has advanced Tibetan-language AI through improvements in multi-dialect adaptation, semantic recognition and offline applications. It has helped the technology evolve from being “basically usable” to more accurate and user-friendly, filling several technological gaps in the industry and helping improve China’s technological framework for AI in ethnic minority languages, noted China’s Party mouthpiece globaltimes.cn Oct 7.

title: Is Xi Jinping all right?
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct06’26) – Chinese President Xi Jinping’a visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit over Sep 12-13 and, especially, his state visit to the USA over Sep 23-25 have reignite rumours about his health, although he is not known to be tied to any specific concerning medical condition. The Wall Street Journal ( WSJ ) said Oct 3 that Xi’s staff requested several breaks during his White House visit and to cut down the duration of some events, raising questions about the 73-year-old’s health. It also follows similar rumours that swirled during Xi’s trip to India for the BRICS summit, noted indianexpress.com Oct 4. People familiar with the planning have told WSJ that Chinese officials asked the White House for a private room where Xi could rest between engagements and sought more downtime during his Washington visit. The most unusual detail was stated to be a request for a private “hold room” inside the White House’s West Wing. Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan was reportedly the only other person allowed inside the room, with even Cai Qi, a senior member of Xi’s delegation and his chief of staff, being not permitted to use it. Dennis Wilder, a former senior China director at the National Security Council, has described the private room arrangement as unusual compared with previous state visits he helped organize. The bilateral meeting at the White House on Sep 24 began close to noon and ended by early afternoon. Xi then left the White House and returned for the state dinner that evening, limiting the time available for substantive discussions, according to the WSJ report. Chinese officials have also turned down a planned working lunch between Xi and US President Donald Trump on Sep 24, the only full day of his Washington visit, saying they wanted more time for Xi to rest. The decision was stated to have created a roughly five-hour gap in the summit schedule. The WSJ report also referred to the fact that at the Joint Base Andrews, footage showed Xi holding Peng’s hand while using the aircraft’s railing as he descended the stairs on his arrival in the USA. Then, two days later, while climbing the National Archives steps alongside Trump and his wife Melania Trump, Xi again held Peng’s hand, with the WSJ reporting that he appeared to rely on her for support. Unusual scheduling was also stated to be visible elsewhere in Xi’s itinerary. No official engagements were planned for him on the evening of his arrival following a roughly 14-hour flight from Beijing, while his visit to the US National Archives the following day lasted only about 10 minutes, far shorter than initially planned. The WSJ report brought renewed focus on an incident during the BRICS summit in New Delhi when the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly appeared to check on Xi, asking his interpreter, “Is it okay?” after the Chinese president appeared uncomfortable. Xi later skipped a gala dinner hosted by Modi for the participating BRICS leaders and other dignitaries after attending the first day of the summit and holding a bilateral meeting with Modi. Taken together, the episodes have renewed questions over Xi’s health, though no specific illness has been established. With Xi holding China’s top political and military posts, any health concerns could have wider implications for Beijing, noted the timesofindia.com Oct 3.

title: County in Qinghai overrun by Chinese tourists following completion of a highway
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct05’26) – The Qilian (Tibetan: Chilen or Dhola) county in Haibei (Tsojang) Prefecture, Qinghai province, which is considered by Tibetans as the bulk of their historical Amdo (or Domey) province, has been overrun by Chinese tourists during China’s week-long National Day holiday which began on Oct 1, following the completion of a national highway. A place with a population of only about 50,000 suddenly found itself receiving more than 100,000 visitors in a single day, reported China’s official globaltimes.cn Oct 5. While all the county’s more than 400 hotels and guesthouses were fully booked, nearly 500 people were accommodated in publicly provided beds on Oct 3, the report said, citing local cultural and tourism authorities. Some tourists have been cited as saying Oct 5 that “it’s like winning the lottery” to find accommodation there. Nearly 35,000 vehicles entered the county on Oct 3, bringing more than 100,000 people into the area, Feng Lingling, head of the local tourism bureau, has said. Nearly 500 people were stated to have been accommodated free of charge in local school dormitories arranged by the Qilian tourism bureau. As rooms ran out, the Qilian tourism bureau activated its emergency response plan. It coordinated with the local education department to open dormitories at two schools as free temporary shelters, accommodating 453 people. Between Oct 3 and 2:30 am on Oct 4, the bureau handled 510 calls for help involving more than 800 visitors, the report said. The sudden influx of tourists, including those passing through the area, was driven by the viral popularity of Highway No. 9. The scenic route has attracted widespread attention online this year, drawing large numbers of tourists to Qilian during the National Day holiday, although the county’s traditional peak tourism season is usually July and August, the report said. The county gets its name from its surrounding mountains and is populated mainly by Tibetans as well as Huis, Hans, Monguors, Gaoshanse, Zhuangs and Koreans. The main religions are Tibetan Buddhism and Islam. Tibetans are mainly concentrated in Arou (Arig Township), Ebao (Kharmar Town), Yeniugou (Dronglung Township), and kekexili (or Kekeli) Township. Mongolians mainly live in Mole (Muri Town) and Yeniugou, while the Huis are concentrated in Babaoxiang (Tsunmoshong Town) and the county itself.

title: Tibet beyond the Dalai Lama and the question of who speaks for its people
author: tibetanreview
content: OPINION While the bill before the US Congress on Assuring the Future of Tibet Act (AFTA) of 2026 – should it become law – will not settle the Sino-Tibetan dispute, nor enable Washington to determine Tibet’s future, what it crucially means is that a people’s political voice should not become uncertain at the very moment when the question of their future becomes most urgent, in the post-Dalai Lama scenario, and that the institutions through which Tibetans speak – under the aegis of the CTA – are not left waiting for the world to decide whom it is prepared to hear, writes Saurabh Chauhan.* A people’s future cannot rest forever on the shoulders of one person, however extraordinary that person may be. Institutions matter. So does memory, language, faith and the right of a people to speak for themselves. For Tibetans, this question has acquired a particular urgency. The 14th Dalai Lama has been the spiritual leader and the most recognised voice of the Tibetan cause for decades. But a political community cannot be expected to leave its future undefined until a moment of succession arrives. That is the larger question behind a new American bill, the Assuring the Future of Tibet Act (AFTA) of 2026. The bill is not law yet. It was introduced in the US House as H.R. 8982 on May 21, 2026, by Congressman James McGovern, with Republican Michael McCaul as cosponsor. A Senate companion, S. 5362, was introduced on August 7 by Senator Jeff Merkley, with a bipartisan group of cosponsors, and referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The House bill was referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Its stated purpose is to direct the Secretary of State to advocate for the “inclusion and recognition” of the Central Tibetan Administration, or CTA. That wording is important. The proposal is not simply another declaration of support for Tibet. It is an attempt to give the Tibetan political administration a more defined place in American foreign policy, including in the period after the present Dalai Lama. For Tibetans, the issue is not only what happens to a revered religious figure. It is also what happens to their political voice when the person who has carried so much of their cause across the world is no longer there. The Dalai Lama has been central to international understanding of Tibet, but Tibetan political life has not stood still around him. In 2011, he devolved his political authority to elected leadership. The CTA now operates as the principal political institution of the Tibetan exile community. AFTA seeks to make that reality more visible in US policy. Its supporters argue that the political future of Tibetans should not be left dependent on the lifetime of one individual, however widely respected he may be. There is a deeper point here. The survival of a people is not only about preserving monuments, religious institutions or cultural practices. It is also about whether that people can maintain institutions through which it can make decisions, express its concerns and represent itself. Tibetan identity has endured through displacement and political upheaval. The question now is whether its political institutions will receive recognition and space to function internationally, particularly as the succession of the Dalai Lama approaches. AFTA’s supporters say this is why the bill should become law: not because it can settle the Tibet question by itself, but because it could establish a more durable relationship between Washington and the Tibetan political leadership before a difficult transition begins. The distinction the bill makes between religious succession and political representation is central to that argument. It does not assign the CTA the task of choosing the next Dalai Lama. The bill refers to the Gaden Phodrang Trust in relation to the recognition of future Dalai Lamas, while identifying the CTA as the political representative of Tibetans. These are separate questions, and treating them as one would create confusion. Religious authority belongs to the religious process. Political representation concerns the institutions through which Tibetans organise and speak in public life. AFTA attempts to keep the two distinct at a time when they could become entangled in a larger geopolitical contest. That contest is not imaginary. Beijing has asserted a role for the Chinese state in the recognition of reincarnate Tibetan Buddhist leaders. The Tibetan position has been that the process belongs to Tibetan religious tradition and should not be controlled by the Chinese government. The next succession could therefore become a question not only of faith, but also of authority and legitimacy. Who has the right to recognise a religious leader? Who speaks politically for Tibetans? And will governments distinguish between those two forms of authority, or allow one to be used to determine the other? AFTA is an attempt by its sponsors to prepare American policy for those questions rather than wait until they become an immediate diplomatic crisis. The bill also proposes a more visible international role for the CTA. It directs the US government to advocate for its inclusion and recognition in international institutions, including support for observer status at the United Nations General Assembly and engagement with relevant UN agencies. It calls for high-level engagement with the Sikyong and other senior CTA officials, and for the United States to encourage allies and partners to engage with the Tibetan administration. These steps would not automatically secure UN status. Nor could a US law compel other governments to recognise the CTA in a particular way. But the proposed change is still consequential. It would make engagement with Tibetan political leadership a stated responsibility of American policy, rather than something left entirely to the discretion of an administration. Congressman McGovern has made the case in direct terms. “Sadly, the Dalai Lama won’t be with us forever,” he said while introducing the House bill. The United States, he argued, needed the “authority and the tools” to continue its advocacy for Tibetan human rights, and support for the CTA was essential to that effort. McCaul has also described the bill as a way to maintain American engagement with Tibetans beyond the present Dalai Lama. These are the sponsors’ arguments, but they point to a real gap in the existing framework. Much of modern international engagement with Tibet has been shaped by the Dalai Lama’s personal standing. The question AFTA raises is whether that engagement can continue with equal seriousness through Tibetan institutions. To understand why this bill has emerged now, it is necessary to look back at the laws that came before it. American Tibet policy did not develop in one stroke. It was built in stages, each responding to a different concern. The Tibetan Policy Act of 2002 created the basic statutory framework. The Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act of 2018 addressed restrictions on access. The Tibetan Policy and Support Act of 2020 expanded the focus on religious freedom, culture and political representation. The Resolve Tibet Act of 2024 sharpened the American approach to the dispute between Tibet and China. AFTA now turns to the question of institutional continuity. The Tibetan Policy Act of 2002 was the foundation. Passed as part of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act and signed by President George W. Bush on September 30, it set out a US policy of supporting the aspirations of the Tibetan people to safeguard their distinct identity. It also established the position of Special Coordinator for Tibetan Issues and called for dialogue between Beijing and the Dalai Lama or his representatives, without preconditions. The law mattered because it moved Tibet policy beyond occasional statements and diplomatic gestures. It created a position inside the US government whose task was to coordinate policy and keep Tibet on the diplomatic agenda. The Special Coordinator became one of the clearest institutional results of the 2002 law. The office could bring together different parts of the US government, engage with Tibetan representatives and raise questions of human rights, religious freedom, cultural preservation and dialogue with Beijing. It gave Congress a continuing point of reference inside the administration. In later years, the State Department described the role as coordinating American policies and programmes on Tibet and promoting dialogue without preconditions. That was not a small change. A concern that could once be pushed aside by shifting diplomatic priorities had acquired a place in the machinery of government. But the limits were also visible. Washington could create an office and call for dialogue. It could not make Beijing enter negotiations. The Tibetan Policy Act did not resolve the political dispute, and the hoped-for dialogue did not produce a settlement. The law changed how the United States organised its own policy more directly than it changed conditions on the ground in Tibet. That distinction runs through the entire history of these laws. Legislation can set priorities, create reporting duties and establish consequences. It cannot, by itself, compel another government to change course. The next major law, the Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act of 2018, approached the problem from a different direction. For years, access to Tibetan areas had been restricted for foreign diplomats, journalists and visitors. The law required the State Department to report annually on the level of access granted to US diplomats and officials, journalists and tourists, and to compare it with access to other parts of China. It also provided for visa restrictions on Chinese officials found to be substantially involved in restricting access. The question was no longer only what Washington believed about Tibet. It was whether outsiders could enter, report and see conditions for themselves. That mattered because restrictions on access make independent reporting difficult and leave the outside world dependent on limited information. RATA put the issue into a formal reporting process. It required the US government to document restrictions, including permits and other measures that impede travel. The State Department’s 2024 report was the sixth annual report under the law. The continuation of those reports itself tells part of the story: the access issue remained unresolved years after the legislation was passed. RATA created a mechanism for accountability and diplomatic pressure, but it did not open Tibetan areas to unrestricted foreign travel. The Tibetan Policy and Support Act of 2020 widened the framework again. It built on the 2002 law and addressed Tibetan religious freedom, language, culture, environmental protection and support for Tibetan communities. It also strengthened the US position that decisions about the succession of the Dalai Lama should be made without interference from the Chinese government. This was a significant development. The question of succession had long been politically sensitive, but the 2020 law placed it more firmly within the language of religious freedom and US policy. It made clear that Washington regarded state interference in the selection of Tibetan religious leaders as an issue it could raise through its own legislation and diplomacy. The 2020 law also matters because it recognised the changing nature of Tibetan political representation. The 2002 act had referred to the Dalai Lama and his representatives. The later framework gave greater space to democratically elected Tibetan leaders. This reflected a political transition that had already taken place within the exile community. The Dalai Lama had devolved his political authority, and an elected leadership had taken on formal responsibilities. American law was beginning to catch up with that institutional reality. AFTA now seeks to take that recognition further, from acknowledging elected leadership to directing the United States to advocate for the CTA’s inclusion and recognition internationally. There were practical consequences under the 2020 framework as well. US officials continued to raise religious and cultural rights, meet Tibetan representatives and support programmes relating to Tibetan language and cultural preservation. The State Department has also announced visa restrictions on Chinese officials over policies affecting Tibetans. These measures do not mean that the situation inside Tibet was transformed. They show, rather, how legislation can give a government tools to sustain pressure and support over time. The difference between a law’s stated purpose and its measurable effect remains important. A statute can make a policy more durable without necessarily producing the outcome it seeks. Then came the Resolve Tibet Act, signed by President Joe Biden on July 12, 2024. Its formal name is the Promoting a Resolution to the Tibet-China Dispute Act. It amended the 2002 Tibetan Policy Act and addressed the dispute itself, including the need to counter claims by Chinese officials about Tibet’s history and to support a negotiated resolution. For the Tibetan side, the law was significant because it challenged the historical narrative advanced by Beijing and gave the United States a stronger legislative basis to address the dispute. The Central Tibetan Administration welcomed it as an important development in US policy. There was, however, a clear boundary. Biden’s signing statement said the Act did not change the longstanding bipartisan US policy recognising the Tibet Autonomous Region and other Tibetan areas as part of the People’s Republic of China. The 2024 law therefore did not amount to recognition of Tibetan independence. It sharpened Washington’s position on the dispute while retaining its existing policy on territorial status. This distinction is often lost in political reactions to the law, but it is essential to understanding the space in which AFTA now operates. Stronger support for Tibetan rights and political representation does not automatically mean a change in the United States’ formal position on sovereignty. Looked at together, these laws form a progression. In 2002, Washington built the policy framework and created the Special Coordinator. In 2018, it made access to Tibetan areas a subject of annual reporting and possible visa restrictions. In 2020, it expanded the focus on religion, culture, language and the succession question, while giving greater recognition to elected Tibetan leadership. In 2024, it addressed the Tibet-China dispute more directly, without changing the US position on territorial status. AFTA, in 2026, asks what political relationship should remain in place when the Dalai Lama is no longer the central figure in that relationship. The case made by its supporters is that the earlier laws leave an institutional question only partly answered. They provide a framework for US policy, but they do not establish the kind of sustained international engagement with the CTA that AFTA proposes. The bill would ask the United States to treat the Tibetan administration as an institution with which it should engage at senior levels and whose participation in international forums it should actively support. It would also encourage other governments to engage with the CTA. That is a shift from expressing support for Tibetans in general to spelling out how one of their political institutions should be included in international affairs. For Tibetans, international recognition is not merely a matter of protocol. It concerns whether their elected representatives can be heard in places where questions affecting their future are discussed. Observer status at the United Nations would not make the CTA a member state, nor would it settle Tibet’s political status. But the effort to secure a place in international forums is tied to a basic political concern: a people affected by decisions should have a means of putting their views before those who make them. The bill’s supporters argue that the CTA should not be pushed to the margins simply because it is based in exile or because the Dalai Lama’s personal role has been so prominent. There are limits, and they should be stated plainly. AFTA cannot decide who the next Dalai Lama will be. It cannot compel the United Nations to grant observer status. It cannot force Beijing to resume dialogue, end restrictions or accept the CTA as a political interlocutor. Nor can it determine how India will respond to the next phase. The CTA is based in Dharamshala, and India’s role as the host country gives the coming transition a regional dimension. But the bill is American legislation. It cannot make decisions on behalf of India or other governments. Still, the India connection cannot be ignored. The institutions of Tibetan exile have developed on Indian soil, and any future succession will have religious, political and diplomatic implications that extend beyond Washington and Beijing. The United States can set out its own approach through legislation, but the practical environment in which Tibetan institutions operate will also be shaped by the policies of the countries around them. AFTA may therefore be read in New Delhi as a signal of how Washington wants to approach Tibetan political representation in the years ahead. What India will do is a separate question, and one that cannot be answered from the text of this bill. There is also a larger question for the Tibetan movement itself. The international standing of the Dalai Lama has been extraordinary, but the future of Tibetan political representation cannot depend only on the moral authority of a spiritual leader. An elected administration has to be able to speak for its people, explain its position and maintain relationships beyond one generation. That does not diminish the Dalai Lama’s role. It recognises that a political community needs institutions capable of carrying responsibility forward. AFTA’s central idea is that the United States should prepare for that continuity now, rather than improvise after the succession. The bill is still before Congress, and its passage cannot be assumed. But the debate it has opened is larger than its legislative status. What does it mean to support a people’s right to preserve their identity if their political representatives remain largely outside international institutions? What happens when the person most closely associated with their cause is no longer there? And can the international community distinguish between a religious succession and the political right of Tibetans to represent themselves? No American law can answer all of these questions. The previous laws did not resolve Tibet’s political future. They did, however, make the issue harder to remove from US policy and gave successive administrations a set of tools, obligations and stated positions. The 2002 law created the framework. The 2018 law made access measurable. The 2020 law expanded protections and addressed succession. The 2024 law sharpened the language around the dispute. AFTA is an attempt to make sure that the political voice of Tibetans has an institutional place in the period that follows the present Dalai Lama. That is the strongest argument its supporters make for enactment. Not that the bill will settle the dispute, or that Washington can determine Tibet’s future, but that a people’s political voice should not become uncertain at the very moment when the question of their future becomes most urgent. The measure would not end the struggle for Tibetan rights. It would seek to ensure that the institutions through which Tibetans speak are not left waiting for the world to decide whom it is prepared to hear. — * Saurabh Chauhan is a journalist and independent researcher based in Himachal Pradesh. He spent nearly eight years with Hindustan Times, reporting from Shimla, Chandigarh and Lucknow, where he covered a wide range of political, social and environmental issues. His work has also appeared in platforms such as The Print, BBC Hindi, Firstpost and several other publications. Currently working independently, Chauhan is engaged in long-form research and writing. He is authoring a forthcoming book, Prayer Wheels in the Cloud, which explores the future of Tibetan culture, religion and political struggle through the lens of technology and a rapidly changing world.

title: China among countries invited to international tourism summit in Tawang
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct04’26) – The government of India is to hold a mega international tourism event in Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh, towards the end of this month, with China being among the invitees. China claims Arunachal Pradesh, especially the Tawang region, as part of its territory on the basis of its claim over Tibet, which has been under its occupation rule for more than seven decades. The International Tourism Mart, being organised by the Ministry of Tourism from Oct 27 to Nov 1, will bring together delegates from around 20 countries, reported the indianexpress.com Oct 2. Delegates from China have also been invited to the annual event which is held, by rotation, in one of the eight North-Eastern states of India. The 2025 edition of the event was held in Sikkim, and was attended by government representatives and industry stakeholders from over19 countries. While the decision to hold the event in Tawang is routine, it is also significant, given the fact that the area is a primary bone of contention in the boundary dispute between India and China, the report noted. Besides, the decision comes weeks after the government of India identified 27 places/features in Arunachal Pradesh by standard place and feature names on the official maps of Survey of India for “their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large”. This was in response to similar exercises carried out six times by China since 2017, with the last one in April this year, as a way to assert its claim over the Arunachal territory, which it calls “Zangnan” (southern Tibet). On each occasion, New Delhi strongly rejects China’s claim, reiterating that Arunachal Pradesh is an “inalienable and integral part of India”.
