The report noted that while government representatives from China have not attended the tourism event traditionally, there have been instances of private tour operators in the country participating at the event since it offers a lot of scope for B2B tie-ups. At the 2018 edition in Agartala, over 60 tour operator delegates from different countries participated, including those from Bangladesh, Australia, Canada, China and France. The report cited sources as saying invitations for the Tawang event had been sent to all participating countries and industry delegations. But the participation confirmation will be known only closer to the event date. While the main focus is on building travel and tourism ties between the region and its neighbours, particularly the ASEAN and SAARC countries, representatives and stakeholders from other parts of the world also attend the event. Delegates from Australia, New Zealand, Spain, Germany, Italy, France, Thailand and Israel were among those at the 2025 edition in Sikkim, the report said. For the edition in Tawang, the Ministry of Tourism is collaborating with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh. Union Ministers and state ministers will be attending the event over five days. Delegates will also be taken on a visit to Tawang Monastery, Buddha Park, Panga Teng Tso lake and Shernup village, the report added.

title: Bollywood war drama Maatrubhumi gets gov’t approval, storyline now shows China in positive light
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct04’26) – The Bollywood film starring superstar Salman Khan that was announced as Battle Of Galwan , based on the brutal 2020 Ladakh-border conflict between India and China, but retitled as Maatrubhumi: May War Rest In Peace earlier this year with significant changes in its storyline, is finally likely set for release, possibly in Nov 2026, reported bollywoodhungama.com Oct 2. The film in its original form could not be released earlier in view of the recent improvement in relations between the two countries because India’s Ministry of Defence had reservations about its content and mention of China, causing its delay, the report said. When an announcement was made about the film’s possible release earlier in its original form, it attracted online criticisms from China, including its official media, for allegedly demonising the country. The criticisms also derided the unrealistic depiction of the fighting skill of Bollywood film stars. However, a major development in the film occurred recently when the government cleared it for a theatrical release. The report quoted an official source as saying: “The officials of the I&B (Information and Broadcasting) Ministry are now satisfied with the new version of Maatrubhumi (meaning, motherland or homeland) submitted by the makers. Hence, they gave an NOC (No Objection Certificate) to the war saga last week. This means that the film can now be made available for public consumption.” The film still needs to be cleared by the country’s censor board, though this may now be a matter of formality. The report quoted the source as saying: “The makers will soon submit it to the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC). If the CBFC clears the film and the process is completed this month, Salman and his team will most probably bring Maatrubhumi to cinemas on November 13. A clearer picture in this regard will emerge in the next 10 days.” Explaining what has changed in the film due to the government directives, the source has replied, “The new version of Maatrubhumi is highly altered compared to the original version. Moreover, it now also talks about the relationship between India and China in a positive light.” The original version of the film highlighted the valour and spirit of sacrifice of Indian troops in the face of border aggressions by Chinese troops which climaxed in the brutal nighttime Galwan Valley clash of Jun 2020, leading to a deep freeze in China-India ties and considerable strengthening of border security by both the sides.

title: Seven Years in Tibet back on Netflix shelves after 20 years
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct03’26) – Subscription-based streaming service Netflix has included on Oct 1 the biographical epic Seven Years in Tibet (1997) among many movies it added to its digital shelves, reported uk.news.yahoo.com Oct 1. The film follows the true story of Heinrich Harrer, an Austrian climber and Nazi Party member who escapes a British POW camp in India, finds solace in Tibet’s holy capital Lhasa, and is transformed by his friendship with the young 14th Dalai Lama. Harrer said he joined the party only in order to be able to pursue his mountaineering interests. The Chinese government objected to the film’s depiction of its occupation of Tibet, particularly its portrayal of Chinese military officials and its positive depiction of the Dalai Lama. Brad Pitt who starred as Harrer, co-star David Thewlis, and director Jean-Jacques Annaud were reportedly banned from entering China as a result. The report also said Annaud had hoped to film in India, but the Chinese government pressured Indian officials to prevent the production from shooting there. The filmmakers ultimately used locations in Argentina and Canada to re-create Tibet. Annaud also obtained footage secretly shot in Tibet, some of which was incorporated into the finished movie. The report said that talking with Interview in 2019 about the film and its ban, Pitt said training and preparing for the role was life-changing. “For an audience it’s two hours, but for me it’s a half year of living,” he had said. “And this one particularly. Being in a different culture for so long, you couldn’t help but walk out of there with something.” The Chinese ban on Pitt was stated to have been slightly flexible. For example, he visited China in 2014 for a Maleficent promotional trip with Angelina Jolie and again in 2016 for an Allied media event. The Associated Press described the 2016 appearance as his first promotional appearance in China since the reported ban nearly 20 years earlier. Other Hollywood celebrities banned or restricted by China over the years over for their Tibet sympathy or support have included Martin Scorsese for his film on the Dalai Lama, Kundun; Melissa Mathison, the film’s screenwriter; Richard Gere for his Tibet activism; Harrison Ford for his outspoken support for a free Tibet and his testimony before the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Tibetan independence; Keanu Reeves for participating in a virtual benefit concert for Tibet House US in 2022; and Sharon Stone for linking the 2008 Sichuan earthquake to China’s treatment of Tibet.

title: New eastern Tibet discovery bolsters China’s lithium reserves by over one million tonnes
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct03’26) – China has greatly increased the amount of lithium deposit present in an already super-large reserve located in the eastern Tibetan city of Barkham (Chinese: Maerkang), in Amdo Ngaba, which is currently part of Sichuan province. The new discovery is expected to help China reduce its dependence on foreign sources for this vital mineral as it pushes to lead the world in the development, use, and export of modern high-tech products. China has announced the expansion of the resource base for a major lithium deposit in Sichuan province by about 70%, strengthening the country’s potential long-term supply for the metal – an essential component in the production of batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage, reported scmp.com Oct 3, citing state news agency Xinhua Oct 1. The report said that after recent detection efforts, the Jiada Lithium Mine had registered about 1.05 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent in the deposit, bringing its total resources to 2.53 million tonnes. The increase has reinforces the mine’s status as a major hard-rock lithium deposit. Dazhong Mining, the project’s developer, has said the additional resources comprised 33.52 million tonnes of ore containing about 423,800 tonnes of lithium oxide, with an average grade of 1.26%. The addition is stated to represents a 70.5% increase from the previously registered 1.48 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent. The company has estimated that the deposit’s initial mining area, with an approved extraction scale of 2.6 million tonnes of ore a year, could support annual production of about 50,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate at full capacity. The report noted that lithium’s utility in the manufacturing of EVs, energy storage systems and consumer electronics makes access to the metal a strategic concern for China, as its battery and clean-energy firms grow into world leaders. In Jan 2025, the China Geological Survey said exploration breakthroughs had increased China’s share of global lithium reserves to 16.5%, placing it second worldwide by the agency’s estimates. Yet the country remains heavily reliant on overseas supplies, counting on overseas sources for about 60% of its lithium resource supply in 2025, the report said, citing China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association. The report said Jiada lies within a lithium belt that stretches across West Kunlun, Songpan and Kardze (Chinese: Garze) in Ngaba (Aba) county, which measures about 2,800km (1,740 miles) and forms part of what Chinese geologists call the “Asian lithium belt”. The region is a major concentration of China’s hard-rock lithium resources, the Xinhua report was cited as saying. China currently imports lithium concentrates from countries such as Australia, Zimbabwe and Brazil, while Chile and Argentina are its main sources of imported lithium carbonate, the report noted.

title: The Reckoning Deferred: Tibet’s Succession Question
author: tibetanreview
content: OPINION Dr Yashwant Singh* argues that the issue concerning the recognition of the reincarnation of the current Dalai Lama, when the time comes eventually, will force governments to adopt what may amount to a position on the political status of Tibet that they have so far managed to avoid by referring to religious repression, human and cultural rights, and so forth. For decades, diplomacy toward Tibet has rested on a single unstated premise: that the hardest question could be deferred indefinitely. Governments could criticize religious repression without contesting sovereignty, host the Dalai Lama without endorsing independence, raise cultural rights in Geneva (UN Human Rights Council) while avoiding the sovereignty question in New York (UN General Assembly). This worked because it was cost-free: a set of positions that never had to resolve into one decision. The succession of the 14th Dalai Lama will end that arrangement, because recognizing a reincarnation is not a statement of values but an act that confers legitimate religious-political authority on one person and delegitimizes any rival. Two incompatible legal architectures The United Nations (UN) Charter itself is split: Article 2(7) bars intervention in matters “essentially within domestic jurisdiction,” while Article 1(2) commits the organization to “self-determination of peoples.” International law never settled whether self-determination survives inside an existing state once decolonization is complete. The International Court of Justice’s 2010 Kosovo advisory opinion sidestepped this, ruling only that a declaration of independence didn’t itself violate international law, without saying international law affirmatively supported one. That evasiveness is now the default posture toward Tibet too: almost no government today disputes People’s Republic of China (PRC) sovereignty over the Tibet Autonomous Region; the old argument about the legality of the 1950-51 incorporation has been displaced by a narrower one about governance: language, religious administration, cultural preservation. A sovereignty claim invites confrontation; a governance claim invites monitoring, and the UN’s machinery is built for the latter. Why Geneva absorbs what New York avoids The UN General Assembly’s (UNGA) high-level week is where heads of state spend scarce rhetorical capital on crises with immediate strategic stakes. The Human Rights Council and its special-procedures system carry reputational, not existential, weight. China’s Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, passed by the National People’s Congress on March 12, 2026, in force since July 1, illustrates the pattern: the UN Human Rights Office and several former UN special rapporteurs warned it could accelerate assimilationist pressure on Tibetan, Uyghur, and Mongol communities, but that concern moved through special-procedures communications and OHCHR statements, not a General Assembly resolution. Tibet hasn’t disappeared from the UN (General Assembly), a recurring lament over the last several years; it has migrated into the venue least likely to generate diplomatic cost, which is exactly why it survives there. At UNGA’s 81st session (opened September 8, 2026; General Debate September 22-28), Tibet-related events entered the General Debate discourse indirectly through the transboundary Himalayan disaster, while Nepal’s official speech itself avoided explicitly naming Tibet (instead referred to the neighbouring region as “China”). The political ‘Tibet Question’ found no mention in the proceedings. Why succession is different Succession cannot be phrased as a governance concern. Beijing has signalled it will control the process through state-approved procedures, a claim UN special-procedures experts have directly challenged , citing the still-unresolved 1995 disappearance of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, the child the Dalai Lama recognized as the 11th Panchen Lama. If Beijing installs its own successor while the Dalai Lama’s institution recognizes a different child, likely born in exile, every government will face a binary with no “ rights-without-recognition ” escape hatch: which reincarnation does each government’s embassy treat as legitimate. Religious legitimacy, unlike governance criticism, isn’t divisible. Three hedges that won’t survive the deadline India : its posture, hosting the Dalai Lama and the Central Tibetan Administration while recognizing Chinese sovereignty, rooted in the 1954 Panchsheel framework, has worked because it never demanded one decisive act. Hosting, or even not obstructing, a recognition ceremony for an exile-based successor would be a decision with consequences for the border dispute and the broader China relationship that can’t be walked back. Washington : a legislation , The Assuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026, introduced by Senators Jeff Merkley, already anticipates Chinese efforts to control succession, which suggests policymakers see the deferral ending, but anticipating a decision isn’t making one. Once a successor is named, “support dialogue, criticize repression, avoid the sovereignty question” stops being an available position. Beijing : its resistance to any external role in succession is inseparable from its anxiety about precedent across Xinjiang, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, which is why this generates more institutional intensity from Beijing than ordinary rights criticism. It is a test of the non-interference doctrine, not a rights dispute. The compression None of this makes the current silence dishonest: it reflects a system that found genuine, low-cost ways to manage a question it never resolved. Succession removes the low-cost options. It will force every government that has spent decades avoiding a decision to make one, in public, with no institutional venue built to absorb the cost. — * Dr Yashwant Singh is an Indian sociologist working at the intersection of urban studies, development, nature and geopolitics. He holds an M Phil in Sociology from the University of Delhi and a PhD from the University of Hyderabad, and recently served as Assistant Professor of Sociology at GITAM (Deemed to be) University, Bengaluru. Alongside his academic work, Dr Singh’s essays and analyses have been published across several international platforms, including Across Voices, Modern Diplomacy, Eurasia Review, Jerusalem Strategic Tribune, Geostrategic Media, South Asia Journal, World Geostrategic Insights, and IA-Forum, where he offers sociological and analytical perspectives on global affairs, strategic developments, and the changing dynamics of contemporary societies.

title: Nearly 22.5% of mining rights across ‘Tibet’ lie within 5km of glaciers
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct02’26) – China says climate change caused the catastrophic Aug 26 Tibet-Nepal avalanche floods, which caused over 1,494 deaths and left more than 6,264 people missing across Nepal and Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), but nearly 22.5% of the global warming mining rights granted by it across the region lie within 5km of glaciers, said an indiatoday.in report Oct 1, citing an official TAR report. These glaciers are located across key transboundary river basins. The finding has sharpened concerns that upstream mining could intensify flood and glacial lake-outburst risks downstream, the report said. Mining can be not only environmentally devastating but it also, according to an https://www.icmm.com/global-datasets/ghg-emissions report Mar 10, 2026, accounts for roughly 4% to 11% of direct global greenhouse gas emissions, depending on how supply chains and metal processing are counted. But climate change is not the whole story. Experts and scientists have increasingly warned that China’s upstream activities in Tibet, including large-scale infrastructure construction, massive militarisation, strategy-driven urbanisation, and dam construction, are destabilising sensitive ecosystems and directly increasing flood and disaster risks across the Himalayas, the report, authored by Tenzin Younten, a Senior Researcher at the 108 Peace Institute, said. Meanwhile, disaster risks posed by Chinese mining operations near glaciers remain largely under-examined. A recently released Chinese environmental assessment for the TAR’s Mineral Resources Master Plan draft (2026–2030) documents that 156 of 694 mining rights across the region lie within five kilometres of glaciers, encompassing 1,810.94 square kilometres of glacier area, including several in the headwaters of trans-boundary rivers flowing toward India, Nepal, and Bhutan, the report said. China’s glacier-adjacent mines in the Himalayas, with their detrimental impact on local hydrology and terrain stability, heighten the risk of disasters rapidly affecting communities far downstream. But instead of addressing these rising disaster risks and the impact of their upstream activities, China has enforced strict information control and moved to normalise the situation in the affected region by rebuilding the G-216 national highway alongside other infrastructure. Yet, China’s own environmental assessment ranking of mining rights and planning units by glacier proximity in TAR shows that the exposure is concentrated on transboundary river basins near the international frontier. In fact, six of the 10 highest-ranked mining rights are located within the Yarlung Tsangpo basin alone. Besides, the two highest-ranked mining rights are both on the India-Tibet border. A third mine lies in Lhozhag (Lhodrag) County, on Tibet’s border with Bhutan, the report pointed out. While these are only a few critically exposed sites on the most sensitive stretch of border disclosed in the top 10 rankings, the broader question is how many glacier-proximate mining operations exist or are planned across the Himalayan border between Tibet and its downstream neighbours, terrain comparable to the already unstable Rasuwa-Kerung corridor. Besides, the Yarlung Tsangpo basin contains TAR’s densest mining footprint, with 48.6% of the region’s mining rights located here, the aforementioned Chinese official report, which is in Chinese, was cited as saying. The report cited ICIMOD ( International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development) and UNDP reports as saying at least 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes are at risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), mainly within the Tibet–Nepal transboundary basins alone. Many more unmapped or unknown lakes likely exist across the major transboundary river basins flowing from Tibet, including the Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Salween, Yangtze, Irrawaddy, and Mekong. The proximity of mining operations near glaciers to the glacier-fed transboundary river system is causing significant additional disturbance to a region that is disaster-prone, the report said. While climate change is already destabilising the region by altering the hydrological and geological conditions, aggressive human interventions such as excavation, blasting, waste generation, and altered drainage associated with mining could compound existing processes of glacier retreat, permafrost degradation, slope instability, and glacial-lake expansion, the indiatoday.in report further said. India, as the primary downstream power with the most at stake, should push Beijing beyond just formal, transparent data-sharing on transboundary rivers and also hold China accountable for its upstream activities such as glacier-adjacent mining that raise such risks. After all, when disaster strikes, it makes no distinction between nationalities, the report concluded.

title: Dozens of Tibetan protesters held near Chinese embassy in New Delhi on China’s national day
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct01’26) – Police in the Indian capital New Delhi detained dozens of Tibetans as they staged a protest near the Chinese Embassy on Oct 1, the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China, reported tribuneindia.com Oct 1. They shouted slogans such as “Tibet is never part of China and will never be”, reported thehindu.com Oct 1. The Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), which organised the protest, has said the purpose was to highlight the Tibetan people’s continued struggle for freedom and justice and to draw attention to China’s policies in Tibet. All the 40 or so protesting men and women were college-going students, who carried Tibetan national flags and stretch banners while shouting “Free Tibet” slogans, said the Voice of Tibet broadcast service Oct 1. It added that all were apprehended and placed under police detention. The group has accused China of denying fundamental rights to Tibetans and suppressing their distinct identity and culture. It has also criticised China for its continued occupation and political control of Tibet. It has condemned China’s assertion of sovereignty and political control over Tibet as well as East Turkestan (Xinjiang), Southern Mongolia and Manchuria. The TYC advocates for Tibet’s independence from Chinese occupation rule, unlike the Central Tibetan Administration, which seeks genuine autonomy for the entirety of the Tibetan homeland through a negotiated settlement. The TYC has expressed confidence that Chinese laws and policies would not succeed in erasing the Tibetan people’s historical claims, identity or their stated aspiration to determine their political future. China is observing a week-long National Day holiday from Oct 1 to 7. Flag-raising ceremonies were held across the country to mark the day, with the main event being held at Tian’anmen Square in Beijing, where a giant flower basket added to the festive atmosphere, state-run Xinhua News reported. At a reception held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to celebrate the occasion, President Xi Jinping has called on the nation to forge ahead with firm confidence and take solid steps to achieve the great national rejuvenation, calling it “unstoppable’. On Taiwan, he has called for efforts to deepen exchanges and cooperation across the Strait, resolutely fight secessionist forces seeking “Taiwan independence,” oppose external interference, and promote the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations to advance national reunification.

title: Bipartisan delegation of US lawmakers meet with Dalai Lama, visiting Dharamshala to deepen their understanding of Tibet issue
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct01’26) – A bipartisan delegation of five US House of Representative members has on Sep 30 called on His Holiness the Dalai Lama at his exile home since Apr 1960 in Dharamshala, India, and also addressed the press, making the point that “we stand with you”, referring to the Tibetan people and their grim, decades-long struggle for freedom against the rising global power China. “We came today in Dharamsala to meet with the Dalai Lama, to learn about an issue that we have supported for many, many years,” the ANI news service quoted Brian Mast, the leader of the delegation and Chairman of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, as saying after he landed at Kangra airport on Sep 29. He has emphasising the importance of the visit, saying gaining a deeper understanding of the issue required members of the US Congress to see Dharamshala in person. “It’s important for us as members of Congress to do everything that we can to learn more about the issue, and that means visiting in person,” he has said. On the concerns of the Tibetan community, Mast has added, “We stand with you.” In their meeting with the Dalai Lama, the delegation members reaffirmed support for the Tibetan people and raised concerns over China’s human rights record and alleged transnational repression, the report said. “Certainly China was among top issues, the freedom of the people of Tibet, his representation of freedom across the globe just as we believe that the United States of America is representation of freedom across the globe. We discussed a great many things,” Mast has told reporters after the meeting. Mast has said the Dalai Lama, like him, supported US President Trump’s meeting with the Chinese President Xi Jinping recently. “His Holiness believed that it was important that President Trump meet with Xi Jinping. They are two leaders of the world’s biggest and strongest countries across the globe. So yes, it’s very important, and it should happen.” And he has explained, “It doesn’t take away in any way from believing that China should not be repressing its people, should not be repressing the Tibetan people or the Uyghur people, but rather working to embrace freedom and support freedom across the globe.” Mast (Republican–Florida) was stated to be accompanied for the Dharamshala visit by Representatives James Gallagher (Republican–California), Jimmy Patronis (Republican–Florida), Haley Stevens (Democrat–Michigan), and Shri Thanedar (Democrat–Michigan). Mast has also said China’s transnational repression was “far-reaching” and alleged that Beijing used surveillance, spies and police in different countries to monitor and suppress people. “They will reach anywhere that they can. They’ve proven that.” Stevens has said, “We will not forget the story of the Tibetans. We will not forget the power of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, what it means to have peace and democracy.” She has also said that it was important for the delegation – usually political opponents – to come together in “a bipartisan way for freedom.” “I came here with a Republican leader who is close to President Trump. I am not afraid to say it because we joined and linked forces,” the Michigan representative said. “This is calling on us to dig deep, to recognize that this is a tough moment, that we are losing sight of why we need to invest and support democracy in the Tibetan people,” rfa.org Sep 30 quoted him as saying Gallagher has called for self-determination and protection of religious and cultural freedoms, saying, “Stop oppressing your people and allow everyone to live free. Allow for self-determination, for freedom of religion, for freedom of culture.” Patronis has praised the 91-year-old Dalai Lama’s wisdom and strength, describing them as important to the delegation’s efforts and continuing dialogue with Beijing. The executive head of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), Sikyong Penpa Tsering, and the CTA’s Representative at the Bureau of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in New Delhi, Jigme Tsering, have accompanied the delegation. The delegation’s Dharamshala visit followed high-level engagements with Indian officials in New Delhi along with five other House members. Their meetings included those with Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, and Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, the ANI report said.

title: Trump discussed release of certain political prisoners with Xi, but seen as silent on rights issues generally
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Oct01’26) – US President Donald ​Trump has said on Sep 30 that he discussed the release of ‌certain political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping when they met in the White House last week. However, he is seen as silent on rights issues generally. “I did with President Xi. I did,” Reuters Sep 30 quoted Trump as telling reporters when asked if ​he brought up the cases of political prisoners like Myanmar ​scholar and US citizen Min Zin, who was arrested in ⁠June, and Hong Kong’s most vocal China critic and media ​tycoon Jimmy Lai. “We talked, and I think we had some very, very ​important discussions. Hopefully, fruitful discussions,” Trump has added. The report noted that ahead of Xi’s visit, the White House had said Trump was expected to bring up cases of people wrongfully ​detained in China with the Chinese leader. However, it did not say if Trump aimed to directly raise broader rights issues related to Tibet, the ‌Uyghur ⁠Muslim minority group, and China’s new “ethnic unity” law. The report noted that Trump had made winning freedom for Americans held overseas a priority, including in China, even as he had largely avoided talking about China’s treatment of Tibetans, Uyghurs ​and voices of ​dissent. Lai’s case had sparked ⁠global concerns over China’s national security clampdown in Hong Kong, in part reflecting his prominence as founder ​of the now-shuttered Apple Daily newspaper. The 78-year-old Hong Kong democracy supporter was ​sentenced to ⁠20 years in jail in February on two counts of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces and one count of publishing seditious materials as perceived by China. Washington in August designated ⁠Myanmar ​scholar and US citizen Min Zin as wrongfully ​detained after his arrest by Chinese authorities in June.

title: Exile administration releases revised vision paper for Tibet and its democratic governance
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep30’26) – The Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) at Dharamshala, India, has on Sep 30 released a revised version of its “Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future”, encapsulating the totality of its political, administrative, and socio-economic policies, programmes, and goals. The paper defines CTA’s two key responsibilities as: seeking an early resolution to the Sino-Tibet conflict and promoting the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile, while also ensuring efficient and effective administrative functioning of the CTA through strengthening its capacity. Guided by the principles of Equitable Justice, Cooperative Effort, and Moving Forward, the revised paper aims to provide clear direction and guidance to the staff and leadership of the CTA. It seeks to further strengthen institutional efficiency, enhance productivity, foster cohesive collaboration, promote sustainability, and ensure greater self-reliance in the face of emerging challenges, said the CTA on its Tibet.net website Sep 30. Sikyong Penpa Tsering has introduced the key issues outlined in the paper to a gathering of the CTA staff, as well as to the general Tibetan public through Tibet TV online telecasting, using a PowerPoint presentation. In his message for the occasion, the Sikyong has said: “The 16th Kashag (the Tibetan cabinet, 2021-26) published the Vision Paper: Securing Tibet’s Future to help officials, the public, and all concerned understand the importance of Tibet and the Tibetan people; strategies for realising the just cause of Tibet; policies for the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile; and plans to strengthen the CTA. It sought to bring everyone’s collective efforts together and has yielded positive results. Building on that foundation, we now present a revised paper setting out the 17th Kashag’s overall position, working approaches, and long-term vision for the attention of all relevant stakeholders.” The first of the paper’s three sections talks about “the realisation of the just cause of Tibet through strengthening the existing Permanent Strategy Committee; engaging with Chinese people and affected groups; securing recognition of Tibet’s historical status; countering the Chinese government’s interference in the reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama; countering the Chinese government’s infiltration and deception; and strengthening Tibetan advocacy.” The paper’s second section, which focuses on the welfare of the Tibetan community in exile, seeks to address “the reinforcement of social cohesion through safeguarding and sustaining democratic practices, ensuring transparency in administration, strengthening relations between the administration and the public, providing additional care for those in need, empowering women and youth, and strengthening relations with organisations and other bodies.” It also sets out the goal of “protecting Tibetan identity and sustaining the community by building and sustaining compact Tibetan communities, supporting monastic and religious institutions, promoting healthy settlements, and creating opportunities for sustainable livelihoods.” It “underscores the promotion of Tibetan education and language through consolidating Tibetan schools in India, sustaining the Basic Education Policy for Tibetans-in-Exile, and promoting the use and development of the Tibetan language and script.” The emphasis of the paper’s third section is on strengthening the capacity of the CTA. It “addresses programme planning, implementation, and follow-up in accordance with the laws of the host country, with the aim of ensuring financial transparency and a sound system of accountability. It further highlights the strengthening of institutional capacity through the controlled and appropriate use of artificial intelligence, the establishment of an Institutional Development Index Data Management (IDI-DM) system, and the timely delivery of staff capacity-building training.” The Tibet.net report said that along with the CTA’s revised Vision Paper, two additional documents outlining the current, 17th Kashag’s position and providing guidelines for the working approach of CTA departments were also presented to the gathering.

title: Exile Tibetan education meet focuses on declining enrolment, urgency to preserve identity
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep29’26) – The executive head of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), Sikyong Penpa Tsering, has on Sep 28 cited low birth rate among exile Tibetans as a major reason for the declining trend in Tibetan school enrolments. There are other major reasons also, of course, including a near-total end to new refugee arrivals from Chinese occupied Tibet and many young Tibetans moving to the West due to tough livelihood opportunities in India and Nepal. Both he and the Education Kalon (minister) Urgen Tenzin have emphasized the urgency to strengthen the implementation of the CTA’s Basic Education Policy (BEP) in light of China’s recently enacted Ethnic Unity and Progress promotion Law (Ethnic Unity Law). Presiding over the two-day, 14th meeting of the CTA’s Education Council and Advisory Committee, the Tibetan Sikyong has said the issues present a growing challenge to the CTA’s Department of Education, requiring more than simply offering advice or raising awareness. Referring to the declining enrolments, he emphasised the need to understand the underlying demographic and social factors and to develop practical and sustainable measures to address the changing circumstances of Tibetan schools and communities, reported the CTA’s Tibet.net Sep 28. He has also highlighted the financial challenges faced by the Tibetan schools in Nepal, noting that their sustainability requires close coordination between the CTA’s Department of Education and the Department of Finance. The Sikyong has also addressed the challenges faced by Tibetans in exile, particularly among the younger generation living abroad. He has highlighted concerns over the declining use of Tibetan language and the difficulties faced in maintaining language proficiency among younger Tibetans. He has called for the strengthening of Tibetan language education and improvement in teaching methods. He has also emphasised the urgent need to ensure that younger generation of Tibetans remain informed about the current situation in Tibet, expressing concern over policies and laws being implemented by China that are increasingly undermining the use and preservation of Tibetan language. He has stressed that the erosion of Tibetan language poses a serious challenge to the preservation of Tibetan identity, culture and heritage, and called on the younger generation to recognise the importance of safeguarding their language and maintaining their connection to Tibet. The Education Council and Advisory Committee held its 14th meeting in Dharamshala on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo courtesy: CTA) The new Chair of the Education Council, Thupten Lungrig, has underlined the importance of the CTA’s BEP of 2004 whose core vision is to ensure the long-term preservation of Tibetan language and values. Education Kalon Urgen Tenzin has said the implementation of the BEP had received overwhelmingly positive feedback and paved the way for a progressive implementation of BEP guidelines across various Tibetan schools in exile. He has highlighted the transformative impact of the BEP within the Tibetan community, pointing, for comparison, out how India’s National Education Policy (NEP) seeks to foster independent, and holistic learning for future generations. He has stressed the indispensable role of parents in understanding and upholding the policy at home, emphasising that family engagement is crucial to nurturing native language proficiency and traditional ethical values. In light of China’s recently enacted Ethnic Unity Law, The education kalon has emphasized the urgent need to challenge the forced assimilation policies and protect Tibetan cultural and linguistic identity against China’s systematic erasure.

title: India says ties with China improving, emphasizes imperative of border stability
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep29’26) – Relations with China today are “better” today than they were a year or two ago, India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has said Sep 28, attributing the improvement to the easing of tensions along the border and the gradual restoration of normal bilateral engagement. Speaking at an Asia Society conversation event in New York, Jaishankar has said if he was to compare the ties between India and China at present against before, his answer would be positive. “After the 2020 standoff, all “normal contacts” between the two countries had stopped. While trade continued, official exchanges, visa issuance and flights were affected,” indiatoday.in Sep 29 quoted Jaishankar as saying. “Once the border standoff was resolved, it was natural that this would start to improve,” hindustantimes.com Sep 29, likewise, quoted Jaishankar as saying. “What we’ve had is that, as the border comes back more towards normalcy, the relationship comes back more towards normalcy… If it happens, it helps both of us.” India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar speaking at an Asia Society conversation event in New York on Sept 28, 2026. (Photo courtesy: Dr. S. Jaishankar/X) India’s approach was based on the principle that the state of the border influences the broader relationship, newindianexpress.com Sep 29 cited Jaishankar as saying. “We came down to a very fundamental principle, which is that the state of the border determines the state of the relationship. You can’t have tension…on the border and say the relationship should be normal.” Referring to the current state of bilateral relations, Jaishankar has clarified that this was not so much a “structural change”, but that ties had improved partly because they had gone “so much off-track” after the 2020 border standoff, according to the indiatoday.in report. Regarding this, the newindianexpress.com report said India and China had taken steps since 2024 to stabilise their relationship, while significant strategic differences remain.

title: A Remarkable Child Who Connected Nepal to the Buddhist World
author: tibetanreview
content: Nepal honoured Bhrikuti, Bhelsa Tritsun in Tibetan, who was married to Tibet’s 33rd Yarlung Dynasty King Songtsen Gampo, the founder of the 7 th to 9 th century Tibetan empire, as a N ational Luminary in 1955 for being a bearer of Nepal’s Buddhist culture and a symbol of peace, but then removed her from the list in 2017, ostensibly due to lack of sufficient historical records about her in the country’s archives. Now, as a case is sought to be made to restore her status with a twist to colour her contributions in light of Kathmandu’s current One China policy stand, Biswo Ulak* gives an account of her as a real historical figure who carried the teachings of the Buddha from Nepal to Tibet and beyond, with a hope to encourage younger generations to appreciate the deep civilisational ties between Nepal and Tibet. At just eight years of age, Bhrikuti left her homeland on a remarkable journey to Tibet, carrying the Nepali Buddhist culture and traditions. Through her marriage to King Songtsen Gampo and the cultural exchange that followed, the influence of Nepali Buddhism reached in Tibet and eventually extended into China and other parts of East and Southeast Asia. Her history was largely overlooked in Nepal because, according to this account, she was born in Kurpasi (Khopasi) while her family was living in exile, outside the Kathmandu Valley. French Professor Sylvain Lévi, who was among the first scholars to write about Nepal’s history, has made a mention of Bribtsn, the daughter of the Nepali king Go Cha (a Tibetan term meaning “Rising Light”) from the Tibetan and Chinese chronology. However, he suspected that her father might have been Amshuvarma Thakuri, as he was the most powerful and influential ruler of Nepal during that period, although Lévi did not reach a definitive conclusion. Nepali historian Baburam Acharya renamed Bribtsn as Bhrikuti Devi and described her as the daughter of Amshuvarma Thakuri, an interpretation later followed by several other contemporary scholars. However, Lilabhakta Munankarmi was not convinced that Bhrikuti was Amshuvarma Thakuri’s daughter. In an article published in Gorkhapatra in 2020 BS, historian Bhuvan Pradhan presented Bhrikuti as the daughter of Lichhivi King Udaya Deva. ((Editor’s note: BS stands for Bikram Sambat [also spelled Vikram Samvat[, which is the official historical calendar used in Nepal.) Unfortunately, some Nepali scholars have questioned whether there was a princess named Bhrikuti in Nepal, suggesting that she was merely a fictional character. The Government of Nepal’s Ministry of Education, through the Janak Education Materials Centre, introduced Bhrikuti as the daughter of Amshuvarma Thakuri in the Grade 7 textbook Mahendramala, published in 2031 BS. This conflicting claim appears to have been incorporated into the school curriculum without adequate historical verification. As a result, despite Bhrikuti having been honoured with the title of “National Luminary” in 2012 BS, her historical legacy was later diminished when her name was removed from the list of National Luminaries without a detailed study by the authorities responsible for making such decisions. The Bhrikuti Smriti Pratisthan subsequently conducted a number of studies on Bhrikuti’s life and historical background in Nepal, including a year-long rigorous details study with the financial support from the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation. The study established her birthplace and identified her parents, findings that were subsequently recognized and accepted by the Government of Nepal. The following are the key findings of the study: According to traditions, Amshuvarma Thakuri was born in Kurpasi in the 550s AD and became a Samanta (feudal lord of a principality) following the death of his father, Manvarma, in the 570s AD. He continued to serve as a Samanta when the Licchhavi King Shiva Deva I ascended to the throne of Nepal in 590 AD. Local legends say that Amshuvarma Thakuri resided in the former residence of King Birat in Kurpasi, on the present-day premises of Narasingh Math, while his administrative office was located in the then palace of Kailash on the banks of Jhilpu Khola. King Shiva Deva faced growing challenges to his governance as the influence of the Guptas increased. To counter this influence, he established a matrimonial alliance with the powerful Samanta Amshuvarma Thakuri by giving his daughter to him in marriage around 595 AD. He also sent his eldest son, Prince Udaya Deva, and his wife, Bhadrawati Devi, to Kurpasi to stay with Amshuvarma Thakuri, receiving knowledge and skills of governance. Considering Amshuvarma Thakuri’s competence, integrity, and matrimonial connection with the royal family, King Shiva Deva granted him greater authority in 598 AD through a royal inscription, elevating him to the position of Maha-Samanta (Great Samanta) and later allowing him to exercise de facto kingly authority. He effectively entrusted Amshuvarma Thakuri with the affairs of the kingdom, as King Shiva Deva devoted much of his time to religious and spiritual activities. Following the death of King Shiva Deva, Amshuvarma Thakuri, who had already been exercising de facto authority, declared himself Maharajadhiraja (King) in 605 AD, reportedly because Prince Udaya Deva was considered unable to govern effectively. However, as Amshuvarma Thakuri had no children of his own, Udaya Deva was reinstated as Crown Prince in 613 AD. Prince Udaya Deva ascended to the throne in 621 AD following the death of Amshuvarma Thakuri, who died at the age of 70 after a long life. Unfortunately, Udaya Deva was unable to withstand the growing influence and attacks from his own brother, Dhrubadeva, who was supported by Jishnu Gupta, Bishnu Gupta, and others. As a result, Udaya Deva was overthrown and removed from the throne in 623 AD. King Udaya Deva, Queen Bhadrawati Devi, and their one-year-old son, Prince Narendradeva, went into exile and sought refuge at Bhadrawati’s maternal home in Manjushree Tole, Lagan, Kathmandu. According to the tradition presented in the study, Bhrikuti was conceived there in Queen Bhadrawati’s womb while they were in Bhadrawati’s maternal home. Exiled King Udaya Deva attempted to regain the throne through a revolt, but he was unsuccessful. He was subsequently driven out of Kathmandu and moved to Patan, where he made another attempt to regain his power, but again failed. He then moved to Bhaktapur. After this attempt also proved unsuccessful, the exile royal family moved to Kurpasi, where they settled in the former residence of the Mahasamanta, Amshuvarma Thakuri. This was the place where Udaya Deva and his wife had previously stayed while gaining knowledge and skills of governance. According to traditions, Bhrikuti was born in Kurpasi in 624 AD in the former residence of Amshuvarma Thakuri. Bhrikuti was raised and groomed in a Buddhist cultural environment, deeply influenced by the traditions of the Kirat and Thakuri periods and the local Pahari inhabitants. In 632 AD, at the age of eight, Bhrikuti was sent to Tibet to marry King Songtsen Gampo, accompanied by a Tibetan delegation led by the Tibetan ministers Thonmi Sambhota and Gar Tongtsen. The ancient route through the Rasuwa Pass was used to take her to Lhasa, and the journey included a pilgrimage to Gosaikunda, which was regarded as an important pilgrimage center for Tibetans. The journey to Lhasa took more than six months. Upon her arrival in Lhasa, Bhrikuti formally married King Songtsen Gampo in 633 AD, at the age of nine. After Bhrikuti’s departure, the royal palace in Kathmandu continued to persecute the exiled King Udaya Deva. As a result, he could no longer remain in Kurpasi and left for Lhasa with his wife, Queen Bhadrawati Devi, and their son, Prince Narendra Deva, seeking political asylum. They reached Lhasa after Bhrikuti’s formal marriage with King Songtsen Gampo. An opportunity subsequently arose for Prince Narendra Deva to seek Chinese support for the release of a Chinese envoy from Kannauj of Magadh (India), at the request of his brother-in-law, King Songtsen Gampo. With the support of the Paharis and others, he returned to Nepal and regained his father’s throne in 642 AD, and relocate capital to Bhaktapur from Kathmandu. However, his parents, Udaya Deva and Bhadrawati Devi, did not return to Nepal. Queen Bhrikuti returned to her motherland, Nepal, around 645 AD to meet her brother, King Narendra Deva, travelling through the Kodari Pass. During her visit, she advised her brother to build a palace named “Bhadradhiwas” in honour of their mother, Queen Bhadrawati Devi. The palace is believed to have been built in Bhaktapur, although its historical identification and location require further study and investigation. In 650 AD, King Songtsen Gampo announced the date and time of his death. According to tradition, Queen Bhrikuti chose voluntary death (स्वेच्छिक मृत्यु) at the age of 25, dying in the king’s lap at the time of his death. It is also believed that Bhrikuti’s body was buried alongside King Songtsen Gampo in the royal burial ground in the Chongye Valley of Lhasa, which is now an important tourist destination. Exiled Princess Bhrikuti, who carried the Buddhist culture and teachings of the Buddha from her motherland as a spiritual dowry, shared them with her husband, King Songtsen Gampo. Through her influence, these teachings reached the royal palace and capital of Lhasa, spread throughout Tibet, and eventually extended into mainland China and Southeast Asia. Although she lived only a short life, her remarkable contribution and spiritual influence earned her lasting reverence. She came to be venerated as Green Tara, a tradition that was widespread across Tibet and Southeast Asia. The history of Bhrikuti is not merely a story of the past; it is a history of cultural exchange, resilience, and peace. From the 8th century, Buddhism experienced periods of decline and suppression in Nepal and India, while continuing to flourish in China and other parts of Asia. In Nepal, the revival of Buddhism gained new momentum following the political changes of 1950s in Nepal, strengthened by renewed cultural and intellectual connections with Buddhist communities beyond the Himalayas, especially from mainland China. Bhrikuti’s legacy reminds us that ideas, cultures, and spiritual teachings can cross borders and endure even through the most difficult periods. As a princess who carried the teachings of the Buddha from Nepal to Tibet and beyond, she represents a historic bridge connecting Nepal, Tibet, China, and the wider Buddhist world. Honouring Bhrikuti today would therefore be more than commemorating a historical figure; it would be a celebration of Nepal’s enduring contribution to peace, compassion, cultural dialogue, and friendship in the globe. — * Biswo Ulak, President and founder-member of the Bhrikuti Memorial Academy, has a master’s degree in political science and a diploma in business administration and commerce from the Tribhuvan University of Nepal and a degree in postgraduate studies in Human Resources Studies from Manchester University. He has worked in the Nepal Government and international development agencies over the four decade s in different fields. He presently holds advisory positions in a few local NGOs and has published articles on culture, tourism and development in national and international journals.

title: Why the Official Policy of the Tibetan Government-in-Exile Can Only Be the ‘Middle Way’
author: tibetanreview
content: OPINION Bembya Mitruev* argues that the middle way policy, “the only sustainable official policy of the Central Tibetan Administration”, envisioned by His Holiness the Dalai Lama way back in the 1970s, is an outcome of rigorous democratic and legal procedures, and could not be changed by the simpleness of a private member’s bill, as attempted in the recent Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile session. Recently, during the second session of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, a private member’s motion was tabled seeking to establish “Tibetan independence” as the official policy of the Central Tibetan Administration. The motion failed to secure a majority at the threshold vote on whether it should proceed to debate, receiving 15 votes in favour and 23 against, and was ultimately rejected. This episode once again underscores that, within the current legal framework, democratic procedures, international realities, and strategic considerations, the “Middle Way” remains the only sustainable official policy of the Central Tibetan Administration. Legal and Charter Basis The Charter of the Tibetans-in-Exile establishes the fundamental institutional framework of the Central Tibetan Administration. Under the relevant provisions (particularly Article 56 and related clauses concerning referendums and major policy matters), issues involving the fundamental interests of Tibet or significant policy changes cannot be altered lightly through an ordinary private member’s motion. They require higher thresholds and, where necessary, a public referendum. Sikyong Penpa Tsering’s procedural objections were grounded precisely in this institutional logic: if established policy could be overturned at will by ordinary resolutions, the stability of parliamentary procedures and the authority of the Charter would be undermined. The Middle Way is not a temporary decision. It is an official position that emerged from prolonged internal discussion, was advocated by His Holiness the Dalai Lama, has been repeatedly affirmed by the Parliament, and enjoys majority support within the exile community. In the mid-1990s, an opinion survey on policy direction showed that a majority supported the Middle Way or deferred to the decisions of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Establishing it as official policy accords with the Charter’s requirement of caution on matters of major importance. Any shift to an independence policy would likewise have to follow equally rigorous democratic and legal procedures, and could not be effected by a single private member’s motion. Historical Legitimacy and Democratic Consensus The Middle Way was proposed by His Holiness the Dalai Lama in the 1970s and formally elaborated in the late 1980s. Its core is to seek genuine national regional autonomy for the three traditional provinces of Tibet within the framework of recognising China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, in order to protect language, religion, culture, and national identity. It explicitly rejects the repressive policies of the current situation while forgoing the immediate pursuit of complete independence. This position has been repeatedly confirmed by successive Parliaments-in-Exile and has been upheld by the elected leadership after His Holiness devolved political authority in 2011. Discussion within the exile Tibetan community between independence and autonomy has never ceased; some continue to uphold the Rangzen (independence) demand. This is a legitimate expression of democratic pluralism. Nevertheless, the formation of official policy is the outcome of a collective democratic process, not of individual will. Sikyong Penpa Tsering’s reaffirmation of the Middle Way after his re-election reflects the mainstream political direction expressed through the elections. A forced shift to independence without broad consensus and formal procedures would weaken the institutional legitimacy of the exile government itself and undermine internal unity. International Impact and External Recognition At the international level, virtually all major countries—including the United States, India, and European Union member states—officially recognise Tibet as part of the People’s Republic of China. They support dialogue, express concern for human rights and cultural protection, and have repeatedly stated their support for the Middle Way or for “resolving the Tibet issue through dialogue.” The White House, the European Parliament, the Canadian Parliament, and others have publicly affirmed this non-violent, mutually beneficial path. Were the exile government formally to adopt an independence policy, it would face serious risk of international isolation: many governments that currently support human rights and dialogue might reduce engagement for fear of being labelled as supporting “separatism.” India, as the host country of the exile administration, has strategic considerations that favour border stability rather than open support for independence. The Middle Way, by contrast, enables the international community to continue focusing on the Tibet issue, promoting dialogue, and maintaining diplomatic and moral support for the Central Tibetan Administration without challenging China’s sovereignty narrative. This is the key reason its external acceptance far exceeds that of the independence position. Practical Feasibility and Strategic Rationality China’s overwhelming military, economic, and diplomatic advantages render the immediate realisation of complete independence unrealistic in the foreseeable future. Insisting on an independence policy could reinforce China’s “separatist forces” narrative, further tighten controls over Tibetans inside Tibet, and shrink the space for international mediation. The Middle Way seeks genuine autonomy within the framework of the Chinese Constitution. It corresponds to Deng Xiaoping’s statement that “apart from independence, all other issues can be discussed,” and was concretised in the 2008 Memorandum on Genuine Autonomy for the Tibetan People. Although China has so far given no substantive response, the Middle Way keeps the window for dialogue open and avoids pushing the issue into zero-sum confrontation. It balances the core Tibetan interest in cultural survival with China’s concerns for sovereignty and stability, constituting a “win-win” design that also accords with Buddhist middle-path thought and the principle of non-violence. In a prolonged stalemate, it enables the exile government to continue international advocacy, human-rights monitoring, and community-building rather than descending into an isolated extreme position. Maintaining Unity and the Sustainability of the Long-Term Movement Tibetans in exile are dispersed worldwide and hold diverse views. Frequent shifts in official policy would easily exacerbate divisions and weaken collective capacity for action. As a democratically affirmed consensus foundation, the Middle Way helps concentrate strength on the urgent task of protecting the language, religion, and culture of Tibetans inside Tibet. At the same time, it does not prohibit individuals or organisations from expressing independence aspirations; it merely defines the official position and the boundaries of official action. Sikyong Penpa Tsering has recently emphasised that even if dialogue yields no results for a long time, the Tibetan movement will continue for decades. The key lies in institutional development, unity, and non-violence. The Middle Way is precisely the vehicle of this long-term strategy. — * Bem Mitruev is a Buddhist Scholar & Tibetan Translator, the first Acharya in Russia and specialist in Buddhist Philosophy & Kalmyk Heritage.

title: Arrests reported as Tibetans, other protesters dogged President Xi on second day of his US state visit
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep25’26) – Protests against Chinese President Xi Jinping, including by a large crowd of Tibetans, continued into the second of his three-day state visit to the United States with Washington DC Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) citing five arrests and counting, according to a wusa9.com report Sep 24. As Xi arrived on the South Lawn of the White House for his summit meeting with US President Donald Trump, Tibetans from across the country as well as Canada gathered near the Chinese embassy in Washington DC on Sep 24 to launch their protest. An organizer put the number of Tibetan protesters at around 1,200. The protesters carried or wrapped themselves in Tibetan national flags, including large ones held by their ends by several people, as well as US flags, placards, and banners with slogans calling for a free or independent Tibet and so forth. “We stand for a free Tibet!” and “Xi Jinping is guilty — guilty of genocide,” cnbctv18.com Sep 25 quoted three of the placards as reading. They also shouted slogans, such as “Free Tibet! China out of Tibet now!” The Tibetan protesters, in particular, sough to draw attention to China’s implementation on Jul 1 this year of its so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which has been condemned across the outside world, including by UN human rights experts and many parliaments, as a tool for a forced assimilation of the ethnic minorities in the People’s Republic of China. They also highlighted Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen’s protest self-immolation in front of the United Nations Headquarters the day after China began implementing this law. “They are trying to sinicize Tibet. Therefore, we are out here to unwelcome him to America and to send a message to the world that we don’t like him,” wusa9.com quoted a protester as saying. “The main things that we can do right now is just spread awareness for the situation in Tibet and share sort of our story with people who are just passing by in the city and really just want to make our voices heard,” it quoted another protester as saying. * * * Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi speaks to Tibetan demonstrators outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy: TYC) Former US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, long known for her strong concern about the situation in Chinese ruled Tibet, addressed the protesters from a stage after the Tibetans marched to the US Capitol. “It’s really important for elected officials and for the president of the United States and the president of China to hear what you have to say, because we put forth ourselves as a country who cares about human rights and respecting the dignity and worth of the people.” Rep. Jim McGovern, speaks to Tibetan demonstrators outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026. Rep. Jim McGovern was also among the speakers at the event. “The main reason for this protest is that Xi Jinping cannot hear the voices of the people inside China,” Chinese democracy activist Wang Dan, has told rfa.org Sep 24. “In fact, many people in China oppose the rule of the Chinese Communist Party. So, I believe those of us overseas have a responsibility and an obligation to speak out for those who cannot speak freely inside China.” The protest continued into the night of Sep 24 as Trump hosted a 134-guest dinner for Xi. protesters chanted for a free Tibet and Hong Kong and told the Chinese leader he was “not welcome”, reported thestatesman.com Sep 25. The gathering outside the White House gates chanted slogans such as “Free Hong Kong”, “Free Tibet”, “CCP, you’re not welcome” and “Xi Jinping, you’re not welcome”, the report said. The chants could be heard from the North Portico, where members of the White House press pool were waiting, the report said. The demonstrators represented a range of causes, from calls for religious autonomy and greater freedoms in Tibet, Hong Kong and the ethnic region of Xinjiang to demands to keep China out of self-governed Taiwan, said AP Sep 24. Tibetan demonstrators march near the Chinese Embassy in Washington as Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with U.S. President Trump at the White House, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy: TYC) The wusa9.com citedMPD as announcing they made five arrests – two adult males for assault on a police officer, one adult male for taking property without right, two adult males for simple assault – with more information to be released as investigation continued. * * * Various rights groups and organisations, including the International Campaign for Tibet, Student for a Free Tibet, and Regional Tibetan Youth Congress, were involved in the protest rallies since Xi landed in Washington, DC, on Sep 23 evening. The White House protest formed part of a wider series of demonstrations planned by Tibetan, Uyghur, Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Southern Mongolian and Chinese democracy groups during Xi’s visit. Protests were also planned outside the Chinese Embassy, at the US Capitol and at Franklin Park, reported thestatesman.com Sep 25. A day before Trump met Xi, International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) President Tencho Gyatso joined Congressman Jim McGovern on Capitol Hill to call for human rights concerns, including Tibet, to be raised during the talks. Also ahead of Xi’s visit, 32 rights organisations, including Amnesty International, Freedom House and Reporters Without Borders, wrote an open letter to the Chinese leader urging him to take steps to address human rights concerns. * * * Despite the fanfare, the two leaders’ talks are not expected to lead to significant breakthroughs. The day so far has brought a trade war truce extension until January and the promise of a student exchange. The display of pomp and pageantry, meanwhile, has attracted criticism from both Republican and Democratic politicians. But as our North America editor Sarah Smith explains in this video, Trump has made no secret of his admiration for Xi and other strongman leaders around the world, said bbc.com Sep 25. At the dinner, Trump declared that the two countries had “never gotten along better” while Xi called on both sides to give their relationship “new substance” and “new strategic guidance”, the report said. And it cited Xi as saying his exchanges with Trump had produced a “common understanding on many issues”, though he did not identify those issues or announce a specific agreement in his toast. Xi has also sought to cast the two leaders’ domestic ambitions as compatible. Referring to Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda and China’s pursuit of what he called “great national rejuvenation”, he said the goals could be “mutually reinforcing”. But while Trump spent Sep 24 lavishing praise on Xi, the Chinese leader used his visit to the White House to deliver a power move with a warning for America to stay in its lane, noted thedailybeast.com Sep 24. In front of Trump, and for the second time in four months, Xi urged the two countries to avoid the so-called “Thucydides Trap”—the historical theory that tensions between a rising power and an established one can spiral into war. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi has said, calling for the two countries to “coexist in peace” and for US competition to be “kept within bounds.” Also, after Trump opened his remarks by describing Xi as a “truly great friend” and boasted about their relationship, the latter effectively reminded his host that this was not simply a friendship between two men—but a strategic contest between two rival superpowers. And so, beneath that pomp and ceremony, the visit has already proved contentious for Trump, the report said.

title: Chinese supporters attack Tibetan, other protesters as President Xi lands in US for state visit
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep24’26) – Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, DC, on Sep 23 evening for a three-day state visit with a prior warning that the US should not cross four “red lines” – Taiwan, democracy and human rights, China’s development path and political system, and its development rights – reported the New York Post Sep 12, citing ambassador Xie Feng. However, he still faced protests from wide range of groups advocating issues such as national independence or self-rule, human rights, democracy, religious freedom, and so forth. They included Chinese democracy activists, Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, Falun Gong followers, Hong Kong activists, and others who were attacked by a large pro-Beijing Chinese crowd as Xi landed on US soil. As Xi landed on Joint Base Andrews, Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, were warmly greeted by President Donald Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the airport in a rare planeside welcome amid pomp and ceremony that included a 100ft (30m) red carpet, 21-gun salute, the playing of the national anthems of both countries, and a military flyover. However, the protesters remained busy with their own version of reception for him. Earlier on Sep 22, a Tibetan student activist from the group Students for a Free Tibet (SFT) was taken into police custody after he climbed an electric pole near the US Capitol Building and hung on it a banner and a Tibetan national flag. The banner read: “Dictator Xi, Your Empire Will Fall, Free Tibet.” Tenzin Namgyal, a Students for a Free Tibet activist, climbed an electric pole near the U.S. Capitol Building and hung a banner and the Tibetan national flag from it. (Photo courtesy: SFT) The activist, 20-year-old Tenzin Namgyal, climbed the pole at around 2:30am. He was taken down and away after a squad of 10 or so police cars arrived on the scene at 10:30 am, said the Tibetan service of rfa.org Sep 23. And as a group of Tibetan and other protesters arrived outside the main entrance of Joint Base Andrews, they were met by a much larger crowd of pro-Beijing Chinese crowd already present on the scene to welcome Xi and his entourage, which included Cai Qi, a member of the party’s Politburo Standing Committee widely seen as his right-hand man, Vice Premier He Lifeng, Foreign Minister Wang Yi, as well as other delegates. This crowd not only attacked the protesters physically but also played loud music to drown their slogans. Police intervened to pull away the protesters, telling them to protest at a location far away from the scene of Xi’s motorcade. Meanwhile, more than 2,000 Tibetans from across North America are expected to join Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, Taiwanese, Southern Mongolians and Chinese democracy activists in Washington on Sep 24 to protest Xi’s visit, reported IANS news service Sep 24. The daylong mobilisation will include demonstrations outside the Chinese Embassy, marches through central Washington, a rally near the US Capitol and an evening candlelight vigil at Franklin Park. The report cited organisers as saying the protesters would declare Xi “not welcome” and highlight concerns over political prisoners, religious freedom, transnational repression and threats to cultural and linguistic identities under his government. The Tibetan Youth Congress and the Capital Area Tibetan Association are leading the Tibetan mobilisation. They are being supported by the International Campaign for Tibet, Students for a Free Tibet, the Tibetan National Congress and other organisations. They will call for the release of the 11th Panchen Lama Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, and other Tibetan political prisoners. They will also demand the resumption of dialogue between Chinese leaders and Tibetan representatives. Besides, they are seeking the repeal of laws and policies they say promote forced assimilation and erode distinct cultural, religious and linguistic identities. Also, the International Campaign for Tibet has joined a coalition of 30 human rights organisations in sending an open letter to the Chinese president. The coalition is calling on China to release prisoners of conscience, end transnational repression and take concrete steps to address its human rights record. Earlier, on Sep 20, Several Chinese democracy and human rights groups organized a march through the Flushing neighborhood of Queens in New York City, calling for an end to Chinese Communist Party rule despite bomb and death threats surrounding the demonstration. Police later detained a man after he rushed toward the demonstrators, grabbed activist Yang Lei’s protest sign, and kicked him, reported theepochtimes.com Sep 22. Yang is chairman of the China Democracy Party International Alliance.

title: China’s new Tibet Party chief vows to ‘intensify struggle ​against separatism’ etc
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep23’26) – The new Party chief of Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), Mr Hu Changsheng, has on Sep 22 vowed to fully and absolutely implement Beijing’s top policy measures there that include building ethnic unity, opposing separatism and strengthening the management of religious affairs. Hu, 62, has been the party chief of Gansu province since late 2022. Qinghai’s party ​chief, Wu Xiaojun, is taking over Hu’s ⁠post in Gansu, while Qinghai Governor Luo Dongchuan ​has been promoted to Qinghai party chief, reported China’s official Xinhua news agency Sep 22. Both Gansu and Qinghai have significant Tibetan populations. The former includes Kanlho (Chinese: Gannan) prefecture, which was part of the traditional Tibetan province of Amdo (or Domey), while Qinghai constitutes the bulk of Amdo. The ​reshuffle announced on Sep 22 took place ahead of a key party conclave ​set for October and the 21st Communist Party ​Congress expected in autumn 2027. Such regional transfers offer clues about broader political line-up ahead of national party congress, said scmp.com Sep 22. Hu has assumed his post at a meeting in Tibet’s capital ‌Lhasa ⁠on Sep 22 itself, with pledges to “remain unswervingly and absolutely loyal to the party,” safeguard lasting peace and stability in Tibet, forge ethnic unity and to “intensify the struggle ​against separatism and ​strengthen the ⁠rule-of-law-based management of religious affairs,” reported Reuters Sep 22, citing state media. His predecessor, Wang Junzheng, 63, would no ​longer serve as TAR’s party chief ​after ⁠five years on the job due to his age, a Xinhua report was stated to show. Before coming to TAR, Wang was the secretary of the Party Committee of the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps—a state-owned economic and paramilitary organization—where he was accused of perpetrating serious human rights violations against the Uyghur people. He was put on an unprecedented coordinated sanctions list of the United States, Canada, Britain and the European Union in Mar 2021. Hu, the TAR’s new Party Secretary, spent the early years of his career in Sichuan province – which includes the historical Tibetan regions of Kardze (Ganzi) and Ngaba (Aba) – before transferring to Qinghai in 2015. In 2017, he was sent to Fujian province, where he headed the provincial party organisation department. He was appointed party secretary of the city of Xiamen in 2019 and was promoted to deputy party secretary of Fujian in 2020 while continuing as Xiamen’s party secretary, noted the scmp.com report. President Xi Jinping spent more than a decade working in Fujian, where he served as party secretary of the provincial capital Fuzhou from 1990 to 1996, and as the province’s deputy party secretary from 1995 to 2002. Luo Dongchuan, 60, the new Party secretary of Qinghai, has a background in law and holds a doctorate in the field. He earlier served in Beijing’s local courts and the Supreme People’s Court and at the Communist Party’s Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. He was the head of the regional commission for discipline inspection in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region from 2017 to 2018, returned to the Supreme People’s Court as vice-president, worked in Fujian as chief of the provincial political and legal affairs commission from 2020 to 2021, and as the provincial deputy party secretary from 2021 to 2024. Luo was made the deputy party secretary of Qinghai in 2024 and its governor last year, the report said. Wu, the new Party chief of Gansu, spent most of his career in Jiangxi province until being relocated to Qinghai in 2021. He was appointed the governor of Qinghai in 2022 and party secretary in 2024, the report said. Provincial party chiefs hold significant political influence in China, making such appointments closely watched ahead of a national congress, noted firstpost.com Sep 22.

title: Sikyong launches ‘Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week’
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep23’26) – The executive head, Sikyong Penpa Tsering, of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), has on Sep 23 launched his administration’s annual “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week” to be observed worldwide. The move is meant “to confront and counter the various methods and systematic policies implemented by the Chinese Communist Government to eradicate Tibetan identity, particularly its recently enacted so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” which, under the guise of law, further intensifies the assimilation and eradication of national identities, said the CTA on its Tibet.net website Sep 23. The launch of the exile Tibetan campaign followed a resolution adopted at the 11th session of the 17th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, calling for designating the fourth week of every September as “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week”. “I hereby proclaim the commencement of this observance effective Sep 23, 2026. ‘Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week’ will be observed annually, from the fourth Wednesday of September through the following Wednesday,” the Tibetan Sikyong has said. “Our campaign must effectively counter the Chinese Communist Government’s observance of the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Propaganda Week,” during which the state organs are directed to execute various forms of state-sponsored assimilation propaganda and re-education campaigns.” This referred to China’s recent launch of its “Ethnic Unity and Progress Publicity Week” set to run from Sep 21 to 27 under the theme of “Promoting ethnic unity and progress, advancing on the journey toward national rejuvenation,” as reported by China’s Party mouthpiece globaltimes.cn Sep 16. The report said that the Chinese week-long, nationwide public education activities will include “seminars on ethnic theory and policy to be held by research institutes”, “legal education,” and “lecturers to explain the new law to government officials and people working in education, culture, publicity and legal affairs, as well as representatives from ethnic minority communities and religious circles.” Local authorities were required to “distribute posters, handbooks and short videos and provide legal consultations at the community level.” “Schools will organize activities through classes, assemblies and student organizations, while youth groups will send volunteers to communities to provide public services and take part in cultural programs. Museums, libraries, cultural centres and intangible cultural heritage venues will also host exhibitions and performances,” the report added.
